p.seg: The nobleman says:
Learning should never cease.
Indigo blue is extracted from the indigo plant,
yet it is bluer than the plant;
ice is formed from water,
yet it is colder than water.
A piece of wood straight as a plumb line,
when steamed and bent into a wheel,
its curvature matches the compass,
even if it dries out under the sun,
it will not return to being straight,
for the steaming has made it so.
Thus, wood marked by the line becomes straight,
metal sharpened on a whetstone becomes sharp;
the nobleman who studies extensively
and reflects on himself daily
then gains clear wisdom
and acts without fault.
Therefore, without climbing high mountains,
one does not know the height of the sky;
without facing deep valleys,
one does not know the thickness of the earth;
without hearing the legacy words of the ancient kings,
one does not know the greatness of learning.
The children of Gàn, Yuè, Yí, and Mò,
are born with the same cries,
yet grow up with different customs,
for education makes them so.
The Book of Songs says:
"Ah, you noblemen,
do not constantly seek comfort and rest.
Be reverent in your duties,
and love what is upright and just.
The spirits will heed this,
and grant you great blessings."
No spirituality is greater than transforming with the Way,
no blessing is longer lasting than being free from misfortune.
I have spent whole days in thought,
but it does not compare to a moment of learning;
I have stood on tiptoe to look afar,
but it does not compare to the broad view from a high place.
Standing high and waving,
the arms are not lengthened,
yet they are seen from afar;
calling with the wind,
the voice is not intensified,
yet it is heard clearly.
Those who use carriages and horses,
do not have faster feet,
yet they reach a thousand miles;
those who use boats and oars,
are not skilled swimmers,
yet they cross rivers and seas.
The nobleman is not born different,
but is good at making use of things.
In the south, there is a bird,
named Méngjiū,
which builds its nest with feathers,
weaving them with hair,
and ties it to reed tips.
When the wind comes, the reeds break,
the eggs break and the chicks die.
The nest is not incomplete,
but what it is tied to causes this.
In the west, there is a tree,
named Yègàn,
its stem four inches long,
growing atop a high mountain
and overlooking a hundred-ren deep abyss;
the stem is not inherently long,
but its position makes it so.
When péng grass grows among hemp,
it stands straight without support;
white sand in black mud,
turns black along with it.
The root of Lánhuái is called Zhǐ.
If it is soaked in filthy water,
the nobleman will not approach it,
the common people will not wear it.
Its substance is not un-beautiful,
but what it is soaked in causes this.
Therefore, the nobleman in dwelling
must choose his neighborhood,
in travel must seek out scholars,
so as to guard against depravity
and draw near to what is upright.
The rise of all things,
must have a beginning.
The coming of honor or disgrace,
must reflect one's virtue.
Rotted flesh breeds worms,
dried fish attracts moths.
Negligence and self-forgetfulness,
bring about disaster.
The rigid invite breaking,
the flexible invite binding.
With depravity and filth in oneself,
resentment gathers.
If firewood is piled evenly,
fire seeks the dry;
if ground is leveled evenly,
water seeks the damp.
Plants and trees grow in clusters,
birds and beasts live in groups,
each thing follows its kind.
Thus, when the target is set,
arrows arrive at it;
when the forest is lush,
axes come to it;
when a tree forms shade,
birds rest in it;
when vinegar turns sour,
gnats gather on it.
Thus, speech can summon disaster,
action can attract disgrace;
the nobleman is cautious about what he establishes!
Piling earth makes a mountain,
wind and rain arise there;
accumulating water makes a deep pool,
jiāo dragons are born there;
accumulating goodness makes virtue,
and spiritual clarity is naturally attained,
the sage's heart is prepared there.
Thus, without accumulating half-steps,
there is no way to reach a thousand miles;
without gathering small streams,
there is no way to form rivers and seas.
A Qíjì in one leap
cannot cover ten paces;
a slow horse in ten days' journey,
succeeds by not giving up.
Carve and then abandon it,
and even rotten wood won't break;
carve without ceasing,
and metal or stone can be engraved.
The earthworm has no sharp claws or teeth,
no strong sinews or bones,
yet it eats the dust above,
drinks from the yellow springs below,
because it focuses its mind.
The crab has six legs and two pincers,
yet without the burrows of snakes or eels
it has no place to dwell,
because it is restless in mind.
Therefore, without a determined will,
one has no clear understanding;
without dedicated effort,
one has no glorious achievements.
One who walks a forked path does not arrive;
one who serves two rulers is not tolerated.
Eyes cannot see two things clearly at once;
ears cannot hear two sounds acutely at once.
The Téngshé flies without feet;
the Wúshǔ with five skills ends in want.
The Book of Songs says:
"The shījiū bird is in the mulberry tree,
its young are seven.
The good man, the nobleman,
his demeanor is one.
His demeanor is one,
his heart is as if tied fast."
Thus, the nobleman is tied to oneness.
In the past, Hùbā played the sè
and swimming fish came to listen;
Bóyá played the qín
and six horses lifted their heads from fodder.
Thus, no sound is too faint to be heard,
no action too hidden not to take form;
with jade in the mountain, plants and trees are moist,
with pearls in the deep, the cliffs are not barren.
Is it that goodness is not accumulated enough?
How could there be any that goes unheard?
Where does learning begin?
Where does it end?
It is said:
In method, it begins with reciting the classics,
and ends with reading the rites;
in meaning, it begins with becoming a scholar,
and ends with becoming a sage.
With genuine accumulation and prolonged effort, one enters in;
learning continues until death and then stops.
Thus, the methods of learning have an end,
but its meaning must not be abandoned for a moment.
To practice it, is to be human;
to abandon it, is to be a beast.
Thus, the Shū is the record of governance,
the Shī is where balanced sounds reside,
the Lǐ is the great division of laws,
the guiding principle of categories.
Therefore, learning culminates in the "Lǐ" and stops there.
This is what is called the ultimate of the Way and virtue.
The reverence and refinement of the "Lǐ,"
the harmony and balance of the "Yuè,"
the breadth of the "Shī" and "Shū,"
the subtlety of the "Chūnqiū,"
encompass all that exists between heaven and earth.
The learning of a noble person:
enters through the ears,
is retained in the heart,
spreads throughout the four limbs,
and manifests in actions.
In speech, it is dignified;
in movement, it is gentle;
all can serve as a model.
The learning of a petty person:
enters through the ears,
and comes out of the mouth.
The distance between the mouth and ears
is only four inches;
how can it beautify a seven-foot body!
The learners of old studied for their own sake;
the learners of today study for the sake of others.
The learning of a noble person
is to beautify their character;
the learning of a petty person
is like treating it as poultry or calves (for show).
Thus, to speak without being asked is called presumptuousness;
to answer one question with two is called garrulity.
Presumptuousness
and garrulity are both wrong;
the noble person responds like an echo.
In learning, nothing is more convenient than being close to the right person.
The "Lǐ" and "Yuè" provide models but do not explain;
the "Shī" and "Shū" contain ancient matters but are not immediate;
the "Chūnqiū" is concise but not swift.
By imitating the right person's practices
and following the noble person's teachings,
one attains reverence and comprehensiveness,
and becomes thorough in worldly affairs.
Hence it is said:
In learning, nothing is more convenient than being close to the right person.
The path of learning is never faster than in admiring the right person;
exalting the "Lǐ" comes next.
If one cannot admire the right person above,
nor exalt the "Lǐ" below,
and merely learns miscellaneous records and texts,
following the "Shī" and "Shū" blindly,
then even after a lifetime of effort,
one cannot avoid being a shallow scholar.
To trace the origins of the ancient kings,
and root oneself in benevolence and righteousness,
the "Lǐ" is the proper guide and path.
It is like grasping the collar of a fur coat;
bend five fingers and shake it,
and the smoothness is beyond count.
Without following the rules of "Lǐ,"
and using the "Shī" and "Shū" instead,
is like using a finger to measure a river,
a spear to pound millet,
or an awl to eat from a pot—
it cannot achieve the goal.
Therefore, one who exalts the "Lǐ,"
even if not fully enlightened,
is a scholar of the law;
one who does not exalt the "Lǐ,"
even if perceptive and eloquent,
is a scattered scholar.
Do not answer those who ask improperly;
do not ask those who speak improperly;
do not listen to those who discuss improperly;
do not argue with those who are contentious.
Thus, only when they come by the proper way
should you engage with them;
if not by the proper way, avoid them.
Therefore, only when they are respectful in "Lǐ"
can you discuss the methods of the Way;
only when their words are compliant
can you discuss the principles of the Way;
only when their expression shows acceptance
can you discuss the essence of the Way.
Hence, to speak when it is not appropriate
is called presumptuousness;
not to speak when it is appropriate
is called concealment;
to speak without observing the countenance
is called blindness.
Therefore, the noble person is not presumptuous, not concealing, not blind,
but cautious in their conduct.
The "Shī" says:
"Not hasty, not negligent,
the Son of Heaven bestows."
This refers to this.
If one misses one shot out of a hundred,
it cannot be called good archery;
if one falls short by half a step over a thousand miles,
it cannot be called good driving;
if one does not comprehend categories and classes,
and is not unified in benevolence and righteousness,
it cannot be called good learning.
Learning, indeed,
is about learning to be unified.
Coming out one way,
going in another,
is the way of ordinary people.
With few good qualities
and many bad ones,
they are like Jié, Zhòu, or Dào Zhí.
To be complete and thorough,
that is the true learner.
The noble person knows that incompleteness and impurity are not enough to be considered beautiful,
so they recite repeatedly to connect it all,
ponder deeply to understand it,
emulate the right person to embody it,
and remove harmful influences to nurture it,
so that the eyes desire not to see what is not this,
the ears desire not to hear what is not this,
the mouth desires not to speak what is not this,
the heart desires not to ponder what is not this.
When it reaches the extreme of loving it,
the eyes love it as the five colors,
the ears love it as the five sounds,
the mouth loves it as the five flavors,
the heart benefits from it as having the world.
Therefore, power and profit cannot sway them,
the multitude cannot shift them,
the world cannot unsettle them.
In life, they follow this;
in death, they follow this;
this is called moral integrity.
With moral integrity, one can be steadfast;
being steadfast, one can respond appropriately;
able to be steadfast and respond,
this is called a complete person.
Heaven shows its brightness,
earth shows its expanse;
the noble person values completeness.
When seeing goodness,
be reflective, and surely find a way to preserve it in oneself;
when seeing badness,
be alarmed, and surely use it for self-examination.
If goodness is in oneself,
be resolute, and surely cherish it;
if badness is in oneself,
be troubled, and surely detest it.
Therefore, those who criticize me appropriately
are my teachers;
those who affirm me appropriately
are my friends;
those who flatter me
are my enemies.
Hence, the noble person honors teachers and befriends others,
to strongly oppose their enemies.
Loving goodness without weariness,
accepting advice and able to heed warnings—
even if they wish not to advance,
how could it be possible!
Petty people are the opposite:
they cause chaos
and hate others for criticizing them;
they act unworthily
yet want others to consider them worthy;
their hearts are like tigers and wolves,
their actions like beasts,
and they hate others for opposing them.
They befriend flatterers,
distance those who admonish,
mock those who cultivate correctness,
and treat the most loyal as enemies;
even if they wish not to perish,
how could it be possible!
The "Shī" says:
"All yes and yes, oh! All no and no,
it is very sorrowful indeed.
When plans are good,
they are all opposed;
when plans are bad,
they are all followed."
This refers to this.
The measure of universal goodness:
in regulating the breath and nurturing life,
one can follow after Péng Zǔ;
in cultivating oneself and strengthening character,
one's name can match Yáo and Yǔ.
Suitable for times of success,
beneficial in times of hardship—
this is what "Lǐ" and trustworthiness are.
In employing vigor and will, knowledge and thought,
following ritual leads to order and comprehension,
while not following it results in confusion and laxity.
In eating and drinking, clothing and residence, movement and stillness,
following ritual brings harmony and moderation,
while not following it leads to stumbling into pitfalls and generating ailments.
In countenance, demeanor, advancing and retreating, hastening and walking,
following ritual yields elegance,
while not following it results in arrogance, obstinacy, perversity, and violation, making one common and crude.
Thus, without ritual, a person cannot live;
without ritual, affairs cannot be accomplished;
without ritual, the state cannot be tranquil.
The Book of Songs says:
"When rituals and ceremonies are fully observed,
laughter and talk are fully appropriate."
This expresses it.
Leading others with goodness is called teaching;
harmonizing with others in goodness is called compliance.
Leading others with what is not good is called flattery;
harmonizing with others in what is not good is called sycophancy.
To affirm what is right and deny what is wrong is called wisdom;
to deny what is right and affirm what is wrong is called foolishness.
Injuring the good is called slander;
harming the good is called villainy.
To call right what is right,
and wrong what is wrong,
is called uprightness.
Stealing goods is called theft;
concealing one's actions is called deceit;
being frivolous in speech is called falsehood;
having no fixed principles in choices is called inconstancy;
preserving profit at the expense of righteousness is called ultimate villainy.
Having broad learning is called erudition;
having little learning is called shallowness.
Having wide experience is called sophistication;
having little experience is called ignorance.
Being slow to advance is called tardiness;
being prone to forgetfulness is called leakage.
What is concise and orderly is called well-governed;
what is numerous and chaotic is called wasteful.
The methods for regulating one's vital energy and nurturing the heart:
If one's vigor is strong and forceful,
soften it with harmony.
If one's thoughts and schemes are overly profound,
unify them with simplicity and goodness.
If one is brave, daring, fierce, and violent,
assist with guidance and compliance.
If one is hasty and impetuous,
restrain with action and stillness.
If one is narrow-minded and petty,
expand with breadth and greatness.
If one is base, sluggish, and greedy for profit,
elevate with high aspirations.
If one is mediocre, common, and negligent,
constrain with teachers and friends.
If one is indolent, careless, and abandoned,
enlighten with the prospect of calamity.
If one is simple, honest, and upright,
combine with ritual and music,
and penetrate with thought and reflection.
In all methods for regulating vital energy and nurturing the heart,
none is more direct than following ritual,
none more essential than obtaining a teacher,
and none more spiritual than single-minded devotion.
This is what is meant by the methods for regulating vital energy and nurturing the heart.
With cultivated will, one can disdain wealth and honor;
valuing the Way and righteousness, one can look down upon kings and dukes;
through introspection, external things become light.
The Tradition says:
"The noble person masters things,
the petty person is mastered by things."
This expresses it.
If the body labors but the heart is at peace,
do it;
if the benefit is small but the righteousness great,
do it.
Serving a disorderly ruler and achieving success
is not as good as serving an impoverished ruler and following the Way.
Thus, a good farmer does not refrain from plowing due to flood or drought;
a good merchant does not refrain from the market due to losses;
a scholar and noble person does not neglect the Way due to poverty.
With a body of reverence and a heart of loyalty and trustworthiness,
practicing ritual and righteousness with a feeling of love for others,
one may traverse the world,
and even if stranded among the barbarians,
all will honor them.
In matters of toil and hardship, they strive to be first;
in matters of abundance and pleasure, they are able to yield;
upright, honest, sincere, and trustworthy,
adhering strictly and acting with care,
they may traverse the world,
and even if stranded among the barbarians,
all will trust them.
With a body of arrogance and obstinacy
and a heart of craftiness and deceit,
practicing compliance and obscurity
with a spirit of impurity,
they may traverse the world,
and even if reaching all quarters,
all will despise them.
In matters of toil and hardship, they shirk and evade;
in matters of abundance and pleasure, they are glib and sharp without restraint;
perverse and disobedient without honesty,
pursuing base endeavors without refinement,
they may traverse the world,
and even if reaching all quarters,
all will reject them.
Walking with hands clasped
is not due to mud and mire;
walking with bowed head
is not due to being struck;
lowering one's gaze when meeting eyes
is not due to fear.
Rather, it is that the scholar wishes to cultivate himself alone,
not to offend against common customs.
A fine steed can travel a thousand lǐ in a day,
but a nag with ten days of travel
can also reach it.
Would one try to exhaust the infinite
and pursue the boundless?
Then even with broken bones and severed tendons,
one could never reach it in a lifetime.
But if there is a stopping point,
then even a thousand lǐ, though far,
may be reached slowly or quickly, earlier or later—
why should it be unreachable?
Do those who do not know the path
intend to exhaust the infinite
and pursue the boundless?
Or do they also have a stopping point?
The investigations into hardness and whiteness, similarity and difference, thickness and non-thickness,
are not unperceptive,
yet the noble person does not debate them—
he stops there.
Eccentric and extraordinary actions,
are not without difficulty,
yet the noble person does not perform them—
he stops there.
Thus, in learning, if one is slow,
and the goal stops and waits for me,
and I proceed toward it,
then whether slow or fast, first or later,
why can we not arrive together?
Hence, taking small steps without rest,
a lame turtle can journey a thousand lǐ;
piling earth without ceasing,
a mound or mountain can be raised;
blocking its source,
and opening its channels,
even rivers and seas can be drained;
advancing one step and retreating another,
turning left and right,
even six fine steeds cannot reach the destination.
The disparity in talent and nature between people—
is it as great as that between a lame turtle and six fine steeds?
Yet the lame turtle reaches it,
while the six fine steeds do not—
this is for no other reason
than that one acts,
and the other does not.
Though the Way is near,
without walking, one does not reach it;
though affairs are small,
without acting, they are not accomplished.
One who has many idle days in their life
will not surpass others by far.
Loving the model and acting accordingly—
this is the scholar;
firm in will and embodying it—
this is the noble person;
clear and unceasing—
this is the sage.
Without a model, a person
is bewildered;
with a model but no understanding of its meaning,
they are anxious;
relying on the model
and deeply comprehending its categories,
then they are serene.
Ritual is that by which one rectifies the self;
the teacher is that by which one rectifies ritual.
Without ritual, how can one rectify the self?
Without a teacher, how can I know what ritual is correct?
If ritual dictates thus and one acts thus,
then one's feelings are at ease with ritual;
if the teacher says thus and one speaks thus,
then one's knowledge is like the teacher's.
With feelings at ease in ritual
and knowledge like the teacher's,
one is a sage.
Thus, to oppose ritual principles
is to be without law;
to oppose teachers
is to be without teachers.
Not to approve of teachers and the model
but to prefer to use one's own ideas
is like using a blind man to distinguish colors
or a deaf man to distinguish sounds—
it is to abandon reason and act absurdly.
Hence, learning means
to model oneself on ritual principles.
The teacher is one who takes his own person as the correct standard
and values achieving personal tranquility.
An Ode says:
"Without knowing or understanding,
he conforms to the ordinances of God."
This expresses my meaning.
If he is honest, diligent, obedient, and brotherly,
then he may be called a good youth.
If to these he adds a love of learning, modesty, and agility,
then he will have equals but no superiors
and can become a gentleman.
If he is indolent, cowardly, and ashamed of nothing,
and has no sense of shame but is fond of food and drink,
then he may be called a bad youth.
If to these he adds a savage ferocity and disobedience
and a dangerous and malicious disregard for his elders,
then he may be called an ominous youth,
and even though he suffer punishment and execution, it is acceptable.
If you honor the aged, then the strong will come to you.
If you do not persecute the unfortunate, then the able will gather about you.
If you act in secret and bestow favors without seeking recompense,
then the worthy and unworthy will be united.
If a man possesses these three forms of conduct,
even though he has great faults,
Heaven would not allow him to perish.
The gentleman in his search for profit is relaxed,
in avoiding harm is early,
in his escape from disgrace is cautious,
and in his practice of the Way and its Virtue is courageous.
Although the gentleman is impoverished, his intentions are expansive.
Although he is wealthy and eminent, his demeanor is respectful.
Although he is at ease, his spirit is not indolent.
Although he is tired and weary, his appearance is not disrespectful.
In anger he does not punish excessively,
in joy he does not reward excessively.
The gentleman is impoverished but his intentions are expansive
because he honors benevolence.
He is wealthy and eminent yet his demeanor is respectful
because he does not presume upon his authority.
He is at ease yet his spirit is not indolent
because he chooses what is reasonable.
He is tired and weary yet his appearance is not disrespectful
because he loves formal patterns.
In anger he does not punish excessively;
in joy he does not reward excessively
because the model overcomes his private feelings.
A Document says:
"Do not follow your personal desires;
follow the Way of the ancient kings.
Do not follow your personal aversions;
follow the path of the ancient kings."
This refers to the fact that the gentleman is able to use public morality to overcome his private desires.
In conduct, the gentleman does not esteem what is difficult without good reason.
In theories, he does not esteem what is abstruse without good reason.
In names, he does not esteem what is widely transmitted without good reason.
He esteems only what is appropriate.
Thus, "to embrace a stone and throw oneself into a river"
is a form of conduct difficult to perform,
and Shentu Dí was capable of it.
However, the gentleman does not esteem it
because it is not in accord with the mean of ritual and moral principles.
"Mountains and abysses are level,"
"Heaven and Earth are on the same level,"
"Qí and Qín are adjacent,"
"it enters the ear
and comes out the mouth,"
"a hook has a beard,"
"an egg has hair"
—these are theories difficult to maintain,
and Huì Shī and Dèng Xī were capable of them.
However, the gentleman does not esteem them
because they are not in accord with the mean of ritual and moral principles.
The name of Dào Zhǐ was on everyone's lips;
his reputation was like that of the sun and moon,
and like that of Yǔ and Shùn, it has been transmitted without cease.
However, the gentleman does not esteem it
because it is not in accord with the mean of ritual and moral principles.
Hence, it is said:
In conduct, the gentleman does not esteem what is difficult without good reason.
In theories, he does not esteem what is abstruse without good reason.
In names, he does not esteem what is widely obtained without good reason.
He esteems only what is appropriate.
An Ode says:
"Things have their being,
but only in their proper season."
This expresses my meaning.
The gentleman is easy to get along with but difficult to be intimate with.
He is easily apprehensive but difficult to intimidate.
He is fearful of hardship but will not avoid dying for a moral cause.
He desires gain but will not do what is wrong to obtain it.
In personal relations he is affectionate but not cliquish.
In discussions he is argumentative but not contentious.
Vast and comprehensive, he possesses what makes him different from the vulgar lot.
Whether the gentleman is capable or not,
he is admirable.
Whether the petty man is capable or not,
he is despicable.
If the gentleman is capable,
he is magnanimous, tolerant, straightforward, and open in instructing others.
If he is incapable,
he is respectful, humble, and restrained in serving others.
If the petty man is capable,
he is arrogant, perverse, and contemptuous in looking down on others.
If he is incapable,
he is envious, resentful, and slanderous in undermining others.
Hence, it is said:
If the gentleman is capable, others consider it an honor to learn from him.
If he is incapable, they are pleased to inform him.
If the petty man is capable, others consider it base to learn from him.
If he is incapable, they are ashamed to inform him.
This is the distinction between the gentleman and the petty man.
The gentleman is magnanimous but not negligent.
He has sharp corners but does not cut.
He is argumentative but not quarrelsome.
He is perceptive but not extreme.
He is upright but not overbearing.
He is strong but not violent.
He is soft and compliant but not unprincipled.
He is respectful, reverent, and cautious, yet composed.
This may indeed be described as the perfection of good form.
An Ode says:
"How mild and respectful is he!
The foundation of his character is virtue."
This expresses my meaning.
The gentleman exalts the virtue of others
and promotes their good points,
but this is not flattery.
He sets forth what is just and directly points out,
citing the faults of others,
but this is not slander or carping.
He speaks of the glory and beauty in himself,
comparing himself to Yǔ and Shùn,
and placing himself on a level with Heaven and Earth,
but this is not boasting or exaggeration.
In accordance with the times, he bends and stretches,
being as soft and pliant as a rush or reed,
but this is not cowardice or timidity.
He is strong, forceful, fierce, and resolute,
and in all his conduct he is unbending,
but this is not arrogance or violence.
It is because he responds to change with what is morally right
and knows when to yield and when to stand firm.
An Ode says:
"To the left, to the left:
the gentleman is fit for it.
To the right, to the right:
the gentleman possesses it."
This refers to the fact that the gentleman is able to bend and stretch, to respond to change, because of his moral principles.
The gentleman is the opposite of the petty man.
When the gentleman is broad-minded, he reveres Heaven and follows the Way.
When he is narrow-minded, he is in awe of moral principles and acts with restraint.
When he is intelligent, he is penetrating and comprehends the various categories.
When he is stupid, he is honest, diligent, and follows the model.
When he is employed, he is respectful and restrained.
When he is unemployed, he is reverent and composed.
When he is happy, he is harmonious and well-ordered.
When he is sad, he is calm and well-ordered.
When he is successful, he is cultured and enlightened.
When he is frustrated, he is restrained and careful.
The petty man is not like this.
When he is broad-minded, he is arrogant and violent.
When he is narrow-minded, he is dissolute and subversive.
When he is intelligent, he is rapacious and thievish and given to treachery.
When he is stupid, he is cruel and malicious and creates anarchy.
When he is employed, he is pleased and arrogant.
When he is unemployed, he is resentful and treacherous.
When he is happy, he is frivolous and flighty.
When he is sad, he is despondent and fearful.
When he is successful, he is arrogant and prejudiced.
When he is frustrated, he abandons himself and becomes despondent.
A tradition says:
"The gentleman progresses in both circumstances;
The noble person governs order,
not chaos.
What does this mean?
It is said:
What is called order is ritual and righteousness,
and what is called chaos is the absence of ritual and righteousness.
Therefore, the noble person
is one who governs ritual and righteousness,
not one who governs what lacks ritual and righteousness.
Then, should a chaotic state not be governed?
It is said:
To govern a chaotic state
does not mean governing according to its chaos,
but rather removing the chaos and replacing it with order;
to rectify a person who is defiled
does not mean rectifying according to the defilement,
but removing the defilement and substituting it with rectitude.
Thus, it is removing chaos, not governing chaos;
it is removing defilement, not rectifying defilement.
The term "governing"
means that the noble person acts for order and not for chaos,
for rectitude and not for defilement.
The noble person purifies his distinctions, and those who agree unite with him;
he refines his words, and those of his kind respond to him.
Thus, when a horse neighs, other horses respond,
not out of knowledge,
but because it is the natural tendency.
Therefore, one who has just bathed shakes out his clothes,
one who has just washed his hair brushes his hat,
such is human nature.
Who would be willing to accept others' filth
with their own cleanliness?
For the noble person, nothing is better than sincerity in cultivating the heart-mind.
To achieve sincerity requires no other efforts—
only hold fast to benevolence,
only practice righteousness.
With a sincere heart holding to benevolence, it manifests;
when it manifests, it becomes spiritual;
when spiritual, it can transform.
With a sincere heart practicing righteousness, it becomes orderly;
when orderly, it becomes clear;
when clear, it can change.
When transformation and change arise in succession,
it is called heavenly virtue.
Heaven does not speak, yet people acknowledge its height;
earth does not speak, yet people acknowledge its thickness;
the four seasons do not speak, yet the common people anticipate their cycles.
These have constancy
because of their utmost sincerity.
The noble person, with utmost virtue,
is understood without speaking,
becomes close without bestowing favors,
commands authority without showing anger.
This is following the mandate
by being cautious when alone.
For those who practice the Way of goodness,
without sincerity, there is no solitude (integrity);
without solitude, there is no manifestation;
without manifestation, even if it arises in the heart,
appears in the countenance,
and emerges in words,
the people will still not follow,
and if they do, they will doubt.
Heaven and earth are great,
yet without sincerity, they cannot transform all things;
the sage is wise,
yet without sincerity, he cannot transform the people;
father and son are intimate,
yet without sincerity, they become distant;
the ruler is esteemed,
yet without sincerity, he becomes lowly.
Sincerity
is what the noble person holds fast to,
and the foundation of governance.
Wherever it resides, its kind gathers.
Grasp it, and you attain it;
abandon it, and you lose it.
Grasp and attain it, and it becomes light;
light, then it acts alone;
acting alone without ceasing,
then it succeeds;
succeeding and exhausting one's talents,
long progressing without returning to the beginning,
then transformation occurs.
The noble person, though in a high position, has a respectful will;
his heart is small, but his Way is great;
what he hears and sees is near,
yet what he comprehends is far.
Why is this?
It is because of the method he employs.
Thus, the nature of thousands and tens of thousands of people
is the same as that of one person;
the beginning of heaven and earth
is like today;
the Way of the hundred kings
is that of the later kings.
The noble person examines the Way of the later kings
and discusses it before the hundred kings,
as if deliberating with a measuring tool.
Extending the system of ritual and righteousness,
distinguishing the boundaries of right and wrong,
grasping the essentials of the world,
governing the masses within the seas,
as if directing one person—
thus, the more concise his grasp,
the greater his achievements.
A square of five inches
can measure all the squares under heaven.
Therefore, the noble person, without leaving his chamber,
can accumulate all circumstances within the seas here,
because of the method he employs.
There are the comprehensive scholar,
the impartial scholar,
the upright scholar,
the sincere scholar,
and the petty person.
Above, he can honor the ruler;
below, he can love the people;
when things come, he responds;
when affairs arise, he discerns—
such a one may be called a comprehensive scholar.
Not colluding below to obscure the superior,
not agreeing above to harm the inferior,
in internal disputes,
not allowing personal interests to cause harm—
such a one may be called an impartial scholar.
His strengths,
even if unknown by the superior,
do not lead him to oppose the ruler;
his shortcomings,
even if unknown by the superior,
do not lead him to seek rewards;
not concealing strengths or shortcomings,
he exhausts himself with truth—
such a one may be called an upright scholar.
In common speech, he must be trustworthy;
in common actions, he must be cautious;
fearing to follow vulgar customs,
and not daring to insist solely on his own views—
such a one may be called a sincere scholar.
In speech, without constant trustworthiness;
in action, without constant integrity;
wherever profit lies,
he inclines without exception—
such a one may be called a petty person.
Impartiality produces clarity,
bias produces darkness;
uprightness and sincerity produce comprehension,
deceit and falsity produce obstruction;
honesty and trustworthiness produce spirituality,
boastfulness and exaggeration produce confusion.
These six productions
the noble person carefully considers,
and they distinguish Yǔ from Jié.
The measure for desires, aversions, choices, and rejections:
when seeing something desirable,
one must consider its detestable aspects before and after;
when seeing something beneficial,
one must consider its harmful aspects before and after;
weighing both sides,
calculating carefully,
then determining desires, aversions, choices, and rejections.
Thus, one often avoids great pitfalls.
The common trouble for people
is being harmed by one-sidedness.
Seeing something desirable,
they do not consider its detestable aspects;
seeing something beneficial,
they do not consider its harmful aspects.
Therefore, acting inevitably leads to pitfalls,
doing inevitably brings disgrace—
this is the harm of one-sidedness.
What people detest,
I also detest.
As for the wealthy and noble,
to generally arrogantly despise them;
as for the poor and lowly,
to seek to soften towards them—
this is not the nature of a benevolent person,
but rather of a treacherous person seeking to steal fame in a dark age,
and nothing is more dangerous.
Therefore, it is said:
Stealing fame is worse than stealing goods.
Tián Zhòng and Shǐ Qiū are worse than thieves.
Arrogance and carelessness
are human calamities,
while respectfulness and frugality
ward off all weapons.
Even the thrust of spears and lances
is not as sharp as the edge of respectfulness and frugality.
Thus, kind words to others
are warmer than cloth and silk;
harming others with words
cuts deeper than spears and halberds.
Therefore, on a vast and treacherous terrain,
one cannot tread safely.
It is not that the ground is unstable,
but that there is no safe place to set one's feet.
All lies in one's words.
On a broad road, one yields;
on a narrow path, one is in peril.
Even if one wishes not to be cautious,
it seems unavoidable.
Those who perish in recklessness do so out of anger;
those who are ruined despite their astuteness do so due to jealousy;
those who exhaust themselves in breadth do so because of slander;
those who become more turbid the more they purify do so because of their speech;
those who grow thinner the more they are nourished do so because of their associations;
those who argue but fail to persuade do so because of contention;
those who are upright yet unrecognized do so because of their competitiveness;
those who are honest yet unvalued do so because of their harshness;
those who are brave yet unfeared do so because of their greed;
those who are trustworthy yet disrespected do so because they insist on acting arbitrarily:
These are what petty people pursue
but noble persons avoid.
Those who engage in fights
forget their own selves,
forget their parents,
and forget their rulers.
Acting on a moment's anger
and losing their lives forever,
yet they still do it—
this is forgetting their own selves;
their households are immediately ruined,
their relatives cannot escape punishment and execution,
yet they still do it—
this is forgetting their parents;
it is what their rulers detest,
what the laws severely prohibit,
yet they still do it—
this is forgetting their rulers.
Below, they forget their own selves;
within, they forget their parents;
above, they forget their rulers.
Such people are not spared by the law,
nor are they kept by sage kings.
A nursing sow does not provoke a tiger,
a nursing dog does not wander far—
they do not forget their offspring.
As for humans,
if they forget their own selves below,
forget their parents within,
and forget their rulers above,
then such people
are not even equal to dogs and pigs.
All who engage in fights
must consider themselves right
and others wrong.
If they are truly right
and others truly wrong,
then they are noble persons
and others are petty people.
For a noble person to harm a petty person—
below, forgetting their own selves,
within, forgetting their parents,
above, forgetting their rulers—
is that not excessively wrong!
Such a person
is said to "use a Húfǔ spear to stir cow dung."
Is this considered wise?
Then nothing is more foolish.
Is this considered beneficial?
Then nothing is more harmful.
Is this considered honorable?
Then nothing is more disgraceful.
Is this considered safe?
Then nothing is more dangerous.
Why do people fight?
I would attribute it to madness or illness,
but that cannot be,
for sage kings also punish them.
I would classify them as birds, rats, or beasts,
but that cannot be, for their form is human,
and their likes and dislikes are mostly the same.
Why do people fight?
I deeply despise it!
There is the courage of dogs and pigs,
the courage of merchants and thieves,
the courage of petty people,
and the courage of scholars and noble persons:
fighting over food and drink,
without shame or integrity,
ignorant of right and wrong,
not avoiding death or injury,
unafraid of the many and strong,
greedily seeing only food and drink—
this is the courage of dogs and pigs.
Acting for profit,
contending over goods and wealth,
without courtesy or yielding,
decisive yet cruel,
fiercely greedy and violent,
greedily seeing only profit—
this is the courage of merchants and thieves.
Taking life lightly and being brutal—
this is the courage of petty people.
Where righteousness lies,
not swayed by power,
disregarding personal gain,
not changing one's view even if the whole country opposes,
valuing life yet upholding righteousness without yielding—
this is the courage of scholars and noble persons.
The Tiáoyáo fish
is a sun-loving fish;
once stranded on sand and longing for water,
it is too late.
Once entangled in trouble and seeking caution,
it is of no use.
Those who know themselves do not blame others;
those who understand fate do not blame heaven.
Those who blame others are destitute;
those who blame heaven lack will.
Having erred themselves,
they turn to blame others—
is that not misguided indeed!
The great distinction between honor and disgrace,
the constant nature of safety and danger, benefit and harm:
those who put righteousness before profit are honored;
those who put profit before righteousness are disgraced;
the honored are often successful;
the disgraced are often destitute;
the successful often control others;
the destitute are often controlled by others—
this is the great distinction between honor and disgrace.
The talented and sincere are often safe and benefited;
the reckless and violent are often endangered and harmed;
the safe and benefited are often joyful and at ease;
the endangered and harmed are often anxious and perilous;
the joyful and at ease often live long;
the anxious and perilous often die young—
this is the constant nature of safety and danger, benefit and harm.
Heaven gives birth to the multitude,
and there are reasons for what they attain.
With aspirations highly cultivated,
virtuous conduct deeply sincere,
and wisdom and thought profoundly clear,
this is how the Son of Heaven attains the world.
With laws and decrees as standards,
actions and measures timely,
judgments and decisions fair,
above able to follow the Son of Heaven's commands,
below able to protect the common people,
this is how the feudal lords attain their states.
With aspirations and conduct cultivated,
governing official duties well,
above able to follow superiors,
below able to preserve their positions,
this is how scholars and officials attain their fields and towns.
Following laws, regulations, punishments, and maps and records, without understanding their principles,
carefully preserving their measures,
cautiously daring not to reduce or increase them,
passed down from father to son,
to serve the kings and dukes—
thus, even though the Three Dynasties have perished,
their governing methods still remain,
this is how officials and clerks attain their salaries and ranks.
Filial, fraternal, honest, diligent, and hardworking, striving diligently in their tasks without daring to be lazy or arrogant—
this is how common people attain warm clothing and full bellies,
long life and enduring vision,
avoiding punishment and execution.
Embellishing wicked theories,
adorning deceitful words,
engaging in crooked affairs,
boasting and cheating,
sneaking and stealing,
reckless, violent, arrogant, and brutal,
sneaking to survive and turning restlessly in the chaos of a troubled age—this is how deceitful people attain danger, disgrace, and death penalties.
Their thoughts are not deep,
their choices not cautious,
their decisions on what to take or discard are crude and negligent—this is why they are endangered.
In innate nature, intelligence, and ability,
noble persons and petty people are the same.
Loving honor and hating disgrace,
loving benefit and hating harm—
this is what noble persons and petty people share.
But the ways they seek these differ.
The petty person
is quick to engage in deception yet desires others to trust him,
quick to practice fraud yet desires others to be close to him,
behaves like beasts yet desires others to think well of him.
His thoughts are difficult to understand,
his actions are difficult to settle,
his maintenance is difficult to establish.
When he succeeds, he inevitably fails to obtain what he likes
and inevitably encounters what he hates.
Thus the noble person,
being trustworthy,
also desires others to trust him;
being loyal,
also desires others to be close to him;
being cultivated, correct, well-governed, and discerning,
also desires others to think well of him.
His thoughts are easy to understand,
his actions are easy to settle,
his maintenance is easy to establish.
When he succeeds, he inevitably obtains what he likes
and inevitably avoids what he hates.
Therefore, in obscurity he is not hidden,
in prominence he is greatly illustrious,
and after death his name becomes even more renowned.
Petty people all crane their necks and stand on tiptoe, wishing:
"In wisdom, thought, talent, and nature,
we surely have what makes others superior."
They do not realize that they are no different from them;
it is that the noble person's application is appropriate,
while the petty person's application is mistaken.
Thus, upon careful examination of the petty person's knowledge and ability,
it is sufficient to know that he has enough
to accomplish what the noble person accomplishes.
Compare it to a Yuè person being at ease in Yuè,
a Chǔ person being at ease in Chǔ,
a noble person being at ease in refinement.
This is not due to differences in knowledge, ability, talent, or nature,
but to the distinctions in application, custom, and habit.
Benevolence, righteousness, virtuous conduct
are constant ways to safety,
yet they are not necessarily without danger;
depravity, indolence, aggression, and theft
are constant ways to danger,
yet they are not necessarily without safety.
Thus the noble person follows the constant way,
while the petty person follows the strange.
All people share certain similarities:
when hungry, they desire food;
when cold, they desire warmth;
when tired, they desire rest;
they like benefit and hate harm.
These are what people are born with;
they are so without dependence on anything else,
and are the same for Yǔ and Jié.
The eyes distinguish white, black, beauty, and ugliness;
the ears distinguish musical notes and their clarity or turbidity;
the mouth distinguishes sour, salty, sweet, and bitter;
the nose distinguishes fragrance, aroma, fishy, and rank;
the bones, body, skin, and texture distinguish cold, heat, illness, and comfort.
These too are what people are constantly born with;
they are so without dependence on anything else,
and are the same for Yǔ and Jié.
One can become a Yáo or a Yǔ,
can become a Jié or a Zhí,
can become a craftsman,
can become a farmer or merchant.
It depends on the accumulation of circumstances, application, custom, and habit.
This too is what people are born with;
it is so without dependence on anything else,
and is the same for Yǔ
and Jié.
To be a Yáo or Yǔ is to be constantly safe and honored;
to be a Jié or Zhí is to be constantly endangered and disgraced;
to be a Yáo or Yǔ is to be constantly joyful and at ease;
to be a craftsman, farmer, or merchant is to be constantly troubled and toilsome.
Yet people mostly do the latter
and seldom do the former.
Why is that?
The answer is:
ignorance.
Yáo and Yǔ
were not born complete;
they arose from transformative efforts,
accomplished through diligent cultivation,
and became fully prepared only after exhaustive effort.
Humans are born as petty persons by nature;
without teachers and models, they only see profit.
Humans are born as petty persons by nature;
if they encounter a chaotic age
and acquire chaotic customs,
then pettiness is compounded by pettiness,
and chaos is obtained through chaos.
Unless noble persons gain authority to oversee them,
there is no way to open and instill [virtue] in them.
Now, as for people's mouths and stomachs,
how would they know ritual and righteousness?
How would they know deference and humility?
How would they know integrity, shame, corners, and accumulations?
They only chew noisily
and eat to fullness.
If people have no teachers or models,
their minds are just like their mouths and stomachs.
Suppose a person from birth has never seen livestock and fine grains,
only beans, coarse vegetables, dregs, and husks;
then he would consider these most sufficient.
Suddenly, if someone appears splendidly carrying livestock,
he would stare wide-eyed and say:
"What strangeness is this?"
He smells it and finds it pleasing to the nose,
tastes it and finds it sweet to the mouth,
eats it and finds it comfortable to the body;
then none would fail to abandon the former and take the latter.
Now, take the way of the former kings,
the system of benevolence and righteousness,
used for communal living,
for mutual support and nurture,
for mutual adornment and refinement,
for mutual safety and stability.
Compare it with the way of Jié and Zhí:
the difference between them
is hardly just that between livestock and fine grains versus dregs and husks!
Yet people mostly do the latter
and seldom do the former.
Why is that?
The answer is:
ignorance.
Ignorance
is the common affliction of the world,
the great calamity and harm to people.
Therefore it is said:
The benevolent like to instruct and show others.
Instruct them, show them,
refine them, make them alert, lead them, and reinforce them;
then those who are blocked will soon be open,
the ignorant will soon be broad-minded,
the foolish will soon be wise.
If this is not practiced,
what benefit would Tāng and Wǔ bring if above?
What harm would Jié and Zhòu bring if above?
With Tāng and Wǔ present,
the world follows and becomes orderly;
with Jié and Zhòu present,
the world follows and becomes chaotic.
In this case,
is it not that human nature
can be led this way
or that way?
Human nature
desires livestock for eating,
embroidered silk for clothing,
carriages and horses for travel,
and also desires abundant wealth and accumulated riches;
yet year after year, generation after generation, they do not know insufficiency
—this is human nature.
Now in people's lives,
they already know to raise chickens, dogs, pigs,
and also raise cattle and sheep,
yet they dare not have wine and meat for eating;
they have surplus coins,
have granaries and cellars,
yet they dare not have silk and brocade for clothing;
even the frugal have boxes and chests of stored goods,
yet they dare not have carriages and horses for travel.
Why is this?
It is not that they do not desire them, (
but almost) because they take long-term thought and consider the future,
fearing they will have nothing to continue with.
Thus they further regulate expenses and restrain desires,
gathering, storing, and accumulating to continue.
Is this not taking long-term thought for themselves and considering the future,
almost extremely good?
Now those who belong to the careless-living and shallow-knowledge type
do not even know this;
they eat too extravagantly,
without considering their future,
and soon are reduced to poverty;
this is why they cannot avoid freezing and starvation,
carrying gourds and bags to become emaciated in ditches and valleys.
How much more so for the way of the former kings,
the system of benevolence and righteousness,
the distinctions in the "Shī",
"Shū", "Lǐ", and "Yuè". They are indeed the great planning for the world,
intended for the people of the world
to take long-term thought, consider the future, and preserve ten thousand generations.
Their flow is long,
their warmth and thickness great,
their achievement flourishing and far-reaching.
Unless one is a noble person who follows,熟悉, and cultivates them,
none can know them.
Thus it is said:
A short rope cannot draw water from a deep well,
and those whose knowledge is inadequate cannot comprehend the words of the sages.
The distinctions found in the Odes, Documents, Rites, and Music
are certainly beyond the understanding of ordinary people.
Thus it is said:
Master one and it can be repeated,
possess it and it can endure,
extend it and it can be universally applied,
ponder it and it can bring peace,
and by repeatedly examining it, it becomes increasingly cherished.
Used to govern emotions, it brings benefit;
used to establish reputation, it brings honor;
in community, it brings harmony;
in solitude, it brings contentment
and joy. Is this not indeed the case?
To be honored as the Son of Heaven
and possess the wealth of the entire world
is what all human desires share alike.
However, if we follow human desires,
circumstances cannot accommodate them,
and goods cannot satisfy them.
Therefore, the ancient kings established rituals and righteousness to create distinctions,
making hierarchies between noble and base,
differences between elder and younger,
and distinctions between wise and foolish, capable and incapable,
so that all people would bear their responsibilities
and each would obtain what is appropriate,
then distributing grain and emoluments in measures matching their worth.
This is the Way for communities to dwell together in harmony and unity.
Thus, when a benevolent person is in authority,
farmers exert their strength in the fields,
merchants use their discernment in wealth,
artisans employ their skill in tools and vessels,
and from scholar-officials up to dukes and marquises,
all fulfill their official duties with benevolence, integrity, wisdom, and ability.
This is called perfect peace.
Thus, some who receive emoluments from the entire world
do not consider it excessive,
while others guarding gates, receiving travelers,
holding passes, or striking night watches
do not consider it meager.
Thus it is said:
"Uneven yet uniform,
crooked yet aligned,
different yet unified."
This is called human relations.
The Odes say:
"Receiving small and large jades,
he became the majestic protector of the lower states."
This expresses it.
Physiognomy
did not exist among the ancients,
and scholars do not speak of it.
In ancient times, there was Gūbù Zǐqīng;
in the present age, in Liáng there is Táng Jǔ,
who examine people's physical forms and facial colors
to know their fortune, misfortune, and omens,
which common customs praise.
But the ancients had no such practice,
and scholars do not speak of it.
Thus, examining form is not as good as evaluating the heart;
evaluating the heart is not as good as selecting the proper method.
Form cannot overcome the heart,
and the heart cannot overcome method.
When method is correct and the heart compliant,
even with an ugly physical form, if the heart and method are good,
it does not prevent one from being a noble person;
even with a handsome physical form, if the heart and method are evil,
it does not prevent one from being a petty person.
The noble person is called auspicious,
the petty person inauspicious.
Thus, tall or short, large or small,
good or bad physical appearance
does not determine fortune or misfortune.
The ancients had no such practice,
and scholars do not speak of it.
For instance, Emperor Yáo was tall,
Emperor Shùn was short;
King Wén was tall,
the Duke of Zhōu was short;
Zhòngní was tall,
Zǐgōng was short.
Formerly, Duke Líng of Wèi had a minister named Gōngsūn Lǚ,
whose body was seven feet tall,
his face three feet long,
his forehead three inches wide,
with nose, eyes, and ears all present,
yet his fame shook the world.
Sūnshū Áo of Chǔ,
a humble man from Qīsī,
bald with a projecting left side,
shorter than the chariot rail,
yet made Chǔ hegemonic.
Lord Yè Gāo
was tiny, short, and emaciated,
walking as if he could not bear his clothes. Yet
during the rebellion of Duke Bái,
the Prime Minister Zǐxī
and Minister of War Zǐqī
all died there;
Lord Yè Gāo entered and secured Chǔ,
executed Duke Bái,
stabilized the state of Chǔ,
as easily as turning his hand,
his benevolence, righteousness, achievements, and fame praised by later generations.
Thus, for scholars, one should not measure height,
not gauge size,
not weigh lightness or heaviness,
but only consider their hearts.
Tall or short, large or small,
beautiful or ugly physical appearance—
how can these be criteria!
Moreover, the appearance of King Xú Yǎn
allowed his eyes to see over his horse;
Zhòngní's appearance
had a face like a masked exorcist;
the Duke of Zhōu's appearance
was like a broken stump;
Gāoyáo's appearance
had a color like a pared melon;
Hóng Yāo's appearance
had a face with no skin visible;
Fù Yuè's appearance
was like a standing fin;
Yī Yǐn's appearance
had a face without beard or eyebrows;
Yǔ limped, Tāng was lopsided,
Yáo and Shùn had double pupils.
Will followers then discuss intentions and will,
compare literature and learning?
Or merely differentiate tall and short,
distinguish beautiful and ugly,
to deceive and despise each other?
In ancient times, Jié and Zhòu were tall, huge, handsome, and beautiful,
the heroes of the world,
with sinews and strength surpassing and vigorous,
a match for a hundred men.
Yet they died and their states perished,
becoming the great shame of the world,
when later generations speak of evil,
they must refer to them.
This is not a calamity of appearance,
but rather from the scarcity of their learning and observation,
and the baseness of their discussions.
Now, the disorderly rulers of common customs,
the foppish youths of the villages,
are all beautiful, elegant, and seductive,
wearing strange clothes and feminine adornments,
with vital energy and demeanor imitating women;
no woman fails to wish them as husbands,
no maiden fails to wish them as suitors,
those who abandon their parents and families to elope with them
are shoulder to shoulder in rising numbers.
Yet, a middling ruler would be ashamed to have them as ministers,
a middling father ashamed to have them as sons,
a middling brother ashamed to have them as brothers,
and middling people ashamed to have them as friends.
Soon they are bound by the authorities
and executed in the great market,
all crying out to heaven, weeping and wailing,
bitterly lamenting their present
and regretting their beginning.
This is not a calamity of appearance,
but from the scarcity of their learning and observation,
and the baseness of their discussions.
Then,
which approach should followers adopt?
There are three inauspicious traits in a person:
being young yet unwilling to serve the elder,
being base yet unwilling to serve the noble,
being unworthy yet unwilling to serve the worthy—
these are the three inauspicious traits in a person.
There are three certain paths to distress in a person:
being superior yet unable to love inferiors,
being inferior yet fond of criticizing superiors—
this is the first certain path to distress.
In person, not complying;
behind the back, slandering—
this is the second certain path to distress.
With shallow knowledge and meager conduct,
and clear disparity in right and wrong,
yet unable to promote the benevolent,
unable to honor the wise—
this is the third certain path to distress.
—Whoever has these several traits,
if placed above, will certainly be imperiled,
if placed below, will certainly be ruined.
The Odes say:
"The snow falls thickly,
then brightly melts away.
None will condescend,
but remain repeatedly proud."
This expresses it.
What is it that makes a human truly human?
I say:
It is their capacity for distinction.
To desire food when hungry,
to seek warmth when cold,
to crave rest when weary,
to favor benefit and avoid harm—
these are innate to human existence,
arising without external cause,
and are common to both Yǔ and Jié.
Thus, what makes a human human
is not merely having two legs and no fur,
but their capacity for distinction.
Now consider the xīngxīng: it stands on two legs and is furry,
yet the gentleman sips its broth
and eats its meat.
Therefore, what makes a human human
is not merely their two legs and lack of fur,
but their capacity for distinction.
Beasts have fathers and sons
but lack paternal affection,
have males and females
but lack gender distinctions.
Thus, in the human way, none lack distinction.
Distinction finds its greatest expression in social divisions,
divisions find their greatest expression in ritual,
and ritual finds its greatest expression in the sage-kings.
With hundreds of sage-kings,
whom should I emulate?
Hence it is said:
Patterns fade with time,
cadences vanish with age,
and officials guarding the statutes
grow distant from ritual and strip it away.
Therefore it is said:
To observe the traces of sage-kings,
look to their brilliant manifestations—
the later kings.
These later kings
are the lords of the world.
To abandon later kings and praise antiquity
is like abandoning one's own lord
to serve another's.
Thus it is said:
To observe a thousand years,
examine the present day;
to know millions,
scrutinize one or two;
to understand ancient times,
study the Way of Zhōu;
to know the Way of Zhōu,
study the gentlemen it honors.
Hence it is said:
Use the near to know the distant,
use one to know ten thousand,
use the subtle to know the evident.
This expresses that idea.
The deluded claim:
"Ancient and modern differ in circumstances,
their ways of order and chaos diverge."
And the masses are confused by this.
These masses
are ignorant and lack explanation,
crude and without measure.
What they witness
can still deceive them,
let alone traditions from a thousand generations!
As for the deluded,
they can deceive even in courtyards and halls,
how much more about eras a thousand years past!
Why can sages not be deceived?
I say:
Sages
measure by themselves.
Thus they measure others by themselves,
measure feelings by feelings,
measure categories by categories,
measure achievements by discourse,
observe totality through the Dào.
Past and present are one.
Categories do not contradict;
though ages pass, principles remain constant.
Thus, facing distortion they do not stray,
observing complexity they are not confused—
they measure by this.
Beyond the Five Emperors, no figures are transmitted,
not for lack of worthy men,
but due to antiquity.
From the Five Emperors, no governance is transmitted,
not for lack of good governance,
but due to antiquity.
Yǔ and Tāng have transmitted governance, yet not as clearly as Zhōu,
not for lack of good governance,
but due to antiquity.
Transmissions grow sketchier with time,
fuller with recency;
sketchy accounts highlight major points,
full accounts include minor details.
Fools hear the sketch and miss the details,
hear the small and miss the grand.
Thus patterns fade with time,
cadences vanish with age.
Any speech discordant with former kings,
contrary to ritual and righteousness,
is called treacherous talk;
though eloquent,
the gentleman does not heed it.
To emulate former kings,
follow ritual and righteousness,
align with scholars,
yet dislike speech,
take no joy in discourse,
is surely not the mark of a sincere scholar.
Thus, regarding goodness, the gentleman
cherishes it in heart,
embodies it in action,
delights in speaking of it.
Hence the gentleman must engage in discourse.
All people enjoy speaking of what they value,
and the gentleman especially so.
Thus, offering words to others
outweighs gold, stone, pearls, and jade;
presenting words to others
surpasses the beauty of embroidered patterns;
hearing others' words
brings more joy than bells, drums, zithers, and lutes.
Therefore, the gentleman never tires of words.
The vulgar are the opposite,
prizing substance but neglecting refinement,
thus never escaping meanness and vulgarity.
Hence the Yì Jīng says:
"Tying the sack: no blame, no praise."
This refers to the pedantic scholar.
The difficulty of persuasion lies in
meeting the lowest with the highest,
engaging the most chaotic with the most orderly.
One cannot proceed directly;
citing distant examples risks fallacy,
citing recent ones risks vulgarity.
The skilled, in such cases,
cite distant examples without fallacy,
cite recent ones without vulgarity,
adapt with the times,
move with the world,
adjust urgency and slack,
like a master carpenter shaping wood with his tools,
skillfully achieving the intended meaning
without breaking or damaging.
Thus, the gentleman measures himself with a plumb line,
but guides others with a towline.
Measuring oneself with a plumb line
makes one fit to be a model for the world;
guiding others with a towline
enables tolerance,
relying on the multitude to accomplish great tasks under heaven.
Thus, the gentleman, being worthy, can tolerate the incompetent;
being wise, can tolerate the foolish;
being broad, can tolerate the shallow;
being pure, can tolerate the mixed.
This is called the art of inclusiveness.
The Shī Jīng says:
"The Xú region is united,
all by the Son of Heaven's merit."
This expresses that idea.
The art of discourse:
approach it with dignity,
handle it with sincerity,
maintain it with firmness,
illustrate it with analogies,
clarify it with distinctions,
convey it with joyful fragrance,
treasure it,
cherish it,
honor it,
revere it.
Thus, persuasion will always be accepted.
Even if not pleasing others,
none will fail to value it.
This is called valuing what is truly valuable.
The tradition says:
"Only the gentleman can value what is truly valuable."
This expresses that idea.
The gentleman must engage in discourse.
All people enjoy speaking of what they value,
and the gentleman especially so.
Thus, the petty man argues dangerously,
the gentleman argues humanely.
If speech lacks humaneness at its core,
then speaking is worse than silence,
eloquence worse than stammering;
if speech embodies humaneness,
then those who love speech are superior,
those who dislike it inferior.
Thus, humane speech is of great importance.
What originates from the sovereign to guide the people below
are government decrees;
what arises from the people below to show loyalty to the sovereign
are remonstrances and rescues.
Thus, the noble person never tires of practicing benevolence.
They cherish it in their aspirations,
practice it with ease in their conduct,
and delight in speaking of it.
Therefore, the noble person must engage in discourse.
Minor disputation is inferior to revealing the starting point,
and revealing the starting point is inferior to understanding fundamental distinctions.
Through minor disputation, one examines;
through revealing the starting point, one clarifies;
through understanding fundamental distinctions, one attains order.
In this, the distinctions of sages, scholars, and noble persons are fully embodied.
There is the discourse of petty persons,
the discourse of scholars and noble persons,
and the discourse of sages:
Without prior contemplation,
without early planning,
when they speak, it is appropriate;
when they form compositions, they are well-categorized;
whether in repose or in movement,
they respond to change inexhaustibly—
this is the discourse of sages.
Contemplating beforehand,
planning early,
their brief words are sufficient to listen to,
elegant yet substantial,
broad yet partial to correctness—
this is the discourse of scholars and noble persons.
Listening to their words, they are eloquent but lack coherence; employing them in person, they are full of deceit and achieve nothing.
Above, they are inadequate to comply with enlightened kings;
below, they are inadequate to harmonize and unite the common people.
Yet in their glibness of tongue,
they are sparing in their utterances,
sufficient to be considered extraordinary and arrogant—
this is called the champion of the treacherous.
When a sage king arises,
they are the first to be executed.
Then come the bandits and thieves.
Bandits and thieves can reform,
but these cannot reform.
In the present age,
there are those who adorn perverse theories,
embellish treacherous words,
to confuse and disrupt the world,
deceiving and deluding the foolish masses,
with bizarre and trivial arguments, making the world chaotic and unaware of where right and wrong, order and disorder lie.
Such people exist.
Indulging their innate nature,
content with willfulness and recklessness,
behaving like beasts,
incapable of conforming to culture and comprehending governance—
yet they uphold their views with reasons,
and their words form a coherent logic,
sufficient to deceive and delude the foolish masses.
These are Tā Xiāo and Wèi Móu.
Suppressing their innate nature,
extreme and aloof, striving for distinction,
arbitrarily considering themselves superior by differing from others,
incapable of uniting with the masses
or clarifying great distinctions—
yet they uphold their views with reasons,
and their words form a coherent logic,
sufficient to deceive and delude the foolish masses.
These are Chén Zhòng and Shǐ Qiū.
Not knowing the standard for unifying the world and establishing the state,
emphasizing utility and effort,
promoting frugality and thrift,
and neglecting distinctions in rank,
utterly incapable of accommodating differences
or distinguishing between ruler and minister—
yet they uphold their views with reasons,
and their words form a coherent logic,
sufficient to deceive and delude the foolish masses.
These are Mò Dí and Sòng Xíng.
Honoring laws but having no law,
not following traditions but fond of innovation,
above, they seek the approval of superiors,
below, they follow the customs of the masses,
all day speaking of established texts and codes,
yet upon reverse examination,
they are adrift without any foundation,
incapable of governing the state and fixing distinctions—
yet they uphold their views with reasons,
and their words form a coherent logic,
sufficient to deceive and delude the foolish masses.
These are Shèn Dào and Tián Pián.
Not modeling after the ancient kings,
not affirming ritual and righteousness,
but fond of crafting strange theories,
playing with extraordinary rhetoric,
very meticulous but not urgent,
disputatious but useless,
multitasking but achieving little,
incapable of serving as the guiding principles for governance—
yet they uphold their views with reasons,
and their words form a coherent logic,
sufficient to deceive and delude the foolish masses.
These are Huì Shī and Dèng Xī.
Partially modeling after the ancient kings but not knowing their system,
yet still with abundant talent and great ambitions,
and broad but miscellaneous knowledge.
They fabricate theories based on old traditions,
calling them the Five Phases,
extremely perverse and unclassifiable,
obscure and unexplained,
cryptic and unresolved.
They adorn their words
and reverently respect them,
saying:
"These are truly the words of the former noble persons."
Zǐsī initiated this,
Mèng Kē echoed it,
and the vulgar, confused Confucians clamor without knowing their errors,
thus accepting and transmitting it,
believing that Zhòngní and Zǐyóu thereby bestowed厚 upon later generations.
This is the crime of Zǐsī and Mèng Kē.
As for unifying strategies,
aligning words and actions,
unifying categories and classes,
and gathering the heroes of the world
to instruct them in the great antiquity,
teaching them the ultimate harmony,
in the hidden corners
and on the matted seats,
the brilliant writings of the sage kings are fully present,
and the customs of a peaceful age majestically arise.
Then the six theories cannot enter,
the twelve masters cannot approach,
even without a place to stick an awl,
kings and dukes cannot contend with their reputation;
holding the position of a single great officer,
then a single ruler cannot exclusively keep them,
a single state cannot solely contain them,
their fame overshadows that of the feudal lords,
and none are unwilling to have them as ministers.
These are the sages who did not attain power,
namely, Zhòngní and Zǐgōng.
Unifying the world,
managing all things,
nurturing and raising the people,
benefiting all under heaven,
wherever communication reaches, none do not submit and follow,
the six theories immediately cease,
the twelve masters transform and shift,
these are the sages who attained power,
namely, Shùn and Yǔ.
Now, what should the benevolent person
devote themselves to?
Above, they should emulate the systems of Shùn and Yǔ,
below, they should emulate the righteousness of Zhòngní and Zǐgōng,
striving to cease the theories of the twelve masters.
Thus, the harms of the world are eliminated,
the tasks of the benevolent person are completed,
and the traces of the sage kings become evident.
To believe what is believable is trustworthiness;
to doubt what is doubtful is also trustworthiness.
To honor the worthy is benevolence;
to despise the unworthy is also benevolence.
To speak appropriately is wisdom;
to be silent appropriately
is also wisdom.
Thus, knowing when to be silent stems from knowing when to speak.
Therefore, to speak much yet be well-categorized
is the sage;
to speak little yet be lawful
is the noble person;
to speak much or little without law
and indulge recklessly,
even if eloquent,
is the petty person.
Thus, to labor physically yet not meet the people's needs
is called treacherous affairs;
to labor intellectually yet not conform to the ancient kings
is called a treacherous mind;
to dispute, argue, analogize,
be quick and facile
yet not comply with ritual and righteousness
is called treacherous discourse.
These three treacheries
are what the sage kings prohibit.
Knowledge coupled with perilousness,
malice combined with supernatural cunning,
ingenuity in practicing fraud and deceptiveness,
eloquence though of no practical usefulness,
keen observation in matters of no urgency—
these are a great curse to good government.
Conduct that is eccentric and obstinate,
skill in concealing faults and making them look attractive,
fondness for villainy and making it seem polished,
speech that is eloquent but perverse—
these were strictly forbidden in antiquity.
Knowledge that lacks a model,
courage that is without fear,
keen observation and eloquence coupled with eccentric conduct,
extravagance and excess in their application,
fondness for villainy and gathering a crowd,
being swift-footed but losing the way,
carrying a heavy stone but stumbling and falling—
these are what the world rejects.
To win the hearts of the whole world:
do not use lofty position, high rank, or honored status to be arrogant toward others;
do not use keen intelligence, sage wisdom, or awareness to embarrass others;
do not use quickness of mind and rapid comprehension to get ahead of others;
do not use firm resolution, decisive strength, bravery, or daring to hurt others.
When you do not know something, ask about it;
when you lack an ability, learn it.
Even if you have ability, you must be modest,
and only then will you have inner power.
When with your lord, cultivate the duties proper to a minister.
When with your village, cultivate the duties owed by the young to their elders.
When with your elders, cultivate the duties proper to a younger brother or a son.
When with friends, cultivate the duties of polite and considerate behavior and of deference.
When with those who are humble and young,
cultivate the duties of offering guidance and of tolerance.
There should be no one you do not treat with kindness,
no one you do not treat with respect,
and you should never contend with anyone.
Be as all-encompassing and vast as heaven and earth in their embrace of the myriad things.
If you are like this,
then the worthy will hold you in high esteem
and the unworthy will be affectionate toward you.
If you are like this
and there are still those who are not obedient,
then they can be described as perverse, strange, and cunningly crafty men.
Even if they are among your younger brothers or sons,
it is fitting that punishment be extended to them.
An Ode says:
"It is not that God is being unseasonable—
it is that Yin does not follow the old ways.
Although there are no old, mature men,
still there are the statutes and punishments.
Why is none of this heeded?
The great mandate is therefore about to topple."
This expresses my meaning.
What in antiquity was called a "scholar-official"
was a man who was generous and honest,
who harmonized with the group,
who enjoyed sharing wealth and noble rank with others,
who delighted in distributing gifts to others,
who kept his distance from crime and error,
who devoted himself to the rational ordering of affairs,
and who was ashamed to be wealthy alone.
What today is called a "scholar-official"
is a man who is vile and slovenly,
who is injurious and disruptive,
who is arrogant and self-indulgent,
who is greedy for profit,
who is offensive and contrary,
and who has no sense for ritual and moral principles but is only fond of authority and power.
What in antiquity was called a "retired scholar"
was a man whose inner power was abundant,
who was capable of calmness,
who cultivated correctness,
who understood fate,
and who made clear what is right.
What today is called a "retired scholar"
is a man of no ability who claims to be able,
of no knowledge who claims to be knowledgeable,
whose greedy heart is never satisfied
but who pretends to have no desires,
whose conduct is deceptive, dangerous, and filthy
but who strongly proclaims himself to be cautious and sincere,
who makes unconventionality his convention,
and who, having left the herd, walks on his toes and engages in criticism.
What the scholar and gentleman can do and cannot do:
The gentleman can make himself worthy of honor,
but he cannot cause others necessarily to honor him.
He can make himself worthy of being trusted,
but he cannot cause others necessarily to trust him.
He can make himself worthy of employment,
but he cannot cause others necessarily to employ him.
Hence, the gentleman is ashamed not to cultivate himself,
but is not ashamed to be insulted.
He is ashamed of not being trustworthy,
but is not ashamed to lack the trust of others.
He is ashamed of lacking ability,
but is not ashamed to be unused.
As a consequence, he is not enticed by praise
and is not alarmed by slander.
He follows the Way and treads it,
corrects himself with unflattering integrity,
and is not swayed by external things.
This indeed is what is meant by the "true gentleman."
An Ode says:
"How mild and deferential he is!
Only thus is virtue made firm."
This expresses my meaning.
The demeanor of the scholar and gentleman:
His cap is lofty,
his garments are roomy,
and his countenance is refined.
He is grave,
imposing,
serene,
relaxed,
broad-minded,
generous,
self-possessed,
and unconstrained—such is the demeanor of a father or elder brother.
His cap is lofty,
his garments are roomy,
and his countenance is respectful.
He is modest,
compliant,
assisting,
correct,
thoughtful,
penetrating,
submissive,
and restrained—such is the demeanor of a son or younger brother.
Let me describe to you the perverse demeanor of the pedant:
His cap is pushed forward on his head,
the ribbons of his cap are tied loosely,
and his countenance is composed and self-satisfied.
He is satisfied with himself,
frivolous,
indifferent,
staring vacantly,
startled and alarmed,
frozen in place,
wide-eyed and blank,
in the midst of wine, food, music, and women,
he is bemused,
dazed;
in the midst of ritual and ceremonies,
he is irritable,
discontented;
in the midst of toilsome, bitter labors and professional duties,
he is slack and indolent,
negligent and careless,
lazy and cowardly, shameless,
and able to endure insults and reproaches—such is the perversity of the pedant.
With his cap askew on his head,
and his speech insipid and bland,
imitating the gait of Yǔ and the walk of Shùn—
such is the base Ru of the school of Zǐzhāng.
With his cap and garments correctly arranged,
his facial expression composed,
pretending to be humble and saying not a word the whole day—
such is the base Ru of the school of Zǐxià.
Lazy and cowardly, shirking his duties,
