without sense of shame or disgrace, but fond of drink and food,
and always saying that the gentleman, being firmly settled, does not exert himself—
such is the base Ru of the school of Zǐyóu.
The gentleman is not like this.
When at ease, he is not lazy;
when toiling, he is not remiss.
He complies with the fundamental principles in his response to changing circumstances,
and in every detail he hits on the proper course of action.
Being like this, he can then be considered a sage.
Among the followers of Zhòngní,
even a boy five feet tall
would be ashamed to mention the Five Lords-Protector.
Why is this?
I say:
Indeed,
they truly deserve to be regarded with shame.
Duke Huán of Qí was the most illustrious of the Five Lords-Protector.
In an earlier affair, he murdered his elder brother and seized control of the state.
In his private conduct, he had seven of his own sisters and cousins who remained unmarried.
Within the women's quarters,
he indulged in music and was wasteful and extravagant,
and the revenues of the whole state of Qí were insufficient to supply his needs.
In his external undertakings, he deceitfully invaded Zhū and made a surprise attack on Jǔ,
annexing a total of thirty-five states.
His conduct of affairs was as dangerous, vile, wasteful, and excessive as this.
How could he be worthy of mention at the gate of the great gentleman!
If such a state does not perish,
but becomes hegemonic, why is that?
The answer is:
Alas! Duke Huán of Qí possessed the great integrity of the world;
who could destroy him?
Calmly recognizing Guǎn Zhòng's ability to entrust the state to him,
this was the great wisdom of the world.
He peacefully forgot his anger, (
out) forgot his enmity,
and thereby established him as Zhòngfù,
this was the great decisiveness of the world.
Establishing him as Zhòngfù,
and the noble relatives dared not be jealous;
giving him positions equal to Gāo and Guó,
and the ministers of his own court dared not resent it;
granting him three hundred registered communities,
and the wealthy dared not oppose.
Noble and humble, old and young,
orderly and proper,
none failed to follow Duke Huán in honoring and respecting him,
this was the great integrity of the world.
If a feudal lord had one such quality,
then none could destroy him;
Duke Huán combined several such qualities and possessed them all,
so how could he be destroyed?
His becoming hegemon
was fitting indeed!
It was not luck,
but inevitability.
Yet at the school of Zhòngní,
even a youth of five feet
speaks of being ashamed to praise the Five Hegemons,
why is that?
The answer is:
Yes.
They did not level governance and education,
did not achieve lofty excellence,
did not perfect cultural order,
did not win people's hearts.
They inclined towards strategies,
examined toil and leisure,
carefully accumulated stores, prepared for battle,
and thus could overthrow their enemies.
They won through deceitful hearts.
They adorned contention with yielding,
relying on benevolence while treading the path of profit,
they were the outstanding among petty men,
how could they be worthy of praise at the gate of the great gentleman!
The true king is not so.
He attains worthiness and thereby saves the unworthy,
attains strength and thereby is lenient to the weak,
in war he can surely defeat them but is ashamed to fight them,
gracefully forming patterns
to show the world,
and violent states naturally transform themselves,
only those with calamitous errors
are then punished.
Thus the punishments of the sage king are extremely few.
King Wén punished four,
King Wǔ punished two,
Duke Zhōu completed the task,
reaching King Chéng,
then peacefully without punishment.
So how could the Way not prevail!
King Wén, with a hundred lǐ of land,
unified the world;
Jié and Zhòu abandoned it,
though thick with the power of having the world,
could not even die as common men.
Thus, if well used,
even a state of a hundred lǐ can stand independently;
if poorly used,
even Chǔ with six thousand lǐ becomes servant to enemies.
Therefore, if a ruler does not strive to attain the Way
but broadly holds power,
this is why he is endangered.
The method to maintain favor and hold position
without ever wearying:
If the lord honors you,
be respectful and modest;
if the lord trusts and loves you,
be cautious and humble;
if the lord fully employs you,
be restrained and careful;
if the lord is close and familiar,
be prudent in association and not devious;
if the lord distances you,
remain whole and loyal without betrayal;
if the lord demotes you,
be fearful but not resentful.
Honored but not boastful,
trusted but not forgetting to be humble,
burdened with heavy tasks but not daring to be arbitrary,
when wealth and profit come,
speak of goodness as beyond reach,
must fully perform the duty of declining and yielding
before accepting.
When blessings come, harmonize and manage them;
when disasters come, be calm and handle them;
wealthy then spread generosity widely,
poor then use frugally;
able to be honored or humbled,
able to be rich or poor,
can be killed but not made to do evil.
This is the method to maintain favor and hold position without wearying.
Even in the state of poverty and solitude,
also take this as a model;
this is called a fortunate person.
The "Shī" says:
"Loved is this one man,
responding to virtue accordingly.
Ever speaking filial thoughts,
bright indeed is the succession."
This refers to it.
Seeking to well handle great responsibilities, (
manage) great tasks,
and exclusively enjoy favor in a state of ten thousand chariots,
the method to surely have no future troubles:
none better than to delight in harmony,
support the worthy and broadly bestow,
remove grievances without harming others. (
Able) to endure the responsibility,
then cautiously practice this way.
If unable to endure it,
and fearing to lose favor,
then none better than to early seek harmony,
promote the worthy and yield to the able,
and peacefully follow behind.
Thus,
if favored, surely honored;
if favor lost, surely without blame;
this is the treasure for serving a lord
and the method to surely have no future troubles.
Therefore, those who understand warfare, in their actions,
when full, consider deficiency;
when level, consider danger;
when safe, consider peril;
doubly prepare carefully,
still fearing to meet disaster,
thus a hundred actions and never fall.
Confucius said:
"Skillful and fond of measure,
must be restrained;
brave and fond of harmony,
must be victorious;
wise and fond of humility,
must be worthy."
This refers to it.
The foolish are the opposite.
Holding heavy responsibilities and monopolizing power,
then delight in controlling affairs and envy the worthy and able,
suppress the meritorious and push forth the guilty,
mind arrogant and轻视 old grievances,
due to stinginess not practicing generosity,
above, act as important,
below, seize power to harm others,
though wishing to be without danger,
is it possible!
Thus, if position is honored, surely endangered;
if tasks are heavy, surely ruined;
if favor is monopolized, surely disgraced;
can be stood and waited for,
can be cooked and accomplished.
Is this the way?
Then those who would ruin it are many
and those who would uphold it are few.
The universal method of conduct:
to serve a lord, surely successful;
to practice benevolence, surely sage;
establish loftiness without doubt.
Then with reverence and respect lead it,
with loyalty and trust guide it,
with caution and care practice it,
with uprightness and sincerity guard it,
in sudden hardship then exert strength to reinforce it.
Though the lord may not know,
have no resentful heart;
though achievements are very great,
have no boastful expression;
reduce desires, increase merits,
love and respect tirelessly:
thus, then always without不顺.
To serve a lord, surely successful;
to practice benevolence, surely sage;
this is called the universal method of conduct.
The young serve the elders,
the lowly serve the noble,
the unworthy serve the worthy—
this is the universal principle of the world.
If there is someone
whose position is not above others
yet feels ashamed to be subordinate,
this is the mind of a treacherous person.
If one's aspirations are not free from treacherous thoughts,
and one's actions are not free from treacherous ways,
yet seeks to have the reputation of a gentleman or sage,
it is like
trying to lick the sky while lying prostrate,
or pulling someone's feet to save them from hanging—
such endeavors will certainly not succeed,
and the more one strives, the farther one gets.
Thus, the gentleman bends when it is time to bend,
and extends when it is time to extend.
The efficacy of the great Ru:
When King Wǔ died,
and King Chéng was young,
the Duke of Zhōu shielded King Chéng and succeeded King Wǔ
to maintain the unity of the world,
fearing that the world would betray the Zhōu.
He trod the registry of the Son of Heaven,
decided the judgments of the world,
calmly as if it were inherently his,
yet the world did not call him greedy:
he executed Guǎn Shū,
emptied the state of Yīn,
yet the world did not call him cruel;
he unified and governed the world,
established seventy-one states,
with the Jī clan alone occupying fifty-three,
yet the world did not call him biased.
He taught and guided King Chéng,
enabling him to understand the Way,
so that he could follow in the footsteps of King Wén and King Wǔ.
When the Duke of Zhōu returned the rule to Zhōu,
restoring the registry to King Chéng,
the world did not cease to serve Zhōu,
yet the Duke of Zhōu faced north and paid homage to him.
The Son of Heaven
cannot be lightly assumed,
nor can it be held by proxy.
If capable, the world will submit to him;
if incapable, the world will abandon him.
Therefore, the Duke of Zhōu shielded King Chéng and succeeded King Wǔ
to maintain the unity of the world,
fearing that the world would desert Zhōu.
When King Chéng was capped,
reaching adulthood,
the Duke of Zhōu returned the rule to Zhōu
and restored the registry,
clarifying the principle of not overshadowing the sovereign.
The Duke of Zhōu no longer possessed the world; formerly he had the world,
now he did not—
this was not usurpation;
King Chéng formerly had no world,
now he had it—
this was not seizure:
it was due to the natural order of changing circumstances.
Thus, for a branch to replace the main was not overstepping,
for a younger brother to execute an elder brother was not violence,
for ruler and minister to exchange positions was not improper.
Relying on the harmony of the world,
fulfilling the achievements of King Wén and King Wǔ,
clarifying the principle of branch and main,
it was indeed a transformation,
yet the world remained peacefully united as one.
None but a sage could accomplish this—
this is called the efficacy of the great Ru.
King Zhāo of Qín asked Master Xúnzǐ:
"Are Ru of no benefit to a state?"
Master Xúnzǐ said:
"The Ru emulate the former kings,
honor ritual and righteousness,
and are careful as ministers to honor their superiors.
If the ruler employs them,
their influence in the court is appropriate;
if not employed,
they retire among the common people and remain sincere,
inevitably becoming obedient subordinates.
Even in poverty and hunger,
they will never resort to wicked ways for gain;
without even a place to stick an awl,
they understand the great principles of upholding the state;
though none respond when they call out,
they comprehend the methods to manage all things
and nurture the people.
In a position above others,
they are fit to be kings or dukes;
in a position below others,
they are ministers of the state,
treasures of the ruler.
Even if hidden in poor alleys and leaky huts,
none fail to honor them, for
the Way truly resides in them.
"When Confucius was about to become Minister of Crime in Lǔ,
Shěnyóu Shì did not dare to water his sheep in the morning,
Gōngshèn Shì divorced his wife,
Shènkuì Shì crossed the border and moved away,
and those selling cattle and horses in Lǔ did not inflate prices—
they all corrected themselves early in anticipation.
Residing in Quèdǎng,
the youths of Quèdǎng divided the catch of their nets fairly,
with those having parents taking more—
this was transformed by filial piety and fraternal duty.
The Ru in court beautify governance,
in lower positions beautify customs—
such is the Ru as subordinates."
The King said:
"Then what are they like as superiors?"
Master Xúnzǐ said:
"As superiors, they are
vast and great:
their will is firm within,
ritual and courtesy are cultivated at court,
laws and measures are rectified among officials,
loyalty, trust, love, and benefit are manifested below.
To commit one unjust act
or kill one innocent person
to gain the world—
they would not do it.
This is the righteousness and trust of the gentleman recognized by others,
reaching throughout the four seas,
so the world responds to him with cheers.
Why is this?
Because his noble reputation is clear and the world is well-ordered.
Thus, those nearby sing and rejoice in him,
those afar hasten exhaustedly to him,
the four seas are like one family,
all within reach submit and follow—
this is called a teacher of men.
The Odes say:
'From west, from east,
from south, from north,
none think not of submitting.'
This expresses it.
As subordinates, they are like that;
as superiors, they are like this—
how can they be said to be of no benefit to a state?"
King Zhāo said:
"Good."
The Way of the former kings
is the height of benevolence,
followed by adhering to the mean.
What is called the mean?
It is said:
Ritual and righteousness are it.
The Way—
not the Way of Heaven,
nor the Way of Earth—
is what humans should follow,
what the gentleman follows.
What the gentleman calls worthy
does not mean being able to do all that others can;
what the gentleman calls wise
does not mean knowing all that others know;
what the gentleman calls discerning
does not mean discerning all that others discern;
what the gentleman calls perceptive
does not mean perceiving all that others perceive—
there are limits.
Assessing high and low land,
observing barren and fertile soil,
arranging the five grains—
the gentleman is not equal to the farmer;
handling wealth and goods,
judging quality,
distinguishing value—
the gentleman is not equal to the merchant;
setting compass and square,
applying the ink line,
preparing tools—
the gentleman is not equal to the artisan;
disregarding right and wrong,
the reality of so and not so,
to mutually suppress and restrain,
to mutually shame and humiliate—
the gentleman is not equal to Huì Shī and Dèng Xī.
But as for evaluating virtue to fix rank,
measuring ability to assign office,
enabling the worthy and unworthy each to find their place,
the capable and incapable each to obtain their position,
so all things find their proper place,
and changing events meet their appropriate response,
so that Shěn and Mò cannot advance their theories,
and Huì Shī and Dèng Xī dare not insert their scrutinies—
speech that must accord with principle,
actions that must suit the task,
this is where the gentleman excels.
In all actions,
those beneficial to governance
are established,
while those unbeneficial to order
are abolished—
this is called balanced governance.
In all knowledge and theories,
those beneficial to order
are practiced,
while those unbeneficial to order
are discarded—
this is called balanced theory.
Actions deviating from balance
are called treacherous deeds,
theories deviating from balance
are called treacherous ways.
Treacherous deeds and ways
are rejected in well-ordered times
but followed in chaotic times.
As for the mutual transformation of fullness and emptiness,
the distinctions of "hardness/whiteness" and "sameness/difference",
these cannot be heard by the sharpest ears,
seen by the keenest eyes,
nor articulated by the most eloquent debaters.
Even with a sage's wisdom,
one cannot fully enumerate them.
Not knowing them doesn't hinder becoming a noble person,
knowing them doesn't prevent becoming a petty person.
If craftsmen don't know them,
it doesn't affect their skill;
if noble persons don't know them,
it doesn't affect governance.
If rulers favor them, laws become chaotic;
if common people favor them, affairs become disordered.
Yet wildly deluded and foolish people
begin leading their followers,
debating their theories,
clarifying their analogies,
growing old with children
without realizing their error.
This is called supreme folly—
even less commendable than those known for breeding chickens and dogs.
The Book of Songs says:
"When you're ghosts or monsters,
you cannot be apprehended.
But with human faces visible,
your endless deceptions are perceptible.
I make this good song
to expose your fickleness."
This describes them.
Can I transform from humble to noble,
from ignorant to wise,
from poor to rich?
Is it possible?
The answer:
Only through learning.
Those who learn
and practice it
are called scholars;
those diligent in it
become noble persons;
those who fully comprehend it
become sages.
Reaching upward to become sages,
remaining below as scholars and noble persons—
who can stop me?
Once, I was an ordinary person among the masses,
yet suddenly I stand with Yáo and Yǔ—
is this not transforming from humble to noble?
Once, I couldn't distinguish between gates and rooms,
completely unable to make decisions,
yet suddenly I trace the sources of benevolence and righteousness,
distinguish right from wrong,
rotate the world in my palm
and differentiate black from white—
is this not transforming from ignorant to wise?
Once, I was an insignificant person,
yet suddenly the great vessel of governing the world rests here—
is this not transforming from poor to rich?
Suppose someone here
hoards treasures worth thousands of yì,
even if begging for food while traveling,
people call them wealthy.
Those treasures
cannot be worn as clothing,
cannot be eaten as food,
cannot be quickly sold,
yet people call them wealthy—
why?
Is it not because the instrument of great wealth truly lies here?
Thus, abundant learning also makes one wealthy—
is this not transforming from poor to rich?
Therefore, noble persons are honored without official rank,
wealthy without salary,
trusted without speaking,
authoritative without anger,
glorious in poverty,
joyful in solitude.
Is this not because the essence of supreme honor, wealth, importance, and dignity all accumulates here?
Hence it is said:
Honorable reputation cannot be won through cliquishness,
cannot be possessed through exaggeration,
cannot be coerced through power.
One must achieve sincerity in this to attain it.
Striving for it leads to loss,
yielding brings attainment,
modesty accumulates it,
boasting empties it.
Therefore, noble persons focus on cultivating their inner selves
and practice humility outwardly,
focus on accumulating virtue within
and dwell in modesty.
Thus,
their honorable reputation rises like sun and moon,
and the world responds like thunder.
Hence it is said:
Noble persons are obscure yet illustrious,
subtle yet brilliant,
yielding yet victorious.
The Book of Songs says:
"The crane cries in the nine-fold marsh,
its voice reaches heaven."
This describes it.
Mean persons are the opposite.
The more they form cliques, the less praise they receive;
the more they contend basely, the more dishonored their names become;
exhausting themselves seeking safety and profit,
they only endanger themselves more.
The Book of Songs says:
"When people are unvirtuous,
they blame each other from their positions.
Accepting ranks without yielding,
they perish because of this."
This describes them.
Thus, small ability undertaking great tasks
is like little strength bearing heavy burdens—
nothing but crushing collapse awaits.
The unworthy pretending to be virtuous
is like a hunchback loving to climb high—
the more point at their head.
Therefore, enlightened rulers assess virtue to assign positions,
thereby preventing disorder;
loyal ministers dare accept office only when truly capable,
thereby avoiding inadequacy.
When ranks above aren't confused,
and abilities below aren't exhausted,
this is the pinnacle of orderly governance.
The Book of Songs says:
"Equitable to left and right,
thus all follow."
This means superiors and subordinates do not confuse each other.
Considering conformity to customs as good,
valuing material wealth as treasure,
regarding self-preservation as the ultimate way—
this is the virtue of common people.
not letting personal desires distort what they've learned—
such persons
may be called resolute scholars.
Practicing laws with utmost firmness,
diligently correcting what they've learned
to rectify their nature,
their words often appropriate
though not fully comprehended,
their actions often proper
though not fully settled,
their thoughts often fitting
though not completely thorough—
above, they can magnify what they esteem,
below, they can guide those inferior to them;
such persons
may be called sincere noble persons.
Mastering the laws of numerous kings
like distinguishing black from white,
responding to contemporary changes
like counting one-two,
practicing rituals and essentials naturally,
like moving four limbs;
seizing opportunities to achieve merits skillfully,
like commanding the four seasons;
governing fairly and harmonizing the people so well
that millions unite as one—
such persons
may be called sages.
Orderly, oh, they possess principle;
Majestic, oh, they are able to respect themselves;
Resolute, oh, they have constancy from beginning to end;
Content, oh, they are able to endure long;
Joyful, oh, they hold to the Way without peril;
Brilliant, oh, their use of knowledge is clear;
Disciplined, oh, their conduct follows the guiding categories;
Graceful, oh, they possess refined patterns;
Harmonious, oh, they delight in others' goodness;
Anxious, oh, they fear others' impropriety;
(Then they may be called sage persons).
This Way of theirs emerges from unity.
What is called unity?
It is said:
Holding to the divine and being firm.
What is called divine?
It is said:
Perfecting goodness and embracing order is called divine.
What is called firm? It is said: That which nothing in the myriad things can overturn is called firm.
Divine and firm is called a sage person.
The sage person
is the conduit of the Way;
the Ways of the world are channeled through this;
the Ways of the hundred kings are unified in this;
thus the Ways of the "Shī," "Shū," "Lǐ," and "Yuè" return to this.
The "Shī" speaks of this, expressing its intent;
the "Shū" speaks of this, recording its affairs;
the "Lǐ" speaks of this, guiding its conduct;
the "Yuè" speaks of this, achieving its harmony;
the "Chūnqiū" speaks of this, revealing its subtleties.
Thus, the reason the "Guófēng" does not chase frivolity
is that it draws on this to regulate it;
the reason the "Xiǎoyǎ" is considered minor
is that it draws on this to embellish it;
the reason the "Dàyǎ" is considered great
is that it draws on this to glorify it;
the reason the "Sòng" reaches the ultimate
is that it draws on this to penetrate it:
the Ways of the world are all complete in this.
Those who align with this prosper;
those who oppose this perish;
to align with this and not prosper,
or oppose this and not perish,
from ancient times to the present,
has never occurred.
A guest once argued, saying:
"Confucius said:
'Was not the Duke of Zhōu magnificent!
His person noble, yet increasingly humble;
his family wealthy, yet increasingly frugal;
having defeated enemies, yet increasingly cautious.'"
I responded:
"This is likely not the conduct of the Duke of Zhōu,
nor the words of Confucius."
When King Wǔ passed away,
and King Chéng was young,
the Duke of Zhōu shielded King Chéng and succeeded King Wǔ,
ascended the Son of Heaven's registry,
sat with his back to the screen,
and the feudal lords hastened to pay respects in the hall below.
At that time,
who was he being humble to!
He unified control over the world, established seventy-one states,
with the Jī clan alone occupying fifty-three of them;
the descendants of Zhōu
who were not insane or deluded
all became illustrious feudal lords of the world—
who can say the Duke of Zhōu was frugal!
When King Wǔ set out to punish Zhòu,
he departed on a day taboo for military action,
faced east toward Tàisuì,
reached Fàn and encountered flooding,
reached Huái and faced collapse,
reached Gòngtóu and a mountain landslide.
Huò Shū feared, saying:
'After three days, five disasters have occurred;
is this not inadvisable?'
The Duke of Zhōu said:
'Having disemboweled Bǐgān and imprisoned Jīzǐ,
with Fēilián and Èlái in power,
how can there be anything inadvisable?'
Thereupon, they selected horses and advanced,
breakfasted at Qī,
lodged at Bǎiquán by dusk,
and at dawn pressed on to the wilds of Mù,
where, at the drum's beat, Zhòu's troops turned their spears,
and they rode the momentum of the Yīn people to punish Zhòu.
Thus, it was not the Zhōu people who did the killing,
but they utilized the Yīn people.
Hence, there were no captures of heads or prisoners,
no rewards for braving dangers,
and upon return, they secured the three armors,
laid aside the five weapons,
unified the world,
established music,
whereupon the "Wǔ" and "Xiàng" arose, and the "Sháo" and "Hù" were set aside.
Within the four seas,
all transformed their hearts and minds to follow in obedience,
so the outer gates remained unclosed,
and they spanned the world without borders.
At that time,
who was he being cautious of!"
Zàofǔ,
the world's expert charioteer,
without carriage or horse, could not display his skill.
Yì,
the world's expert archer,
without bow or arrow, could not show his cleverness.
The great Ru,
expert at harmonizing and unifying the world,
without a hundred lǐ of land
could not manifest his achievements.
With a sturdy carriage and selected horses,
yet unable to reach distant places,
covering a thousand lǐ in a day, he would not be Zàofǔ.
With a tuned bow and straight arrows,
yet unable to shoot far and hit the subtle target,
he would not be Yì.
Using a hundred lǐ of land,
yet unable to harmonize and unify the world,
subdue the strong and violent,
he would not be a great Ru.
That great Ru,
even if hidden in poor alleys and leaky huts,
without land enough to stick an awl,
kings and dukes cannot contend with his reputation;
in the position of a single great officer,
one ruler cannot alone retain him,
one state cannot alone contain him,
his fame surpassing that of feudal lords,
all wish to have him as a minister; using a hundred lǐ of land,
and states of a thousand lǐ cannot compete with him in victory,
he chastises violent states,
unifies and orders the world,
and none can overturn him.
This is the mark of a great Ru.
His words have categories,
his actions have ritual,
his undertakings are without regret,
his handling of perils and responses to change are perfectly appropriate,
moving with the times,
adapting with the age,
through a thousand actions and myriad changes,
his Way remains one.
This is the standard of a great Ru.
In obscurity, vulgar Ru laugh at him;
in prominence, the heroic are transformed by him,
the petty and trivial flee from him,
heretical doctrines fear him,
the multitude feels ashamed before him.
In prominence, he unifies the world;
in obscurity, he stands alone with esteemed name;
Heaven cannot cause his death,
Earth cannot bury him,
the age of Jié and Zhì cannot defile him;
none but a great Ru can establish this—
such were Zhòngní and Zǐgōng.
Thus, there are the vulgar person,
the vulgar Ru,
the refined Ru,
and the great Ru.
Those who do not study or inquire,
lack correct righteousness,
and exalt wealth and profit—
these are vulgar persons.
With loose garments and shallow belts,
wearing crooked caps,
superficially imitating the former kings enough to confuse the methods of a chaotic age,
erroneous in learning and miscellaneous in pursuits,
not knowing to emulate the later kings and unify institutions,
not knowing to exalt ritual righteousness and demote the "Shī" and "Shū";
their attire and conduct already identical to the common customs,
yet unaware of their odiousness;
their speech and discourse no different from that of Mòzǐ,
yet their clarity cannot distinguish it;
invoking the former kings to deceive the foolish and seek food and clothing,
gaining enough stores to cover their mouths
and they strut about proudly;
following the elders,
serving the favorites,
praising the honored guests,
submissively as if lifelong captives without daring other ambitions—
these are vulgar Ru.
Emulating the later kings,
unifying institutions,
exalting ritual righteousness and demoting the "Shī" and "Shū,"
their words and actions already follow great models,
yet their clarity cannot fully reach where laws and teachings fall short,
When one's hearing and sight have not reached certain realms,
then knowledge cannot be categorized.
To know is to say one knows,
and not to know is to say one does not know.
Internally, one does not use deception
externally;
externally, one does not use deceit
internally.
By this, one respects the worthy and reveres the laws,
daring not to be negligent or arrogant—such is the refined scholar.
They model themselves on the ancient kings,
unify ritual and righteousness,
and consolidate institutions.
They use the shallow to grasp the broad,
the ancient to hold the present,
and the one to control the myriad.
If it pertains to the category of benevolence and righteousness,
even among birds and beasts,
it is as distinct as black and white.
Unusual phenomena and strange changes,
never before heard of,
never before seen,
suddenly arising from one direction—
they raise the guiding categories to respond,
with no hesitation or doubt.
Applying the laws to measure them,
they fit as seamlessly as tallying tokens—such is the great scholar.
Thus, if a ruler employs common people,
a state of ten thousand chariots will perish;
if he employs vulgar scholars,
a state of ten thousand chariots may survive;
if he employs refined scholars,
a state of a thousand chariots will be secure;
if he employs great scholars,
even a territory of a hundred li
will endure long; and after three years,
the world will be unified,
the feudal lords will become ministers.
Employing them in a state of ten thousand chariots,
decisions and actions will bring stability,
and in one morning, hegemony is achieved.
Not hearing is not as good as hearing,
hearing is not as good as seeing,
seeing is not as good as knowing,
knowing is not as good as acting.
Learning culminates in action.
Action
leads to clarity,
and clarity makes one a sage.
The sage
is rooted in benevolence and righteousness,
judges right and wrong appropriately,
and aligns words and deeds,
without the slightest error.
There is no other way—
it stops at acting.
Thus, hearing without seeing,
though broad, is bound to be mistaken;
seeing without knowing,
though remembered, is bound to be delusional;
knowing without acting,
though substantial, is bound to be hindered.
Without hearing or seeing,
even if correct,
it is not benevolent,
and such a way will fail in every attempt.
Thus, if a person has no teacher or laws
yet is knowledgeable, they will surely become a thief;
if brave, they will surely become a bandit;
if capable, they will surely cause chaos;
if perceptive, they will surely engage in strangeness;
if eloquent, they will surely be deceitful.
If a person has a teacher and laws
and is knowledgeable, they will quickly attain understanding;
if brave, they will quickly gain authority;
if capable, they will quickly achieve success;
if perceptive, they will quickly exhaust matters;
if eloquent, they will quickly reason clearly.
Thus, having a teacher and laws
is a great treasure for a person;
lacking a teacher and laws
is a great calamity for a person.
Without a teacher and laws,
one exalts their innate nature;
with a teacher and laws,
one exalts accumulated effort.
And teachers and laws
are obtained through accumulation,
not received from nature.
Nature is insufficient to govern independently.
Nature
is what we cannot create,
yet it can be transformed;
accumulation
is not what we inherently possess,
yet it can be achieved.
Guidance and customs
are the means to transform nature;
concentrating on one without division
is the way to complete accumulation.
Customs shift one's will,
and prolonged stability changes one's substance.
Concentrating on one without division
leads to communion with the divine
and alignment with heaven and earth.
Thus, accumulating earth makes a mountain,
accumulating water makes a sea,
and the accumulation of dawns and dusks is called a year.
The highest is called heaven,
the lowest is called earth,
and the six directions in space are called the extremes.
An ordinary person among the hundred surnames,
accumulating goodness to the fullest,
is called a sage.
They seek it and then attain it,
act and then accomplish it,
accumulate and then rise high,
exhaust it and then become sage.
Thus, the sage
is what a person accumulates.
One accumulates plowing and weeding to become a farmer,
accumulates carving and cutting to become a craftsman,
accumulates trading goods to become a merchant,
accumulates ritual and righteousness to become a noble person.
The sons of craftsmen
none fail to continue the work,
and the people of cities and states are accustomed to their duties.
Living in Chǔ, one becomes like Chǔ;
living in Yuè, one becomes like Yuè;
living in Xià, one becomes like Xià.
This is not innate nature
but the result of accumulated influence.
Thus, if a person knows to be careful in guidance,
cautious with customs,
and greatly accumulates influence,
they become a noble person;
if they indulge their nature and lack inquiry and learning,
they become a petty person.
As a noble person, one is often safe and honorable;
as a petty person, one is often endangered and disgraced.
All people desire safety and honor and detest danger and disgrace,
thus only the noble person can attain what they love,
while the petty person daily invites what they hate.
The "Shī" says:
"These good people,
are not sought or advanced;
those cruel-hearted ones,
are cherished and repeated.
The people's craving for chaos
leads them to inflict cruelty."
This expresses it.
On the character of people:
If one's will is not free from crooked selfishness
yet hopes others see them as public-spirited,
if one's conduct is not free from污秽
yet hopes others see them as cultivated,
if one is extremely foolish and ignorant
yet hopes others see them as wise—
such are the common masses.
If one's will restrains selfishness,
then they can be public-spirited;
if one's conduct restrains their nature,
then they can be cultivated;
if one is knowledgeable and fond of inquiry,
then they can become talented.
Public-spirited, cultivated, and talented—
they may be called a minor scholar.
If one's will is at ease with public spirit,
one's conduct is at ease with cultivation,
and one's knowledge penetrates guiding categories—
thus, they may be called a great scholar.
The great scholar
serves as the Three Dukes of the Son of Heaven;
the minor scholar
serves as feudal lords, high officials, and scholars;
the common masses
are the artisans, farmers, and merchants.
Rites are the ruler's means to measure officials by inches, feet, and yards,
and human relations are fully expressed.
The noble person's speech has its boundaries,
conduct has its standards,
and the Way has its emphasis.
In seeking the Way and virtue,
they do not descend below safety and preservation;
in seeking aspirations and intentions,
they do not descend below the level of scholars;
in seeking the Way and virtue,
they do not deviate from the later kings.
A way that passes beyond the Three Dynasties is called dissipated;
laws that differ from those of later kings are termed unrefined.
Elevating or lowering,
diminishing or enlarging them,
it does not go beyond this principle.
This is how the noble person gives free rein to their intentions within the hallmarks of propriety.
Thus, when feudal lords inquire about governance,
if they do not address safety and survival,
they are not answered;
when commoners ask about learning,
if it does not pertain to becoming scholars,
they are not taught;
the doctrines of the hundred schools,
if they do not reach the level of the ancient kings,
are not heeded.
This is what is meant by the noble person having boundaries in speech
and guidelines in conduct.
May I ask about governing?
The reply:
Promote the worthy and capable without waiting for their turn;
dismiss the incompetent and unworthy without delay;
execute the arch-villains without awaiting instruction;
transform the mediocre and common people without relying on administration.
Before distinctions are settled,
there should be clear hierarchy.
Even the descendants of kings, dukes, or officials,
if they cannot adhere to ritual and righteousness,
should be relegated to commoners.
Even the descendants of commoners,
if they accumulate literary learning,
rectify their conduct,
and can adhere to ritual and righteousness,
should be elevated to ministers and officials.
Therefore, for those who engage in deceitful speech,
deceptive theories,
unrighteous acts,
or corrupt skills,
and for the restless and evasive people,
assign them duties and educate them,
wait with patience,
encourage them with rewards,
and punish them with penalties.
Those who are content in their duties are nurtured;
those who are not are discarded.
For the five types of disabilities,
the ruler should gather and support them,
employ them according to their abilities,
provide official positions, clothing, and food,
covering all without omission.
Those whose conduct and talents oppose the times shall die without pardon.
This is what is called heavenly virtue,
the governance of a true king.
The great principle in administering governance:
treat those who come with good intentions with courtesy;
treat those who come with ill intentions with punishment.
When the two are distinguished,
then the worthy and unworthy do not mix,
and right and wrong are not confused.
If the worthy and unworthy do not mix,
then the heroic and outstanding will come;
if right and wrong are not confused,
then the state will be well-governed.
If so,
reputation will grow daily,
the world will look up with admiration,
orders will be carried out and prohibitions heeded,
then the tasks of a true king are accomplished.
In all administration,
if one is stern, severe, and harsh
and does not favor guiding others with accommodation,
then subordinates will fear and not be close,
concealing and not revealing all;
if so,
then major affairs will risk neglect,
and minor affairs risk obstruction.
If one is conciliatory and accommodating,
favors guiding others with indulgence
without any restraint,
then deceitful words will arise together,
and speculative theories will sprout like spikes;
if so,
then administration becomes burdensome and affairs troublesome,
which is also damaging.
Thus, having laws without deliberation,
then what the laws do not cover will surely be neglected;
having duties without flexibility,
then what duties do not reach will surely fall through;
therefore, with laws and deliberation,
duties and flexibility,
there will be no hidden schemes,
no good left undone,
and all affairs will be without error—
none but the noble person can achieve this.
Thus, fairness is
the balance of administration;
impartiality and harmony are
the plumb line of administration.
Where there are laws, act by them;
where there are none, use analogy to decide—
this is the perfection of administration;
partiality and factionalism without principle
are the crookedness of administration.
Hence, there have been cases
where good laws existed yet disorder arose;
but from ancient times to the present,
it has never been heard
that there was a noble person and yet disorder.
The tradition says:
"Order is born from the noble person,
and disorder from the petty person."
This expresses it.
If shares are equal, there is no distinction;
if status is uniform, there is no unity;
if the masses are equal, they cannot be directed.
Heaven and earth exist,
and high and low have differences;
when an enlightened king first establishes,
he sets rules for the state's structure.
Two nobles cannot serve each other;
two commoners cannot direct each other—
this is the natural order.
If status and position are equal
and desires and aversions the same,
goods cannot satisfy and contention must arise;
contention leads to disorder,
and disorder leads to exhaustion.
The ancient kings hated such disorder,
so they established ritual and righteousness to differentiate,
creating grades of poverty, wealth, nobility, and baseness,
sufficient for mutual oversight—
this is the foundation of nurturing the world.
The Documents say:
"Equality lies in inequality."
This expresses it.
If horses are startled by the carriage,
the noble person is not safe in it;
if the common people are startled by governance,
the noble person is not secure in position.
If horses are startled by the carriage,
nothing is better than calming them;
if the common people are startled by governance,
nothing is better than benefiting them.
Select the worthy and good,
promote the sincere and respectful,
encourage filial piety and fraternal duty,
support the orphaned and widowed,
aid the poor and needy;
thus,
the common people will be content with governance.
When the common people are content with governance,
then the noble person is secure in position.
The tradition says:
"The ruler is like a boat;
the common people are like water.
The water can carry the boat,
the water can capsize the boat."
This expresses it.
Therefore, the ruler
who desires security should do nothing better than equitable governance and loving the people;
who desires glory should do nothing better than exalting ritual and respecting scholars;
who desires to achieve merit and fame should do nothing better than honoring the worthy and employing the capable—
these are the great essentials for a ruler.
If these three essentials are correct,
then all else will inevitably be correct;
if these three essentials are incorrect,
then even if the rest are partially correct,
it will still be of no benefit.
Confucius said:
"If the great essentials are correct,
and the minor details are correct,
that is a superior ruler.
If the great essentials are correct,
but the minor details are not, sometimes deviating,
sometimes conforming,
that is a middling ruler.
If the great essentials are incorrect,
even if the minor details are correct,
I do not consider the rest."
Chéng Hóu and Sì Gōng were rulers who amassed wealth and calculated gains,
but did not reach the level of winning the people;
Zhèng Zǐchǎn won the people,
but did not reach the level of governing;
Guǎn Zhòng governed,
but did not reach the level of cultivating ritual.
Thus, those who cultivate ritual become kings;
those who govern become strong;
those who win the people gain security;
those who amass wealth perish.
Thus, the kingly ruler enriches the people,
the hegemonic ruler enriches his scholars,
the barely surviving state enriches its high officials,
and the doomed state enriches its coffers and storehouses.
When the coffers are filled
and the storehouses are full,
but the common people are impoverished,
this is called overflowing above while leaking below.
Such a state cannot defend internally
nor campaign externally,
and its collapse and destruction can be expected imminently.
Thus, what I hoard leads to my demise,
while the enemy gains it to become stronger.
Hoarding wealth is the way to summon invaders, enrich enemies, destroy the state, and endanger oneself,
so an enlightened ruler does not tread this path.
The kingly way wins over people,
the hegemonic way wins over allies,
the forceful way seizes territory.
Winning over people makes feudal lords submit,
winning over allies makes feudal lords friendly,
seizing territory makes feudal lords hostile.
Subduing feudal lords leads to kingship,
befriending feudal lords leads to hegemony,
antagonizing feudal lords leads to peril.
Using force to overcome others' city defenses
and others' battlefield engagements
inevitably harms their people severely.
Severely harming their people
makes their people detest me intensely;
when their people detest me intensely,
they daily desire to fight me.
Using force to overcome others' city defenses
and others' battlefield engagements
inevitably harms my own people severely.
Severely harming my own people
makes my people detest me intensely;
when my people detest me intensely,
they daily refuse to fight for me.
Others' people daily desire to fight me,
while my people daily refuse to fight for me—
this is how strength turns into weakness.
Gaining territory while losing people,
accumulating burdens with little achievement—
though defended land increases,
the means of defense diminish.
This is how great possessions become reduced.
Feudal lords all harbor resentment and alliances,
never forgetting their enemies,
awaiting moments of weakness in the strong,
and capitalizing on their decline.
Understanding the vulnerabilities of strength
reveals the perilous time for the powerful.
Those who know the way of strength do not pursue force,
but consider the kingly mandate
to preserve their power
and consolidate their virtue.
With power preserved, feudal lords cannot weaken them;
with virtue consolidated, feudal lords cannot reduce them.
When there is no true king or hegemon in the world,
they remain constantly victorious.
Such are those who know the way of strength.
The hegemon acts differently:
opening up fields and wilderness,
filling granaries and storehouses,
preparing equipment and supplies,
carefully recruiting and selecting men of talent and skill,
then gradually encouraging them with rewards and honors,
and restraining them with strict punishments.
Preserving the perishing and continuing the extinct,
protecting the weak and prohibiting violence—
without ambitions of annexation—
then feudal lords become close to him.
Cultivating the way of befriending rivals,
receiving feudal lords with respect,
then feudal lords become pleased with him.
The reason they become close
is his non-annexation;
if annexation appears,
feudal lords would distance themselves.
The reason they become pleased
is his befriending of rivals;
if subjugation appears,
feudal lords would turn away.
Thus, demonstrating non-annexation conduct
and proving the way of befriending rivals—
when there is no true king in the world,
he remains constantly victorious.
Such are those who know the hegemonic way.
King Mǐn was defeated by the five states,
Duke Huán was humiliated by Lord Zhuāng of Lǔ—
for no other reason
than attempting the kingly way without following its true path.
The kingly ruler acts differently:
his benevolence surpasses the world,
his righteousness surpasses the world,
his majesty surpasses the world.
With benevolence surpassing the world,
all under Heaven become close to him;
with righteousness surpassing the world,
all under Heaven honor him;
with majesty surpassing the world,
none under Heaven dare oppose him.
With unopposable majesty
assisting the way of winning people's hearts,
he triumphs without fighting,
gains without attacking,
and all under Heaven submit without mobilizing troops.
Such are those who know the kingly way.
Understanding these three methods,
one can become kingly when desiring kingship,
hegemonic when desiring hegemony,
and strong when desiring strength.
The personnel of a kingly ruler:
adorn actions with ritual and righteousness,
decide cases according to law,
discern the finest details,
and respond to changes inexhaustibly.
This is called having foundation.
Such are the personnel of a kingly ruler.
The institutions of a kingly ruler:
principles not exceeding the Three Dynasties,
laws not differing from later kings.
Principles exceeding the Three Dynasties are called ungrounded,
laws differing from later kings are called improper.
Clothing has regulations,
palaces have measures,
retinues have numbers,
funeral vessels and ritual implements all have appropriate grades.
Music: all non-elegant sounds are abolished;
colors: all non-traditional patterns are discontinued;
implements: all non-classical vessels are destroyed.
This is called restoring antiquity.
Such are the institutions of a kingly ruler.
The evaluations of a kingly ruler:
none without virtue are honored,
none without ability are appointed,
none without merit are rewarded,
none without crime are punished.
Court has no undeserved positions,
people have no unearned livelihoods.
Honoring the worthy and employing the capable,
so that ranked positions are not misassigned;
restraining the cautious and prohibiting the violent,
so that punishments are not excessive.
The people clearly understand that doing good at home
brings rewards at court,
and doing evil in secret
incurs punishment in public.
This is called established evaluation.
Such are the evaluations of a kingly ruler.
The regulations of a kingly ruler:
graded taxes, governance affairs, and managing all things
are to nourish the myriad people.
Field taxes at one-tenth,
border markets inspected but not taxed,
mountains, forests, and weirs
closed or opened seasonally without taxation.
Adjust levies according to land quality,
determine tribute based on road distance.
Circulating goods, grain, and rice
without stagnation,
enabling mutual exchange.
All within the Four Seas become like one family:
thus the near do not conceal their abilities,
the far do not resent their labors,
no remote or isolated land
fails to serve willingly and contentedly.
This is called being a teacher of humanity.
Such are the regulations of a kingly ruler.
The northern seas have running horses and barking dogs,
yet the central states obtain and raise them;
the southern seas have feathers, ivory, hides, azurite, and cinnabar,
yet the central states obtain and utilize them;
the eastern seas have purple dye, hemp cloth, fish, and salt,
yet the central states obtain and consume them;
the western seas have leather and patterned yak tails,
yet the central states obtain and use them.
Thus, lake dwellers have sufficient wood,
mountain dwellers have sufficient fish,
farmers without carving or smelting have sufficient tools,
artisans and merchants without farming have sufficient grain.
Though tigers and leopards are fierce,
the gentleman skins and uses them.
Thus, what Heaven covers and
what Earth supports
all manifest their full beauty
and serve their functions,
used above to adorn the worthy and virtuous,
and below to nourish the common people, bringing them peace and joy.
This is called the Great Divinity.
The Book of Songs says:
"Heaven made the high mountain,
King Tài cultivated it.
He began the work,
and King Wén brought it to tranquility."
This expresses the idea.
To use categories to manage complexity,
to use unity to govern multiplicity,
beginning leads to end,
end leads to beginning,
like a circle without a break—
if this is abandoned, the world declines.
Heaven and Earth are
the origin of life;
ritual and righteousness are
the foundation of order;
the noble person (jūnzǐ) is
the source of ritual and righteousness.
To practice them,
persist in them,
accumulate them deeply,
and perfect them—
this is the noble person (as the origin).
Thus, Heaven and Earth produce the noble person,
and the noble person brings order to Heaven and Earth.
The noble person is
the counterpart of Heaven and Earth,
the summation of all things,
and the parent of the people.
Without the noble person,
Heaven and Earth would lack order,
ritual and righteousness would have no system,
above there would be no ruler or teacher,
below no father-son
or husband-wife relationships—this is called utter chaos.
Ruler and minister, father and son, elder and younger brother, husband and wife—
beginning leads to end,
end leads to beginning,
sharing the same principle with Heaven and Earth,
enduring as long as all generations—
this is called the great foundation.
Thus, mourning and sacrifice, court audiences and diplomatic missions (and military affairs) are one;
noble and base, execution and life, giving and taking are one;

ruler being ruler, minister being minister, father being father, son being son, elder brother being elder brother, younger brother being younger brother are one; farmer being farmer, scholar being scholar, artisan being artisan, merchant being merchant are one.
Water and fire have energy but no life;
plants and trees have life but no awareness;
birds and beasts have awareness but no righteousness;
humans have energy, life, and awareness,
and also possess righteousness,
thus they are the most noble under Heaven.
Their strength is not like that of an ox,
their speed not like that of a horse,
yet oxen and horses are used by them—
why is that?
The answer:
humans can form societies,
while those cannot.
How can humans form societies?
The answer:
through division (of roles).
How can division be implemented?
The answer:
through righteousness.
Thus, with righteousness to guide division, there is harmony;
harmony leads to unity;
unity brings greater strength;
greater strength leads to power;
power enables overcoming things;
hence, palaces and dwellings can be inhabited.
Thus, arranging the four seasons,
managing all things,
benefiting all under Heaven—
there is no other reason
than having obtained division and righteousness.
Therefore, in life, one cannot be without society;
but society without division leads to strife;
strife leads to chaos;
chaos leads to disintegration;
disintegration leads to weakness;
weakness means inability to overcome things;
hence, palaces and dwellings cannot be inhabited—
this is why it is said one cannot for a moment abandon ritual and righteousness.
Being able to serve parents is called filial piety;
being able to serve elder brothers is called fraternal duty;
being able to serve superiors is called obedience;
being able to command subordinates is called being a ruler.
The ruler is
one who excels at organizing society.
When the way of society is proper,
then all things find their appropriate place,
the six domestic animals all thrive,
and all living beings fulfill their destinies.
Thus, if nurturing and growth are timely,
the six domestic animals multiply;
if harvesting and preservation are timely,
plants and trees flourish;
if government decrees are timely,
the common people are unified
and the worthy and virtuous submit.
The system of the sage ruler:
when plants and trees are blooming and bearing fruit,
axes do not enter the forests,
so as not to cut short their life
or halt their growth;
when turtles, alligators, fish, turtles, loaches, and eels are spawning,
nets and poisonous drugs are not used in the marshes,
so as not to cut short their life
or halt their growth;
plowing in spring, weeding in summer, harvesting in autumn, storing in winter—
if these four are not mistimed,
then the five grains are uninterrupted
and the common people have surplus food;
for ponds, deep pools, marshes, rivers, and lakes,
strictly enforcing seasonal prohibitions,
so fish and turtles are abundant
and the common people have surplus for use;
if felling and nurturing are not mistimed,
then the mountains and forests are not barren
and the common people have surplus timber.
The application by the sage king:
observing above to Heaven,
applying below to Earth,
filling the space between Heaven and Earth,
extending over all things,
subtle yet clear,
short yet long,
narrow yet broad,
divinely brilliant and vast, yet reaching the utmost simplicity.
Thus it is said:
one who unifies and makes one is called
a sage.
On the ordering of officials:
The Minister of Ceremonies knows the numbers for guests, sacrifices, banquets, and sacrificial animals;
the Minister of the Land knows the numbers of clans, city walls, and established implements;
the Minister of War knows the numbers of armies, armor, weapons, and chariots.
To revise statutes and commands,
examine poetry and songs,
prohibit licentious music,
and timely adjust and revise,
so that barbarian customs and corrupt sounds dare not confuse the elegant—
this is the duty of the Grand Master.
To repair dikes and bridges,
dredge ditches and canals,
channel floodwaters,
stabilize water storage,
and regulate openings and closures seasonally;
so even in years of flood or drought disaster,
the people have means to farm and harvest—
this is the duty of the Minister of Works.
To survey high and low land,
inspect fertile and lean soil,
arrange the five crops,
oversee agricultural work,
carefully manage storage,
and timely adjust and revise,
so that farmers focus on effort with few distractions—
this is the duty of the Field Supervisor.
To establish fire regulations,
conserve mountains, forests, marshes, plants, trees, fish, turtles, and all resources,
and enforce seasonal bans and allowances,
so the state has ample supplies
and wealth and goods are not exhausted—
this is the duty of the Forester.
To harmonize villages and neighborhoods,
settle dwellings and homes,
raise the six domestic animals,
promote planting and cultivation,
encourage education and transformation,
urge filial piety and fraternal duty,
and timely adjust and revise,
so the common people follow commands
and live peacefully and joyfully in their villages—
this is the duty of the Village Supervisor.
To assess various artisans,
examine seasonal tasks,
distinguish well-made from crude work,
value durability and utility,
ensure readiness for use,
so that carved and patterned items are not privately made at home—
this is the duty of the Artisan Supervisor.
To observe yīn and yáng,
interpret omens and signs,
drill tortoise shells and arrange hexagrams,
preside over exorcisms and selections using the five divinations,
knowing auspicious, inauspicious, and ominous signs—
this is the duty of the hunchbacked shamans and lame invokers.
To clean and collect refuse,
to repair the roads,
to be vigilant against thieves and robbers,
to equalize the taxes on shops and inns,
to make timely adjustments and repairs,
so that merchants and travelers feel secure and goods circulate freely—these are the duties of the market administration.
To restrain the violent and prohibit the fierce,
to guard against excesses and eliminate depravity,
to execute them with the five punishments,
causing the violent and fierce to reform,
so that treachery and depravity do not arise—these are the duties of the Minister of Justice.
To base on government and instruction,
to correct laws and standards,
to listen broadly and regularly inspect,
to measure their achievements,
to deliberate on rewards and honors,
to make timely adjustments and repairs,
so that all officials are diligent
and the common people are not negligent—these are the duties of the Prime Minister.
To deliberate on rites and music,
to rectify personal conduct,
to broaden education and transformation,
to beautify customs and practices,
to universally cover and harmonize them into one—these are the duties of the feudal lords.
To perfect the Way and its Power,
to reach the peak of loftiness,
to make patterns and order utmost,
to unify the world,
to stir even the finest details,
so that all under heaven follow and submit without exception—these are the duties of the Son of Heaven.
Thus, if governmental affairs are in disorder,
it is the fault of the Prime Minister;
if the state loses its customs,
it is the error of the feudal lords;
if the world is not unified,
and the feudal lords are inclined to rebel,
then the Son of Heaven is not the right person.
When the conditions are fully present, one becomes king;
when the conditions are fully present, one becomes hegemon;
when the conditions are fully present, one survives;
when the conditions are fully present, one perishes.
For a state of ten thousand chariots,
the means by which authority and strength are established,
the means by which reputation and fame are beautified,
the means by which enemies are subdued,
the means by which the state's safety, danger, good, and bad are determined—
the control lies here,
not in others.
To be king, hegemon, safe and surviving, endangered, or perishing—
the control lies with oneself,
not in others.
If authority and strength are not enough to endanger neighboring enemies,
and reputation and fame are not enough to awe the world,
then the state cannot stand independently;
how can it avoid troubles?
When the world is coerced by violent states,
and one is forced to do what one does not wish,
daily working and acting alongside a Jié,
it does no harm to being a Yáo;
this is not the source of achievements and fame,
nor what determines survival, danger, or safety.
The source of achievements and fame,
what determines survival, danger, or safety,
must lie in the place of sincere and joyful heart during prosperous times.
Truly, if one makes one's state a place for a king, one becomes king;
if one makes it a place for danger and destruction, one faces danger and destruction.
In times of prosperity,
one should remain neutral
without bias
and engage in neither vertical nor horizontal alliances,
calmly keeping troops at rest without movement,
to observe the violent states clash with each other.
Then, stabilize government and instruction,
examine rhythms and regulations,
sharpen the people,
and on the day this is done,
one's military will be the strongest in the world;
cultivate humanity and righteousness,
exalt loftiness,
correct laws and standards,
select the worthy and good,
nurture the people,
and on the day this is done,
one's reputation will be the finest in the world.
Authority is made weighty,
military is made strong,
reputation is made beautiful.
As for Yáo and Shùn, who unified the world,
they could not add a hair's breadth to this.
Thus, when those who use cunning and subversion are dismissed,
the worthy, wise, and sagely scholars naturally advance;
when punishments and government are equitable,
the people are harmonious,
and state customs are restrained,
then the military is strong and cities firm,
and enemy states naturally submit;
focus on fundamental tasks,
accumulate wealth and goods,
and do not forget to avoid waste and dispersal,
so that all ministers and people act according to the system,
then wealth and goods accumulate,
and the state naturally becomes rich.
If these three are embodied, the world submits,
and the rulers of violent states naturally cannot use their military.
Why?
They have no one to follow them.
Those who would follow them
must be their people,
but their people feel toward me as joyfully as toward parents;
they like me as fragrance of orchids;
looking back at their rulers, they see them as branding and tattooing,
as enemies.
By their human nature,
even a Jié
or a Zhí, would they be willing to do what they hate,
and harm what they like? They have been won over.
Thus, the ancients
had those who took the world with one state—
not by going to enforce it,
but by cultivating government in their own place,
so that the world had no unwillingness;
thus, they could punish the violent and restrain the fierce.
Hence, when the Duke of Zhōu campaigned south, the northern states complained,
saying:
"Why only not come to us?"
When he campaigned east, the western states complained,
saying:
"Why only later to us?"
Who could fight against this?
One who can make his state such becomes king.
In times of prosperity,
to secure with stilled troops and rested people,
to be kind and loving to the people,
to open up fields and lands,
to fill granaries and storehouses,
to prepare for convenient use,
to carefully recruit, select, and review men of talent and skill;
then gradually use rewards and honors to lead them,
strict punishments and penalties to guard against them,
select scholars who understand affairs
to have them lead and oversee,
thus amassing and cultivating with satisfaction,
so that goods and resources are sufficient.
As for weapons, armor, and equipment,
they will daily be exposed and destroyed in the open plains,
while I will repair and maintain them,
care for them,
and store them in the treasuries;
as for goods, wealth, grain, and rice,
they will daily be scattered and wasted in the wild fields,
while I will accumulate and gather them in the granaries;
as for men of talent, skill, strong aides, and brave warriors,
they will daily be worn out and exhausted by enemies,
while I will summon them,
review them,
and sharpen them at the court.
Thus,
they daily accumulate decay,
while I daily accumulate completeness;
they daily accumulate poverty,
while I daily accumulate wealth;
they daily accumulate toil,
while I daily accumulate ease.
Between rulers and ministers, superiors and inferiors,
they will fiercely daily drift apart and resent,
while I will sincerely daily grow closer and love,
thus awaiting their decline.
One who can make his state such becomes hegemon.
If in personal conduct one follows common customs,
in actions one follows common practices,
in promotions, demotions, honors, and disgraces one elevates common scholars,
and in dealing with the common people one uses generosity and kindness,
such a one survives safely.
If in personal conduct one is frivolous and crude,
in actions one is doubtful and hesitant,
in promotions, demotions, honors, and disgraces one elevates flatterers and sycophants,
and in dealing with the common people one is fond of seizing and encroaching,
such a one is endangered.
If in personal conduct one is arrogant and violent,
in actions one is subversive,
in promotions, demotions, honors, and disgraces one elevates the sinister, dangerous, deceitful, and crafty,
and in dealing with the common people,
one is fond of using their labor and strength to death,
but neglects their achievements;
fond of using their taxes and levies,
but forgets their fundamental duties—
such a one perishes.
——These five categories
must be carefully chosen,
for they are the instruments of kingship, hegemony, security, peril, and ruin.
Those who choose well control others,
while those who choose poorly are controlled by others;
those who choose well become kings,
while those who choose poorly perish.
The distinction between a king and one who perishes,
between controlling others and being controlled by them,
is vastly different indeed.
All things share the same universe but have different forms,
having no inherent suitability yet being useful to humans,
is a matter of natural order.
Humans live together,
share common desires but follow different paths,
have similar wants but different understandings,
which is inherent to life.
All have their approvals,
the wise and foolish alike;
but what they approve differs,
thus distinguishing the wise from the foolish.
When status is equal but understanding differs,
when acting selfishly brings no calamity,
when indulging desires meets no limit,
then people's minds become agitated and cannot be persuaded.
In such circumstances,
the wise cannot attain governance,
and if the wise cannot govern,
then achievements and fame cannot be established;
without achievements and fame,
then the masses remain undifferentiated,
with the masses undifferentiated,
then the relationship between ruler and minister cannot be established.
Without a ruler to control ministers,
without superiors to control inferiors,
the world suffers from harm born of indulgent desires.
Desiring and disliking the same things,
with many desires but scarce goods,
scarcity inevitably leads to contention.
Thus the products of various skills
serve to sustain a single person.
But ability cannot encompass all skills,
one person cannot hold all offices,
living apart without mutual support leads to poverty,
gathering without distinction leads to contention.
Poverty is a trouble,
contention is a calamity,
to rescue from trouble and eliminate calamity,
nothing is better than clarifying distinctions to organize society.
The strong coercing the weak,
the wise terrifying the foolish,
inferiors disobeying superiors,
the young bullying the old,
not governing with virtue;
in such cases, the old and weak face the worry of lacking support,
while the strong face the calamity of divisive contention.
Work is what people dislike,
profit and gain are what they prefer,
without distinction in occupations;
thus people face the trouble of establishing affairs,
and the calamity of contending for achievements.
The union of man and woman,
the distinction between husband and wife,
the marriage ceremonies and betrothal presents
without proper etiquette in sending and receiving;
thus people face the worry of failed unions,
and the calamity of contending for beauty.
Therefore the wise establish distinctions for them.
The way to enrich the state
is to economize expenditures and enrich the people,
while properly storing the surplus.
Economize expenditures according to ritual,
enrich the people through governance.
By enriching the people,
thus there is abundant surplus.
Enriching the people makes them wealthy,
wealthy people make fields fertile and well-tended,
fertile and well-tended fields yield a hundredfold produce.
The ruler collects according to law,
while the people economize expenditures according to ritual.
The surplus piles up like hills and mountains,
sometimes needing burning,
with nowhere to store it;
how could the gentleman worry about lacking surplus?
Thus knowing to economize expenditures and enrich the people,
one will certainly possess the reputation for benevolence, righteousness, sageliness, and goodness,
and moreover have accumulated wealth as abundant as hills and mountains.
This is for no other reason,
but arises from economizing expenditures and enriching the people.
Not knowing to economize expenditures and enrich the people makes the people poor,
poor people make fields barren and weed-filled,
barren and weed-filled fields yield less than half the produce;
even if the ruler likes to take and plunder,
he will still gain little,
and if some use without ritual restraint,
then there will certainly be the reputation for greed and extortion,
and moreover the reality of emptiness and poverty.
This is for no other reason,
but arises from not knowing to economize expenditures and enrich the people.
The "Kànggào" says:
"Vast like heaven's covering,
such virtue enriches your person
without neglect in the royal court." This expresses it.
Ritual
means the noble and humble have their ranks,
the elder and younger have their differences,
the poor and wealthy, light and heavy, all have their appropriate correspondence.
Thus the Son of Heaven wears the red dragon robe and crown,
feudal lords wear the black dragon robe and crown,
high officials wear the ceremonial robe and crown,
scholars wear leather caps and garments.
Virtue must correspond to position,
position must correspond to emolument,
emolument must correspond to use.
From scholars upward, they must be regulated by ritual and music,
while the common people must be controlled by laws and measures.
Measure the land to establish states,
calculate benefits to nurture the people,
assess human strength to assign tasks,
ensure the people can certainly accomplish their tasks,
tasks must produce benefits,
benefits must suffice to sustain the people,
all ensuring that clothing, food, and all expenses balance income and expenditure,
necessarily storing surplus in due season,
this is called appropriate measure.
Thus from the Son of Heaven down to commoners,
affairs whether great or small, many or few,
are deduced from this principle.
Hence it is said:
"In court, no undeserved positions;
among the people, no undeserved livelihoods."
This expresses it.
Lighten the taxes on fields,
equalize the levies at passes and markets,
reduce the number of merchants,
seldom raise labor conscriptions,
do not rob farmers of their seasons,
thus the state will be wealthy.
This is called enriching the people through governance.
Human life cannot exist without community,
but community without distinction leads to contention,
contention leads to disorder,
disorder leads to poverty.
Thus lack of distinction
is humanity's great harm;
having distinction
is the world's fundamental benefit;
and the ruler
is the pivotal mechanism for managing distinctions.
Therefore praising him
is praising the world's foundation;
securing him
is securing the world's foundation;
honoring him
is honoring the world's foundation.
In ancient times, the former kings divided and differentiated with hierarchy,
thus making some beautiful
and some ugly,
some generous
and some meager,
some leisurely and happy,
some toilsome and laborious,
not merely for extravagant, excessive, and boastful display,
but to illuminate the pattern of benevolence,
and penetrate the harmony of benevolence.
Therefore creating carved, engraved, embroidered, and patterned decorations,
suffices to distinguish noble from humble,
not seeking spectacular views;
creating bells, drums, pipes, chimes, lutes, zithers, reed organs, and panpipes,
suffices to distinguish auspicious from inauspicious, unite joy and stabilize harmony,
not seeking anything beyond;
creating palaces, halls, towers, and pavilions,
suffices to avoid dryness and dampness,
nurture virtue, and distinguish importance,
not seeking external display.
The "Shī" says:
"Carve and polish his pattern,
like gold and jade his substance.
Energetic is our king,
ordering all regions."
This expresses it.
As for wearing multiple colored robes,
eating varied flavors,
controlling abundant goods and materials,
uniting the world under his rule,
not merely for extravagant display,
but firmly to unify the world,
govern myriad changes,
utilize all things,
nurture all people,
comprehensively control the world,
none is better than the excellence of the benevolent person!
Thus his knowledge and planning suffice to govern it,
his benevolence and generosity suffice to secure it,
his virtuous reputation suffices to transform it,
Attain it and there is order,
lose it and there is chaos.
The common people truly rely on his wisdom,
thus they follow one another in laboring diligently to ensure his ease,
thereby nurturing his wisdom;
they truly admire his generosity,
thus they brave death and risk their lives to protect and rescue him,
thereby nurturing his generosity;
they truly praise his virtue,
thus they carve, engrave, and adorn with emblems and patterns to embellish him,
thereby nurturing his virtue.
Therefore, when a benevolent person is in authority,
the common people honor him as a sovereign,
cherish him as parents,
and do not hesitate to brave death and risk their lives for him;
there is no other reason—
what he affirms is truly admirable,
what he achieves is truly great,
and what benefits he brings is truly abundant.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"We bear our loads, we pull our carts,
our wagons and our oxen,
our journey now completed,
oh, let us return home!"
This expresses the idea.
Hence it is said:
"The nobleman relies on virtue,
the petty man relies on force."
Force
is subservient to virtue.
The strength of the common people
depends on it to achieve results;
the community of the common people
depends on it to achieve harmony;
the wealth of the common people
depends on it to be gathered;
the stability of the common people
depends on it to be secure;
the longevity of the common people
depends on it to be prolonged.
Father and son cannot but be affectionate,
brothers cannot but be harmonious,
men and women cannot but be joyful.
The young grow up,
the old are cared for.
Thus it is said:
"Heaven and Earth give them life,
the sages bring them to completion."
This expresses the idea.
In the present age, it is not so:
heavy levies on currency
rob them of their wealth,
burdensome taxes on fields
rob them of their food,
harsh duties at passes and markets
hinder their affairs.
Not only that,
there is also grasping, deceit, and spying,
scheming and subversion,
mutually overturning,
to exhaust and ruin them.
The common people clearly know
that such corruption, excess, violence, and disorder will lead to great peril and ruin.
Thus, ministers may assassinate their rulers,
subordinates may kill their superiors,
sell their cities,
betray their integrity,
and not die for their duties;
there is no other reason—
it is brought upon by the rulers themselves.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"No word goes unanswered,
no virtue goes unrewarded."
This expresses the idea.
The way to enrich all under heaven lies in clarifying distinctions.
Covering the land and marking the fields,
weeding and growing grain,
applying much manure to fertilize the soil—
these are the tasks of the farmers and common people.
Observing the seasons and motivating the people,
promoting work and increasing yields,
harmonizing and uniting the common people,
ensuring they are not negligent—
these are the tasks of the commanders and leaders.
The highlands not suffering drought,
the lowlands not flooding,
cold and heat in harmony,
and the five grains ripening in season—
these are the affairs of Heaven and Earth.
As for providing universal coverage,
universal love,
and universal regulation,
so that even in years of poor harvest or flood and drought,
the common people are free from the worries of cold and hunger—
these are the tasks of sage rulers and worthy ministers.
Mòzǐ's words anxiously worry about insufficiency for all under heaven.
But insufficiency is not a universal affliction of the world;
it is merely Mòzǐ's private anxiety and excessive concern.
Now, as for the land producing the five grains,
if people manage it well,
then each mu yields several *pen*,
and in one year, it can be harvested twice;
then melons, peaches, dates, and plums from one plant yield amounts measured in *pen* and *gu*;
then various vegetables grow in abundance, filling the marshes;
then the six domestic animals and beasts each fill a carriage;
turtles, alligators, fish, and eels breed in season,
each forming large groups;
then flying birds and wild geese are as numerous as a sea of smoke;
then insects and all creatures born among them,
which can be used for food and sustenance,
are too many to count.
Now, when Heaven and Earth produce the myriad things,
there is inherently a surplus
sufficient to feed people;
hemp, kudzu, silk, and the feathers, furs, teeth, and hides of birds and beasts
are inherently abundant
sufficient to clothe people.
Thus, surplus and insufficiency
are not universal afflictions of the world;
they are merely Mòzǐ's private anxiety and excessive concern.
The universal affliction of the world
is injury caused by disorder.
Why not try to seek out who brings about this disorder?
I say that Mòzǐ's
condemnation of music
leads to disorder in the world;
Mòzǐ's
advocacy of frugality
leads to poverty in the world.
It is not that I intend to slander him,
but his doctrines inevitably lead to this.
If Mòzǐ, on a large scale, ruled all under heaven,
or on a small scale, a single state,
he would anxiously wear coarse clothes and eat poor food,
grieving and condemning music.
If so, then there would be austerity;
austerity leads to lack of desires,
and lack of desires means rewards cannot be effective.
If Mòzǐ, on a large scale, ruled all under heaven,
or on a small scale, a single state,
he would reduce followers,
cut official positions,
emphasize toil and hardship,
share tasks equally with the common people,
and equalize achievements and labors.
If so, then there would be no authority;
without authority, rewards and punishments cannot be enforced.
If rewards are not effective,
then the worthy cannot be promoted;
if punishments are not enforced,
then the unworthy cannot be removed.
If the worthy cannot be promoted,
and the unworthy cannot be removed,
then the capable and incapable cannot be properly assigned to office.
If so,
then the myriad things lose their proper order,
events and changes lose their appropriate responses,
above, the timing of Heaven is lost,
below, the advantages of Earth are lost,
in the middle, human harmony is lost,
and all under heaven become agitated,
