as if scorched by fire.
Even if Mòzǐ himself wore coarse clothes and rope belts,
ate beans and drank water,
how could he ever suffice?
Having already undermined the root,
exhausted the source,
he would scorch the world.
Therefore, the former kings and sages did not act this way.
They knew that for those who rule over others,
without beauty and adornment, they cannot unify the people;
without wealth and abundance, they cannot govern the subordinates;
without authority and strength, they cannot prohibit violence and overcome brutality.
Thus, they must strike great bells,
beat resounding drums,
blow reed pipes and mouth organs,
and pluck zithers and lutes
to fill their ears;
they must carve, engrave,
and adorn with emblems and patterns
to fill their eyes;
they must provide livestock, rice, and millet,
with the five flavors and fragrant aromas
to fill their mouths;
then, with numerous followers,
complete official positions,
graduated rewards and honors,
and strict punishments
to warn their hearts.
So that all the living people under heaven
know that all their desires and wishes are fulfilled here,
thus rewards are effective;
and know that all their fears and dreads lie here,
thus punishments are authoritative.
When rewards are implemented and punishments carry authority,
then the worthy can be advanced,
and the incompetent can be removed,
enabling the capable and incapable to be properly assigned to office.
If so, then all things find their proper place,
and changing events receive appropriate responses,
above, the timeliness of heaven is obtained,
below, the advantages of earth are gained,
and in between, human harmony is achieved,
wealth and goods gush forth like a spring,
flow abundantly like rivers and seas,
pile up massively like hills and mountains,
and even if occasionally burned,
there is nowhere to store it all,
so how could the world worry about insufficiency?
Thus, if Confucian methods are genuinely practiced,
then the world becomes vast and rich,
efforts lead to achievement,
and the striking of bells and drums brings harmony.
The Book of Songs says:
"The bells and drums sound loud,
the pipes and stone chimes clear and harmonious,
bringing down abundant blessings.
Blessings descend in great measure,
dignified and solemn is the demeanor.
When full and drunk,
fortune and prosperity come in return."
This expresses it.
Hence, if Mohist methods are genuinely practiced,
then the world values frugality yet becomes poorer,
condemns strife yet daily contends,
toils bitterly and exhaustedly
with increasingly less achievement,
and is gloomily sorrowful, rejecting music
while daily losing harmony.
The Book of Songs says:
"Heaven repeatedly sends calamities,
death and disorder are widespread.
The people's words hold no praise,
yet none take warning and sigh."
This expresses it.
To attend to minor tasks in nurturing the people,
patting and comforting them,
cooing and babying them,
providing congee in winter,
and giving melons and gruel in summer,
to stealthily gain a moment's praise,
is the way of deceit;
it may briefly win the praise of the deceitful,
but it is not a lasting way.
Tasks will surely not be accomplished,
achievements will surely not be established,
this is governance by deceit.
Rashly seizing the moment to drive the people,
pushing tasks and seeking quick results,
disregarding praise or blame and being indifferent to losing the people,
may advance affairs,
but the common people resent it,
this is yet another partial and reckless approach.
It leads to collapse and decline,
and inevitably results in no achievement.
Thus, attending to minor tasks to cultivate reputation
is not acceptable,
and pursuing achievements while neglecting the people
is also not acceptable,
both are deceitful ways.
Therefore, the ancients did not do it this way;
they ensured the people did not suffer from heatstroke in summer,
nor freeze from cold in winter,
did not overstrain them in urgency,
nor lag behind the seasons in leisure,
thus tasks were accomplished and achievements established,
and both above and below prospered;
and the common people all loved their superiors,
flocking to them like flowing water,
feeling as joyful as with their parents,
willing to risk death and destruction for them without reluctance,
for no other reason
than that loyalty, trustworthiness, harmony, and fairness were at their utmost.
Hence, those who rule the state and lead the people,
wishing to seize the moment and achieve success,
find harmony and relaxation
quicker than haste;
loyalty and trustworthiness with fairness
are more pleasing than rewards and honors;
they must first correct what lies in themselves,
then gradually demand it of others,
making their authority
more formidable than punishments.
If these three virtues are sincerely upheld above,
then those below respond like shadow and echo,
and even if one wished not to be enlightened and penetrating,
how could it be possible!
The Book of Documents says:
"When greatly enlightened, you are obeyed,
the people will diligently harmonize their efforts.
But there are those who resent it."
This expresses it.
Thus, to punish without teaching
leads to numerous penalties yet evil remains unconquered;
to teach without punishing
leaves the deceitful unpunished;
to punish without rewarding
fails to encourage the diligent people;
to punish and reward without categorization
causes those below to doubt, customs to become stingy, and the people to lack unity.
Therefore, the ancient kings clarified rituals and righteousness to unify them,
promoted loyalty and trustworthiness to care for them,
honored the worthy and employed the capable to rank them,
used ranks, robes, honors, and rewards to emphasize and reinforce this,
timed their tasks
and lightened their burdens
to regulate and balance them,
broadly covering and protecting all,
nurturing and raising them,
as if safeguarding infants.
If so,
then deceit and evil do not arise,
thieves and bandits do not emerge,
and those transformed to goodness are encouraged.
Why is this?
Because the way is easy,
the barriers firm,
the governance and decrees unified,
and the guidelines clear.
Hence it is said:
If those above are unified, those below will be unified;
if those above are divided, those below will be divided;
like plants, the leaves must resemble the root.
This expresses it.
To benefit them without first being beneficial
is not as good as being beneficial first and then benefiting from it;
to use them without first showing love
is not as effective as loving first and then using them.
Benefiting first and then benefiting from it
is not as good as benefiting without seeking benefit;
loving first and then using them
is not as effective as loving without using them.
Benefiting without seeking benefit
and loving without using them
leads to winning the world. Benefiting
first and then benefiting from it
and loving first and then using them
leads to preserving the state. Not
benefiting them yet seeking benefit
and not loving them yet using them
endangers the state.
Observing a state's order or chaos, good or bad,
can be discerned right up to its borders.
If its patrols are intricate and overlapping,
and its border policies are excessively scrutinized, it is a chaotic state.
Entering its territory,
if its fields are weedy,
and its cities exposed, it is a state of a greedy ruler.
Observing its court,
if the esteemed are not worthy;
observing its offices,
if the administrators are incapable;
observing its close attendants,
if the trusted are not sincere; it is a state of a benighted ruler.
As for the rulers, ministers, and all officials,
in matters of wealth, taking and giving, and calculations,
they are meticulous and exhaustive;
but in rituals, righteousness, and decorum,
they are negligent and crude; it is a disgraced state.
If its farmers enjoy the fields,
its soldiers endure hardships,
its officials uphold the law,
its court honors rituals,
and its ministers deliberate harmoniously, it is a well-governed state.
Observing its court,
if the esteemed are worthy;
observing its offices,
if the administrators are capable;
observing its close attendants,
if the trusted are sincere; it is a state of an enlightened ruler.
As for the rulers, ministers, and all officials,
in matters of wealth, taking and giving, and calculations,
they are lenient and simple;
but in rituals, righteousness, and decorum,
they are rigorous and thorough; it is an honorable state.
When worthiness is equal, those who are close are honored first;
when capability is equal, those with old ties are appointed first;
and among its ministers and all officials,
the corrupt are transformed to become upright,
the fierce are transformed to become honest,
and the reckless are transformed to become sincere; this is the achievement of an enlightened ruler.
There are signs to observe a state's strength or weakness, wealth or poverty:
If the ruler does not exalt ritual, the military will be weak,
if the ruler does not love the people, the military will be weak,
if promises are not kept, the military will be weak,
if rewards and honors are not gradually bestowed, the military will be weak,
if generals are incompetent, the military will be weak.
If the ruler is fond of aggressive achievements, the state will be poor,
if the ruler is fond of profit, the state will be poor,
if there are too many officials and scholars, the state will be poor,
if there are too many artisans and merchants, the state will be poor,
if there are no regulations and measures, the state will be poor.
When the lower classes are poor, the ruler is poor;
when the lower classes are wealthy, the ruler is wealthy.
Thus, fields and rural areas
are the root of wealth;
walls, granaries, and storehouses
are the branches of wealth;
when the common people are timely harmonious
and their work is properly ordered,
that is the source of goods;
graded taxes and treasuries
are the flow of goods.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler must carefully nurture harmony,
regulate the flow,
open the source,
and constantly deliberate,
so abundantly that the world must have surplus,
and the ruler need not worry about insufficiency.
In this way,
both upper and lower are wealthy,
and there is nowhere to hide the surplus,
this is knowing the ultimate statecraft.
Thus, when Yǔ had ten years of floods
and Tāng seven years of drought,
the world had no starved faces,
and after ten years,
when the grains ripened again,
there were accumulated reserves in surplus.
This is for no other reason
than knowing what is called the root and branch, source and flow.
Thus, if fields are barren but granaries full,
if the people are empty but treasuries overflowing,
this is called the state's collapse.
To cut off its root,
drain its source,
and merge into its branches,
yet the ruler and ministers do not know to detest it,
then their overthrow and destruction can be awaited standing.
To rely on the state
and yet not suffice to shelter oneself,
this is called extreme poverty,
the ultimate folly of a ruler.
Seeking wealth, they lose their state;
seeking profit, they endanger themselves.
In ancient times there were ten thousand states,
now only a dozen or so remain.
This is for no other reason
than that they lost it in the same way.
The ruler of men should awaken to this.
A state of a hundred lǐ
is sufficient to stand independently.
Generally, those who attack others
do so either for fame,
or for profit,
or else out of anger.
When a benevolent person employs the state,
they will cultivate their will,
rectify their conduct,
elevate the lofty,
achieve loyalty and trustworthiness,
and aim for cultural order.
If a scholar in coarse clothes and hempen shoes is truly thus,
then even in poor alleys and leaky huts,
kings and dukes cannot contend with him for fame;
if entrusted with the state,
none in the world can conceal him.
If so, then those seeking fame will not attack.
They will open up fields and lands,
fill granaries,
prepare useful equipment,
unite upper and lower hearts,
combine the three armies' strength,
and if engaged in distant campaigns and extreme battles, it cannot be done.
The gatherings within the borders are securely fortified,
observing the opportune moment,
confronting their army,
capturing their general,
like brushing off chaff.
What they gain
is not enough to heal wounds or repair losses.
They cherish their claws and teeth,
fear their enemies,
if so, then those seeking profit will not attack.
They will cultivate the principles of great and small, strong and weak,
to handle them with caution,
their rituals will be very refined,
their jade tokens very ample,
their gifts and bribes very generous,
those sent to persuade them
will surely be gentlemen of elegant speech and discerning wisdom.
If they have any human sense,
who could be angered by them?
If so,
then those acting out of anger will not attack.
Those for fame refrain,
those for profit refrain,
those for anger refrain,
then the state is secure as a firm rock,
long-lived as the banner and wings.
When all others are in chaos,
I alone am ordered;
when all others are in peril,
I alone am safe;
when all others are losing and perishing,
I rise up and control them.
Thus, when a benevolent person employs the state,
it is not merely to maintain what they have,
but also to encompass others.
The Shī says:
"The good man, the noble man,
his demeanor is without fault.
His demeanor is without fault,
he rectifies the four states."
This refers to this.
On the difficulty and ease of maintaining a state:
Serving a strong and violent state is difficult,
making a strong and violent state serve me is easy.
If serving them with treasures and valuables,
then treasures are exhausted
and alliances not formed;
if swearing oaths and making covenants,
then agreements are fixed but betrayal is imminent;
if ceding slivers of the state to bribe them,
then after ceding, their desires are insatiable.
The more one serves them,
the more they invade,
inevitably leading to exhausted resources and the state's takeover before it ends.
Even with Yáo on the left and Shùn on the right,
none can avoid this fate by such means.
It is like a maiden adorned with precious pearls,
wearing precious jade,
carrying gold on her back
meeting bandits in the central mountains;
even if she looks askance like Péng Méng,
bends her waist and knees,
like a servant girl of a hut,
still it will not suffice to escape.
Thus, without the way of unifying people,
merely skillfully and busily bowing and pleading in fearful service,
is not enough to maintain the state and secure oneself,
so an enlightened ruler does not follow this path.
They must cultivate ritual to unify the court,
rectify laws to unify the officials,
equalize governance to unify the people,
then rhythms are unified in the court,
all affairs are unified among officials,
the masses are unified below.
In this way,
the near compete to be close,
the distant express willingness,
upper and lower are of one heart,
the three armies united in strength;
their reputation is enough to scorch them,
their mighty power enough to whip them,
with hands folded or pointing,
and no strong, violent state fails to hasten to serve,
like Wū Huó wrestling with Jiāo Yáo.
Therefore it is said:
"Serving a strong and violent state is difficult,
making a strong and violent state serve me is easy."
This refers to this.
The state
is the most useful instrument in the world,
the ruler
holds the most advantageous position in the world.
If one attains the Dào to maintain it,
then there is great security,
great glory,
the source of accumulated beauty.
If one does not attain the Dào to maintain it,
then there is great danger,
great burden,
having it is worse than not having it,
and at its extreme,
one cannot even become a commoner,
as with Qí Mǐn and Sòng Xiàn.
Thus, the ruler holds the most advantageous position in the world,
yet cannot secure it by himself;
to secure it, he must follow the Dào.
Therefore, those who employ the state:
if righteousness is established, they become kings,
if trustworthiness is established, they become hegemons,
if deceit and stratagem are established, they perish.
—These three are what the enlightened ruler carefully chooses,
and what the benevolent person strives to clarify.
To lead a state by advocating ritual and righteousness
without harming them,
to commit one unjust act
or kill one innocent person
and gain the world,
is what the benevolent would not do.
Firmly upholding mind and state,
they are as solid as this.
Those with whom one acts
are all righteous men;
the laws and punishments displayed throughout the state
are all righteous laws;
what the ruler earnestly leads his ministers toward
is all righteous intent.
Thus, the subordinates look up to the superior with righteousness,
and this foundation is secure.
When the foundation is secure, the state is stable;
when the state is stable, the world is at peace.
Though Confucius had not even a place to stick an awl,
he sincerely embodied righteousness in his will,
added righteousness to his conduct,
and expressed it in speech.
In his time,
he was not hidden from the world,
and his name endures to later ages.
Now if the illustrious lords of the world
sincerely embody righteousness in their will,
add righteousness to their laws, standards, and measures,
manifest it in governance,
and repeatedly apply it through distinctions of noble and base, life and death,
making it consistent from start to finish;
then,
the fame that bursts forth between heaven and earth
would it not be like the sun, moon, and thunder?
Hence it is said:
Unify the state with righteousness,
and in one day it will be renowned,
as with Tāng and Wǔ.
Tāng with Bó,
King Wǔ with Hào,
both had only a hundred lǐ of land,
yet united the world,
made the feudal lords their servants,
and all within reach
submitted without exception.
There was no other reason
but that they achieved righteousness.
—This is called establishing righteousness and becoming king.
Though virtue may not be perfect,
and righteousness not fully achieved,
yet the principles of the world are roughly assembled,
punishments, rewards, promises, and prohibitions are trusted by all,
and ministers clearly know what can be relied upon.
When decrees are set forth,
even seeing gains or losses,
they do not deceive their people;
when alliances are made,
even seeing gains or losses,
they do not deceive their partners.
Thus,
their troops are strong, their cities firm,
enemy states fear them,
the state's foundation is clear,
allied states trust them,
and though located in remote lands,
their might shakes the world,
as with the Five Hegemons.
They did not base themselves on governance and education,
did not reach the highest elevation,
did not perfect cultural order,
did not win others' hearts,
but focused on strategy,
carefully managed toil and rest,
prudently accumulated resources,
prepared for war,
and firmly maintained mutual trust between high and low,
so that none in the world dared oppose them.
Thus, Qí Huán, Jìn Wén, Chǔ Zhuāng, Wú Hélǘ, and Yuè Gōujiàn,
all from remote states,
shook the world with their might,
endangering the central states,
for no other reason
than their emphasis on trust.
—This is called establishing trust and becoming hegemon.
To lead a state by advocating profit and gain,
without promoting righteousness
or unifying trust,
seeking only profit,
internally not hesitating to cheat their people
for small gains,
externally not hesitating to cheat their allies
for great profits,
not rectifying what they possess internally,
but greedily always desiring what others have.
Thus,
ministers and commoners all treat their superiors with deceit.
Superiors deceive subordinates,
subordinates deceive superiors,
then high and low are divided.
Thus,
enemy states despise them,
allies distrust them,
scheming is daily practiced,
and the state cannot avoid danger and diminution,
ultimately perishing,
as with Qí Mǐn and Xuē Gōng.
Thus, wielding the strong state of Qí,
they did not cultivate ritual and righteousness,
did not base on governance and education,
did not aim to unify the world,
but constantly engaged in alliances and external ventures.
So strong, south足以 crush Chǔ,
west足以 humble Qín,
north足以 defeat Yān,
center足以 seize Sòng.
But when Yān and Zhào rose to attack them,
it was like shaking withered leaves,
and they died, their states perished,
greatly shamed by the world,
later generations speaking of evil,
must refer to them.
There is no other reason
but that they did not follow ritual and righteousness
but followed scheming.
These three are what enlightened rulers carefully choose,
and what benevolent men strive to clarify.
Those good at choosing control others,
those not good at choosing are controlled by others.
The state is the great vessel of the world,
a heavy responsibility,
and one must carefully choose where to place it,
for misplaced danger brings peril;
one must carefully choose the path to guide it,
for a foul road brings blockage,
and peril with blockage leads to ruin.
That state's placement
does not mean enfeoffment,
but which laws to follow,
and with whom to ally?
Thus, follow the laws of a true king,
and ally with true king's men,
then one becomes king;
follow the laws of a hegemon,
and ally with hegemon's men,
then one becomes hegemon;
follow the laws of a doomed state,
and ally with doomed state's men,
then one also perishes—.
These three are what enlightened rulers carefully choose,
and what benevolent men strive to clarify.
Thus, the state is a heavy responsibility,
and without accumulated principles, it cannot stand.
Hence the state
is renewed through generations,
this is renewal,
not change,
but changing jades and steps.
The days of a morning,
the people of a day,
yet how can there be the stability of a thousand years?
It is said:
By upholding the trusted laws of a thousand years,
and working with the trusted men of a thousand years.
No man lives a hundred years,
yet there are trusted men of a thousand years, how?
It is said:
Those who uphold the laws of a thousand years
are the trusted men of a thousand years.
Thus, with gentlemen accumulated in ritual and righteousness, one becomes king;
with upright, sincere, and complete men, one becomes hegemon;
with scheming, subversive men, one perishes.
—These three are what enlightened rulers carefully choose,
and what benevolent men strive to clarify.
Those good at choosing control others,
those not good at choosing are controlled by others.
Those who hold the state
cannot do it alone,
thus strength, stability, honor, and shame lie in choosing a minister.
If one is capable and the minister capable,
then one becomes king;
if one is incapable,
but knows fear and seeks the capable,
then one becomes strong;
if one is incapable,
does not know fear nor seek the capable,
but only uses flatterers, attendants, and close favorites,
then one faces danger and diminution,
ultimately perishing.
The state,
used greatly becomes great,
used small becomes small,
extremely great leads to kingship,
extremely small leads to ruin,
and those balancing small and great survive.
Those who employ it on a grand scale
prioritize righteousness over profit,
showing no concern for closeness or distance,
no regard for nobility or baseness,
but only seek those with genuine capability.
This is what is called employing it on a grand scale.
Those who employ it on a small scale
prioritize profit over righteousness,
showing no concern for right or wrong,
no attention to crookedness or straightness,
but only use those who are flattering, close, and aligned with themselves.
This is what is called employing it on a small scale.
Those who employ it on a grand scale are like that,
those who employ it on a small scale are like this;
those who diverge between small and grand
are partly like that,
partly like this.
Hence it is said:
"Pure, one becomes king;
mixed, one becomes hegemon;
with neither, one perishes."
This refers to this.
A state without ritual is not properly ordered.
Ritual is that by which the state is properly ordered,
comparable to
a balance for weighing lightness and heaviness,
to a marking line for determining crookedness and straightness,
to a compass and square for shaping square and round.
Once these are applied, no one can deceive about them.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Like the majesty of frost and snow,
like the brightness of the sun and moon,
practice it and it endures,
neglect it and it perishes."
This refers to this.
When the state is in peril, there is no joyful ruler;
when the state is secure, there are no anxious people.
Disorder leads the state to peril,
order leads the state to security.
Now, those who rule others
hastily pursue pleasure and neglect governing the state—
is this not exceedingly mistaken?
It is akin to loving sounds and sights
yet being content without ears and eyes—
is this not lamentable?
Now, human nature
desires the utmost in sights for the eyes,
the utmost in sounds for the ears,
the utmost in flavors for the mouth,
the utmost in scents for the nose,
the utmost in ease for the heart.
—These five utmost desires
are unavoidably part of human nature.
Nurturing the five utmost desires requires means;
without the means,
the five utmost desires cannot be attained.
A state of ten thousand chariots
can be said to be vast, rich, and thick,
and if it possesses the way of good governance and strength,
then it is joyful and free from hardship,
and only then are the means to nurture the five utmost desires in place.
Thus, all joys
arise from a well-governed state,
and worries and troubles
arise from a disordered state.
Those who hastily pursue pleasure and neglect governing the state
do not understand joy.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler
must first govern the state,
and only then can all joys be found within it;
a benighted ruler
will recklessly pursue pleasure and neglect governing the state,
so worries and troubles become innumerable,
inevitably leading to personal death and state destruction before ceasing—
is this not lamentable?
Intending to seek joy,
one instead gains worry;
intending to seek security,
one instead gains peril;
intending to seek blessing,
one instead gains death and destruction.
Is this not lamentable?
Alas!
Those who rule others
should also examine such words.
Thus, governing the state has its way,
and the ruler has his duties.
As for managing details over successive days,
and distinguishing matters in a single day,
these are tasks for the hundred officials and functionaries to perform,
and should not impair the joys of excursions and peaceful repose.
As for selecting one minister to lead them all,
ensuring that all officials and subordinates adhere to the way and direction in their duties,
this is the duty of the ruler.
If so, then achievements unite the world,
and fame matches that of Yáo and Yǔ.
Such a ruler
maintains the utmost simplicity yet with thoroughness,
handles affairs with the utmost ease yet achieves results,
draping his robes,
without leaving his mat,
yet all within the seas wish to have him as emperor or king.
This is called the utmost simplicity,
and there is no greater joy than this.
The ruler
is one who excels in appointing others;
the common man
is one who excels in doing things himself.
The ruler can have others do things for him,
the common man has no one to delegate to.
Managing one hundred acres of land alone,
with exhausting work,
leaves no one to delegate to.
Now, for one person to oversee the entire world,
with time to spare and governance not lacking,
it is because he has others do it for him.
Whether ruling the vast world
or a small state, if one must do everything oneself to manage, then no toil and exhaustion could be greater. In such a case, even a slave
would not exchange places with the Son of Heaven to take on such
tasks. To thus oversee the world,
unify the four seas,
why must one do it oneself?
Doing so oneself
is the way of a laborer,
the doctrine of Mòzǐ.
Evaluating virtue, employing ability, and officiating accordingly
is the way of the sage kings,
which the Rú carefully uphold.
The *Tradition* says:
"Farmers divide the fields to plow,
merchants divide goods to trade,
various artisans divide tasks to encourage,
scholars and officials divide duties to administer,
the lords of established states divide territories to guard,
the three dukes oversee regions and deliberate,
then the Son of Heaven merely rests on his own."
In this way, outward and inward,
all under heaven are equitable,
all are well-governed and distinguished,
this is what all kings have in common,
and the great basis of ritual and law.
With a territory of a hundred lǐ,
one can win the world—
this is not empty talk,
the difficulty lies in the ruler's understanding of it.
Winning the world
does not mean others bring their land to follow you,
but that your way is sufficient to unify people.
If those people are unified,
how could their land leave me and go to another?
Thus, with a territory of a hundred lǐ,
its ranks, titles, and robes
are sufficient to accommodate the worthy scholars of the world;
its offices and tasks
are sufficient to accommodate the capable men of the world;
following its old laws,
selecting the good among them and applying them clearly,
is sufficient to subdue those who love profit.
When worthy scholars are unified,
capable men are officiated,
and profit-lovers are subdued,
with these three in place, the world is fully encompassed,
with nothing beyond.
Hence, a territory of a hundred lǐ
is enough to exhaust its potential,
to extend loyalty and trustworthiness,
to manifest benevolence and righteousness,
is enough to win over people.
When these two are combined, the world is won,
and feudal lords who align later are the first to face peril.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"From the west, from the east,
from the south, from the north,
none think not to submit."
This refers to unifying the people.
Yì and Féngmén
were skilled at mastering archery;
Wáng Liáng and Zàofǔ
were skilled at mastering charioteering;
the intelligent noble
is skilled at mastering people.
When people are mastered, power follows;
when people are not mastered, power departs.
Thus, the king focuses on mastering people.
Therefore, if a ruler wants excellent archers who hit distant, tiny targets,
none are better than Yì and Féngmén;
if he wants excellent charioteers who speed to far places,
none are better than employing Wáng Liáng and Zàofǔ;
if he wants to harmonize and unify the world,
control Qín and Chǔ,
none are better than the intelligent noble.
Its application is very simple,
its tasks require no toil
yet achieve great merit and fame,
being extremely easy to manage and supremely delightful.
Thus, enlightened rulers regard it as a treasure,
while foolish ones consider it difficult.
To be honored as the Son of Heaven,
to possess the wealth of the entire world,
to be named a sage king,
to control others
without being controlled by anyone—
this is what all human desires share,
and the king possesses all of these.
He wears the most exquisite colors,
eats the richest flavors,
controls abundant goods and resources,
unites the world and rules over it;
his food and drink are lavish,
his music grand,
his terraces and pavilions lofty,
his parks and gardens vast,
he commands feudal lords as ministers,
unifies the world—
this too is what all human desires share,
and such are the rites and regulations of the Son of Heaven.
Institutions are established,
decrees are enforced;
officials who fail in their duties are executed,
nobles who violate rites are confined,
states in the four directions
that display extravagant or divisive conduct are inevitably destroyed,
his reputation shines like the sun and moon,
his achievements stand as firm as heaven and earth,
the people of the world respond to him like shadows and echoes—
this again is what all human desires share,
and the king possesses all of these.
Thus, in human nature,
the mouth craves flavors
and no tastes are finer than his,
the ear delights in sounds
and no music is grander than his,
the eye favors beauty
and no patterns are more intricate,
no women more numerous than his,
the body prefers ease
and no tranquility is more pleasurable than his,
the heart seeks profit
and no emoluments are richer than his;
he gathers and possesses all that the world collectively desires,
holding the world in his grasp and controlling it as he would his own descendants—
unless one is mad, deluded, or foolishly ignorant,
who could witness this and not rejoice!
Rulers who desire this
exist side by side,
men capable of achieving this
are never extinct through the ages,
yet for millennia they do not coincide—why?
The answer:
the ruler is not impartial,
the ministers are not loyal.
The ruler excludes the worthy and promotes partially,
the ministers contend for positions and envy the worthy—
this is the reason they do not coincide.
Why does the ruler not broaden his scope,
disregarding closeness or distance,
ignoring rank or humility,
seeking only true capability?
If so,
then ministers would lightly regard their posts, yield to the worthy,
and contentedly follow thereafter;
thus,
Shùn and Yǔ would promptly arrive,
royal enterprise would swiftly arise.
To unify the world in achievement,
to match Shùn and Yǔ in fame—
could anything in the world bring joy
as splendid as this?
Alas!
Those who rule others
should also examine such words.
Yáng Zhū wept at the crossroads,
saying:
"This is where a misstep of half a pace
leads to a stumble a thousand miles away!"
He mourned with tears.
This too is the crossroads of honor and disgrace, safety and danger, survival and ruin,
and here the cause for sorrow
is greater than at the crossroads.
Alas!
How lamentable!
Those who rule others
remain unawares for millennia.
There is no state without laws of order,
no state without laws of chaos;
no state without worthy scholars,
no state without unworthy ones;
no state without honest people,
no state without unruly people;
no state without fine customs,
no state without corrupt customs.
When both coexist, the state survives;
if the superior aspects prevail, the state is secure; (
if) the inferior aspects prevail, the state is endangered;
if entirely superior, it becomes kingly;
if entirely inferior, it perishes.
Thus, when its laws are orderly,
its ministers worthy,
its people honest,
its customs fine,
and all four are aligned,
this is called being entirely superior.
In such a case, victory is won without battle,
gains are made without attack,
arms are not wearied yet the world submits.
Thus, Tāng with Bó,
King Wǔ with Hào,
each had only a hundred lǐ of territory,
yet united the world,
made feudal lords their ministers,
and all within reach
submitted without exception—
for no other reason
than that all four were aligned.
Jié and Zhòu, despite possessing the full power of the world,
could not even attain the status of commoners in the end—
for no other reason
than that all four were lost.
Thus, the laws of a hundred kings differ
as described, yet what they converge upon is one.
The superior must extend love to those below
and govern them with ritual;
the superior's relation to the inferior
should be like protecting an infant.
Decrees and institutions
that connect with the common people below—
if there is the slightest unfairness,
even the orphaned, widowed, or solitary shall not be burdened.
Thus, the people's affection for their superiors
is joyous as for parents;
they can be killed but not made disobedient.
Ruler and minister, superior and inferior,
noble and humble, elder and younger,
down to the commoners,
all take this as the highest standard.
Then each reflects inwardly
to carefully observe their duties—
this is what the hundred kings shared,
and is the essence of ritual and law.
Then farmers divide fields to plow,
merchants divide goods to trade,
artisans divide tasks to encourage diligence,
officials divide offices to administer,
feudal lords divide lands to guard,
the three dukes coordinate regions and deliberate,
and the Son of Heaven need only compose himself.
In all actions,
the world knows no inequality,
no lack of orderly governance—
this is what the hundred kings shared,
and is the great foundation of ritual and law.
As for managing affairs day by day,
weighing things for appropriate use,
regulating clothing,
limiting palace sizes,
setting numbers of attendants,
grading funeral and sacrificial implements suitably—
thus encompassing all things,
from inches to yards,
ensuring all follow regulated measures before proceeding—
these are tasks for officials and clerks,
unworthy of mention before great gentlemen.
Therefore, those who rule others,
if they establish noble governance in their court appropriately,
and those appointed to key posts are truly benevolent,
then they themselves are at ease while the state is well-governed,
achieving great merit and fine reputation;
at best, they can become kings,
at least, hegemons;
if noble governance is established inappropriately,
and those in key posts are not benevolent,
then they toil while the state falls into chaos,
merit is ruined and reputation shamed,
the altars of state surely endangered—
this is the pivotal mechanism for rulers.
Thus, appointing one person rightly can win the world,
misappointing one person can endanger the state;
being unable to appoint one person rightly
yet able to appoint hundreds or thousands—
such a claim is baseless.
If one can appoint rightly,
then what toil remains for oneself?
Robes hang undisturbed, and the world is settled.
Thus, Tāng employed Yī Yǐn,
King Wén employed Lǚ Shàng,
King Wǔ employed Shào Gōng,
and King Chéng employed Zhōu Gōng Dàn.
Among the humbler examples are the Five Hegemons:
Duke Huán of Qí, within his women's quarters, indulged in music, extravagance, and leisurely pleasures,
yet in the eyes of the world, he was not considered cultivated.
Nevertheless, he assembled the feudal lords nine times,
unified and corrected the world,
becoming the foremost of the Five Hegemons.
This was for no other reason
than that he entrusted governance entirely to Guǎn Zhòng.
This is the essential principle for a ruler to uphold.
When the wise are employed, it is easy to generate strength,
and achievements and fame become exceedingly great.
If this is abandoned, what else is worth doing?
Therefore, the ancients
who achieved great merits and fame
invariably followed this path;
those who lost their states and endangered themselves
invariably acted contrary to it.
Hence, Confucius said:
"The wisdom of the wise
is inherently abundant;
if they have few things to guard,
how can they not be perceptive!
The wisdom of the foolish
is inherently scarce;
if they have many things to guard,
how can they not be reckless!"
This expresses the idea.
In a well-governed state, once roles are defined,
then the ruler, ministers, and officials
each carefully attend to what they hear,
not striving to hear what they should not;
each carefully attend to what they see,
not striving to see what they should not.
If what is heard and seen is truly unified,
then even in secluded and remote places,
the common people will not dare to neglect their duties or violate the system,
but will instead be transformed by their superiors through ritual,
which is the sign of a well-governed state.
The way of the ruler is to govern the near, not the distant;
to govern the manifest, not the obscure;
to focus on one, not on many.
If the ruler can govern the near, the distant will be orderly;
if the ruler can govern the manifest, the obscure will be transformed;
if the ruler can handle the one correctly, all affairs will be set right.
To oversee the entire world,
with time to spare and governance never lacking—
this is how it is achieved,
and it is the pinnacle of governance.
To be able to govern the near
and yet strive to govern the distant;
to be able to govern the manifest
and yet strive to perceive the obscure;
to be able to handle the one
and yet strive to correct the many—
this is excess.
Excess is as bad as deficiency,
akin to planting a straight tree and expecting its shadow to be crooked.
To be unable to govern the near
and yet strive to govern the distant;
to be unable to discern the manifest
and yet strive to perceive the obscure;
to be unable to handle the one
and yet strive to correct the many—
this is perversity,
akin to planting a crooked tree and expecting its shadow to be straight.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler prefers essentials,
while a benighted ruler prefers details.
If the ruler prefers essentials, all affairs will be detailed;
if the ruler prefers details, all affairs will be neglected.
The ruler's role is to select one prime minister,
establish one law,
clarify one directive,
to cover all comprehensively,
to illuminate all thoroughly,
and to observe the flourishing results.
The prime minister's role is
to evaluate the heads of various offices,
oversee the hearing of all affairs,
to regulate the duties of court ministers and officials,
assess their achievements,
deliberate on rewards,
and at year's end present their accomplishments to the ruler.
If suitable, they are retained;
if not, they are dismissed.
Thus, the ruler labors in seeking them out
but rests in employing them.
He who governs a state:
gains wealth by winning the people's labor,
gains strength by winning the people's willingness to die,
gains honor by winning the people's praise.
When these three virtues are present, the world submits to him;
when these three virtues are absent, the world abandons him.
The world's submission is called kingship;
the world's abandonment is called ruin.
Tāng and Wǔ
followed the Way,
practiced righteousness,
promoted benefits shared by all under heaven,
eliminated harms shared by all under heaven,
and thus the world submitted to them.
Therefore, they enhanced their virtuous reputation to lead the people,
clarified rituals and righteousness to guide them,
manifested loyalty and trust to care for them,
rewarded the worthy and employed the capable in proper order,
used ranks, robes, and rewards to emphasize importance,
timed their tasks appropriately,
managed their responsibilities systematically
to harmonize and balance them,
broadly covering all with generosity,
nurturing and fostering them,
as if protecting infants.
In nurturing the people, they were extremely lenient;
in employing the people, they were highly reasonable.
They formulated policies, orders, and institutions
to connect with the common people below;
if there was the slightest unreasonableness,
even towards the orphaned, widowed, or solitary,
it would never be imposed.
Therefore, the people esteemed them as gods,
loved them as parents,
and were willing to risk death for them without hesitation—
for no other reason than that their virtue was truly illustrious,
and their benefits and kindness truly profound.
In chaotic times, it is not so:
filth, excess, and plunder come first,
schemes and subversion are displayed,
the requests of actors, dwarfs, and women cause confusion,
the foolish instruct the wise,
the unworthy oversee the worthy,
the people are made extremely poor and constrained,
and employing them is excessively toilsome.
Hence,
the people despise them as if they were cripples,
hate them as if they were ghosts,
daily seeking opportunities to conspire and overthrow them,
to drive them away.
If suddenly there is an invasion or calamity,
and they hope the people will die for them,
it is impossible to obtain,
and there is no way to persuade them otherwise.
Confucius said:
"Examine how I treat others,
and how others will treat me in return."
This expresses the idea.
What harms a state?
It is said:
Elevating petty men to dominate the people and wield authority,
and skillfully taking from the people what is not rightfully theirs—these are great calamities that harm the state.
The ruler of a great state
who delights in petty gains
harms the state;
who, regarding music, women, towers, pavilions, gardens, and parks,
grows weary and constantly seeks novelty,
harms the state;
who does not properly manage what he possesses,
but greedily always desires what others have,
harms the state.
With these three evils in his heart,
and furthermore favoring those who use schemes and subversion
to decide affairs externally,
then his authority will be light and his reputation stained,
the altars of land and grain will surely be endangered—
this is what harms the state.
The ruler of a great state
who does not honor fundamental conduct,
does not respect ancient laws,
but delights in deceit and cunning—
then the court ministers
will also follow suit, forming a custom of not honoring ritual and righteousness but favoring subversion.
If the customs of the court ministers are such,
then the common people will also follow, forming a custom of not honoring ritual and righteousness but favoring greed for profit.
If the customs of ruler and ministers, high and low, are all like this,
then even if the territory is vast,
authority will surely be light;
even if the population is large,
the military will surely be weak;
even if punishments are numerous,
orders will not reach below.
This is called an endangered state,
and it is what harms the state.
The Confucian approach is not so;
they must rectify distinctions:
the court must honor ritual and righteousness and clarify honors and ranks,
and if so, then the scholars and officials will all be diligent in upholding their duties and dying for the system.
The various officials will then align with the regulations,
value their official ranks,
and if so, then all officials will fear the law and follow the rules.
Checkpoints and markets will inspect but not levy taxes,
standards and prohibitions will be impartial, and if so, then merchants will all be honest and without deceit.
When the various artisans are to fell trees in due season,
and are lenient with their deadlines
yet value skillful workmanship,
then,
all artisans will be loyal and trustworthy without shoddy work.
If outlying districts lighten taxes on fields and lands,
reduce levies in coinage,
seldom impose labor services,
and do not disrupt farming seasons,
then, all farmers will devote their strength and have few other pursuits.
When scholar-officials are committed to integrity and dying for regulations,
then the military will be strong.
When all officials fear the law and follow rules,
then the state's order will not be disrupted.
When merchants are honest without deceit,
then commerce will be secure,
goods and wealth will circulate,
and the state's needs will be supplied.
If artisans are loyal and trustworthy without shoddiness,
then tools will be skillful and convenient, and resources will not be lacking.
If farmers devote their strength with few other pursuits,
then above, they will not miss celestial timing,
below, they will not lose terrestrial advantages,
and in between, they will achieve human harmony,
so all affairs will not be neglected.
This is called the enforcement of governance and orders,
and the beauty of customs.
In defense, it will be firm;
in campaigns, it will be strong;
at rest, it will have reputation;
in action, it will achieve merit.
This is what the Rú call comprehensive discernment.
There are rulers who bring chaos,
but no states that are inherently chaotic;
there are people who bring order,
but no laws that inherently create order.
Yì's archery method is not lost,
yet Yì is not born in every generation;
Yǔ's laws still exist,
yet the Xià dynasty did not produce kings in every generation.
Thus, laws cannot stand alone,
and categories cannot act by themselves.
With the right person, they survive;
without the right person, they perish.
Laws are the beginning of order,
but the noble person is the source of laws.
Hence, with a noble person,
even if laws are sparse,
they suffice to be comprehensive;
without a noble person,
even if laws are complete,
they lose the sequence of application,
cannot adapt to changing events,
and are enough to cause chaos.
Those who do not understand the meaning of laws
but only correct the details of laws,
though broadly learned, will inevitably be confused when facing affairs.
Thus, an enlightened ruler urgently seeks the right person,
while a benighted ruler urgently seeks power.
Urgently seeking the right person,
the ruler's person is at ease and the state is well-governed,
achieving great merit and fine reputation,
enabling him to become a king above,
or a hegemon below;
not urgently seeking the right person
but urgently seeking power,
the ruler's person is toiled and the state is chaotic,
merit is ruined and reputation disgraced,
and the state will surely be endangered.
Therefore, the ruler of people
labors in searching for them,
but rests in employing them.
The Shū says:
"Only King Wén was reverent and cautious,
choosing for the one."
This refers to this.
Matching tallies and tokens,
distinguishing contracts and deeds,
are means to create trust;
but if the superior favors power and schemes,
then ministers and officials, being deceitful, will seize this to deceive.
Drawing lots and casting hooks,
are means to create fairness;
but if the superior favors crooked selfishness,
then ministers and officials will seize this to be partial.
Weights, measures, and balances,
are means to create equity;
but if the superior favors overturning,
then ministers and officials will seize this to be treacherous.
Bushels, pecks, and levelers,
are means to create exactness;
but if the superior favors greed for profit,
then ministers and officials will seize this to take abundantly and give stingily,
extracting from the people without measure.
Thus, tools and methods
are the streams of governance,
not the source of governance;
the noble person
is the source of governance.
Officials guard the methods,
the noble person nurtures the source.
If the source is clear, the streams are clear;
if the source is turbid, the streams are turbid.
Hence, if the superior values ritual and righteousness,
honors the worthy and employs the capable,
and has no greedy heart for profit,
then subordinates will also highly practice deference,
offer loyalty and trustworthiness,
and be diligent in their roles as ministers and sons.
Thus, even among common people,
without waiting to match tallies and tokens,
or distinguish contracts and deeds, there is trust;
without waiting to draw lots or cast hooks, there is fairness;
without waiting for weights and balances, there is equity;
without waiting for bushels and levelers, there is exactness.
Hence, without using rewards, the people are encouraged;
without using punishments, the people are submissive;
officials are not toiled, yet affairs are well-managed;
governance and orders are not burdensome, yet customs are beautiful.
The common people dare not disobey the ruler's laws,
emulate the ruler's will,
and are encouraged in the ruler's tasks,
finding peace and joy in them.
Thus, in taxation, they forget the cost;
in public works, they forget the toil;
in facing invaders and difficulties, they forget death.
City walls need no decoration to be firm;
weapons need no tempering to be strong;
enemy states need no subjugation to yield;
the people within the four seas need no orders to be unified.
This is called the utmost peace.
The Shī says:
"The king's plans were truly sincere,
and the Xú region came."
This refers to this.
May I ask about being a ruler?
The answer:
Distribute with ritual,
equally and universally without bias.
May I ask about being a minister?
The answer:
Serve the ruler with ritual,
loyal and obedient without negligence.
May I ask about being a father?
The answer:
Kind, generous, and with ritual.
May I ask about being a son?
The answer:
Reverent, loving, and exceedingly refined.
May I ask about being an elder brother?
The answer:
Compassionate, loving, and manifesting friendship.
May I ask about being a younger brother?
The answer:
Reverent, yielding, and not careless.
May I ask about being a husband?
The answer:
Achieving merit without dissipation,
and exceedingly close yet with distinction.
May I ask about being a wife?
The answer:
If the husband has ritual, be gentle, obedient, and attentive;
if the husband lacks ritual, be fearful and alert on one's own.
This is the Dào.
If partially established, there is chaos;
if fully established, there is order.
This is sufficiently verifiable.
May I ask how to comprehensively achieve this?
The answer:
Be meticulous in ritual.
In ancient times, the former kings were meticulous in ritual, extending it pervasively throughout the world,
so that no action was inappropriate.
Thus, the noble person is respectful without distress,
reverent without stiffness,
in poverty not constrained,
in wealth not arrogant,
encountering changes and responding without exhaustion—
all due to being meticulous in ritual.
Hence, the noble person towards ritual,
is reverent and at ease with it;
towards affairs,
is direct yet without error;
towards people,
has few resentments, is generous, and without flattery;
in self-conduct,
is cautious in cultivation and without danger;
in responding to changes and events,
is quick and adept without confusion;
towards heaven, earth, and all things,
does not strive to explain their reasons,
but excels in utilizing their materials.
Regarding the affairs of the hundred officials and the skilled artisans,
he does not contend with them in abilities
but ensures the excellent use of their efforts;
in serving his superiors,
he is loyal and diligent without laxity;
in employing his subordinates,
he is equitable and impartial;
in his social interactions,
he adheres to righteousness and associates with the appropriate class;
in his residence among the village community,
he is tolerant and does not cause disorder.
Therefore, in obscurity, he is sure to have a reputation,
and in prominence, he is sure to have achievements;
his benevolence and magnanimity cover all under heaven without exhaustion,
his wisdom penetrates heaven and earth, and he manages myriad changes without doubt;
his vital energy is harmonious and balanced,
his will and aspirations are broad and great,
his righteous conduct fills the space between heaven and earth—
this is the ultimate in benevolence and wisdom.
Such a one is called a sage,
who thoroughly understands ritual.
May I ask about governing the state?
The reply: I have heard of cultivating one's person,
but never of governing the state.
The ruler is like the sundial's gnomon,
the people are like the shadow;
if the gnomon is straight, the shadow is straight.
The ruler is like the basin,
the people are like the water;
if the basin is round, the water is round;
the ruler is like the vessel—if the vessel is square, the water is square. When the ruler shoots, his ministers draw the bowstring.
King Zhuāng of Chǔ favored slender waists,
so there were starving people at his court.
Hence it is said:
I have heard of cultivating one's person,
but never of governing the state.
The ruler is
the source of the people;
if the source is clear, the stream is clear;
if the source is turbid, the stream is turbid.
Therefore, if one who possesses the altars of soil and grain cannot love the people,
cannot benefit the people,
yet seeks the people's affection and love for himself,
it cannot be obtained.
If the people do not feel affection or love,
yet seeks their service for himself,
their death for himself,
it cannot be obtained.
If the people do not serve him,
do not die for him,
yet seeks strong soldiers,
fortified walls,
it cannot be obtained.
If the soldiers are not strong,
the walls not fortified,
yet seeks that enemies do not come,
it cannot be obtained.
When enemies come and one seeks to avoid danger, reduction,
and destruction,
it cannot be obtained.
The circumstances of danger, reduction, and destruction
all accumulate from this;
yet to seek peace and joy
in such a situation,
is it not difficult?
Such a one is a reckless man.
Reckless men
do not wait for their time to perish.
Therefore, if the ruler desires strength, stability, peace, and joy,
then nothing is better than turning to the people;
if he desires to unite and harmonize the people,
then nothing is better than turning to governance;
if he desires to cultivate governance and beautify customs,
then nothing is better than seeking the right person.
Those who accumulate and obtain such men are not cut off from generation to generation.
Such a person
lives in the present age
but aspires to the Way of antiquity.
Though the kings and dukes of the world do not favor it,
yet this man alone favors it;
though the people of the world do not practice it,
yet this man alone practices it;
those who favor it become poor,
those who practice it become destitute,
yet this man alone still practices it,
not ceasing for a moment.
He alone clearly understands how the former kings succeeded,
how they failed,
knowing the safety, danger, good, and bad of the state
as if distinguishing white from black.
Such a person,
if greatly employed,
will unify the world,
and the feudal lords will become his ministers;
if employed in a lesser capacity,
his authority will extend to neighboring enemies;
even if he cannot be employed,
if he is kept from leaving the borders,
the state will remain without calamity for a lifetime.
Therefore, the ruler of men
loves the people and achieves peace,
esteems scholars and achieves glory;
lacking both, he perishes.
The Odes say:
"The good men are the hedge,
the Grand Master is the wall."
This expresses it.
What is the Way?
The reply:
It is what the ruler follows.
What is the ruler?
The reply:
He who can form a community.
What is meant by 'can form a community'?
The reply:
He who is good at nurturing and supporting people,
good at governing and ordering people,
good at appointing and establishing people,
good at adorning and decorating people.
He who is good at nurturing and supporting people is cherished by them;
he who is good at governing and ordering people brings them peace;
he who is good at appointing and establishing people brings them joy;
he who is good at adorning and decorating people brings them honor.
When these four essentials are all present,
the world turns to him;
this is called 'able to form a community.'
He who cannot nurture and support people
is not cherished by them;
he who cannot govern and order people
does not bring them peace;
he who cannot appoint and establish people
does not bring them joy;
he who cannot adorn and decorate people
does not bring them honor.
When these four essentials are lost,
the world abandons him;
this is called a common man.
Hence it is said:
If the Way is preserved, the state is preserved;
if the Way is lost, the state is lost.
Reduce the artisans and merchants,
increase the farmers,
prohibit theft and robbery,
eliminate the treacherous and evil—
these are the means to nurture and support them.
The Son of Heaven has three ducal ministers,
the feudal lords have one prime minister,
the great officers hold specific offices,
the scholars preserve their duties—
all act according to law and with impartiality;
these are the means to govern and order them.
Determine rank by assessing virtue,
confer office by measuring ability,
ensuring that each person carries out their duties
and each finds their appropriate place.
Employ the most worthy as the three ducal ministers,
the next worthy as feudal lords,
the lesser worthy as scholars and great officers;
these are the means to appoint and establish them.
Adorn caps, robes,
embroidered patterns, colors and designs,
carvings, engravings,
all with distinctions of rank;
these are the means to adorn and decorate them.
Thus, from the Son of Heaven to the common people,
all give full play to their abilities,
attain their aspirations,
find joy in their tasks—
this is what they share.
Being clothed warmly and fed fully,
living securely and enjoying leisure,
handling affairs timely, with clear regulations and sufficient resources—
this is also what they share.
As for multiplying colors to complete patterns,
multiplying flavors to prepare
rare delicacies, this is abundance.
The sage king uses abundance
to clarify distinctions:
above, to adorn the worthy and good, making noble and base clear;
below, to adorn the old and young, making closeness and distance clear.
Above, in the court of kings and dukes,
below, in the homes of the common people,
all under heaven clearly know that these are not for creating disparity,
but to clarify social roles, achieve good governance, and preserve the state for ten thousand generations.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven and feudal lords have no wasteful expenditures,
scholars and great officers have no dissolute conduct,
the hundred officials have no negligent affairs,
the masses and common people have no treacherous or strange customs,
no crimes of theft or robbery—
they are able to be called righteous throughout.
Hence it is said:
"In order, abundance reaches the common people;
in disorder, even the kings and dukes lack enough."
This expresses it.
The ultimate Way manifests its grand form,
when exalted rituals and perfected laws prevail, the state maintains constancy;
when the virtuous are esteemed and the capable employed, the people know direction;
when collective deliberation and public scrutiny are practiced, the people harbor no doubts;
when the diligent are rewarded and the indolent punished, the people do not slacken;
when broad listening and comprehensive understanding are embraced, all under heaven submit to it.
Thereafter, duties are clarified,
enterprises are ordered,
talents and skills are officially recognized,
all without exception are well governed,
then public justice prevails and private favoritism is blocked,
public righteousness is illuminated and private affairs cease.
Thus,
the deeply virtuous advance while flatterers are halted,
the greedy retreat while the incorruptible rise.
The *Book of Documents* says:
"Those who act prematurely shall be executed without pardon,
those who fail to meet the timing shall be executed without pardon."
When people are accustomed to their tasks, they become steadfast;
the hundred affairs of people
are like the eyes, ears, nose, and mouth, which cannot substitute for one another;
thus, with divided responsibilities, the people do not neglect their duties;
with hierarchy established, order is not disrupted;
with broad listening and comprehensive understanding, all affairs proceed without delay.
Thus,
from ministers and officials down to the common people,
none dare not cultivate themselves before presuming to be secure in correctness,
nor dare accept office without genuine capability;
the common people change their customs,
petty men transform their hearts,
and all deceitful and aberrant types revert to sincerity.
This is called the pinnacle of governance and education.
Hence, the Son of Heaven sees without looking,
hears without listening,
knows without pondering,
achieves without acting,
sitting solidly alone while all under heaven follow him as one body,
like the limbs obeying the heart.
This is called the grand manifestation.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Gentle and reverent people,
are the foundation of virtue."
This expresses it.
As for the ruler,
none do not desire strength and detest weakness,
desire safety and detest danger,
desire honor and detest disgrace,
this is common to both Yǔ and Jié.
To attain these three desires,
and avoid these three aversions,
what path indeed is most expedient?
The answer:
lies in carefully selecting the chancellor,
no path is more direct than this.
Thus, having knowledge but lacking benevolence
is unacceptable;
having benevolence but lacking knowledge,
is unacceptable.
One who possesses both knowledge and benevolence
is the treasure of the ruler,
and the support of kings and hegemons.
Not urgently seeking such a person
is unwise;
finding but not employing them
is unbenevolent.
Without the right person yet hoping for their achievements,
no folly is greater.
Now rulers suffer from six afflictions:
having the worthy perform tasks,
yet allowing the unworthy to direct them;
having the wise deliberate,
yet allowing the foolish to discuss them;
having the cultivated execute affairs,
yet allowing the corrupt and wicked to doubt them.
Even if they wish to succeed,
how could they?
It is like
erecting a straight pole yet fearing its shadow will be crooked,
no delusion is greater.
As the saying goes:
"The beauty of a lovely woman
is a calamity to the ugly.
The man of public integrity
is a sore to the multitude.
One who follows the Way
is a scourge to the corrupt and wicked."
Now having the corrupt and wicked
judge those they resent and harm
while expecting impartiality,
how could it be?
It is like
erecting a crooked pole yet seeking a straight shadow,
no disorder is greater.
Thus, the ancients did not act this way.
They had principles for selecting people,
and methods for employing them.
The principle for selecting people
is to assess them with ritual;
the method for employing them
is to restrain them with hierarchy.
Their actions and conduct,
are measured by ritual;
their judgments and choices,
are verified by outcomes;
over time and accumulation,
they are evaluated by merit.
Thus, the lowly cannot oversee the noble,
the light cannot outweigh the heavy,
the foolish cannot counsel the wise,
thereby all endeavors avoid error.
Hence, evaluate them with ritual,
and observe their ability to remain reverent;
place them in changing situations,
and observe their adaptability;
give them comfort and leisure,
and observe their resistance to dissipation;
expose them to sounds and sights, power and profit, anger and hatred, peril and hardship,
and observe their ability to not abandon their duties.
Whether they truly possess these qualities
or truly lack them
becomes as clear as black and white,
how could they be distorted?
Thus, as Bólè cannot be deceived about horses,
the gentleman cannot be deceived about people,
this is the way of the enlightened king.
If a ruler desires skilled archers who hit distant, minute targets,
he hangs noble titles and heavy rewards to attract them.
Internally, he must not favor his sons and brothers,
externally, he must not neglect those from afar,
those who can hit the target are selected,
is this not the way to surely obtain them?
Even a sage could not improve it.
If he desires skilled drivers who cover great distances swiftly, a thousand lǐ in a day,
he hangs noble titles and heavy rewards to attract them,
internally, he must not favor his sons and brothers,
externally, he must not neglect those from afar,
those who can achieve this are selected,
is this not the way to surely obtain them?
Even a sage could not improve it.
But when it comes to governing the state and guiding the people,
harmonizing superiors and subordinates,
securing the interior to fortify the city,
defending the exterior against calamities,
so that in order, they control others,
and are not controlled by others,
while in disorder, danger, disgrace, and ruin
stand imminent,
yet in seeking ministers and chancellors for assistance,
he alone does not act with such impartiality,
instead employing only flatterers and those close to him,
is this not exceedingly mistaken?
Hence, those who possess the altars of soil and grain
all desire strength,
yet soon become weak;
all desire safety,
yet soon face danger;
all desire preservation,
yet soon meet ruin.
In antiquity, there were ten thousand states,
now only several tens remain,
this is for no other reason
than that all erred in this matter.
Thus, an enlightened ruler may privately gift gold, stone, pearls, and jade,
but never privately bestow offices and responsibilities,
why is that?
The answer:
it fundamentally does not benefit those favored.
If they lack ability yet the ruler employs them,
then the ruler is benighted;
if ministers lack ability yet pretend to have it,
then the ministers are deceitful.
With a benighted ruler above
and deceitful ministers below,
ruin is not far off,
a path harmful to all.
Thus, only the enlightened ruler can truly cherish those he loves,
while the benighted ruler inevitably endangers those he loves.
Now, King Wén was not without noble relatives,
not without sons and brothers,
not without favorites,
yet impartially he elevated Tàigōng from among the common people and employed him,
was it out of personal favor?
Did he consider him kin?
But Zhōu was of the Jī lineage,
while he was of the Jiāng lineage.
Did he consider him an old acquaintance?
They had never met before.
Did he consider him handsome?
That man was seventy-two years old,
with teeth gaping and fallen.
However, when employing them,
King Wén, wishing to establish noble principles,
desiring to make his illustrious name known,
and to benefit all under heaven,
could not do it alone.
Without this man, none was sufficient to assist him,
so he raised this man and employed him.
Thereupon, the noble principles were indeed established,
his illustrious name indeed became renowned,
he universally governed all under heaven,
established seventy-one states, with fifty-three occupied solely by those of the Jī surname,
and the descendants of Zhōu,
unless they were mad or deluded,
all became prominent feudal lords under heaven.
In this way, he was able to love others.
Therefore, by promoting the great Way of all under heaven,
and establishing the great achievements for all under heaven,
then concealing those he pitied and loved,
their descendants were still sufficient to become prominent feudal lords under heaven.
Hence it is said:
"Only an enlightened ruler is capable of loving those he loves,
while a benighted ruler will inevitably endanger those he loves."
This expresses that idea.
Beyond the wall,
the eye does not see;
before the village,
the ear does not hear;
yet the responsibilities of the ruler
extend to the far reaches of all under heaven,
and the near confines within the borders;
he cannot but have a general knowledge of them.
Changes throughout the realm,
and affairs within the borders,
may have relaxations, alterations, discrepancies, and errors,
yet if the ruler has no means to know of them,
then this is the beginning of constraint, coercion, and obstruction.
The clarity of eyes and ears
is so limited;
the responsibilities of the ruler
are so vast;
that what lies within them cannot be unknown,
making the situation so perilous.
Then how shall the ruler come to know?
It is said:
Trusted attendants and close aides
are the windows and openings through which the ruler peers afar and gathers the multitude;
they cannot but be prepared early.
Thus, the ruler must have trusted attendants and close aides who are sufficiently reliable
before he can act;
their wisdom must be adequate to assess things,
their integrity sufficient to settle matters
before they can serve.
These are called the instruments of the state.
The ruler cannot avoid times of leisure, excursions, and repose,
nor can he escape the changes of illness and death.
In such a state,
affairs and tasks arrive like a spring's source,
and if one matter is not addressed,
it becomes the beginning of disorder.
Hence it is said:
The ruler cannot act alone.
Ministers and chancellors who assist
are the foundation and staff of the ruler;
they cannot but be prepared early.
The ruler must have ministers and chancellors who are sufficiently competent to assist
before he can act;
their virtuous reputation must be adequate to pacify the common people,
their wisdom and foresight sufficient to respond to myriad changes
before they can serve.
These are called the instruments of the state.
Relations with the feudal lords of the four neighboring states
cannot be without interaction,
yet they need not be intimate.
Therefore, the ruler must have those who can adequately convey his will and resolve doubts in distant lands
before he can act.
Their persuasive speech must suffice to resolve complexities,
their wisdom and foresight to decide uncertainties,
their decisive judgment to ward off difficulties,
without deferring to private interests,
without opposing the ruler,
and thus able to meet pressing needs and defend against perils
to maintain the altars of soil and grain
before they can serve.
These are called the instruments of the state.
Thus, if the ruler lacks trusted attendants and close aides who are sufficiently reliable,
it is called benighted;
if he lacks ministers and chancellors who are sufficiently competent to assist,
it is called isolated;
if those sent to the feudal lords of the four neighboring states are not the right persons,
it is called solitary.
Being solitary, isolated, and obscure
is termed perilous.
Though the state may seem to exist,
the ancients would say it is lost.
The Book of Songs says:
"With many scholars, grand and dignified,
King Wén found tranquility."
This expresses that idea.
On types of talent:
Those who are earnest, cautious, diligent,
meticulous in calculation and frugal,
daring not to omit or lose anything,
are the talent of officials and clerks.
Those who cultivate themselves, are upright and correct,
revere laws and respect duties,
without inclining to partiality,
maintain their posts and follow their tasks,
daring not to reduce or increase,
can transmit through generations,
but should not be allowed to encroach or usurp,
are the talent of scholar-officials and master officials.
Those who understand that exalting ritual and righteousness honors the ruler,
that cherishing scholars enhances reputation,
that loving the people stabilizes the state,
that having constant laws unifies customs,
that honoring the worthy and employing the capable prolong achievements,
that focusing on fundamentals and restricting non-essentials multiplies resources,
that not contending with inferiors over petty benefits facilitates affairs,
that clarifying institutions,
weighing things, and adapting their use prevents obstinacy,
are the talent of ministers and chancellors who assist,
but they have not yet reached the way of the ruler.
Being able to evaluate and appoint these three types of talent without misordering their sequence
is called the way of the ruler.
If so, then the ruler's person is at ease while the state is well-governed,
his achievements great and his name glorious,
at best he can become a true king,
at least a hegemon;
this is the essential maintenance of the ruler.
If the ruler cannot evaluate these three types of talent,
does not know this way,
then how can he, demeaning his position and toiling personally,
abandoning the pleasures of eyes and ears,
personally manage details throughout the day,
and try to settle everything in a single day,
contend with subordinates in minor scrutinies and extreme partial abilities?
From ancient times to the present,
there has never been such a case that did not lead to disorder.
This is what is called "looking at what cannot be seen,
listening to what cannot be heard,
doing what cannot be accomplished."
This expresses that idea.
On the classification of ministers:
There are posturing ministers,
usurping ministers,
meritorious ministers,
and sage ministers.
—Those who inwardly are inadequate to unify the people,
outwardly inadequate to ward off difficulties;
whom the people do not cherish,
and feudal lords do not trust;
yet who are clever, agile, flattering, and persuasive,
skilled at gaining favor from the superior,
are posturing ministers.
Those who are not loyal to the ruler above,
but skilled at gaining praise from the people below,
disregarding just principles and universal righteousness,
forming cliques and conspiring together,
devoted to misleading the ruler and scheming for private gain,
are usurping ministers.
Those who inwardly are adequate to unify the people,
outwardly adequate to ward off difficulties,
whom the people cherish,
and scholars trust,
who are loyal to the ruler above,
and love the common people tirelessly below,
are meritorious ministers.
Those who above can honor the ruler,
below can love the people,
in governance, orders, education, and transformation,
influence the lower like a shadow,
respond to emergencies and encounters with change,
swiftly as an echo,
extend categories and connect praises,
to deal with the unforeseeable,
adaptively complete and establish models,
are sage ministers.
Thus, employing sage ministers leads to true kingship,
employing meritorious ministers leads to strength,
employing usurping ministers leads to peril,
employing posturing ministers leads to ruin.
If posturing ministers are employed, the state will surely perish;
if usurping ministers are employed, the state will surely be endangered;
if meritorious ministers are employed, the state will surely flourish;
if sage ministers are employed, the state will surely be honored.
Thus, Sū Qín of Qí,
Zhōu Hóu of Chǔ,
Zhāng Yí of Qín,
may be called posturing ministers.
Zhāng Qùjí of Hán,
Fèng Yáng of Zhào,
Mèng Cháng of Qí,
may be called usurping ministers.
Guǎn Zhòng of Qí,
Jiù Fàn of Jìn,
Sūn Shū'áo of Chǔ,
can be called meritorious ministers.
Yī Yǐn of Yīn,
Tàigōng of Zhōu,
can be called sage ministers.
— This is the discourse on ministers,
the ultimate standard for auspiciousness and inauspiciousness, worthiness and unworthiness,
one must carefully record it
and cautiously choose for oneself,
which is sufficient for reference.
Obeying commands and benefiting the ruler is called compliance,
obeying commands but not benefiting the ruler is called flattery;
opposing commands and benefiting the ruler is called loyalty,
opposing commands and not benefiting the ruler is called usurpation;
not considering the ruler's honor or disgrace,
not considering the state's good or ill,
but merely accommodating and preserving oneself, to hold onto salary and nurture connections,
is called a state traitor.
If the ruler has erroneous plans or actions,
and there is fear of endangering the state and toppling the altars of soil and grain,
ministers, fathers, sons, elder
or younger brothers who can advise the ruler,
if employed, they stay,
if not employed, they leave,
this is called remonstrance;
those who can advise the ruler,
if employed, they stay,
if not employed, they die,
this is called contention;
those who can unite in wisdom and strength,
leading all officials and officers to jointly compel and correct the ruler,
even if the ruler is uneasy,
he cannot but listen,
thereby resolving the state's great calamities,
removing the state's great harms,
achieving the honor of the ruler and the security of the state,
this is called assistance;
those who can resist the ruler's commands,
take over the ruler's authority,
reverse the ruler's actions,
to secure the state in peril,
remove the ruler's disgrace,
whose achievements are sufficient to accomplish the state's great benefits,
this is called opposition.
Thus, those who remonstrate, contend, assist, or oppose,
are ministers of the altars of soil and grain,
treasures of the state ruler,
honored and valued by enlightened rulers,
but confused rulers misunderstand them, considering them personal enemies.
Thus, those rewarded by enlightened rulers,
are punished by deluded rulers;
those rewarded by deluded rulers,
are executed by enlightened rulers.
Yī Yǐn, Jīzǐ, can be said to have remonstrated;
Bǐ Gàn,
Zǐxū, can be said to have contended;
Lord Píngyuán regarding Zhào, can be said to have assisted;
Lord Xìnlíng regarding Wèi, can be said to have opposed.
The tradition says:
"Follow the Way, not the ruler."
This expresses it.
Therefore, when righteous ministers are established,
the court is not biased;
when those who remonstrate, contend, assist, or oppose are trusted,
the ruler's errors do not persist;
when brave warriors are employed,
enemies do not arise;
when border ministers are stationed,
the frontiers are not lost.
Thus, enlightened rulers favor collaboration while deluded rulers favor solitude,
enlightened rulers esteem the worthy and employ the capable, enjoying their achievements,
deluded rulers envy the worthy and fear the capable, destroying their accomplishments.
