Punishing the loyal,
rewarding the traitorous,
this is called extreme delusion,
the reason for the downfall of Jié and Zhòu.
Serving a sage ruler,
one obeys and follows, without remonstrance or contention;
serving a mediocre ruler,
one remonstrates and contends, without flattery or sycophancy;
serving a tyrannical ruler,
one mends and corrects, without compulsion or opposition.
Forced into chaotic times,
living in hardship under a tyrannical state,
with no means of escape,
then exalt its virtues,
promote its good deeds,
avoid its evils,
conceal its failures,
speak of its strengths,
not mention its weaknesses,
making this a common practice.
The Book of Songs says:
"The state has great decrees,
that cannot be told to others,
guard them in your own person."
This expresses it.
Reverent and deferential,
obedient and diligent,
not daring to make private decisions,
not daring to privately take or give,
making obedience to the superior one's aim,
this is the principle of serving a sage ruler.
Loyal and trustworthy without flattery,
remonstrating and contending without sycophancy,
firmly upright and unyielding, with correct intent and no devious heart,
calling right what is right,
wrong what is wrong,
this is the principle of serving a mediocre ruler.
Harmonious but not drifting,
gentle but not yielding,
tolerant but not chaotic,
clearly understanding the highest Way and harmonizing all,
able to transform and adapt,
timely guiding inwardly,
this is the principle of serving a tyrannical ruler.
Like driving an untrained horse,
like nurturing an infant,
like feeding a starving person,
thus, using their fear to correct their faults;
using their worries to discern the causes;
using their joy to introduce the Way;
using their anger to eliminate their resentments;
indirectly achieving the intended result.
The Book of Documents says:
"Obey commands without opposition,
subtly remonstrate without weariness,
as a superior, be enlightened,
as a subordinate, be deferential."
This expresses it.
Serving others without obedience,
is due to lack of diligence;
diligent but not obedient,
is due to lack of respect;
respectful but not obedient,
is due to lack of loyalty;
loyal but not obedient,
is due to lack of achievement;
achieving but not obedient,
is due to lack of virtue.
Thus, the way of lacking virtue
harms diligence, ruins achievements, and nullifies toil,
so the gentleman does not practice it.
There is the highest loyalty,
the secondary loyalty,
the lower loyalty,
and the state traitor.
Using virtue to restore and transform the ruler,
is the highest loyalty;
using virtue to harmonize and supplement the ruler,
is secondary loyalty;
using right to admonish wrong and anger the ruler,
is lower loyalty;
not considering the ruler's honor or disgrace,
not considering the state's good or ill,
but accommodating and preserving oneself, to hold onto salary and nurture connections,
is a state traitor.
Like the Duke of Zhōu regarding King Chéng,
can be called the highest loyalty;
like Guǎn Zhòng regarding Duke Huán,
can be called secondary loyalty;
like Zǐxū regarding Fūchāi,
can be called lower loyalty;
like Cáo Chùlóng regarding Zhòu,
can be called a state traitor.
The benevolent must respect others.
All people, if not worthy,
are then unworthy.
If one does not respect the worthy,
then one is a beast;
if one does not respect the unworthy,
then one is teasing a tiger.
Beasts cause chaos,
teasing tigers brings danger,
disaster reaches one's person.
The Book of Songs says:
"I dare not attack a tiger with bare hands,
I dare not cross a river on foot.
People know one danger,
but not others.
Trembling with fear, as if approaching a deep abyss,
as if treading on thin ice."
This expresses it.
Thus, the benevolent must respect others.
Respecting others has its way:
for the worthy, honor and respect them;
for the unworthy, fear and respect them;
for the worthy, be close and respect them;
for the unworthy, keep distant and respect them.
Their reverence is one,
their emotions are twofold.
As for being loyal, faithful, upright, and sincere without causing harm,
then there is no interaction where this is not so,
this is the substance of a benevolent person.
Taking loyalty and faithfulness as the substance,
uprightness and sincerity as the guiding principle,
ritual and righteousness as the refinement,
and human relations and categories as the rationale,
even their breathing while speaking,
and subtle movements,
can all serve as models.
The Book of Songs says:
"Without error or harm,
rarely do they not become a standard."
This refers to this.
Respectfulness is ritual,
harmony is music,
caution is beneficial,
conflict and anger are harmful.
Thus, the noble person finds peace in ritual and joy in music,
is cautious and avoids conflict and anger,
thereby ensuring that all actions are without fault.
──The petty person is the opposite.
The smoothness that comes from thorough loyalty,
the balance achieved by weighing dangers,
and following the voice of calamity and chaos,
these three, none but an enlightened ruler can understand.
Strife then leads to goodness,
opposition then leads to achievement,
facing death without selfishness,
utmost loyalty and public-mindedness,
this is what is called the smoothness from thorough loyalty,
and Lord Xìnlíng resembled this.
Seizure then becomes righteousness,
killing then becomes benevolence,
the reversal of superior and inferior positions then becomes integrity,
achievements matching heaven and earth,
blessings covering the living people,
this is what is called the balance achieved by weighing dangers,
and Tāng, Wǔ were such.
Faults yet understanding feelings,
harmony without principles,
disregarding right and wrong,
not rectifying crooked and straight,
compromising and tolerating for survival,
deluded and recklessly living,
this is what is called following the voice of calamity and chaos,
and Fēilián, Èlái were such.
The Tradition says:
"Cut yet even,
bent yet smooth,
different yet unified."
The Book of Songs says:
"Receiving the small and large jades,
to be the dangling banner for the lower states."
This refers to this.
The methods of impartial hearing,
revealing the hidden,
doubling the bright,
expelling the treacherous, and advancing the virtuous:
praises from cliques and factions,
the noble person does not listen to;
slanders that add accusations,
the noble person does not employ;
people who are envious and obstructive,
the noble person does not approach;
requests with goods, wealth, or livestock,
the noble person does not permit.
All rumors,
circulating talk,
circulating events,
circulating schemes,
circulating praises, circulating accusations,
that come not through official channels but sideways,
the noble person is cautious of them.
Hearing and clearly assessing them,
determining what is appropriate and right,
then applying punishments or rewards accordingly,
thus,
then treacherous words,
treacherous talk,
treacherous deeds,
treacherous schemes,
treacherous praises, treacherous accusations
none dare to try,
loyal words,
loyal talk,
loyal deeds,
loyal schemes,
loyal praises, loyal accusations all become clearly understood,
and widely arise to be fully expressed.
This is what is called the methods of impartial hearing,
revealing the hidden,
doubling the bright,
expelling the treacherous, and advancing the virtuous.
When rivers and abysses are deep, fish and turtles return to them,
when mountains and forests are lush, birds and beasts return to them,
when punishments and governance are fair, the common people return to them,
when ritual and righteousness are complete, the noble people return to them.
Thus, when ritual reaches the person, conduct is cultivated,
when righteousness reaches the state, governance is clear,
being able to embrace ritual makes one's noble reputation evident,
the world is content,
orders are followed and prohibitions heeded,
the tasks of a true king are complete.
The Book of Songs says:
"Bless this central state,
to pacify the four quarters."
This refers to this.
Rivers and abysses are the dwelling of dragons and fish,
mountains and forests are the dwelling of birds and beasts,
the state is the dwelling of scholars and people.
If rivers and abysses dry up, then
dragons and fish leave them,
if mountains and forests become hazardous,
then birds and beasts leave them,
if the state fails in governance, then scholars and people leave it.
Without land, people cannot settle peacefully,
without people, land cannot be defended,
without the Way and laws, people will not come,
without noble persons, the Way is not upheld.
Thus, land and people,
the Way and laws,
are the foundation of the state.
The noble person,
is the essential pivot of the Way and laws,
and cannot be lacking even for a moment.
With them, there is order,
without them, there is chaos;
with them, there is safety,
without them, there is danger;
with them, there is survival,
without them, there is perish.
Thus, there have been cases of having good laws yet chaos,
but having noble persons yet chaos,
from ancient times to the present,
has never been heard of.
The Tradition says:
"Order arises from noble persons,
chaos arises from petty persons."
This refers to this.
Gaining the multitude moves heaven.
A joyful mind prolongs years.
Sincerity and trust are like spirits.
Boastfulness and exaggeration chase away the soul.
The trouble with rulers,
lies not in speaking about employing the worthy,
but in not being sincere and determined to employ them.
Speaking of employing the worthy—
is with the mouth,
rejecting the worthy—
is with actions,
mouth and actions contradicting,
yet wanting the worthy to come—
and the unworthy to retreat,
is it not difficult!
Those who catch cicadas by torchlight
focus on brightening their fire
and shaking the tree,
if the fire is not bright,
even shaking the tree
is of no use.
If a ruler can make his virtue bright, then the world will return to him,
like cicadas returning to a bright fire.
Handling affairs and interacting with the people
with righteousness, adapting with
tolerance and broad acceptance,
leading with respectfulness,
is the beginning of governance;
then assisting with balanced and discerning judgment,
is the height of governance;
then advancing, retreating, punishing, and rewarding,
is the end of governance.
Thus, start with them in the first year,
and conclude with them in the third year.
Using the end as the beginning,
then government orders will not be carried out
and superiors and inferiors will resent and hate,
which is how chaos arises on its own.
The Book of Documents says:
"Righteous punishments and righteous killings,
do not hastily implement,
you should only say
'I have not yet managed affairs properly.'"
This speaks of teaching first.
Standards are the measure of things,
and ritual principles are the measure of conduct.
Standards establish quantities,
ritual principles define social relationships,
virtue determines rank,
and ability assigns office.
In all matters, discipline should be rigorous,
but the people's livelihood should be generous.
With rigorous discipline comes refinement,
and with generous livelihood comes peace.
When superiors are refined and inferiors at peace,
this is the pinnacle of achievement and reputation,
beyond which nothing can be added.
The ruler is the exalted one of the state,
the father is the exalted one of the family.
With one exalted there is order,
with two there is chaos.
From ancient times to the present,
there has never been a case where two exalted ones contended for supremacy
and were able to endure long.
There are four qualifications for a teacher, but broad learning is not among them:
being dignified and inspiring awe
qualifies one to be a teacher;
being advanced in years and trustworthy
qualifies one to be a teacher;
reciting and explaining without transgressing or violating
qualifies one to be a teacher;
understanding subtle points and discussing them
qualifies one to be a teacher.
Thus, there are four qualifications for a teacher, but broad learning is not among them.
Deep water creates eddies,
fallen leaves fertilize the roots,
and when students achieve success, they think of their teacher.
The Book of Songs says:
"No word goes unanswered,
no virtue unrequited."
This expresses that idea.
Rewards should not be excessive,
punishments should not be indiscriminate.
Excessive rewards benefit the unworthy,
indiscriminate punishments harm the noble.
If unfortunately one must err,
it is better to be excessive in rewards than indiscriminate in punishments;
rather than harming the good,
it is better to benefit the wicked.
Línwǔ Jūn and Sūnqīng Zǐ debated military affairs in the presence of King Xiàochéng of Zhào.
The King said:
"May I ask about the essentials of warfare?"
Línwǔ Jūn replied:
"Above, gain the favor of heaven;
below, secure the advantages of earth;
observe the enemy's movements;
strike after them,
but arrive before them—
this is the essential art of using troops."
Sūnqīng Zǐ said:
"Not so.
What I have heard of the ancient Way
is that the foundation of all military operations
lies in uniting the people.
If the bow and arrows are not adjusted,
even Yì could not hit the smallest target;
if the six horses are not in harmony,
even Zàofǔ could not go far;
if the officers and people are not attached,
even Tāng and Wǔ could not be certain of victory.
Thus, he who is good at attaching the people
is the one who is good at using troops.
Therefore, the essential point of warfare lies solely in attaching the people well."
Línwǔ Jūn said:
"Not so.
What is valued in warfare is advantageous position,
what is practiced is deception and stratagem.
Those skilled in using troops
move mysteriously and unpredictably,
so none know where they come from;
when Sūn and Wú used such methods, they were invincible under heaven.
How can one necessarily rely on attaching the people!"
Sūnqīng Zǐ said:
"Not so.
What I advocate
is the army of a benevolent person,
the ambition of a true king.
What you value, sir,
is tactical advantage and power;
what you practice,
seizing by attack and deception,
are the affairs of the feudal lords.
The army of a benevolent person
cannot be deceived.
Those who can be deceived
are the negligent and lazy,
the exhausted and weak,
those among whom,
between ruler and minister, superior and inferior, there is a disunity of virtue.
Thus, when Jié deceives Jié,
there may still be a chance for the clever to overcome the clumsy.
But when Jié deceives Yáo,
it is like
throwing an egg at a stone,
or stirring boiling water with a finger,
or rushing into water or fire—
one enters only to be scorched or drowned.
Therefore, with a benevolent person, superiors and inferiors,
all generals are of one mind,
the entire army united in strength.
The minister's relation to the ruler,
the inferior's to the superior,
is like a son serving his father,
a younger brother serving his elder brother,
like using arms and hands to protect the head and eyes or cover the chest and belly.
To deceive and attack them
or to alert them first and then strike—
it is all the same.
Moreover, if a benevolent person rules a state of ten lǐ,
he will have intelligence from a hundred lǐ;
if he rules a state of a hundred lǐ,
he will have intelligence from a thousand lǐ;
if he rules a state of a thousand lǐ,
he will have intelligence from the four seas.
He will surely be clear-sighted and vigilant, harmonious and united as one.
Thus, the army of a benevolent person
gathers into squads,
disperses into formations,
extends like the long blade of Mòyé sword,
cutting down whoever confronts it;
concentrates like the sharp edge of Mòyé,
crushing whoever stands against it;
whether encamped circularly or arrayed squarely,
it is like a solid rock;
those who touch it have their corners broken,
and
fall scattered
and routed in retreat.
Moreover, with the ruler of a violent state,
who will follow him to war?
Those who follow him
must be his own people.
Yet his people feel closer to us, delighting as if we were their parents;
their affection for us is fragrant as pepper and orchid;
when they look back at their superiors,
they see them as branded criminals,
as hated enemies.
By human nature,
even Jié or Zhí
would hardly be willing to do harm
to those they love for the sake of those they detest!
This is like making a man's children harm their own parents—
they would surely come and report it;
how then can deception be used?
Thus, when a benevolent person is employed, the state grows daily brighter;
the feudal lords who submit first are safe,
those who submit later are endangered,
those who consider being enemies are weakened,
and those who oppose are destroyed.
The Book of Songs says:
'King Wǔ set out,
gripping his axe with reverence,
blazing like fierce flames,
and none dared to stop us.'
This expresses that idea."
King Xiàochéng and Línwǔ Jūn said:
"Excellent!
May we ask what principles
the army of a true king employs, and what conduct is acceptable?"
Sūnqīng Zǐ said:
"All lies with the great king;
generals and commanders are minor matters.
Allow me to explain the effects of strength and weakness, survival and destruction among kings and feudal lords,
and the conditions of safety and danger.
When the ruler is worthy, the state is well-governed;
when the ruler is incompetent, the state is chaotic;
when ritual principles are exalted and righteousness valued, the state is well-governed; when
ritual principles are neglected and righteousness despised, the state is chaotic.
A well-governed state is strong,
a chaotic state is weak—
this is the foundation of strength and weakness.
When the superior is worthy of emulation, the inferiors can be used;
when the superior is not worthy of emulation, the inferiors cannot be used.
When inferiors can be used, there is strength;
when they cannot be used, there is weakness—
this is the constant pattern of strength and weakness.
Exalting ritual principles and rewarding achievement
is the best way;
valuing emoluments and honoring integrity
is the next best;
emphasizing achievement and despising integrity
is the worst—
this is the general principle of strength and weakness."
He who values scholars is strong,
he who does not value scholars is weak;
he who loves the people is strong,
he who does not love the people is weak;
he whose governance and commands are trustworthy is strong,
he whose governance and commands are untrustworthy is weak;
he whose people are united is strong,
he whose people are not united is weak;
he whose rewards are generous is strong,
he whose rewards are meager is weak;
he whose punishments are awe-inspiring is strong,
he whose punishments invite contempt is weak;
he whose weapons and armor are well-crafted and effective is strong,
he whose weapons and armor are crude and ineffective is weak;
he who employs military force judiciously is strong,
he who employs it lightly is weak;
he whose authority is unified is strong,
he whose authority is divided is weak:
These are the constants of strength and weakness.
"The Qí people emphasized martial skills;
their method was
to award a fixed sum of metal
for each enemy head taken,
with no fundamental reward.
This works for minor engagements or weak foes
and can be used carelessly,
but in major confrontations or against staunch enemies,
they scatter and flee.
Like birds in flight,
they may capsize and scatter any day—
this is the army of a doomed state,
no army is weaker than this,
it is little more than mercenaries hired from the market to fight.
"The Wèi clan's warrior recruits
were selected by standards:
clad in three layers of armor,
wielding a twelve-dàn crossbow,
carrying fifty arrows,
with a spear atop,
helmeted and belted with a sword,
provisioned for three days,
marching a hundred lǐ by noon.
Those who passed the test had their households exempted from taxes
and granted fertile lands and homes.
Though their vigor declines after some years,
their benefits cannot be revoked,
and replacing them is not easily manageable.
Thus, even with vast territory,
tax revenue is necessarily meager—
this is the army of an endangered state.
"The Qín people, their livelihood constrained,
drive their people harshly,
compelling them by force,
cornering them with hardship,
accustoming them with rewards,
and disciplining them with punishments,
so that all under heaven's people
seeking benefit from the ruler
have no way but through combat.
They use them under duress,
rewarding only after achievements,
where merit and reward grow together:
capturing five armored heads grants authority over five households.
This makes them most numerous, strong, and enduring,
with ample land to govern.
Hence, four generations have seen victories—
not by luck,
but by method.
"Thus, Qí's martial skills
cannot withstand Wèi's warrior recruits;
Wèi's warrior recruits
cannot withstand Qín's sharp troops;
Qín's sharp troops
cannot match the discipline of Huán or Wén;
the discipline of Huán and Wén
cannot oppose the benevolence and righteousness of Tāng or Wǔ.
Any who encounter them
are like scorching themselves against a stone.
These several states' armies
all pursue rewards and profits,
following the way of hired sellswords,
with no principle of honoring superiors, securing order, or utmost discipline.
If any feudal lord subtly perfects this with discipline,
he would rise and overcome all others.
Thus, recruiting and selecting,
exalting force and deceit,
prizing merit and profit—
this is to corrupt them.
Ritual, righteousness, and education—
this is to unify them.
So, deceit meeting deceit
may still have cleverness or clumsiness;
but deceit meeting unity
is like using a dagger to topple Mount Tài—
none but the world's greatest fool would dare try.
Thus, the true king's army does not need to try.
When Tāng and Wǔ punished Jié and Zhòu,
they merely gestured and commanded,
and the violent states all hastened to serve,
punishing Jié and Zhòu as if they were lone scoundrels.
Hence, the 'Great Declaration' says,
'the lone scoundrel Zhòu'—
this refers to this.
Thus, great unity in the army controls all under heaven;
lesser unity manages neighboring foes.
As for recruiting and selecting,
exalting force and deceit,
prizing merit and profit—
such armies have no constancy in victory or defeat,
alternately expanding and contracting,
now surviving, now perishing,
vying for dominance.
This is called bandit troops,
which the noble man does not employ.
"Thus, Qí's Tián Dān,
Chǔ's Zhuāng Qiāo,
Qín's Wèi Yāng,
Yān's Miào Jǐ—
these are all what the world calls skilled generals;
their cleverness or clumsiness, strength or weakness
may not surpass each other,
but their way is one:
they never achieved harmony and unity.
Grasping at opportunities, practicing deceit,
using stratagems for overthrow—
they are not free from being bandit troops.
Qí Huán, Jìn Wén, Chǔ Zhuāng, Wú Hé Lǘ, Yuè Gōu Jiàn—these all had harmonious and unified armies,
and may be said to have entered the realm,
yet they lacked the fundamental system;
thus, they could hegemonize but not become true kings.
This is the effect of strength and weakness."
King Xiàochéng and Lord Línwǔ said:
"Excellent!
May we ask about being a general?"
Master Xúnqīng said:
"No knowledge is greater than discarding doubt,
no action greater than being without error,
no affair greater than having no regrets.
When an affair reaches no regrets, it is enough;
success cannot be guaranteed.
Thus, regulations, commands, and governance should be stern and awe-inspiring;
rewards and punishments should be certain and trustworthy;
encampments and stores should be thorough and secure;
movements and advances should be steady and weighty,
yet swift and rapid;
observing the enemy and changes should be covert and deep,
and verified through multiple sources;
in meeting the enemy and deciding battles, follow what we know clearly,
not what we doubt—
this is called the six techniques.
Do not desire command and hate dismissal,
do not rush for victory and forget defeat,
do not be stern internally and轻视 externally,
do not see only benefits and ignore harms;
in all planning, be thorough, and in using resources, be generous—
this is called the five balances.
A general may not accept the ruler's command in three cases:
he may be killed but not sent to an untenable position,
he may be killed but not ordered to attack without hope of victory,
he may be killed but not made to deceive the common people—
this is called the three utmost principles.
Whenever receiving the ruler's command to lead the three armies,
once the three armies are settled,
officials in order,
all matters rectified,
then the ruler cannot sway him with favor,
the enemy cannot provoke him with anger—
this is called the utmost minister.
Plan always before the affair,
and reinforce it with reverence,
cautious at the end as at the start,
consistent from beginning to end—
this is called great fortune.
In all affairs, success
lies in reverence;
their failure
lies in negligence.
Thus, reverence overcoming negligence brings fortune,
negligence overcoming reverence brings ruin;
plan overcoming desire brings compliance,
desire overcoming plan brings disaster.
Fight as if defending,
march as if fighting,
treat achievement as fortune.
Revere planning without neglect,
revere affairs without neglect,
revere the end without neglect,
revere the masses without neglect,
revere the enemy without neglect—
this is called the fivefold neglectlessness.
Carefully practice these six techniques, five balances, and three utmost principles,
and handle them with reverence and neglectlessness—
this is called the general of all under heaven,
then he is in communion with the divine and enlightened."
Línwǔ Jūn said:
"Excellent!
May I ask about the military system of a true king?"
Master Xúnzǐ replied:
"The general dies at his drum,
the charioteer dies at his reins,
all officers die at their posts,
and the gentry die in their ranks.
They advance upon hearing the drum,
and retreat upon hearing the gong.
Obedience to commands is paramount,
achieving merit is secondary.
To advance when not ordered to advance
is like retreating when not ordered to retreat -
the crime is equal.
Do not kill the old and weak,
do not trample the crops,
do not capture those who surrender,
do not spare those who resist,
and do not take prisoners of those who flee.
In all executions,
it is not the common people who are executed,
but those who bring chaos to the common people.
If common people shield the rebels,
then they too are rebels.
Therefore, those who yield survive,
those who resist die,
and those who flee are presented as tribute.
Wēizǐ was enfeoffed in Sòng,
while Cáo Chùlóng was executed in the army.
The people who submitted to Yīn
were provided for
no differently from the Zhōu people.
Thus those nearby sing praises and rejoice,
while those from afar hasten eagerly.
No remote or isolated country
fails to come serve and find peace and joy.
Within the four seas, it is like one family;
all accessible regions submit and obey.
This is what is called being a teacher of men.
The Book of Songs says:
'From west, from east,
from south, from north,
none thinks but to submit.'
This expresses it.
A true king executes but does not wage war,
does not attack cities that defend themselves,
does not strike troops that resist.
When superiors and subordinates rejoice together, he celebrates.
He does not massacre cities,
does not attack secretly,
does not detain the masses,
and his campaigns do not exceed one season.
Thus the troubled delight in his governance,
and though unsettled under their rulers,
they desire his arrival."
Línwǔ Jūn said:
"Excellent!"
Chén Xiāo asked Master Xúnzǐ:
"You, sir, discuss military affairs
always based on benevolence and righteousness.
The benevolent love others,
the righteous follow principle.
Then why use military force at all?
The purpose of having armies
is for contention and seizure."
Master Xúnzǐ said:
"This is beyond your understanding.
The benevolent love others,
and because they love others, they hate harm coming to them;
the righteous follow principle,
and because they follow principle, they hate chaos disrupting it.
Military force is for prohibiting violence and eliminating harm,
not for contention and seizure.
Thus the army of the benevolent
works wonders where it stays,
transforms where it passes,
like the falling of timely rain -
none fail to rejoice.
Therefore Yáo attacked Huāndōu,
Shùn attacked the Yǒumiáo,
Yǔ attacked Gònggōng,
Tāng attacked the Xià,
King Wén attacked Chóng,
King Wǔ attacked Zhòu -
these four emperors and two kings
all exercised armies of benevolence and righteousness
throughout the world.
Thus those nearby cherished their goodness,
while distant lands admired their righteousness;
their weapons remained unstained by blood,
and near and far came to submit.
Virtue so flourishing
extended to the four extremes.
The Book of Songs says:
'The good man, the gentleman,
his demeanor is without fault.'
This expresses it."
Lǐ Sī asked Master Xúnzǐ:
"Qín has been victorious for four generations,
its military strength dominates the realm,
its might commands the feudal lords -
not through benevolence and righteousness,
but by acting expediently."
Master Xúnzǐ said:
"This is beyond your understanding.
What you call expedient
is the expediency of the inexpedient;
what I call benevolence and righteousness
is the great expediency.
Benevolence and righteousness
are what cultivate good governance.
With good governance, the people cherish their superiors,
delight in their ruler,
and lightly die for them.
Therefore it is said:
'In military matters,
generals and commanders are minor affairs.'
Qín has been victorious for four generations,
yet trembles with constant fear that all under heaven might unite against it -
this is what is called the army of a declining age,
lacking fundamental principles.
Thus when Tāng exiled Jié,
it was not merely when he drove him out at Míngtiáo;
when King Wǔ executed Zhòu,
it was not merely on the morning of Jiǎzǐ that he prevailed -
both had cultivated virtue beforehand,
this is what is called the army of benevolence and righteousness.
Now you seek not the root
but demand the branches -
this is why the age is in chaos."
Ritual principles are the ultimate standard for orderly governance,
the foundation of a strong state,
the way to exercise authority,
the summation of achievement and fame.
Kings and dukes who follow them thereby gain the world;
those who do not follow them thereby lose their altars of soil and grain.
Thus strong armor and sharp weapons do not suffice for might,
high walls and deep moats do not suffice for defense,
harsh commands and numerous punishments do not suffice for authority.
Following the proper way leads to success,
not following it leads to ruin.
The Chǔ people made armor from shark skin, rhinoceros, and wild buffalo hide,
hard as metal or stone;
they had lances of Yuán's great iron,
vicious as bees or scorpions;
their troops moved swiftly and lightly,
sudden as a whirlwind;
yet their army was defeated at Chuíshā,
and Táng Miè died.
Zhuāng Qiāo rose up,
and Chǔ divided into three or four parts.
Was this because they lacked strong armor and sharp weapons?
It was because their way of governance was not correct.
They used the Rǔ and Yǐng rivers as natural barriers,
the Yángzǐ and Hàn rivers as moats,
bounded by the Dèng Forest,
and surrounded by the Fāngchéng walls;
yet when the Qín army arrived
Yān and Yǐng fell
like shaking dead leaves.
Was this because they lacked strong defenses and narrow passes?
It was because their way of governance was not correct.
Zhòu cut open Bǐgān's chest,
imprisoned Jīzǐ,
created the roasting pillar punishment,
and killed indiscriminately.
His ministers trembled, uncertain of their lives;
yet when the Zhōu army arrived
his commands were not obeyed below,
and he could not use his people.
Was this because his commands were not harsh
or his punishments not numerous?
It was because his way of governance was not correct.
The armies of antiquity
had only spears, halberds, bows, and arrows,
yet enemy states submitted without testing them;
without building inner and outer walls,
without digging moats and ponds,
without erecting strongholds,
without setting up mechanical devices,
the state remained secure, unafraid of external threats and firm -
for no other reason than
illuminating the Way and distributing equally,
employing people seasonably and loving them sincerely,
so the people responded to their superiors like shadow and echo.
Only those who disobeyed commands
were then punished accordingly."
Thus, when one person is punished, the whole world submits;
the offender does not resent his superiors,
knowing the fault lies within himself.
Therefore, penalties are sparingly applied yet authority flows like water,
for no other reason
than because the proper way is followed.
In ancient times, when Emperor Yáo governed the world,
he executed only one person
and punished two others,
yet the world was well-governed.
The "Record" says:
"Authority is stern yet untested,
punishments are in place yet unused."
This expresses it.
Generally, when people act
for the sake of rewards and honors,
they stop when they see harm or injury.
Thus, rewards, punishments, authority, and deception
are insufficient to exhaust people's strength
or drive them to death.
If a ruler
in dealing with his subjects and common people
lacks ritual principles, loyalty, and trustworthiness,
but instead hastily employs rewards and honors,
punishments,
authority, and deception,
endangering his subordinates
merely to seize their services,
then when great bandits arrive,
if ordered to defend a precarious city, they will surely rebel;
if encountering the enemy in battle, they will surely flee;
if faced with toil and hardship, they will surely run away;
swiftly dispersing,
the subordinates turn against and control their superiors.
Thus, the way of rewards, punishments, authority, and deception
is the method of hired laborers and sellers,
insufficient to unite the masses
or strengthen the state.
Hence, the ancients were ashamed and did not speak of it.
Instead, they amplified virtuous reputation to guide them,
clarified ritual principles to instruct them,
achieved loyalty and trustworthiness to care for them,
honored the worthy and employed the capable to rank them,
used ranks, robes, honors, and rewards to encourage them,
timed their tasks
and lightened their burdens
to harmonize and adjust them,
nurturing and rearing them
as if protecting infants.
When government decrees are established,
and customs are unified,
if any deviate from custom and disobey their superiors,
then all the common people will deeply detest them,
and regard them as poisonous pests,
as if exorcising an ill omen.
Only then are punishments applied.
When such great penalties are imposed,
what disgrace could be greater?
If they seek profit,
then great penalties befall them.
Unless they are insane, foolish, or ignorant,
who, seeing this, would not reform?
Thereafter, the common people clearly understand to follow the ruler's laws,
emulate the ruler's will,
and find peace and joy in it.
Then, those capable of transforming to goodness, cultivating themselves, correcting conduct, accumulating ritual principles, and honoring the Way and its power
are all respected and revered by the people,
all cherished and praised.
Only then are rewards bestowed.
When such high ranks and generous emoluments are granted,
what honor could be greater?
If they fear harm,
then high ranks and generous emoluments support and nurture them.
Among living people,
who would not desire this?
Clearly displaying noble ranks and substantial rewards before them,
and suspending clear punishments and great disgrace behind them,
even if they wish not to transform,
how can they avoid it?
Thus, the people turn to him like flowing water;
where he resides becomes divine,
what he does transforms all;
they become obedient.
The violent, fierce, and brave are transformed into honesty;
the biased, crooked, and selfish are transformed into fairness;
the contentious, contentious, and contentious are transformed into harmony.
This is called the great transformation and ultimate unity.
The "Book of Songs" says:
"The king's plans were truly sincere,
and the Xú region came."
This expresses it.
Generally, there are three methods to annex others:
some do so by virtue,
some by force,
some by wealth.
They value my reputation,
admire my moral conduct,
and wish to become my people.
Thus, they open their gates and clear the roads
to welcome my entry.
Following their people,
occupying their dwellings,
all the common people are content.
Establishing laws and issuing decrees,
none fail to comply.
Thus, gaining land, authority increases;
annexing people, the military grows stronger.
This is annexing others by virtue.
They do not value my reputation,
nor admire my moral conduct.
They fear my authority
and are coerced by my power.
Thus, though the people may have divisive thoughts,
they dare not contemplate rebellion.
In such a case,
the more armor and troops increase,
the more provisions must be spent.
Thus, gaining land, authority lightens;
annexing people, the military weakens.
This is annexing others by force.
They do not value my reputation,
nor admire my moral conduct.
Using poverty to seek wealth,
using hunger to seek fullness,
with empty bellies and open mouths,
they come to me for food.
In such a case,
one must distribute grain from storehouses to feed them,
bestow wealth and goods to enrich them,
appoint good officials to receive them.
Only after a full three years
can the people be trusted.
Thus, gaining land, authority lightens;
annexing people, the state grows poorer.
This is annexing others by wealth.
Therefore, it is said:
He who annexes others by virtue becomes king;
he who annexes others by force becomes weak;
he who annexes others by wealth becomes poor.
This holds true from ancient to modern times.
Annexation is easy to achieve,
but firm consolidation is difficult.
Qí could annex Sòng
but failed to consolidate it,
so Wèi seized it;
Yān could annex Qí
but failed to consolidate it,
so Tián Dān seized it;
the upper lands of Hán,
spanning several hundred li,
fully intact and wealthy, defected to Zhào,
but Zhào failed to consolidate them,
so Qín seized them.
Thus, if one can annex
but not consolidate,
it will surely be seized;
if one cannot annex
nor consolidate what one has,
it will surely be lost.
If one can consolidate,
then one can surely annex.
Gaining it and consolidating it,
no military power can rival it.
In ancient times, Tāng with Bó
and King Wǔ with Hào,
each had only a hundred li of land,
yet united the world,
with the feudal lords as ministers.
For no other reason
than their ability to consolidate.
Thus, consolidate scholars with ritual,
consolidate the people with governance.
When ritual is cultivated, scholars submit;
when governance is fair, the people are content.
Scholars submit and the people are content—
this is called great consolidation.
In defense, it is secure;
in attack, it is strong;
orders are followed, prohibitions heeded.
The tasks of a true king are complete.
If the mold is correct,
the bronze and tin fine,
the craftsmanship skillful,
the fire and alloy right,
opening the mold yields a Mòyé sword.
Yet without stripping the rough cast,
without grinding and sharpening,
it cannot cut a rope.
Once stripped
and sharpened,
it can slice through bronze basins
and behead oxen and horses
effortlessly.
That state,
is but a fragment of a strong state's penal code.
However, without instruction and guidance,
without harmonization and unification,
it cannot defend internally,
nor can it wage war externally;
with instruction and guidance,
harmonization and unification,
then the military becomes powerful and the city walls strong,
and enemy states dare not provoke it.
That state also has its whetstone,
which is ritual principles, righteousness, moderation, and restraint.
Thus, a person's fate lies with Heaven,
a state's fate lies with ritual.
The ruler of men
who exalts ritual and honors the worthy becomes a true king,
who emphasizes laws and loves the people becomes a hegemon,
who craves profit and is full of deceit faces danger,
and who employs schemes, subversion, darkness, and peril meets destruction.
There are three kinds of authority:
the authority of the Way and virtue,
the authority of violent scrutiny,
and the authority of reckless arrogance.
—These three kinds of authority,
must be carefully examined.
When ritual and music are cultivated,
when distinctions and righteousness are clear,
when actions and measures are timely,
when love and benefit are manifested,
then,
the people honor him as a deity,
elevate him as Heaven,
cherish him as parents,
and fear him as divine spirits,
thus rewards are not used yet the people are encouraged,
punishments are not used yet authority prevails.
This is called the authority of the Way and virtue.
When ritual and music are not cultivated,
when distinctions and righteousness are not clear,
when actions and measures are untimely,
when love and benefit are not manifested;
yet his prohibitions against violence are thorough,
his punishment of the disobedient is precise,
his penalties are severe and trustworthy,
his executions are fierce and inevitable,
suddenly striking like thunder,
crushing like a collapsing wall.
In such a case,
the people are coerced into fear,
but when weak, they become arrogant toward superiors,
when seized, they gather in crowds,
when given an opportunity, they scatter,
when hit by the enemy, they are easily taken,
unless coerced by physical force,
unless intimidated by executions,
there is no way to control the masses.
This is called the authority of violent scrutiny.
Without a heart to love others,
without deeds to benefit others,
yet daily practicing the ways of disturbing others,
when the people clamor and protest,
he then seizes and binds them,
punishes and burns them,
without harmonizing the people's hearts.
In such a case,
the masses form cliques, riot, and disperse, alienating the ruler,
collapse and destruction,
can be expected to occur immediately.
This is called the authority of reckless arrogance.
—These three kinds of authority,
must be carefully examined.
The authority of the Way and virtue results in security and strength,
the authority of violent scrutiny results in danger and weakness,
the authority of reckless arrogance results in destruction and ruin.
Gōngsūnzǐ said:
"Zǐfā led the army to attack Cài,
conquered Cài,
and captured the Marquis of Cài;
upon returning to report, he said:
'The Marquis of Cài offered his state
and surrendered it to Chǔ,
I left it to a few subordinates to govern his land.'
Afterward,
Chǔ distributed rewards,
but Zǐfā declined, saying:
'Issuing warnings and orders caused the enemy to retreat,
that is the sovereign's authority;
moving troops and attacking caused the enemy to retreat,
that is the general's authority;
joining battle and exerting force caused the enemy to retreat,
that is the masses' authority.
I should not receive a reward based on the masses' authority.'
It was criticized, saying:
"Zǐfā's report was respectful,
but his declining the reward was rigid.
Honoring the worthy and employing the capable,
rewarding the meritorious,
punishing the guilty,
is not done by one person alone,
it is the way of the former kings,
the foundation for uniting people,
the response to praising good and condemning evil,
governance must follow this,
it is the same in ancient and modern times.
When the enlightened kings of old undertook great tasks
and achieved great merits,
once the great tasks were accomplished,
the great merits achieved,
the ruler enjoyed the success,
the ministers shared in the achievements,
the officials had their ranks increased,
the functionaries had their positions elevated,
the common people had their stipends augmented.
Thus, those who did good were encouraged,
those who did evil were deterred,
superiors and inferiors were of one mind,
the three armies united in strength,
hence all tasks succeeded
and fame and merit were great.
Now Zǐfā alone does otherwise,
opposing the way of the former kings,
disrupting the laws of Chǔ,
discouraging the ministers who achieved merit,
shaming those who received rewards,
not only disgracing his clan
but also demeaning his descendants,
presuming it to be personal integrity,
is that not extremely mistaken!
Therefore, it is said:
Zǐfā's report was respectful,
but his declining the reward was rigid."
Xúnqīngzǐ advised the Prime Minister of Qí, saying:
"Occupying a position to overcome others,
practicing the way to overcome others,
no one in the world resents,
such were Tāng and Wǔ;
occupying a position to overcome others,
but not practicing the way to overcome others,
despite having the power over the world,
one cannot even hope to remain a commoner,
such were Jié and Zhòu.
Thus, those who possess the position to overcome others,
fall far short of those who practice the way to overcome others.
The ruler and minister,
overcome others by position,
affirming what is right as right,
condemning what is wrong as wrong,
acknowledging ability as ability,
inability as inability,
setting aside personal desires,
and adhering to the Way
—the public way and universal righteousness that can be mutually compatible—
this is the way to overcome others.
Now, the Prime Minister above can solely influence the sovereign,
below can solely govern the state,
the Prime Minister, regarding the position to overcome others,
truly possesses it.
Then why not drive this position to overcome others,
toward the way to overcome others,
seek benevolent, generous, wise, and understanding gentlemen and entrust the king to them,
share with them in state governance,
and correct right and wrong?
If so,
then who in the state would dare not act righteously?
Ruler and minister, superior and inferior,
noble and humble, old and young,
down to the common people,
all act righteously,
then who in the world would not wish to align with righteousness?
Worthy scholars would wish to serve in your court,
capable men would wish to hold office under you,
profit-seeking people would all wish to make Qí their home,
this is to unify the world.
If the Prime Minister abandons this and does not act,
but merely follows what the common practice does,
then women will bring chaos to the palace,
deceitful ministers will bring chaos to the court,
greedy officials will bring chaos to the administration,
the masses and common people will all make greed, profit-seeking, and contention their custom,
how can one govern the state like this?
Now, the great state of Chǔ hangs before us,
the great state of Yān presses behind us,
the powerful state of Wèi hooks our right,
the western border is as thin as a thread,
and the people of Chǔ have Xiāngféi and Kāiyáng to threaten our left.
If one state plots against us,
the other three will surely rise and take advantage of us.
In that case,
Qí will surely be cut into three or four pieces,
the state will be like a borrowed city,
and will surely be greatly laughed at by the world.
Which of the two options is worth pursuing?
Jié and Zhòu,
were descendants of sage kings,
heirs to those who possessed the empire,
holders of the authority and registry,
the ancestral house of the empire.
With vast territories,
their domains spanned a thousand li,
and their populations numbered in the hundreds of millions.
Yet suddenly, the entire empire unanimously turned away from Jié and
Zhòu and fled to Tāng and Wǔ,
instead unanimously detesting Jié and
Zhòu while esteeming Emperor Tāng and Wǔ.
Why is this?
What did Jié and Zhòu lose?
And what did Tāng and Wǔ gain?
There is no other reason:
Jié and Zhòu excelled at doing what people detest,
while Tāng and Wǔ excelled at doing what people desire.
What do people detest?
Answer:
Filth, deceit,
strife, contention, greed, and profit-seeking.
What do people desire?
Answer:
Ritual principles, righteousness, deference, humility, loyalty, and trustworthiness.
Now, those who rule over others,
when drawing analogies, wish to compare themselves to Tāng and Wǔ,
but in their methods of governance,
they are no different from Jié and Zhòu.
Yet they seek to achieve the merits and fame of Tāng and Wǔ—
is this possible?
Thus, all who achieve victory
must unite with people;
all who win over people
must align with the Way.
What is the Way?
Answer: Ritual principles, righteousness, deference, humility, loyalty, and trustworthiness.
Hence, for states with forty to fifty thousand people and beyond,
strength and victory do not come from numerical force,
but from emphasizing trustworthiness.
For states spanning several hundred li and beyond,
stability and security do not come from vast size,
but from cultivating good governance.
Now, those who already have tens of thousands of followers
engage in deceit, boasting, and cliquishness to compete for allies;
those who already have territories of several hundred li
resort to filth, deceit, aggression, and theft to contend for land.
Thus, they abandon what brings them stability and strength,
and pursue what leads to danger and weakness,
depleting what they already lack,
while amplifying what they already have in excess.
Such perversity and contradiction—
and yet they seek the merits and fame of Tāng and Wǔ,
is this possible?
To analogize,
it is like lying down and licking the sky,
or trying to save someone from hanging by pulling their feet.
Such proposals are bound to fail,
and the more one strives, the farther one gets.
As for ministers,
they do not care whether their actions are righteous or not,
but only seek wealth and profit.
This is like driving a siege chariot into a burrow to seek gain—
something the benevolent would be ashamed of and not do.
Thus, nothing is more precious to humans than life,
nothing more joyful than security;
and nothing is greater for nurturing life and joy in security
than ritual principles and righteousness.
If people know to value life and cherish security yet discard ritual principles and righteousness,
to analogize,
it is like wishing for longevity while cutting one's own throat—
no folly is greater.
Therefore, a ruler who loves the people
achieves security,
and who delights in scholars attains glory;
lacking both, he perishes.
The Odes say:
'Good men are the hedge,
the great masses the wall.'
This expresses it.
The method of force has its limits,
the method of righteousness prevails.
What does this mean?
Answer:
It refers to Qín.
In might, it surpasses Tāng and
Wǔ,
and Yǔ;
in expanse, it exceeds Shùn. Yet its worries and troubles are innumerable;
it is constantly fearful that the empire might unite and crush it.
This is what is meant by "the method of force has its limits."
Wǔ?
Tāng and
What does "surpassing Tāng and Wǔ in might" mean?
It means being able to make even those who oppose you serve you.
Now, though Chǔ's ruler has died,
and the state is occupied,
bearing the temples of the three kings,
it hides between Chén and Cài,
watching for an opportunity, awaiting a gap,
planning to raise its legs and trample Qín's heartland.
Yet Qín can command it to go left or right at will,
making it obey as if a servant.
This is called "surpassing Tāng and Wǔ in might."
What does "exceeding Shùn and Yǔ in expanse" mean?
Answer:
In ancient times, when the hundred kings unified the empire
and subjugated the feudal lords,
none had domains exceeding a thousand li.
Now, Qín extends south to Shāyì and beyond,
reaching south of the river;
north, it borders the Hú and Mò tribes,
and the Róng;
west, it holds Bā. In Chǔ, it borders Qí;
in Hán, it crosses Chángshān to Línlǜ;
in Wèi, it occupies Wéijīn, merely a hundred and twenty li from Dàliáng.
In Zhào, it securely holds Líng and controls the Sōngbǎi Pass,
backed by the Western Sea and fortified by Chángshān.
Thus, its land spans the empire.
Its might shakes the world,
its strength threatens the central states.
This is what is meant by "exceeding Shùn and Yǔ in expanse."
Yet its worries and troubles are innumerable,
and it is constantly fearful that the empire might unite and crush it.
What then is to be done?
Answer: Restrain might and return to civility,
employ gentlemen who are upright, sincere, trustworthy, and virtuous to govern the empire,
bringing them into the state's administration,
correcting right and wrong,
adjudicating straight and crooked,
and hearing cases in Xiányáng.
Those who submit are left in peace,
those who resist are then punished. If so,
then armies need not march beyond the borders
yet orders are obeyed throughout the empire.
If so,
even building a Mingtáng
beyond the borders to receive feudal lords
would be nearly possible.
In the present age,
the task of increasing trust is more urgent than expanding territory.
Marquis Yìng asked Master Xúnzǐ:
"What have you seen in Qín?"
Master Xúnzǐ said:
"Its terrain is fortified and strategic,
its configuration advantageous,
its mountains, forests, rivers, and valleys beautiful,
its natural resources abundant—
this is topographical supremacy.
Entering its borders,
observing its customs,
the common people are simple,
their music is not decadent or corrupt,
their clothing not frivolous,
they deeply respect officials and are obedient—
they are like the people of antiquity.
In its cities and government offices,
all officials are solemn,
each respectful, frugal,
sincere, reverent, loyal, and trustworthy, not negligent—
they are like the officials of antiquity.
Entering the state,
observing its scholar-officials,
they leave their homes
and enter the public gates;
leaving the public gates,
they return to their homes,
with no private affairs.
They do not form cliques,
or engage in factionalism,
but are uniformly enlightened, impartial, and public-spirited—
they are like the scholar-officials of antiquity.
Observing its court,
during court sessions,
all matters are decided without delay,
yet it is serene as if untroubled—
it is like the courts of antiquity.
Thus, four generations have seen victories,
not by luck,
but by principle.
This is what I have seen.
Hence it is said:
'Leisurely yet orderly,
simple yet thorough,
effortless yet effective—
this is the pinnacle of governance.'
Qín resembles this.
However,
it has its fears.
Though it possesses all these qualities,
when measured against the achievements and fame of a true king,
it falls far short.
Why is this so?
It is probably because they had no Confucian scholars!
Hence the saying:
'He who is pure becomes king,
he who is mixed becomes hegemon,
he who has neither perishes.'
This was also the shortcoming of Qín.
On accumulating small things:
The month cannot compare with the day,
the season cannot compare with the month,
the year cannot compare with the season.
Ordinary people tend to neglect small matters,
and only when major events arise do they exert themselves to attend to them.
If this is the case,
they will always be inferior to those who diligently handle small matters.
Why is this so?
Because small matters occur frequently,
their duration is extensive,
and their accumulation is great;
while major events occur rarely,
their duration is brief,
and their accumulation is small.
Thus, he who makes good use of days becomes king,
he who makes good use of seasons becomes hegemon,
he who mends leaks faces danger,
and he who lets things go to waste perishes.
Therefore, the true king values each day,
the hegemon values each season,
while a state barely surviving feels anxious only when in danger.
A perishing state realizes its doom only when it is about to perish,
and realizes death only when facing it.
The disasters and failures of a perishing state
are too numerous to regret.
The excellence of a hegemon
can be recorded by seasons,
while the achievements and fame of a true king
are too numerous to count and can be recorded by days.
Material wealth and treasures are valued for their size,
but governance, education, achievements, and fame are the opposite—he who can accumulate small things achieves success quickly.
The Book of Songs says:
"Virtue is as light as a hair,
yet few can lift it."
This expresses the meaning.
The reason villains arise
is that those above do not value righteousness
nor revere righteousness.
Righteousness is that which
restrains people from evil and villainy.
If those above do not value righteousness
nor revere righteousness,
then
the common people below
will all have the intention to abandon righteousness
and a mind inclined toward villainy.
This is why villains arise.
Moreover, those above are the models for those below.
The response of those below to those above
is like an echo responding to a sound,
or a shadow resembling a form.
Therefore, those in high positions
must be careful.
Righteousness is that which
internally regulates people
and externally regulates all things,
bringing security to the ruler above
and harmony to the people below.
When internal and external, above and below, are regulated,
this is the essence of righteousness.
Thus, the essential principle for governing the world
is righteousness as the foundation,
with trustworthiness next.
In ancient times, Yǔ and Tāng upheld righteousness and practiced trustworthiness, bringing order to the world;
Jié and Zhòu abandoned righteousness and betrayed trust, bringing chaos to the world.
Therefore, those in high positions
must carefully observe ritual and righteousness,
and devote themselves to loyalty and trustworthiness,
only then can they succeed.
This is the great foundation for rulers.
If the hall is not swept,
then the grass in the suburbs will not be weeded;
when a bright blade is pointed at one's chest,
the eyes do not see flying arrows;
when a halberd is pressed against one's head,
the ten fingers do not hesitate to be cut off.
It is not that one does not consider these important,
but there is an order of priority in urgency and importance.
Heaven's operation is constant,
it does not exist because of Yáo,
nor does it perish because of Jié.
Respond to it with order, and there will be good fortune;
respond to it with disorder, and there will be misfortune.
Strengthen the fundamentals and practice frugality,
and Heaven cannot make you poor;
provide ample nourishment and act timely,
and Heaven cannot make you ill;
follow the Way and do not err,
and Heaven cannot bring disaster upon you.
Thus, floods and droughts cannot cause hunger (and thirst),
cold and heat cannot cause illness,
and supernatural phenomena cannot bring misfortune.
If the fundamentals are neglected and extravagance is practiced,
Heaven cannot make you wealthy;
if nourishment is insufficient and action is rare,
Heaven cannot make you whole;
if you betray the Way and act recklessly,
Heaven cannot bring you good fortune.
Thus, hunger occurs even before floods and droughts arrive,
illness occurs even before cold and heat approach,
and misfortune occurs even before supernatural phenomena arise.
The time received is the same as in an orderly age,
yet calamities differ from those in an orderly age;
one cannot blame Heaven,
for it is the Way that causes this.
Therefore, one who understands the distinction between Heaven and humanity
may be called a perfect person.
Achieving without acting,
obtaining without seeking,
this is called Heaven's function.
In such cases,
no matter how profound, the sage does not ponder it;
no matter how great, he does not apply his ability to it;
no matter how subtle, he does not examine it;
this is called not competing with Heaven in its function.
Heaven has its seasons,
Earth has its resources,
and humanity has its governance;
this is called the ability to form a triad.
If one abandons what enables this triad
and only desires what the triad achieves,
then one is deluded.
The stars follow one another in rotation,
the sun and moon alternate in shining,
the four seasons succeed one another,
Yīn and Yáng undergo great transformations,
wind and rain are widely bestowed,
all things obtain their harmony to live,
and obtain their nourishment to mature.
We do not see the process
but see the results;
this is called divinity.
All know how things are accomplished,
but none know the formless;
this is called Heaven's achievement.
Only the sage does not seek to know Heaven.
Once Heaven's function is established,
and Heaven's achievement is complete,
the form is constituted and the spirit is born.
Likes, dislikes, joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure reside within;
this is called natural emotions.
The ears, eyes, nose, mouth, and body each have their objects of perception but cannot interchange functions;
this is called the natural organs.
The mind resides in the central void
to govern the five organs;
this is called the natural ruler.
Using things not of one's kind to nourish one's kind;
this is called natural nourishment.
Following what suits one's kind is called blessing;
opposing what suits one's kind is called calamity;
this is called natural governance.
If one darkens the natural ruler,
disorders the natural organs,
abandons natural nourishment,
opposes natural governance,
violates natural emotions,
and thereby loses Heaven's achievement,
this is called great misfortune.
The sage clarifies the natural ruler,
rectifies the natural organs,
provides natural nourishment,
follows natural governance,
nurtures natural emotions,
and thereby preserves Heaven's achievement.
Thus,
he knows what to do
and what not to do;
then Heaven and Earth are employed and all things are utilized.
His actions are completely orderly,
his nourishment is completely appropriate,
his life is unharmed;
this is called knowing Heaven.
Therefore, great skill lies in not doing certain things,
and great wisdom lies in not pondering certain things.
What one aims to know about Heaven
is limited to the visible signs that can be anticipated;
what one aims to know about Earth
is limited to the suitable conditions that can be utilized for growth;
what one aims to know about the four seasons
is limited to the regularities that can be used for activities;
what one aims to know about Yīn and Yáng
is limited to the harmony that can be used for governance.
Officials guard Heaven's laws,
while the ruler guards the Way.
"Is order and disorder a matter of Heaven?"
The reply:
"The sun, moon, stars, and celestial phenomena
were the same under Yǔ and Jié alike;
Yǔ brought order,
while Jié brought disorder,
so order and disorder are not a matter of Heaven."
"Is it a matter of timing?"
The reply:
"Things sprout and flourish in spring and summer,
and are stored and gathered in autumn and winter;
this too was the same under Yǔ and Jié alike;
Yǔ brought order,
while Jié brought disorder;
so order and disorder are not a matter of timing."
"Is it a matter of earth?"
The reply:
"With land, they live;
without land, they die;
this too was the same under Yǔ and Jié alike;
Yǔ brought order,
while Jié brought disorder;
so order and disorder are not a matter of earth.
The Book of Songs says:
'Heaven made the high mountain,
King Tài cultivated it.
He began the work,
and King Wén dwelt in peace.'
This expresses the idea."
Heaven does not cease winter because people dislike cold;
earth does not cease vastness because people dislike distance;
the gentleman does not cease his actions because of the clamor of petty men.
Heaven has constant ways,
earth has constant measures,
the gentleman has constant substance.
The gentleman follows his constants,
while the petty man calculates his gains.
The Book of Songs says:
"If there is no transgression of ritual and righteousness,
why worry about what people say!"
This expresses the idea.
The King of Chǔ having a thousand chariots in his retinue
is not due to wisdom;
the gentleman eating beans and drinking water
is not due to stupidity:
these are matters of circumstance.
As for cultivating one's will and intentions,
enriching one's moral conduct,
clarifying one's knowledge and thoughts,
living in the present but aspiring to the ancient ways,
these lie within oneself.
Thus the gentleman admires what lies within himself,
and does not admire what lies with Heaven;
the petty man neglects what lies within himself,
and admires what lies with Heaven;
the gentleman reveres what lies within himself,
and does not admire what lies with Heaven,
thus he daily advances;
the petty man neglects what lies within himself,
and admires what lies with Heaven,
thus he daily regresses.
Therefore the reason the gentleman daily advances,
and the petty man daily regresses,
is one and the same.
The reason why gentlemen and petty men are so far apart
lies precisely in this.
When stars fall or trees make sounds,
all people in the state are frightened.
They ask:
"What is this?"
The reply:
"It is nothing.
It is a transformation of Heaven and earth,
a change of yīn and yáng,
something rarely encountered.
To find it strange
is permissible;
but to fear it
is not.
Eclipses of the sun and moon,
untimely wind and rain,
the occasional appearance of strange stars
—these occur in every age.
If the ruler is enlightened and governance fair,
then even if these occur simultaneously,
there is no harm;
if the ruler is benighted and governance perilous,
then even if not one such event occurs,
there is no benefit.
The falling of stars,
the sounding of trees,
are transformations of Heaven and earth,
changes of yīn and yáng,
things rarely encountered;
to find them strange
is permissible;
but to fear them is not."
"Among things that have already occurred,
human omens are what should be feared:
poor plowing that damages crops,
weeding poorly that leaves weeds,
perilous governance that loses the people,
fields weedy and crops bad,
grain expensive and people starving,
dead bodies on the roads—
these are called human omens.
Government orders unclear,
measures taken at wrong times,
fundamental affairs not properly managed—
these are called human omens.
Forced labor at improper times,
so that oxen and horses give birth to each other,
banditry and calamities arising together—
these are called human omens.
Omen arise from disorder;
if these three types interlace,
the state will have no peace.
The explanation is quite simple,
but the disaster is extremely grievous.
It may be considered strange,
but should not be feared.
The tradition says:
'The strange phenomena of things, books do not discuss.
Useless debates,
unurgent investigations,
should be abandoned and not pursued.'
As for the righteousness between ruler and minister,
the affection between father and son,
the distinction between husband and wife,
these should be daily refined and never abandoned."
"It rains after the rain sacrifice;
why is that?"
The reply:
"There is no other reason;
it is just like raining without the rain sacrifice.
Performing rescue rites during eclipses of the sun and moon,
holding rain sacrifices during drought,
divining before deciding major affairs—
these are not done to get what one seeks,
but to ornament things.
Thus the gentleman considers them ornamentation,
while the common people consider them supernatural.
Considering them ornamentation brings good fortune;
considering them supernatural brings misfortune."
Among heavenly things, none are brighter than the sun and moon;
among earthly things, none are brighter than water and fire;
among objects, none are brighter than pearls and jade;
among human things, none are brighter than ritual and righteousness.
Thus if the sun and moon were not high,
their radiance would not be glorious;
if water and fire do not accumulate,
their brilliance and moisture would not be extensive;
if pearls and jade are not visible externally,
kings and lords would not consider them treasures;
if ritual and righteousness are not applied to the state,
then achievements and fame will not be illustrious.
Thus human destiny lies with Heaven,
but the state's destiny lies with ritual.
The ruler who
exalts ritual and honors the worthy becomes king;
who emphasizes laws and loves the people becomes hegemon;
who covets profit and practices much deceit faces danger;
who uses schemes, subversion, secrecy, and peril will perish completely."
To revere Heaven and contemplate it,
how does that compare to treating it as a thing and controlling it?
To follow Heaven and praise it,
how does that compare to mastering the Mandate of Heaven and using it?
To await the season and wait for it,
how does that compare to responding to the season and employing it?
To rely on things and increase them,
how does that compare to developing abilities and transforming them?
To contemplate things and treat them as things,
how does that compare to managing things and not losing them?
To wish for how things are born,
how does that compare to possessing how things are completed?
Thus to neglect humanity and contemplate Heaven
is to miss the true nature of all things."
What remains unchanged through a hundred kings
is sufficient to form the thread of the Way.
Through every rise and fall,
respond with this thread,
and the thread's principle will not be disordered.
Not knowing the thread,
one cannot know how to respond to change,
yet the main substance of the thread has never perished.
Disorder arises from deviation from it,
order is achieved through its complete application.
Thus, what the Way approves,
if it is central, can be followed;
if it is one-sided, it cannot be done;
if it is concealed, it leads to great confusion.
Those who navigate water mark the depths;
if the markers are unclear, they sink;
those who govern the people mark the Way;
if the markers are unclear, there is chaos.
Ritual principles are
the markers;
without ritual,
it is an age of darkness;
an age of darkness
is great disorder.
Therefore, the Way must be clearly illuminated,
with different markers for internal and external,
constancy in the hidden and the manifest,
so that the people's pitfalls are removed.
All things are one aspect of the Way;
one thing is one aspect of all things;
the foolish person is one aspect of one thing,
yet considers themselves to know the Way—
this is ignorance.
Shènzǐ had insight into following,
but none into leading;
Lǎozǐ had insight into yielding,
but none into extending;
Mòzǐ had insight into uniformity,
but none into disparity;
Sòngzǐ had insight into scarcity,
but none into abundance.
Having only following and no leading,
then the masses have no gateway;
having only yielding and no extending,
then nobility and baseness are not distinguished;
having only uniformity and no disparity,
then government decrees cannot be implemented;
having only scarcity and no abundance,
then the masses cannot be transformed.
The *Shū* says:
"Have no selfish preferences,
follow the king's Way;
have no selfish aversions,
follow the king's path."
This refers to this.
A common saying among the世俗 is:
"The ruler's Way benefits from secrecy."
This is not so.
The ruler is the one who leads the people;
the superior is the model for the inferior.
They will listen to the lead and respond,
look to the model and act.
If the lead is silent, the people have nothing to respond to;
if the model is hidden, the inferior have nothing to act upon.
Without response or action,
then superior and inferior have no means to assist each other.
If so,
it is the same as having no superior,
and no misfortune is greater than this.
Therefore, the superior is the root of the inferior;
if the superior is open and clear,
then the inferior are well-ordered;
if the superior is upright and sincere,
then the inferior are honest and careful;
if the superior is fair and just,
then the inferior are straightforward.
Being well-ordered makes them easy to unify;
being honest and careful makes them easy to employ;
being straightforward makes them easy to understand.
Easy to unify leads to strength;
easy to employ leads to achievement;
easy to understand leads to clarity;
this is how order arises.
If the superior is secretive,
then the inferior are suspicious and perplexed;
if the superior is obscure and treacherous,
then the inferior become deceitful;
if the superior is biased and crooked,
then the inferior form cliques.
Suspicious and perplexed, they are hard to unify;
deceitful, they are hard to employ;
forming cliques, they are hard to understand.
Hard to unify leads to weakness;
hard to employ leads to no achievement;
hard to understand leads to obscurity;
this is how chaos arises.
Therefore, the ruler's Way benefits from clarity, not obscurity;
benefits from openness, not secrecy.
Thus, if the ruler's Way is clear, the inferior are secure;
if the ruler's Way is obscure, the inferior are endangered.
Therefore, if the inferior are secure, they honor the superior;
if the inferior are endangered, they despise the superior.
Thus, if the superior is easy to know,
then the inferior are close to the superior;
if the superior is hard to know,
then the inferior fear the superior.
If the inferior are close to the superior, the superior is secure;
if the inferior fear the superior, the superior is endangered.
Therefore, nothing in the ruler's Way is worse than being hard to know,
nothing more dangerous than making the inferior fear oneself.
The *Zhuàn* says:
"If those who hate you are many, it is dangerous."
The *Shū* says:
"Able to make bright his bright virtue."
The *Shī* says:
"Brightly shining below."
Thus, the former kings made it bright—
how could they only obscure it!
A common saying among the世俗 is:
"Jié and Zhòu possessed the world,
and Tāng and Wǔ usurped and seized it."
This is not so.
To say that Jié and Zhòu held the position of the world is true,
but to say they personally possessed the position of the world is not true,
and to say the world belonged to Jié and Zhòu is not true.
In ancient times, the Son of Heaven had a thousand officials,
the feudal lords had a hundred officials.
With these thousand officials,
if his decrees were implemented throughout the states of Xià,
he was called a king;
with these hundred officials,
if his decrees were implemented within his borders,
even if the state was not fully at peace,
it did not reach the point of being overthrown and perishing,
he was called a ruler.
The son of a sage king,
the descendant of one who possessed the world,
the one in the position of authority,
the patriarch of the world—
yet if he is untalented and unworthy,
internally the common people resent him,
externally the feudal lords rebel against him;
nearby, within the borders, there is disunity;
far away, the feudal lords do not obey;
decrees are not implemented within the borders.
In severe cases, feudal lords invade and reduce his territory,
attack and assault him;
if so,
then even if he has not yet perished,
I say he does not possess the world.
When a sage king passes away,
if the one in authority is incompetent and unable to sustain the world,
the world has no ruler;
if among the feudal lords there is one capable of accumulating bright virtue and authority,
and all the people within the seas wish to have him as their ruler and teacher,
yet a violent state alone acts arrogantly
and how can it be punished?
It must harm innocent people;
punishing the ruler of a violent state
is like punishing a lone individual.
If so,
then he can be said to be able to use the world.
Being able to use the world is called being a king.
Tāng and Wǔ did not seize the world;
they cultivated their Way,
practiced their righteousness,
promoted the common benefits of the world,
removed the common harms of the world,
and the world turned to them.
Jié and Zhòu did not lose the world;
they opposed the virtue of Yǔ and Tāng,
disrupted the distinctions of ritual and righteousness,
acted like beasts,
accumulated their cruelty,
perfected their wickedness,
and the world abandoned them.
The world turning to someone
is called being a king;
the world abandoning someone is called perishing.
Thus, Jié
and Zhòu did not possess the world,
and Tāng and Wǔ did not assassinate their rulers—this is evidenced by this.
Tāng and Wǔ are
the parents of the people;
Jié and Zhòu are the hated enemies of the people.
Now, those who hold common世俗 sayings,
considering Jié and Zhòu as rulers
and Tāng and Wǔ as assassins,
then this is to condemn the parents of the people
and emulate the hated enemies of the people—
no misfortune is greater than this.
To consider the one with whom the world unites as the ruler,
then the world never united with Jié and Zhòu.
Thus, to call Tāng and Wǔ assassins,
then there has never been a valid argument for it,
it is merely slander.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven must be the right person.
The world is
of utmost importance,
and none but the most powerful can bear its burden;
it is of the greatest magnitude,
and none but the most discerning can distinguish its parts;
it is of the multitude,
and none but the most enlightened can harmonize it.
These three ultimates
can only be fully realized by a sage.
Hence, none but a sage is fit to be king.
A sage is one who embodies the Way and possesses all virtues,
and thus serves as the universal standard of balance.
Jié and Zhòu,
their thoughts were utterly perilous,
their intentions utterly dark,
and their actions utterly chaotic;
they estranged their kin,
demeaned the worthy,
and incurred the resentment of the people;
though descendants of Yǔ and Tāng,
they could not secure the allegiance of a single person;
they disemboweled Bǐgān,
imprisoned Jīzǐ,
met death and the ruin of their state,
becoming the great shame of the world,
so that all later discussions of evil inevitably refer to them;
this exemplifies the fate of one not even tolerated by his own wife and children.
Thus, the supremely worthy rule all within the Four Seas,
as Tāng and Wǔ did;
the utterly incompetent are not tolerated even by their wives and children,
as Jié and Zhòu were.
Now, those who propose common theories
claim that Jié and Zhòu possessed the world
and had Tāng and Wǔ as their subjects—
is this not excessively erroneous?
It is like
a hunchbacked shaman or a lame exorcist greatly esteeming their own wisdom.
Thus, one may seize a state,
but one cannot seize the world;
one may steal a state,
but one cannot steal the world.
One who seizes may possess a state,
but cannot possess the world;
one may steal to gain a state,
but cannot gain the world thereby.
Why is this?
The answer:
A state is a minor instrument,
which a petty person may hold,
which may be obtained by petty ways,
and maintained by petty strength;
the world is a great instrument,
which a petty person cannot hold,
which cannot be obtained by petty ways,
nor maintained by petty strength.
A state may be held by a petty person,
yet it is not certain to avoid ruin;
the world, being of the greatest magnitude,
can only be held by a sage.
Those who propose common theories say:
"In the well-governed antiquity, there was no corporal punishment,
but symbolic punishments:
ink for tattooing;
a grass collar for nose-cutting;
a hemp garment for castration;
straw sandals for foot-amputation;
and an unhemmed reddish-brown garment for execution.
Such was the well-governed antiquity."
This is not so.
If it was indeed well-governed,
then naturally no one committed crimes,
so not only was corporal punishment unnecessary,
but symbolic punishments were also unneeded.
If it is thought that some might have committed crimes,
and punishments were merely lightened,
then killers would not die,
and injurers would not be punished.
When crimes are grave and punishments light,
ordinary people would not recognize the evil,
and no disorder could be greater.
The fundamental purpose of punishing people
is to prohibit violence and condemn evil,
and to warn against future offenses.
If killers do not die,
and injurers are not punished,
this is called favoring the violent and indulging the harmful,
not condemning evil.
Thus, symbolic punishments likely did not originate in well-governed antiquity,
but arose together in the disordered present.
Well-governed antiquity was not so.
All ranks, offices, rewards, and punishments
are retributions, each corresponding to its kind.
