If one thing is misjudged,
it becomes the beginning of disorder.
When virtue does not match position,
ability does not match office,
rewards do not fit achievements,
punishments do not fit crimes,
no misfortune is greater.
In the past, King Wǔ attacked the Shāng,
executed Zhòu,
cut off his head,
and hung it on a red banner.
To campaign against the violent and execute the brutal
is the pinnacle of governance;
killers die,
injurers are punished—
this is the same for all kings;
none know its origin.
When punishment fits the crime,
there is order;
when it does not fit,
there is disorder.
Thus, in order, punishments are heavy;
in disorder, they are light;
crimes in order are inherently grave,
crimes in disorder inherently minor.
The *Book of Documents* says:
"Punishments are light or heavy according to the age."
This refers to that.
Those who propose common theories:
"Why could Tāng and Wǔ not enforce prohibitions?
What is the reason?"
They say:
"Chǔ and Yuè did not accept their control."
This is not so.
Tāng and Wǔ were the most capable in the world at enforcing prohibitions.
Tāng resided in Bó,
King Wǔ in Hào,
both territories of a hundred *lǐ*,
yet the world was unified,
the feudal lords were their subjects,
and all accessible regions
trembled and submitted, transformed and obedient—
why would only Chǔ and Yuè not accept control?
The system of such kings
adapts tools and implements to the terrain,
and grades tributes according to distance—
how could they be uniform?
Thus, the Lǔ used táng,
the Wèi
used kē,
the Qí used a single leather,
for lands and customs differ,
and tools and ornaments must vary.
Hence, states of Xià shared the same service and rites,
while states of Mán, Yí, Róng, and Dí shared service but not the system.
Within the domain, Diàn service;
outside, Hóu service;
Hóu and Wèi areas, Bīn service;
Mán and Yí, Yāo service;
Róng and Dí, Huāng service.
Diàn service offers daily sacrifices,
Hóu service monthly sacrifices,
Bīn service seasonal offerings,
Yāo service annual tributes,
Huāng service acknowledges the king once.
Daily sacrifices, monthly sacrifices, seasonal offerings, annual tributes—
this is called adapting tools to the terrain
and grading tributes by distance,
the system of kings.
Those states like Chǔ and Yuè,
with seasonal offerings, annual tributes,
and acknowledgment of the king,
must they match the daily and monthly sacrifices
to be considered under control?
This is a distorted view,
like the emaciated in a ditch,
unfit to discuss the kingly system.
As the saying goes:
"The shallow cannot fathom the deep,
the foolish cannot plan with the wise,
the frog in a well cannot be told of the joys of the Eastern Sea."
This refers to that.
Those who propose common theories say:
"Yáo and Shùn abdicated and yielded."
This is not so.
The Son of Heaven
holds the most honored position,
unequaled in the world—
to whom would he yield?
With virtue pure and complete,
wisdom brilliantly clear,
facing south to govern the world,
all people tremble and submit, transformed and obedient,
no scholars are hidden,
no goodness overlooked,
those in agreement are right,
those differing are wrong—
how could there be any yielding of the world?
It is said:
"They abdicated upon death."
This is again incorrect.
When a sage king is on the throne,
he determines rank according to virtue,
assigns offices based on capability,
enabling all people to bear their duties and each to find their proper place;
those who cannot use righteousness to control profit,
or disguise their nature with artifice,
are all made commoners.
After the sage king has passed away,
if there is no sage in the world,
then certainly none is worthy to claim the world.
If there is a sage in the world
among the descendants,
then the world will not disintegrate;
the court positions remain unchanged,
the state system unaltered,
the world tranquil
no different from before;
succeeding Yáo with another Yáo,
what change could there be?
If the sage is not among the descendants but among the three highest ministers,
then the world would turn to him,
as if restored and revitalized,
the world tranquil
no different from before,
succeeding Yáo with another Yáo,
what change could there be?
Only changing courts and altering systems is difficult.
Thus, while the Son of Heaven lives, the world uniformly
submits and is well-governed,
with rank determined by virtue;
upon his death, one capable of ruling the world will surely emerge.
When the distinctions of ritual and righteousness are fully realized,
what use is abdication?
It is said:
"They abdicated due to old age and decline."
This is again incorrect.
While blood, energy, sinews, and strength may decline,
wisdom, deliberation, choice, and rejection do not.
It is said:
"The elderly cannot bear the toil and rest."
This is the argument of those who fear affairs.
The Son of Heaven holds the heaviest responsibility yet enjoys the utmost leisure physically,
his mind most joyful and will unyielding,
his body not laboring,
his honor unsurpassed.
He wears robes of five colors,
mixed with intermediate shades,
layered with embroidered patterns,
adorned with pearls and jades;
his meals feature the grand sacrifice with rare delicacies,
awaiting the finest flavors,
served gracefully,
with attendants replacing him in tasting,
"Yōng" music playing until the clearing of sacrifices to the five gods,
a hundred bearers of offerings
waiting in the western chamber;
residing, he sets up canopies and screens,
sits with his back to the patterned screen,
while feudal lords hasten below the hall;
exiting the door, shamans and wizards perform rites,
leaving the gate, ancestral sacrifices are conducted,
riding the grand carriage, treading on rush mats for comfort,
with fragrant zhǐ orchids placed beside to nourish the nose,
inlaid crossbars ahead to nourish the eyes,
harmonious bell sounds,
steps keeping time with "Wǔ" and "Xiàng" music,
harness bells matching "Sháo" and "Hù" melodies to nourish the ears,
the three highest ministers presenting the yoke and reins,
feudal lords holding wheels and flanking the carriage ahead of the horses,
major lords following in order,
high officials next,
minor lords and chief scholars after them,
common soldiers armored and lining the road,
ordinary people hiding
daring not to look up.
At rest, he is like a great deity,
in action, like the celestial emperor;
to maintain old age and nurture decline,
is there any better way than this?
Old age means rest,
but does rest entail such peace, joy, and tranquility?
Therefore, it is said:
Feudal lords may grow old,
but the Son of Heaven does not.
There may be abdication in states,
but not in the world,
this is consistent throughout history.
To say "Yáo and Shùn abdicated and yielded"
is false words,
the transmission of the shallow,
the theory of the ignorant,
who do not understand the principle of conformity and opposition,
the variations between small and great, ideal and actual,
and cannot be involved in discussing the great principles of the world.
A popular theory says:
'Yáo and Shùn could not transform everyone through education.'
Why is that?
They say:
'Dān Zhū and Xiàng were not transformed.'
This is incorrect.
Yáo and Shùn were the best at educating and transforming in the world,
facing south to govern the world,
all among the living were stirred to obey and follow, transformed to compliance;
yet only Dān Zhū and Xiàng were not transformed,
this was not the fault of Yáo and Shùn,
but the crime of Dān Zhū and Xiàng.
Yáo and Shùn were the heroes of the world;
Dān Zhū and Xiàng were the freaks of the world,
the petty ones of their time.
Now those who hold popular theories
do not blame Dān Zhū and Xiàng
but criticize Yáo and Shùn,
is that not greatly mistaken!
This is what is called a freakish theory.
Yì and Péng Méng were the best archers in the world,
yet could not hit the target with crooked bows and arrows;
Wáng Liáng
and Zào Fǔ were the best charioteers in the world,
yet could not go far with unruly horses and broken carriages;
Yáo and Shùn were the best at educating and transforming in the world,
yet could not transform the freakish and petty.
What era lacks freaks?
What time lacks the petty?
From Tàihào and Suìrén onward, all have had them.
Thus, those who create such theories are unlucky,
learners suffer their harm,
those who reject them are fortunate.
The "Shī" says:
"The calamities of the lower people,
are not sent down from heaven;
gathering to agree, turning backs in hatred,
the strife chiefly comes from men."
This refers to it.
A popular theory says:
"In antiquity, burials were simple,
coffins three inches thick,
burial clothes three layers,
burial fields not interfering with farming,
so they were not dug up.
In the chaotic present, burials are lavish, coffins decorated,
hence they are dug up."
This fails to understand the way of order,
and does not examine the reasons for digging or not digging.
Whenever people steal,
it must be for a purpose,
not to prepare for insufficiency, (
sufficiency) but to add to abundance.
And the sage kings in nurturing the people,
made all wealthy and prosperous,
ample yet not knowing sufficiency,
but not allowing excess beyond measure.
Thus thieves did not steal,
robbers did not stab,
dogs and pigs disdained grains,
and farmers and merchants could all yield goods and wealth;
the beauty of customs,
men and women did not meet on roads,
and the common people were ashamed to pick up lost items.
Therefore, Confucius said:
"When the world has the Way,
thieves are the first to change!"
Even with the body full of pearls and jades,
the coffin filled with embroideries,
the outer coffin stuffed with gold,
added with cinnabar,
layered with azurite,
rhinoceros and ivory as trees,
lánggān, lóngzī, huájìn as fruits,
people still would not dig it up.
Why is that?
Because the cunning pursuit of profit slows,
and the shame of violating one's lot is great.
But the chaotic present is the opposite:
those above rule without laws,
those below act without measure;
the wise cannot plan,
the capable cannot govern,
the worthy cannot be employed.
If so,
then above, nature is lost,
below, earth's benefits are lost,
in between, human harmony is lost;
thus all affairs are abandoned,
goods and wealth are depleted,
and calamity and chaos arise.
Kings and dukes suffer from insufficiency above,
common people freeze, starve, and become emaciated below;
then Jié and Zhòu-like figures gather,
and thieves and robbers assault and plunder to endanger those above;
inevitably behaving like beasts,
greedy as tigers and wolves,
Thus they would cure giants and roast infants.
If so, then what fault is there in digging up people's graves,
prying open their mouths to seek profit?
Even if buried naked,
they would still be dug up,
so how can burial be secure?
Those robbers would devour their flesh and gnaw their bones.
Some claim:
"In ancient times burial was simple,
hence no grave-robbing occurred;
in chaotic modern times burial is lavish,
hence grave-robbing happens."
This is merely deceitful people propagating erroneous theories,
to deceive the foolish and lead them into pitfalls
while stealthily profiting themselves -
this is what we call great wickedness.
The Tradition says:
"Endangering others to secure oneself,
harming others to benefit oneself."
This describes such people.
Zǐ Sòngzǐ said:
"Clearly understanding that being insulted is not disgraceful
prevents people from fighting.
Since all consider being insulted disgraceful,
they fight;
knowing being insulted is not disgraceful,
they would not fight."
I respond:
"Then do you also believe human nature does not resent insult?"
He says:
"They resent it but feel no disgrace."
I say:
"If so,
then you certainly won't achieve your desired outcome.
When people fight,
it's always because they resent something,
not because they feel disgraced.
Now actors, dwarves, and jesters endure insults without fighting -
is this because they know being insulted isn't disgraceful?
They don't fight
because they feel no resentment.
If someone enters another's pigpen,
steals their pigs,
the owner will seize weapons and pursue,
regardless of life or injury -
is this because losing pigs is disgraceful?
They don't fear fighting
because they resent the theft.
Even if feeling insulted is disgraceful,
without resentment, no fighting occurs;
even knowing insult isn't disgraceful,
with resentment, fighting inevitably follows.
Thus whether people fight or not
doesn't depend on feeling disgraced or not,
but on feeling resentful or not.
Now Zǐ Sòngzǐ cannot resolve people's resentment of insult,
but insists on persuading them not to feel disgraced -
isn't this greatly mistaken!
Even with a golden tongue and worn-out mouth,
it would be useless.
Not knowing it's useless
shows ignorance;
knowing it's useless
yet still deceiving people
shows inhumanity.
Both inhuman and ignorant -
no disgrace is greater than this.
If intending to benefit people,
but actually bringing no benefit,
one only retreats with great disgrace.
No doctrine is more flawed than this."
Zǐ Sòngzǐ said:
"Being insulted is not disgraceful."
I respond:
All discussions must establish
lofty standards first.
Without lofty standards, right and wrong remain confused
and disputes unresolved.
Thus I've heard:
'The world's supreme standard,
the boundary between right and wrong,
the origin of duties and designations -
this is the kingly system.'
Therefore all discourse and mandates
take the sage kings as teachers,
and the sage kings' distinction
lies in honor and disgrace.
Here are two aspects:
there is righteous honor,
and positional honor;
there is righteous disgrace,
and positional disgrace.
Cultivated will,
abundant virtue,
clear wisdom -
this is honor arising from within,
called righteous honor.
High rank,
ample salary,
dominant position,
above as Son of Heaven or feudal lords,
below as ministers or officials -
this is honor coming from without,
called positional honor.
Debauchery and sloth,
transgression and chaos,
arrogance and greed -
this is disgrace arising from within,
called righteous disgrace.
Insults and assaults,
beatings and amputations,
executions and dismemberments,
bondage and torture -
this is disgrace coming from without,
called positional disgrace.
These are honor and disgrace's two aspects.
Thus gentlemen may suffer positional disgrace
but not righteous disgrace;
petty men may enjoy positional honor
but not righteous honor.
Positional disgrace doesn't prevent being Yáo,
positional honor doesn't prevent being Jié.
Righteous honor and positional honor
only gentlemen possess both;
righteous disgrace and positional disgrace
only petty men possess both.
This is honor and disgrace's distinction.
Sage kings take this as model,
officials take this as way,
functionaries take this as duty,
common people make this custom -
unchangedable for ten thousand generations."
"Now Zǐ Sòngzǐ acts otherwise:
only bending himself accommodatingly,
hoping to change this overnight -
his doctrine certainly won't work.
It's like
trying to dam rivers and seas with bricks,
or having Jiāoyáo support Tàishān -
he'll stumble and break
in no time.
You followers of Zǐ Sòngzǐ
should probably stop him,
lest he injure himself."
Zǐ Sòngzǐ said:
"Human nature
desires little,
yet all consider their own nature
as desiring much -
this is error."
So he leads his followers,
debates his theories,
illustrates with analogies,
trying to show people's nature desires little.
I respond:
"Then do you also believe human nature desires
eyes not to see extreme colors,
ears not to hear extreme sounds,
mouth not to taste extreme flavors,
nose not to smell extreme scents,
body not to enjoy extreme comfort?
─These five extremes,
does human nature not desire them?"
He says:
"Human nature
desires these indeed."
I say:
"If so,
then your theory certainly won't work.
Claiming human nature desires these five extremes but not abundance
is like
saying human nature desires wealth and status but not goods,
or loves beauty but hates Xī Shī.
"The ancients did otherwise.
Knowing human nature desires abundance not scarcity,
they rewarded with wealth and punished with deprivation -
this all kings shared.
Thus superior worthies receive the world's emolument,
lesser worthies receive a state's,
minor worthies receive land,
while honest commoners have adequate food and clothing.
Now Zǐ Sòngzǐ claims human nature desires little not much.
Then did former kings reward with what people don't desire,
and punish with what they desire?
No disorder is greater than this.
Now Zǐ Sòngzǐ solemnly promotes his doctrine,
gathers followers,
establishes school,
completes texts -
yet his doctrine ultimately mistakes perfect order for perfect disorder,
isn't this greatly mistaken!"
"How did rituals originate?"
The reply:
"Humans are born with desires.
When desires are not fulfilled,
they cannot but seek;
when seeking lacks measure and boundaries,
they cannot but contend;
contention leads to disorder,
disorder leads to exhaustion.
The ancient kings detested such disorder,
thus they established rituals and righteousness to differentiate,
to nurture people's desires,
to supply people's seeking,
ensuring desires do not exhaust resources,
and resources do not yield to desires,
with both sustaining and growing together—
this is why rituals arose.
Therefore, rituals are about nurturing.
Grains, livestock, and fine foods,
harmoniously blended with five flavors,
nurture the mouth;
the fragrance of pepper and orchids,
nurture the nose;
carved and engraved ornaments,
embroidered patterns and designs,
nurture the eyes;
bells, drums, pipes, and chimes,
lutes, zithers, reed pipes, and mouth organs,
nurture the ears;
spacious rooms, fine mats,
bamboo mats, beds, stools, and mats,
nurture the body.
Thus, rituals are about nurturing."
"The noble person, having attained this nurturing,
also values distinction.
What is meant by distinction?"
The reply:
"Nobility and baseness have their ranks,
elder and younger have their differences,
wealth, poverty, lightness, and heaviness all have their correspondences.
Thus, the Son of Heaven's grand carriage with fine mats
nurtures the body;
fragrant herbs placed beside
nurture the nose;
the ornate crossbar in front
nurtures the eyes;
the harmonious sounds of bells,
matching the 'Wǔ' and 'Xiàng' when walking,
and the 'Sháo' and 'Hù' when hastening,
nurture the ears;
the nine-tailed dragon banner
nurtures trust;
the recumbent rhinoceros, standing tiger,
dragon-hide trappings, silk tassels, and dragon decorations,
nurture authority;
thus, the horses for the grand carriage
must be truly trained and obedient
before they are mounted,
to ensure safety.
Who understands that risking death for integrity nurtures life!
Who understands that spending resources nurtures wealth!
Who understands that reverence and deference nurture safety!
Who understands that ritual principles and patterns nurture emotions!
Thus, if one only sees life,
such a person will surely die;
if one only sees profit,
such a person will surely be harmed;
if one seeks ease in laziness and cowardice,
such a person will surely face danger;
if one finds joy solely in emotional indulgence,
such a person will surely perish.
Therefore, if one unifies with ritual righteousness,
then both are attained;
if one unifies with emotions and nature,
then both are lost.
Thus, the Confucians aim to help people attain both,
while the Mohists lead people to lose both—
this is the distinction between Confucians and Mohists."
Rituals have three foundations:
Heaven and Earth
are the foundation of life;
ancestors
are the foundation of kinship;
rulers and teachers
are the foundation of order.
Without Heaven and Earth,
how could life exist?
Without ancestors,
how could one be born?
Without rulers and teachers,
how could there be order?
If any of these three is lacking,
there is no peace for people.
Thus, rituals serve Heaven above,
Earth below,
honor ancestors,
and exalt rulers and teachers—
these are the three foundations of ritual.
Therefore, the king honors Heaven's ancestor,
feudal lords dare not destroy this,
officials and scholars have constant ancestral temples,
to distinguish noble origins.
Honoring origins is the root of attainment.
Suburban sacrifices are reserved for the Son of Heaven,
while altars of the soil stop at feudal lords,
and the Way extends to officials and scholars,
to distinguish noble and humble: the noble serve the noble,
the humble serve the humble,
what is great is made grand,
what is small is kept minor.
Thus, those who possess the empire serve seven generations,
those who possess a state serve five generations,
those with land for five chariots serve three generations,
those with land for three chariots serve two generations,
laborers who eat by hand cannot establish ancestral temples,
to distinguish accumulated merit:
deep accumulation spreads blessings widely,
shallow accumulation spreads blessings narrowly.
In the great sacrifice,
plain water is elevated,
raw fish is offered on the stand,
the unseasoned broth comes first,
honoring the roots of food and drink.
In the great sacrifice,
plain water is elevated yet sweet wine is used;
in meals, millet and sorghum precede fine rice;
in offerings,
the unseasoned broth comes first before various delicacies are enjoyed,
honoring the roots while embracing practicality.
Honoring roots is called refinement,
embracing practicality is called principle,
the two combine to form culture,
returning to the Great One—
this is called the highest excellence.
Thus, elevating plain water in the cup,
offering raw fish on the stand,
presenting the unseasoned broth first in the vessel,
are one in principle.
The libation cup not being drained,
the stand at the ceremony's end not tasted,
the three offerings not eaten,
are one in principle.
Before the grand wedding ceremony begins,
before the ancestral temple receives the impersonator,
before the initial laying out of the deceased,
are one in principle.
The plain canopy of the grand carriage not assembled,
the hemp crown at the suburban sacrifice,
the scattered hemp in mourning garments first,
are one in principle.
In the three-year mourning,
weeping without echo;
the song of the 'Qīng Miào',
one lead with three responses;
a single suspended bell,
with drum and diaphragm preferred,
red strings and open holes,
are one in principle.
All rituals
begin with simplicity,
achieve form through refinement,
and end in joyful fulfillment.
Thus, at their most complete,
emotion and form are both fully expressed;
next,
emotion and form alternate in dominance;
at the lowest, emotion is restored to return to the Great One.
Through it, Heaven and Earth are harmonized,
sun and moon shine,
four seasons follow order,
stars and planets move,
rivers flow,
all things flourish;
likes and dislikes are moderated,
joy and anger are appropriate;
applied below, it brings obedience,
applied above, it brings clarity,
all things change without chaos,
but if neglected, it is lost.
How ultimate rituals are!
Established as the highest standard,
nothing in the world can add or subtract from them.
Root and branch follow each other,
end and beginning respond to each other,
most refined yet with distinctions,
most discerning yet with reasoning.
Those in the world who follow it achieve order,
those who do not fall into chaos;
followers gain safety,
non-followers face danger;
followers survive,
non-followers perish.
Petty minds cannot fathom this.
The principles of ritual are truly profound.
Investigations into "hardness and whiteness" or "sameness and difference" drown when they enter it;
its principles are truly great,
so theories that arbitrarily create canonical systems or are biased and shallow perish when they enter it;
its principles are truly lofty,
so behaviors like arrogance, indulgence, and considering oneself superior by despising customs collapse when they enter it.
Thus, when the marking line is truly laid out,
one cannot be deceived about crookedness and straightness;
when the balance is truly suspended,
one cannot be deceived about lightness and heaviness;
when the compass and square are truly set,
one cannot be deceived about squareness and roundness;
when the gentleman is well-versed in ritual,
one cannot deceive him with fraud and falsehood.
Therefore, the marking line
is the ultimate in straightness,
the balance
is the ultimate in fairness,
the compass and square
are the ultimate in squareness and roundness,
and ritual
is the ultimate of the human way.
However, those who do not model themselves on ritual
nor affirm ritual
are called people without direction;
those who model themselves on ritual
and affirm ritual
are called scholars with direction.
Being able to reflect within the framework of ritual
is called being capable of thought;
being able to remain unwavering within the framework of ritual
is called being capable of steadfastness.
Capable of thought and steadfastness,
and adding a love for it,
this makes a sage.
Thus, heaven
is the ultimate in height,
earth
is the ultimate in depth,
the boundless
is the ultimate in breadth,
and the sage
is the ultimate of the Way.
Therefore, learners
steadfastly learn to become sages,
not merely to be people without direction.
Ritual
uses material goods as its means,
distinguishes noble and base through its patterns,
varies in application according to quantity,
and takes richness and reduction as its essentials.
When the patterns and principles are elaborate,
and emotional expression is restrained,
this is the richness of ritual;
when the patterns and principles are simple,
and emotional expression is abundant,
this is the reduction of ritual;
when patterns and principles, and emotional expression, serve as inner and outer, surface and core,
operating together in mixture,
this is the middle course of ritual.
Thus, the gentleman applies its richness in high matters,
employs its reduction in low matters,
and dwells in the middle course for intermediate matters.
Whether walking, running, or galloping fiercely, he does not go beyond this,
for this is the courtyard and palace of the gentleman.
One who possesses this
is a scholar-gentleman;
one who is outside of this
is a common person;
within this framework,
moving about freely and comprehensively,
perfectly attaining its sequence,
this is the sage.
Therefore, depth
is the accumulation of ritual,
breadth
is the expanse of ritual,
height
is the loftiness of ritual,
and clarity
is the completeness of ritual.
The Book of Songs says:
"The rituals are all in measure,
laughter and talk are all appropriate."
This expresses it.
Ritual
is meticulous in governing life and death.
Life is the beginning of a person,
death is the end of a person:
when both end and beginning are well-handled,
the human way is complete.
Thus, the gentleman reveres the beginning and is cautious about the end.
Being consistent from start to finish
is the way of the gentleman,
the pattern of ritual and righteousness.
To treat life generously but death meagerly
is to respect the conscious state
and neglect the unconscious state,
which is the way of the treacherous and a heart of betrayal.
For a gentleman to treat even a servant or a stable hand with a betraying heart
would still bring shame,
how much more so when serving those he honors and loves!
Thus, death as a principle
occurs once and cannot be repeated,
so the means by which ministers show utmost respect to their ruler,
and sons show utmost respect to their parents,
are fully expressed here.
Therefore, in serving the living, if one is not loyal and generous,
not reverent and cultured,
it is called rudeness;
in sending off the dead, if one is not loyal and generous,
not reverent and cultured,
it is called stinginess.
The gentleman despises rudeness and is ashamed of stinginess,
hence the Son of Heaven has seven layers of inner and outer coffins,
feudal lords have five,
high officials have three,
scholars have two,
and then there are regulations for the amount and quality of burial clothes and goods,
and gradations of decorative shrouds and emblems
to honor and adorn them,
making life and death, end and beginning, as one;
this unity is sufficient to fulfill human wishes,
and is the way of the former kings,
the ultimate standard for loyal ministers and filial sons.
The funeral of the Son of Heaven moves the whole realm
and involves the feudal lords;
the funeral of a feudal lord moves the entire state
and involves the high officials;
the funeral of a high official moves the whole country
and involves the refined scholars;
the funeral of a refined scholar moves the whole district
and involves friends;
the funeral of a commoner assembles the clan and community,
moving the local region.
For the funeral of a punished criminal,
the clan and community may not assemble,
only the wife and children are involved,
with a coffin three inches thick,
three sets of burial clothes and quilts,
no adornment of the coffin,
no procession during the day,
buried at dusk,
with plain edges to the burial garments, and thus buried,
returning without the rituals of weeping,
without mourning garments of hemp,
without distinctions in the duration of mourning for close or distant relatives,
each returning to their normal state,
each restored to their beginning,
once buried,
as if there had been no death, and it ends.
This is called the ultimate disgrace.
Ritual
is meticulous in ensuring that auspicious and inauspicious matters do not interfere with each other.
At the time when listening for breath with floss on the mouth,
even loyal ministers and filial sons know the person is near death,
yet they do not seek the burial implements;
they shed tears and are fearful,
yet the hope for life persists,
and efforts to sustain life do not cease;
only after death occurs
do they begin
to prepare them.
Thus, even a well-prepared household
must wait a day before encoffining,
and three days before donning mourning garments,
then those from afar are notified to come,
and the preparation of items begins.
Therefore, for the encoffining,
the longest does not exceed seventy days,
the shortest is no less than fifty days.
Why is this?
It is said: so that those from afar can arrive,
all requests can be fulfilled,
all matters can be accomplished;
the loyalty is utmost,
the observance is great,
the cultural forms are complete.
Then, in the early part of the month, the burial site is divined,
and in the latter part, the burial day is divined,
then the burial takes place.
At that time,
if it is right to stop,
who can proceed?
If it is right to proceed,
who can stop?
Thus, a burial after three months,
with the appearance in death adorned as in life,
is not merely to detain the dead to comfort the living;
it is to express the principle of honoring and remembering with utmost reverence.
The general principles of funeral rites are:
to transform and adorn,
to move and distance,
to endure and pacify.
Thus, in the way of death,
if not adorned, it becomes repulsive,
and if repulsive, there is no grief;
if too familiar, it becomes trivialized,
and if trivialized, it becomes tiresome,
if tiresome, it is forgotten,
and if forgotten, there is no respect.
To lose one's revered parent in a single morning,
and for those who send off the deceased
to show neither grief nor respect,
is akin to the behavior of beasts;
the gentleman is ashamed of this.
Therefore, transforming and adorning
serves to eliminate repulsiveness;
moving and distancing
serves to fulfill respect;
enduring and pacifying
serves to comfort the living.
Rites involve cutting long and continuing short,
reducing excess,
supplementing insufficiency,
expressing the patterns of love and respect,
and nurturing the beauty of righteous conduct.
Thus, adornment and roughness,
music and weeping,
tranquility and sorrow,
are opposites;
yet rites combine and employ them,
applying each at the appropriate time and alternating their use.
Therefore, adornment, music, and tranquility
serve to maintain balance in auspicious times;
roughness, weeping, and sorrow
serve to uphold stability in inauspicious times.
Thus, in establishing adornment,
it does not become frivolous or seductive;
in establishing rough mourning attire,
it does not lead to emaciation or neglect;
in establishing music and tranquility,
it does not descend into indulgence or laziness;
in establishing weeping and sorrow,
it does not become oppressive or life-damaging:
this is the middle path of rites.
Thus, the changes in emotion and appearance
are sufficient to distinguish auspicious from inauspicious,
to clarify the distinctions of noble and base, close and distant,
and this is the limit;
beyond this,
it is artifice,
and even if difficult,
the gentleman disdains it.
Therefore, one eats according to one's measure of food,
and ties the belt according to the waist's need.
To compete in emaciation through self-harm
is the way of deceitful people
not the pattern of ritual righteousness,
nor the true feeling of a filial child,
but rather done with ulterior motives.
Thus, joy and smoothness,
sorrow and distress,
are the feelings of auspiciousness and inauspiciousness, joy and sorrow, expressed in countenance.
Singing, teasing, and laughter,
weeping, wailing, and crying,
are the feelings of auspiciousness and inauspiciousness, joy and sorrow, expressed in sound.
Livestock,
rice and grain,
wine and ale,
fish and meat,
congee,
beans and greens,
water and broth,
are the feelings of auspiciousness and inauspiciousness, joy and sorrow, expressed in food and drink.
Ceremonial caps,
embroidered robes,
patterned fabrics,
coarse cloth,
mourning garments and hempen bands,
thin and fine hemp,
straw sandals,
are the feelings of auspiciousness and inauspiciousness, joy and sorrow, expressed in clothing.
Spacious rooms,
thatched roofs and rough walls,
mats and rushes,
beds and mats,
thatched huts,
makeshift shelters,
sleeping on brushwood with a clod for a pillow,
are the feelings of auspiciousness and inauspiciousness, joy and sorrow, expressed in dwelling.
These two sets of feelings
have inherent beginnings in human life.
As for cutting and continuing,
broadening and narrowing,
augmenting and reducing,
categorizing and exhausting,
enhancing and beautifying,
so that root and tip, end and beginning
are all in harmonious order
and perfectly complete, sufficient to be a model for ten thousand generations,
this is the work of rites,
and unless one is a gentleman who has diligently cultivated and practiced,
none can understand it.
Therefore it is said:
Human nature is the raw material of beginnings;
conscious effort is the flourishing of pattern and order.
Without nature, effort has nothing to apply to;
without effort, nature cannot beautify itself.
When nature and effort combine
, then the reputation of the sage is achieved,
and the task of unifying the world is accomplished.
Therefore it is said:
Heaven and earth combine and all things are born,
yīn and yáng interact and transformations arise,
nature and effort combine and the world is ordered.
Heaven can produce things,
but cannot distinguish them;
earth can support humans,
but cannot govern them;
all things in the universe, the category of living humans,
await the sage to then be differentiated.
The "Shī" says:
"He pacified the hundred spirits,
and the rivers and lofty peaks."
This expresses it.
Funeral rites
use the living to adorn the dead,
greatly imitating their life to send them off in death.
Thus, to treat death as life,
to treat the departed as present,
is consistent from beginning to end.
At the start of death,
washing the hair and body, tying the hair, placing rice and pearls in the mouth,
imitates the practices of life.
If not washing the hair, then moisten the comb three times and stop;
if not bathing, then moisten the cloth three times and stop.
Fill the ears with jade plugs,
place uncooked rice in the mouth,
put dry bones in the mouth,
reversing the methods of life.
Set out undergarments,
add three layers of clothing,
with a sash but no hook belt.
Set a covering for the face and a blindfold,
tie the hair without cap or hairpin.
Write the name,
place it on the memorial tablet,
so the name is not seen and the coffin alone is prominent.
The offered vessels
include a helmet-like cap without ties,
earthenware jars, empty and not filled,
mats but no bed frames,
wooden vessels unfinished and unpolished,
pottery vessels not fully formed,
thin vessels not usable.
Yú and shēng reed instruments are present but not harmonious,
qín and sè string instruments are strung but not tuned.
The carriage is buried but the horses return,
signifying they are not used,
preparing the vessels of life to go to the tomb,
imitating the way of moving.
Brief and not exhaustive,
resembling but not functional,
the carriage is hurriedly buried,
metal and leather reins and traces not included,
making clear they are not used.
Imitating the way of moving,
and further clarifying non-use,
all these serve to emphasize grief.
Thus, the vessels of life are adorned but not functional,
the ceremonial vessels resemble but are not used.
In all rites,
serving the living
adorns joy;
sending off the dead
adorns grief;
sacrificial offerings
adorn respect;
military affairs
adorn authority:
this is the same for all kings,
consistent in ancient and modern times,
though none know its origin.
Thus, the tomb mound resembles a house;
the inner and outer coffins resemble the boards, covers, and canopies;
the absence of curtains and decorative fringes
resembles the thin curtains and coverings;
the protective frames
resemble the plastered thatch and barriers.
Therefore, funeral rites
have no other purpose
than to clarify the meaning of life and death,
to send off with grief and respect
and finally to conceal completely.
Thus, burial and interment are
to show reverence for the physical form;
sacrificial offerings
are to serve the spirit with reverence;
the inscriptions, eulogies, and genealogical records
are to reverently transmit their names.
Serving the living
is to adorn the beginning,
and sending off the dead
is to adorn the end.
When both end and beginning are fulfilled,
the tasks of a filial son are completed,
and the way of the sage is made complete.
To be harsh to the dead and attached to the living is called cruelty;
to be harsh to the living and attached to the dead is called delusion;
to kill the living to send off the dead is called villainy.
To imitate their life in great detail to send off their death,
so that death and life, end and beginning, are all appropriately and well handled,
this is the model of ritual and righteousness,
and it is the Confucians who embody it.
Why is the mourning period three years?
It is said:
It is established according to human emotions to create form,
thereby adorning the community,
distinguishing the degrees of closeness and distance, nobility and baseness,
and cannot be increased or decreased.
Hence it is said:
It is a rule that nowhere can be altered.
For great wounds, the duration is long;
for severe pain, the healing is slow.
The three-year mourning period,
established according to human emotions to create form,
is for the utmost pain;
the hemmed sackcloth, the rough staff, living in a hut, eating gruel, using straw for a mat, and a clod for a pillow—these are the adornments for the utmost pain.
The three-year mourning period
ends after twenty-five months;
though grief is not yet exhausted,
and longing not yet forgotten,
yet ritual cuts it off here.
Is it not because sending off the dead must have an end,
and returning to life must have its measure?
All that live between heaven and earth,
if they belong to the blood-and-breath kind, must have awareness;
and those with awareness all love their kind.
Now, when great birds and beasts lose their companions or mates,
after passing months and seasons,
they will surely turn back;
passing their old haunts,
they will surely linger there,
crying out,
pacing to and fro,
hesitating,
and only then are able to leave.
As for smaller ones like swallows and sparrows,
they still chirp mournfully for a moment,
and only then can leave.
Thus, among the blood-and-breath kinds, none have greater awareness than humans;
therefore, humans' attachment to their parents
lasts until death without end.
Should we follow the foolish, base, and depraved people?
They would forget by evening if their parent died in the morning;
but if we indulge this,
then they would be inferior even to birds and beasts.
How could they live together in groups without disorder?
Should we follow the cultivated gentlemen?
Then the three-year mourning period,
ending in twenty-five months,
passes like a team of horses galloping past a crack,
yet if we extend it,
it would be endless.
Therefore, the ancient kings and sages established a moderate measure for it,
so that it is sufficient to complete the pattern of principle,
and then it is set aside.
Then how is it divided?
It is said:
For the closest kin, it ends after one year.
Why is this?
It is said:
Heaven and earth have already changed,
the four seasons have completed a cycle,
and all things in the cosmos have made a new beginning.
Thus, the ancient kings used this to symbolize it.
Then why three years?
It is said: To add grandeur to it,
making it double,
hence two cycles.
Why are there periods below nine months?
It is said: To make them less.
Thus, three years is considered grand,
the three-month and
five-month mourning are considered reduced,
and the one-year and nine-month are intermediate.
Above, it takes its image from heaven;
below, it takes its image from earth;
in the middle, it takes its standard from humans;
thus, the principle by which humans live together in harmony is fully expressed.
Therefore, the three-year mourning period
is the ultimate expression of human culture,
and this is called the utmost grandeur;
it is what all kings shared alike, and what is uniform from ancient to modern times.
Why is the mourning for a ruler
set at three years?
It is said:
The ruler is the master of order and distinction,
the source of cultural pattern,
and the fullest expression of emotion and demeanor.
To lead one another in honoring him supremely—
is this not fitting?
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Affable and courteous gentlemen,
are the parents of the people."
Those gentlemen
truly have the saying of being parents to the people.
A father can give birth to them,
but cannot feed them;
a mother can feed them,
but cannot teach and instruct them;
the ruler
can both feed them
and is good at teaching and instructing them.
Is three years not complete?
A wet nurse, who feeds them,
is mourned for three months;
a nurturing mother, who clothes them,
is mourned for nine months;
the ruler, who provides for them comprehensively,
is mourned for three years—is that not complete?
To have this leads to order;
to lose it leads to chaos—
this is the ultimate in culture;
to have it brings safety;
to lose it brings danger—
this is the ultimate in emotion.
When both ultimates are accumulated,
to serve him with three years
is still insufficient,
but there is simply no way to extend it further.
Thus, the altar of soil is for sacrificing to the spirit of soil;
the altar of grain is for sacrificing to the spirit of grain;
the suburban sacrifice
unites all kings in heaven and sacrifices to them.
Why is the encoffining period three months?
It is said: To magnify it,
to honor it;
it is for the utmost grandeur,
for the utmost closeness.
When about to move and place it,
to transfer it,
to leave the palace and return to the mound,
the ancient kings feared it would lack refinement,
so they extended the period,
making the days sufficient.
Thus, for the Son of Heaven, it is seven months;
for feudal lords, five months;
for high officials, three months—
all to allow time sufficient to accommodate the affairs,
the affairs sufficient to accommodate completion,
completion sufficient to accommodate refinement,
refinement sufficient to accommodate full preparation.
To fully prepare and accommodate all things comprehensively is called the Way.
Sacrifice is the accumulation of the thoughts and memories of the mind and will.
Feelings of change and sorrow cannot but arise at times.
Thus, in times of human joy and harmony,
even loyal ministers and filial sons will feel changes and have their moments.
What they feel
is a very great stirring;
if it is simply suppressed,
then for the accumulated thoughts and will, they feel sorrowful and unsatisfied;
for the ritual forms, they feel lacking and incomplete.
Therefore, the ancient kings established forms for it,
and the meaning of honoring the honorable and loving the kin reached its peak.
Hence it is said:
Sacrifice is the accumulation of the thoughts and memories of the mind and will,
the peak of loyalty, faithfulness, love, and reverence,
the height of ritual form and cultural demeanor.
Unless one is a sage,
none can understand it.
Sages understand it clearly;
scholars and gentlemen practice it contentedly;
officials take it as their duty;
the common people make it their custom.
For gentlemen, it is considered the way of humanity;
for the common people, it is considered the affairs of ghosts.
Thus, bells and drums, pipes and chimes,
lutes and zithers, reed organs and mouth organs,
the Sháo, the Xià, the Hù,
the Wǔ, the Zhuó, the Huán, the Shuò, and the Xiàng,
are the means by which the gentleman gives patterned expression to the changes and transformations of his joy and delight.
The sackcloth mourning garments, the staff of wild mulberry, the mourning hut, the eating of gruel, the sleeping on straw, the pillow of earth,
are the means by which the gentleman gives patterned expression to the changes and transformations of his grief and pain.
The army has its regulations,
punishments and laws have their gradations,
and none fails to match the crime,
are the means by which the gentleman gives patterned expression to the changes and transformations of his loathing and hatred.
Divining by shell and stalk, observing the days, fasting and purification,
sweeping and cleaning,
the offerings, the presentations, the prayers and invocations,
as if the spirits were actually enjoying them;
the selection of various items and sacrificing them all,
as if the spirits were actually tasting them;
not seeking benefit from raising the cup,
the host having the honored vessel,
as if the spirits were actually toasting with it;
when the guests depart,
the host bows and escorts them,
returns, changes his clothes,
takes his position and weeps,
as if the spirits had actually left.
How sorrowful!
How reverent!
Serve the dead as you serve the living,
serve the departed as you serve the present,
giving form to what is without shape or
shadow, and yet completing the pattern.
Now music is joy,
an unavoidable expression of human emotion,
so people cannot be without music.
Joy must be expressed in sounds and voices,
manifested in movement and stillness,
and such is the Way of humanity.
Sounds and voices, movement and stillness,
the changes in the arts of life are fully contained herein.
Thus, people cannot be without joy,
and joy cannot be without manifestation,
but if manifested without guidance,
it cannot avoid disorder.
The ancient kings hated such disorder,
so they established the sounds of the Yǎ and Sòng to guide it,
making the sounds sufficient to bring joy without indulgence,
making the patterns sufficient to be distinct without being perverse,
making the twists and turns, complexity and simplicity, sharpness and fullness, rhythm and tempo
sufficient to move people's good hearts,
so that depraved and corrupt influences find no way to connect.
This was the method by which the ancient kings established music,
yet Mòzǐ condemns it—how can this be!
Thus, when music is in the ancestral temple,
rulers and ministers, superiors and inferiors listen to it together,
and none fail to be harmonious and reverent;
within the household,
fathers and sons, elder and younger brothers listen to it together,
and none fail to be harmonious and affectionate;
among village elders and clan leaders,
old and young listen to it together,
and none fail to be harmonious and obedient.
Thus, music examines the fundamental tone to determine harmony,
combines instruments to adorn the rhythm,
unites rhythm to complete the pattern,
sufficient to lead the one Way,
sufficient to govern all changes.
This was the technique by which the ancient kings established music,
yet Mòzǐ condemns it—how can this be!
Thus, listening to the sounds of the Yǎ and Sòng,
one's will and intent are broadened;
grasping the shield and battle-axe,
practicing the bowing and rising, bending and stretching,
one's demeanor becomes dignified;
moving according to the dance positions,
following the rhythm,
the ranks become correct,
advancing and retreating become uniform.
Thus, music is used externally for campaigns and punishments,
and internally for courtesy and deference.
Campaigns and punishments, courtesy and deference,
their principle is one.
Used externally for campaigns and punishments,
then none fail to listen and obey;
used internally for courtesy and deference,
then none fail to submit and follow.
Thus, music is the great unifier of the world,
the guiding principle of balance and harmony,
an unavoidable expression of human emotion.
This was the technique by which the ancient kings established music,
yet Mòzǐ condemns it—how can this be!
Moreover, music is what the ancient kings used to adorn their joy;
armies and battle-axes
are what the ancient kings used to adorn their anger.
The ancient kings' joy and anger were both properly ordered.
Therefore, when they were joyful, the world harmonized with them,
and when they were angry, the violent and disorderly feared them.
In the Way of the ancient kings,
ritual and music are its most flourishing aspects,
yet Mòzǐ condemns them.
Thus it is said: Mòzǐ in relation to the Way
is like a blind man in relation to black and white,
like a deaf man in relation to clear and turbid,
like one who wishes to go to Chǔ but seeks it in the north.
Now musical sounds enter people deeply,
and transform people quickly,
so the ancient kings carefully patterned them.
When music is balanced and peaceful, the people are harmonious and not dissolute;
when music is solemn and dignified, the people are unified and not disorderly.
When the people are harmonious and unified, the military is strong and the cities secure,
and enemy states dare not assail them.
In this way,
the common people all dwell in peace,
delight in their villages,
and fully satisfy their superiors.
Thereafter, their reputation becomes illustrious,
their glory becomes great;
the people within the four seas all wish to have them as teachers.
This is the beginning of a true king.
If music is seductive and perilous,
then the people become dissolute, disrespectful, and base.
Dissoluteness leads to disorder,
baseness leads to contention.
Disorder and contention weaken the military and endanger the cities,
and enemy states threaten them.
In this way,
the common people do not dwell in peace,
do not delight in their villages,
and do not satisfy their superiors.
Thus, when ritual and music are abandoned and depraved sounds arise,
it is the root of danger, diminishment, and disgrace.
Therefore, the ancient kings valued ritual and music and despised depraved sounds.
In the section on ordering offices,
it says:
"Cultivate the laws and commands,
examine punishments and rewards,
prohibit licentious sounds,
and in due season regulate and cultivate,
so that barbarian customs and depraved sounds dare not corrupt the Yǎ,
this is the task of the Grand Master."
Mòzǐ said:
"Music is condemned by the sage kings,
yet the Ru practice it—this is wrong."
The gentleman does not think so.
Music is what the sages delighted in,
and it can improve the people's hearts,
it moves people deeply,
it transforms customs and practices,
so the ancient kings guided with ritual and music,
and the people were harmonious and concordant.
If the people have feelings of liking and disliking
but no response of joy and anger, there will be disorder.
The ancient kings hated such disorder,
so they cultivated their conduct,
rectified their music,
and the world became obedient.
Thus, the garments of mourning,
the sounds of weeping,
make people's hearts sorrowful;
donning armor and helmet, singing
in the ranks,
makes people's hearts stirred;
seductive countenances,
the sounds of Zhèng and Wèi,
make people's hearts licentious;
girdled with the sash, wearing the cap,
dancing the Sháo and singing the Wǔ,
makes people's hearts dignified.
Therefore, the gentleman does not listen to licentious sounds with his ears,
does not look at feminine charms with his eyes,
does not utter harsh words with his mouth.
These three things
the gentleman is careful about.
Whenever depraved sounds move people and perverse energy responds,
perverse energy takes form and disorder arises;
when correct sounds move people and harmonious energy responds,
harmonious energy takes form and order arises.
Call and response correspond,
good and evil mirror each other,
so the gentleman is careful about what he accepts and rejects.
The gentleman uses bells and drums to guide his will,
uses lutes and zithers to gladden his heart,
moves with shield and battle-axe,
adorns with feathers and plumes,
follows with chimes and pipes.
Thus, its clarity and brightness resemble heaven,
its breadth and greatness resemble earth,
its bowing and rising, circling and turning, are like the four seasons.
Thus when music is practiced, aspirations become purified;
when rituals are cultivated, conduct is perfected;
ears and eyes become sharp and clear;
blood and vital energy become harmonious and balanced;
customs are transformed;
the whole world is at peace;
beauty and goodness delight each other.
Hence it is said:
"Music is joy."
The nobleman delights in attaining the Way;
the petty man delights in satisfying his desires.
When desires are restrained by the Way,
there is joy without disorder;
when the Way is forgotten for desires,
there is confusion without joy.
Therefore, music
is what guides joy,
and the instruments of metal, stone, silk, and bamboo
are what guide virtue.
When music is practiced, the people turn toward the proper direction.
Thus music
is the highest means of governing people,
yet Mòzǐ opposed it.
Moreover, music
represents the unchangeable nature of harmony;
ritual
represents the unalterable principle of order.
Music unites and brings agreement;
ritual distinguishes and differentiates.
The unifying principle of ritual and music
governs the human heart.
To penetrate the root and exhaust transformation
is the essence of music;
to manifest sincerity and eliminate falsity
is the constant principle of ritual.
Mòzǐ's opposition to this
nearly approaches criminal error.
Since the enlightened kings have passed away,
there has been no one to correct this.
When foolish people learn from him,
they endanger themselves.
The nobleman's understanding of music
manifests his virtue.
In chaotic times, goodness is hated,
and this is not heeded.
Alas, how sorrowful!
It cannot be accomplished.
Disciples, strive in your learning,
and do not be preoccupied with anything else.
The images of sound and music:
The drum represents heavenly splendor,
the bell represents substantial unity,
the stone chime represents purity and control,
the yú shēng represent solemn harmony,
the guǎn yuè represent vigorous outbursts,
the xūn chí represent vast comprehensiveness,
the sè represents gentle goodness,
the qín represents feminine grace,
singing represents clarity and completeness,
and dance embodies the meaning of harmonizing with the Way of Heaven.
The drum—is it not the ruler of music!
Thus the drum resembles heaven,
the bell resembles earth,
the stone chime resembles water,
the yú shēng (xiāo hé) and guǎn yuè
resemble the stars, sun, and moon,
and the táo, zhù, fǔ, gé, qiāng, and qià resemble the myriad things.
How do we understand the meaning of dance?
It is said:
The eyes do not see themselves,
the ears do not hear themselves,
yet in managing bowing and rising, bending and stretching, advancing and retreating, slow and fast movements,
all are precisely controlled,
exerting the full strength of sinews and bones
to meet the rhythm of bells and drums in coordinated movements,
with none acting contrary,
the accumulated intent of the multitude is profoundly focused!
Confucius said: "By observing the village drinking ceremony,
I understand how easily the Kingly Way can be implemented."
The host personally invites the guest of honor and the secondary guest,
and all the other guests follow them,
arriving outside the gate,
where the host bows to the guest of honor and the secondary guest,
and then all the other guests enter,
thus distinguishing the meaning of noble and humble.
After three bows they reach the steps,
after three deferrals the guest of honor ascends,
the ceremonies of bowing upon arrival, offering wine, and toasting,
with their elaborate rituals of declining and yielding.
With the secondary guest, these are simplified.
As for the other guests,
they ascend, receive, sit to make offerings, stand to drink,
without offering a return toast before descending;
thus the distinction between elaborate and simple ceremonies is made clear.
The musicians enter,
ascend and sing three pieces,
and the host offers them wine;
the reed players enter and play three pieces,
and the host offers them wine;
there is alternating singing and playing of three pieces each,
combined performance of three pieces,
the musicians announce the completion of the music,
and then depart.
Two men raise their zhì cups,
a master of ceremonies is appointed,
showing that they can achieve harmonious joy without dissipation.
The guest of honor toasts the host,
the host toasts the secondary guest,
the secondary guest toasts the other guests,
with order determined by age,
ending with those who performed the washing.
This shows that they can respect elders without omission.
They descend,
remove their shoes and sit down,
with countless rounds of drinking.
The regulation of drinking
does not interfere with morning duties,
nor with evening duties.
When the guests depart,
the host bows in farewell,
and the ceremonial procedures are thus completed.
This shows that they can enjoy repose without disorder.
When noble and humble are distinguished,
elaborate and simple ceremonies are differentiated,
there is harmonious joy without dissipation,
respect for elders without omission,
and repose without disorder;
these five practices
are sufficient to rectify the self and bring peace to the state.
When that state is at peace, the whole world is at peace.
Therefore it is said:
"By observing the village drinking ceremony,
I understand how easily the Kingly Way can be implemented."
The signs of a chaotic age:
its clothing is ornate,
its demeanor effeminate,
its customs decadent,
its aspirations profit-oriented,
its conduct disorderly,
its music dangerous,
its literature concealed yet flashy,
its nurturing of life without measure,
its burial of the dead meager and stingy,
despising ritual and righteousness while valuing courage and strength,
where the poor become robbers,
and the rich become predators.
A well-governed age is the opposite of this.
The common trouble with people
is being blinded by one limited perspective
while remaining ignorant of the great principles.
Good governance returns to the constant norms,
but when two paths seem equally plausible, confusion arises.
There are not two Ways in the world,
nor do sages have two minds.
Now with feudal lords governing differently,
and the hundred schools advocating different doctrines,
people are inevitably confused about right and wrong,
and about order and chaos.
The rulers of chaotic states,
the proponents of chaotic schools,
in their sincere hearts
all seek correctness and act for themselves,
yet they err and distort the Way,
and others lure them according to their predispositions.
They cherish their accumulated views,
fearing to hear them criticized;
relying on their private opinions
to examine different doctrines,
they fear to hear them praised.
Thus they depart further from order
while never ceasing to affirm themselves.
Are they not blinded by one limited perspective
and losing the true pursuit?
When the mind is not applied,
even black and white before the eyes go unseen,
and thunderous drums beside the ears go unheard—
how much more so with those who are misled!
Those who possess the Way and virtue
are condemned above by the rulers of chaotic states,
and condemned below by the proponents of chaotic schools.
Is this not lamentable!
Thus, what causes obscuration:
desire causes obscuration,
aversion causes obscuration,
beginnings cause obscuration,
endings cause obscuration,
distance causes obscuration,
proximity causes obscuration,
breadth causes obscuration,
superficiality causes obscuration,
antiquity causes obscuration,
modernity causes obscuration.
Whenever things differ, none fail to obscure one another,
this is the common affliction of mental methods.
In the past, among rulers who were obscured,
Xià Jié and Yīn Zhòu were such.
Jié was obscured by Mòxǐ and Sīguān,
and did not recognize Guān Lóngpáng,
thus confusing his mind
and disrupting his conduct;
Zhòu was obscured by Dájǐ and Fēilián,
and did not recognize Wēizǐ Qǐ,
thus confusing his mind
and disrupting his conduct.
Therefore, ministers abandoned loyalty and served selfish ends,
the common people grumbled and refused service,
the worthy and good withdrew into seclusion,
this is why they lost the lands of the nine provinces
and made their ancestral temples desolate.
Jié died at Lìshān,
Zhòu was hanged under a red banner;
they themselves lacked foreknowledge,
and none dared admonish them,
this is the calamity of obscuration.
Chéng Tāng reflected upon Xià Jié,
thus mastering his mind and governing it cautiously,
thereby able long to employ Yī Yǐn
while personally not losing the Way,
this is why he replaced the Xià king and received the nine domains.
King Wén reflected upon Yīn Zhòu,
thus mastering his mind and governing it cautiously,
thereby able long to employ Lǚ Wàng
while personally not losing the Way,
this is why he replaced the Yīn king and received the nine provinces.
Distant regions all sent their treasures,
thus his eyes beheld every color,
his ears heard every sound,
his mouth tasted every flavor,
his body dwelled in every palace,
his name received every honor,
in life all under heaven sang his praises,
in death the four seas wept for him,
this may be called the pinnacle of glory.
The Odes say:
"The phoenixes dance gracefully,
their wings like shields,
their voices like panpipes.
There is the female phoenix,
there is the male phoenix, delighting the emperor's heart."
This is the blessing of non-obscuration.
In the past, among ministers who were obscured,
Táng Yāng and Xī Qí were such.
Táng Yāng was obscured by desire for power and expelled Zǎi Zǐ,
Xī Qí was obscured by desire for the state and condemned Shēnshēng,
Táng Yāng was executed in Sòng,
Xī Qí was executed in Jìn.
Expelling worthy ministers and condemning filial brothers,
personally suffering execution,
yet remaining unaware,
this is the calamity of obscuration.
Therefore, those who through greed, baseness,
betrayal,
and power struggles avoid danger, disgrace, and destruction—from ancient times to the present, such has never occurred.
Bào Shū, Nìng Qì, and Xí Péng were benevolent, wise, and unobscured,
thus they could support Guǎn Zhòng and share his fame, profit, and blessings;
Shào Gōng and Lǚ Wàng were benevolent, wise, and unobscured,
thus they could support Zhōu Gōng and share his fame, profit, and blessings.
The Traditions say:
"Understanding the worthy is called clarity,
assisting the worthy is called capability.
Strive and strengthen yourself,
your blessings will surely be long-lasting."
This expresses it.
This is the blessing of non-obscuration.
In the past, among visiting scholars who were obscured,
the disorderly schools were such.
Mòzǐ was obscured by utility and did not understand refinement,
Sòngzǐ was obscured by desires and did not understand attainment,
Shènzǐ was obscured by law and did not understand worthies,
Shēnzǐ was obscured by power and did not understand knowledge,
Huìzǐ was obscured by rhetoric and did not understand reality,
Zhuāngzǐ was obscured by heaven and did not understand humanity.
Thus, speaking from utility, the Way
is wholly profit;
speaking from convention, the Way
is wholly satisfaction;
speaking from law, the Way
is wholly regulations;
speaking from power, the Way
is wholly expedience;
speaking from rhetoric, the Way
is wholly debate;
speaking from heaven, the Way
is wholly accommodation;
these several perspectives
are all one corner of the Way.
The Way embodies constancy while exhausting change,
one corner cannot fully represent it.
Those with partial knowledge,
viewing one corner of the Way without recognizing it fully,
therefore consider it sufficient and adorn it,
internally bringing disorder to themselves,
externally confusing others,
above obscuring those below,
below obscuring those above,
this is the calamity of obscuration.
Confucius was benevolent, wise, and unobscured,
thus his learning of various methods sufficed to continue the former kings.
One school attained the comprehensive Way,
raised it and applied it,
unobscured by accumulated conventions.
Therefore, his virtue matched Zhōu Gōng's,
his fame equaled the Three Kings',
this is the blessing of non-obscuration.
The sage knows the afflictions of mental methods,
sees the calamities of obscuration,
therefore has no desire nor aversion, no beginning nor end, no near nor far, no breadth nor superficiality, no antiquity nor modernity,
presents all things comprehensively while suspending the balance at the center.
Thus, the multitude of differences cannot obscure one another and disrupt their proper order.
What is the balance?
Answer: the Way.
Therefore, the mind must not fail to know the Way.
If the mind does not know the Way,
then it will not approve the Way
but approve what is not the Way.
Who would wish to follow their inclinations
and uphold what they disapprove
to restrain what they approve?
Using a mind that does not approve the Way to select people,
will certainly unite with those not following the Way,
and not unite with those following the Way,
using a mind that does not approve the Way,
to discuss those following the Way with people not following the Way—
this is the root of disorder.
How could one understand!
Answer:
the mind knowing the Way,
then can approve the Way;
approving the Way,
then can uphold the Way and restrain what is not the Way.
Using a mind that approves the Way to select people,
will unite with those following the Way,
and not unite with those not following the Way.
Using a mind that approves the Way,
to discuss what is not the Way with those following the Way—
this is the essence of order. Why worry about not understanding?
Therefore, the essence of order lies in knowing the Way.
How can humans know the Way?
Answer: through the mind.
How can the mind know?
Answer: through emptiness, unity, and stillness.
The mind never fails to store,
yet there is what is called emptiness;
the mind never fails to comprehend diversely,
yet there is what is called unity;
the mind never fails to move,
yet there is what is called stillness.
Humans are born with awareness,
awareness brings memory.
Memory is
storage,
yet there is what is called emptiness—
not allowing what is already stored to harm what is to be received is called emptiness.
The mind is born with awareness,
awareness brings distinction,
distinction is
simultaneously knowing multiple things.
Simultaneously knowing multiple things
is duality,
yet there is what is called unity—
not allowing that one to harm this one is called unity.
The mind—
in sleep dreams,
in idleness wanders freely,
when employed plans.
Therefore, the mind never fails to move,
yet there is what is called stillness—
not allowing dreams and turmoil to disrupt awareness is called stillness.
Those who seek the Way without having attained it are said to cultivate emptiness, unity, and stillness.
Practice them:
then those who aspire to the Way shall embrace emptiness—with emptiness, they enter it;
those who serve the Way shall embrace unity—with unity, they exhaust it;
those who contemplate the Way shall embrace stillness—with stillness, they perceive it.
To know the Way and perceive it,
to know the Way and practice it—
this is to embody the Way.
Emptiness, unity, and stillness
are called the Great Clarity.
Of the myriad things, none take form without being seen,
none are seen without being understood,
none are understood without being properly placed.
Sitting in a room, one sees all within the four seas;
dwelling in the present, one discusses distant times;
broadly observing the myriad things, one knows their true nature;
examining order and chaos, one comprehends their measure;
ordering heaven and earth, one utilizes and governs the myriad things;
grasping the great principle, one encompasses the universe.
Vast and expansive—
who knows its limits?
Brilliant and boundless—
who knows its virtue?
Turbulent and diverse—
who knows its form?
Its brightness rivals the sun and moon;
its greatness fills the eight directions—
this is what is called the Great Person.
How could there be any obscurity?
The mind is the ruler of the body
and the master of spiritual intelligence.
It issues commands but accepts none.
It restrains itself,
employs itself,
deprives itself,
takes for itself,
acts by itself,
and stops by itself.
Thus, the mouth can be forced to speak or be silent;
the body can be forced to bend or stretch;
but the mind cannot be forced to change its intent—
what it affirms, it accepts;
what it denies, it rejects.
Hence it is said:
The capacity of the mind—its choices are unimpeded
and necessarily manifest themselves;
its engagement with things is diverse and broad,
yet in its utmost refinement, it is undivided.
The Book of Songs says:
"I gather and gather the mouse-ear,
but cannot fill a slanting basket.
Alas, I think of my beloved,
and place it there on the Zhou road."
A slanting basket is easily filled;
mouse-ear is easily obtained;
yet one cannot divide attention while on the Zhou road.
Thus it is said:
If the mind branches out, it lacks knowledge;
if it inclines, it lacks refinement;
if it doubts, it becomes confused.
Assisted by examination,
the myriad things can be fully known.
One who fully comprehends their reasons is excellent.
Categories cannot be dual;
thus the wise choose one and concentrate on it.
A farmer skilled in tilling
cannot become the master of farming;
a merchant skilled in the market
cannot become the master of marketing;
a craftsman skilled in tools
cannot become the master of toolmaking.
Yet there are those who, without these three skills,
can be appointed to govern these three offices—
they are called those skilled in the Way,
not those skilled in things.
Those skilled in things manage things;
those skilled in the Way oversee the management of things.
Thus, the gentleman concentrates on the Way and thereby assists in examining things.
Concentrating on the Way brings correctness;
assisting in examining things brings clarity;
with correct intention and clear understanding,
the myriad things are governed.
In ancient times, when Shùn governed the world,
he did not manage affairs directly, yet all things were accomplished.
Abiding in the peril of unity,
his glory filled all around;
nourishing the subtlety of unity,
he was glorious yet unaware.
Thus, the Classic of the Way says:
"The human mind is perilous;
the mind of the Way is subtle."
The subtlety of peril and subtlety
only the enlightened gentleman can know.
Thus, the human mind is like a pan of water:
if placed level and undisturbed,
the sediment sinks and the clear rises to the top,
enough to reflect beard, eyebrows, and skin texture.
If a slight breeze passes over it,
the sediment stirs below,
the clarity is disturbed above,
and it cannot capture the correct form of a large object.
So too is the mind.
Thus, guided by principle,
nourished by clarity,
and undisturbed by things,
it can determine right and wrong and resolve doubts.
If distracted by trivial matters,
its external correctness shifts,
its internal mind inclines,
and it cannot decide on general principles.
Thus, many have loved writing,
but only Cāngjié is remembered—
due to concentration;
many have loved farming,
but only Hòujì is remembered—
due to concentration;
many have loved music,
but only Kuí is remembered—
due to concentration;
many have loved righteousness,
but only Shùn is remembered—
due to concentration.
Chuí made the bow,
Fúyóu made the arrows,
and Yì excelled in archery;
Xīzhòng made the cart,
Sāngdù bred the horses,
and Zàofǔ excelled in driving.
From ancient times to the present,
there has never been one who achieved excellence through duality.
Zēngzǐ said:
"If his courtyard is for catching mice,
how can he sing with me?"
In the cave of Kōngshí dwelled a man
named Jí,
who was skilled in archery and fond of thought.
If sensory desires arose,
they ruined his thought;
if he heard the buzz of mosquitoes,
it disrupted his concentration.
Thus, he shut out sensory desires
and avoided the sound of mosquitoes,
dwelling in solitude and quiet thought to attain understanding.
Is thinking of benevolence in this way considered subtle?
Mèngzǐ, fearing failure, sent his wife away—
this can be called self-discipline;
Yǒuzǐ, fearing sleepiness, burned his palm—
this can be called self-endurance;
but these do not reach the level of true fondness.
Shutting out sensory desires
can be called self-discipline,
but it does not reach the level of thought.
Hearing the buzz of mosquitoes and disrupting one's concentration
can be called perilous,
but it cannot be called subtle.
Subtlety belongs to the ultimate person.
The ultimate person—
what need for discipline?
What need for endurance?
What need for peril?
Thus, turbid brightness reflects externally;
clear brightness reflects internally.
The sage gives free rein to his desires
and embraces his emotions,
yet is governed by principle.
What need for discipline?
What need for endurance?
What need for peril?
Thus, the benevolent person practices the Way
without forced action;
the sage practices the Way
without compulsion.
The benevolent person's thought is reverent;
the sage's thought is joyful.
This is the way to govern the mind.
Whenever observing things with doubt,
if the center is unsettled,
external things are unclear;
if one's thoughts are unclear,
one cannot determine truth and falsehood.
One who walks in darkness
may see a fallen tree and think it a crouching tiger,
see a standing forest and think it people following—
darkness obscures their sight.
A drunkard crossing a hundred-pace ditch
mistakes it for a footpath's gutter;
bending to exit the city gate,
he takes it for a small inner door—
wine has disordered his spirit.
One who presses on his eyes while looking
sees one as two;
one who covers his ears while listening
hears silence as roaring—
external forces disturb his senses.
Thus, viewing an ox from a mountaintop makes it seem like a sheep,
yet one seeking a sheep would not go down to lead it away,
for distance obscures its size;
viewing trees from a foothill,
a ten-ren tree appears like a chopstick,
yet one needing chopsticks would not climb to break it,
for height obscures its length.
Water in motion makes reflections sway,
but people do not use it to judge beauty or ugliness,
for the water's nature is deceptive.
A blind man looking up cannot see stars,
yet people do not rely on him to determine their presence,
for his faculties are impaired.
If someone determines things under such conditions,
they are among the world's fools.
When fools determine matters,
they use doubt to resolve doubt,
and their judgments are inevitably incorrect.
If they are incorrect,
how can they avoid error?
South of Xiàshǒu lived a man
named Juān Shǔliáng,
whose character
was foolish and prone to fear.
Walking by night under a bright moon,
he glanced down and saw his shadow,
taking it for a crouching ghost;
looking up, he saw his hair,
mistaking it for a standing demon.
He fled in terror,
and upon reaching his home,
he collapsed breathless and died.
Is this not lamentable?
Whenever people believe in ghosts,
it must be during moments of sensory confusion or doubtful perception that they affirm them.
This is when humans transform absence into presence and presence into absence.
Yet if one relies on this to rectify affairs,
it is like being afflicted by dampness
and beating drums to cure paralysis—
one will only incur the cost of ruined drums and lost piglets,
with no blessing of healed illness.
Thus, even if not south of Xiàshǒu,
there is no difference.
The capacity to know
is human nature;
being knowable
is the principle of things.
Using humanity's innate capacity to know
to seek the knowable principles of things
without setting limits to inquiry
would leave one unable to exhaust them in a lifetime.
Even if one comprehends millions of principles,
it remains insufficient to embrace all changes in things,
making one no different from a fool.
To study until old, with children grown,
yet remain like a fool,
still unaware of error,
this is called a deluded person.
Therefore, learning
must inherently have its stopping point.
Where should it stop?
The answer:
Stop at ultimate sufficiency.
What is ultimate sufficiency?
Say:
The sage.
The sage
exhausts all ethical relationships;
the king
exhausts all regulations.
When both are exhausted,
it suffices as the highest standard for the world.
Thus, learners take the sage-king as teacher,
adopting the sage-king's institutions as law,
emulating their laws to seek their unifying categories,
and striving to imitate such persons.
Those devoted to this direction
are scholars;
those approximating it
are gentlemen;
those who fully know it
are sages.
Hence, having wisdom not used to contemplate this
is called greed;
having courage not used to uphold this
is called violence;
being astute not used to distinguish this
is called usurpation;
having multiple talents not used to cultivate this
is called cunning;
being eloquent not used to discourse on this
is called verbosity.
The tradition says:
"The world has two aspects:
wrong scrutinizes right,
right scrutinizes wrong."
This means assessing conformity or nonconformity with the kingly institutions.
If the world lacks this as its exalted standard,
how can anyone distinguish right from wrong or judge crooked and straight?
As for not distinguishing right and wrong,
not adjudicating crooked and straight,
not discerning order and chaos,
not governing the human way—
even if capable, it benefits none;
if incapable, it harms none.
They merely cultivate strange theories,
play with bizarre rhetoric,
to confuse and disrupt each other;
they forceably suppress others with sharp tongues,
are thick-skinned and endure disgrace,
lack correctness and act recklessly,
argue wildly while seeking profit;
they dislike courteous deference,
disrespect rituals and礼节,
and prefer pushing and jostling—
these are the doctrines of chaotic times and treacherous people,
and currently, many of the world's theorists
are precisely like this.
The tradition says:
"Splitting hairs to show acuity,
discoursing on things to display argumentation—
gentlemen despise this;
broad learning and strong memory
that contradict the kingly institutions—
gentlemen despise this."
This refers to that.
Doing what does not help achieve success,
seeking what does not help attain gain,
worrying over what does not aid critical moments—
then broadly abandon these things.
Do not let them hinder you,
not even briefly occupying your heart.
Do not yearn for the past,
do not anxiety over the future,
hold no heart of sorrow or pity,
