act when the time comes,
respond when things arrive,
manage when events arise—
order and chaos, possibility and impossibility,
become clearly evident.
Secrecy leads to success,
openness to failure—
enlightened rulers have none of this;
openness leads to success,
secrecy to failure—
benighted rulers have none of this.
Thus, if a ruler is secretive, slanderous words will come,
while straightforward words recede,
petty men draw near and gentlemen distance themselves.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Taking darkness for brightness,
foxes appear bluish."
This speaks of the ruler being obscure and the subjects perilous.
If a ruler is open, straightforward words will come,
while slanderous words recede,
gentlemen draw near and petty men distance themselves.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Brightness below,
radiance above."
This speaks of the ruler being enlightened and the subjects transformed.
Later kings established names thus:
penal names follow Shāng,
rank names follow Zhōu,
ritual names follow the *Rites*.
Miscellaneous names applied to all things
follow the established customs of central states, with nuanced designations
so that distant regions with different customs
may thereby communicate.
Miscellaneous names pertaining to humans:
what makes life be so is called nature;
what arises from nature's harmony,
through essence meeting and responding,
unforced and spontaneous, is called nature.
Nature's likes, dislikes, joys, angers, sorrows, and pleasures are called emotions.
Emotions thus, and the mind selecting among them is called deliberation.
The mind deliberating and the faculties acting accordingly is called conscious activity.
Deliberation accumulated,
faculties habituated,
and only then achieved
is called conscious activity.
Acting for correct benefit
is called business.
Acting for correct righteousness
is called conduct.
That which enables knowledge in humans
is called perception.
When perception corresponds with reality, it is called wisdom.
That which enables ability in humans
is called faculty.
When faculty corresponds with reality, it is called capability.
When nature is harmed, it is called illness.
When encountering circumstances, it is called fate.
These are scattered names applied to humans,
and these are the established names of later kings.
Thus when kings establish names,
once names are fixed, realities are distinguished;
once the Way is practiced, intentions are communicated;
then carefully lead the people to unity.
Hence, those who split phrases and arbitrarily create names to confuse correct terminology,
causing people doubt and confusion,
making many engage in disputes and litigation,
are called great villains;
their crime is like that of forging tallies, measures, or weights.
Therefore, their people dare not rely on strange expressions to confuse correct names.
Thus their people become honest,
honesty makes them easy to command,
being easy to command leads to achievement.
Since their people dare not rely on strange expressions to confuse correct names,
they become unified in the Way and laws and careful in following orders.
In this way, their accomplishments endure.
Enduring accomplishments and successful achievements
represent the pinnacle of governance,
which is the result of carefully maintaining name conventions.
Now that the sage kings have perished,
the maintenance of names has become lax,
strange expressions have arisen,
names and realities have become confused,
the forms of right and wrong are unclear,
so even officials who guard the laws and scholars who recite classics
are all in confusion.
If a king were to arise,
he would necessarily follow some old names
and create some new names.
Therefore, the reason for having names,
the basis for similarity and difference,
and the essential principles for establishing names
must be examined.
Different forms and divergent minds,
describing different things,
names and realities mysteriously entangled,
noble and base unclear,
similar and different undistinguished;
in such cases, intentions will inevitably suffer from miscommunication,
and affairs will inevitably meet with obstruction and failure.
Therefore, the wise make distinctions and establish names to point to realities,
above to clarify noble and base,
below to distinguish similar and different.
When noble and base are clear,
and similar and different are distinguished;
then intentions suffer no miscommunication,
and affairs meet no obstruction or failure,
this is the reason for having names.
Then what is the basis for similarity and difference?
The answer is:
the natural faculties.
All who share the same kind and same emotions
have natural faculties that perceive things similarly,
thus through comparison and approximation they communicate,
this is how they establish conventional names to understand each other.
Forms, bodies, colors, and patterns are distinguished by the eye;
sounds, clear and turbid, harmonious and discordant notes are distinguished by the ear;
sweet, bitter, salty, bland, pungent, sour, and strange flavors are distinguished by the mouth;
fragrant, foul, aromatic, rank, fishy, rancid, and strange odors are distinguished by the nose;
pain, itch, cold, heat, smooth, rough, light, and heavy are distinguished by the body;
reasons, causes, joy, anger, grief, pleasure, love, hate, and desire are distinguished by the mind.
The mind has verifying knowledge.
Through verification, one can know sounds via the ear,
and know forms via the eyes;
however, verification must await the natural faculties recording their respective categories
before it is possible;
if the five faculties record but do not know,
and the mind verifies but cannot explain,
then people invariably call this ignorance,
this is the basis for similarity and difference.
Then accordingly we name them:
similar things receive similar names, different things receive different names;
if simple names suffice for understanding, use simple names;
if simple names are insufficient, use compound names;
if simple and compound names don't conflict, use shared names;
even when shared,
they cause no harm.
Knowing that different realities have different names,
thus ensure that different realities all have different names,
this cannot be confused,
just as ensure that similar realities all have similar names.
Thus although the myriad things are numerous,
sometimes we wish to refer to them comprehensively,
so we call them "things."
"Thing"
is the great shared name.
Extending this sharing,
sharing leads to further sharing,
until reaching no further sharing then stopping.
Sometimes we wish to refer to them partially,
so we call them "birds and beasts."
"Birds and beasts"
are great specific names.
Extending this specification,
specification leads to further specification,
until reaching no further specification then stopping.
Names have no inherent appropriateness,
they are established by convention,
when convention establishes and custom forms, this is called appropriate,
what differs from convention is called inappropriate.
Names have no inherent reality,
they assign reality by convention,
when convention establishes and custom forms
this is called real names.
Names have inherent goodness,
straightforward and unobstructed,
this is called good names.
Some things have similar forms but different substances,
some have different forms but the same substance,
these can be distinguished.
When forms are similar but substances different,
though they may be combined,
they are called two realities.
When form changes but reality remains unchanged though considered different,
this is called transformation.
When there is transformation but no distinction,
this is called one reality.
This is how we examine realities to determine their number,
this is the essential principle of establishing names.
The established names of later kings
must be examined.
"Being insulted is not disgraceful,"
"Sages do not love themselves,"
"Killing robbers is not killing people,"
these confuse by using names to disrupt names.
Test them against the reason for having names and see which can be practiced,
then you can prohibit them.
"Mountains and abysses are level,"
"Desires are few,"
"Animal meats are not more tasty,
great bells are not more pleasurable,"
these confuse by using realities to disrupt names.
Test them against the basis for similarity and difference and see which harmonizes,
then you can prohibit them.
"To deny and yet approach the pillar,"
"There are oxen and horses, therefore no horses,"
these confuse by using names to disrupt realities.
Test them against name conventions,
using what they accept to contradict what they reject,
then you can prohibit them.
All heretical doctrines and perverse statements that deviate from the right Way and are arbitrarily created
resemble these three confusions.
Therefore, enlightened rulers know their distinctions and do not debate with them.
The people can be easily unified through the Way
but cannot share reasons with them,
thus enlightened rulers oversee them with authority,
guide them with the Way,
instruct them with commands,
clarify with discourse,
and prohibit with punishments.
Thus the people's transformation by the Way is miraculous,
what use is debate then!
Now that the sages have perished,
the world is in chaos,
deceitful words have arisen,
gentlemen have no authority to oversee,
no punishments to prohibit,
therefore debate and explanation are necessary.
When reality is not understood, then name it;
when naming doesn't work, then describe it;
when description fails, then explain it;
when explanation fails, then debate it.
Thus description, naming, debate, and explanation
are the great instruments of use,
and the beginning of kingly enterprise.
When names are heard and realities understood,
this is the function of names.
Accumulated to form writing,
this is the adornment of names.
When both function and adornment are achieved,
this is called knowing names.
Names
are means to describe accumulated realities.
Phrases
combine names of different realities to express one meaning.
Debate and explanation
use unchanging names to illustrate the principles of movement and stillness.
Description and naming
are the instruments of debate and explanation.
Debate and explanation
are the mind's representation of the Way.
The mind
is the master craftsman of the Way,
the Way
is the constant principle of governance.
The mind is in accord with the Way,
discourse is in accord with the mind,
and words are in accord with discourse.
Correct names are established to convey meaning,
and the substance of requests is made clear.
Distinguishing differences without error,
inferring categories without contradiction,
listening in accordance with patterns,
and debating to exhaust the reasons—
using the correct Way to distinguish wickedness
is like using a plumb line to determine straight and crooked.
Therefore, perverse doctrines cannot cause confusion,
and the Hundred Schools have nowhere to hide.
Possessing the wisdom to listen broadly
without an arrogant demeanor,
having the magnanimity to embrace all
without a boastful expression—
when such discourse is practiced, the world becomes upright;
when it is not practiced, the Way is made clear without falling into obscurity.
This is the discourse of the sage.
The Book of Songs says:
"Majestic and dignified,
like a jade scepter or tablet,
with renowned fame and prestige.
The amiable gentleman
serves as the model for all regions."
This expresses it.
The ritual of deference is achieved,
the principles of elder and younger are properly ordered;
taboos are not mentioned,
and strange expressions do not emerge.
Speaking with a benevolent heart,
listening with a learning heart,
debating with a fair heart—
unmoved by others' criticism or praise,
not dazzling the eyes and ears of spectators,
not bribing the powerful for influence,
not benefiting from the words of flatterers—
thus able to abide in the Way without wavering,
speaking without being forced to yield,
benefiting without becoming dissipated,
valuing fairness and despising vulgar contention—
this is the discourse of the scholar-gentleman.
The Book of Songs says:
"The long night stretches on,
eternally thinking of my faults.
Not neglecting the ancient ways,
not transgressing ritual and righteousness—
why worry about others' words!"
This expresses it.
The gentleman's words
are profound yet precise,
humble yet categorical,
varied yet consistent.
He rectifies his names
and uses appropriate expressions
to fully clarify his intentions and meanings.
Those names and expressions
are messengers of intention and meaning—
when sufficient for mutual understanding,
they are set aside;
to force them
is wickedness.
Therefore, when names sufficiently indicate reality
and expressions sufficiently reveal the essence,
they are set aside.
Going beyond this is called obstinacy—
this is what the gentleman rejects,
while the foolish pick up as their treasure.
Thus the fool's words
are vague and crude,
contentious and unclassifiable,
clamorous and boiling.
He seduces with names,
dazzles with expressions,
without depth in his intentions and meanings.
Therefore, he exhausts borrowed terms without reaching the essence,
labors intensely without achievement,
and covets without gaining reputation.
Thus the wise person's words
are easily understood when pondered,
easily practiced when acted upon,
easily maintained when upheld—
success necessarily brings what is desired while avoiding what is disliked.
But the fool is the opposite.
The Book of Songs says:
"If you are a ghost or a water demon,
you cannot be caught;
with your human face visible,
people see no limit to your ways.
I make this good song
to expose your fickleness."
This expresses it.
All who discuss governance while waiting to eliminate desires
fail to guide desires and thus are trapped by having desires.
All who discuss governance while waiting to reduce desires
fail to regulate desires and thus are trapped by numerous desires.
Having desires or having none
are different categories—
life and death are inherent to nature,
not what brings order or chaos;
the multitude or paucity of desires
are different categories—
they are quantities of emotion,
not what brings order or chaos.
Desires don't wait to be obtainable—
seeking follows what is permissible.
Desires not waiting to be obtainable
is received from Heaven;
seeking following what is permissible
is received from the mind.
The single desire received from Heaven
is controlled by the multiple seekings received from the mind—
naturally difficult to categorize as received from Heaven.
What people desire, life is extreme;
what people detest, death is extreme;
yet some follow death and reject life—
not that they don't desire life but desire death,
but because life is impermissible and death permissible.
Thus when desires exceed but actions fall short,
the mind stops them;
if what the mind permits aligns with principle,
then even if desires are numerous,
how could they harm order!
When desires are insufficient but actions exceed,
the mind drives them.
If what the mind permits loses principle,
then even if desires are few,
how could they stop chaos!
Thus order and chaos lie in what the mind permits,
not in what emotions desire.
Not seeking where it exists,
but seeking where it doesn't—
though one may say "I've found it,"
has actually lost it.
Nature
is endowed by Heaven;
emotions
are the substance of nature;
desires
are responses of emotions.
Believing desired things obtainable and seeking them
is inevitably unavoidable for emotions;
believing them permissible and pursuing them
is necessarily emerging from knowledge.
Thus even a gatekeeper
cannot eliminate desires;
even the Son of Heaven
cannot exhaust desires.
Though desires cannot be exhausted,
they can be nearly exhausted;
though desires cannot be eliminated,
seeking can be regulated.
Though what is desired cannot be exhausted,
seeking can nearly exhaust it;
though desires cannot be eliminated,
if seeking fails,
the thoughtful will regulate their seeking.
The Way—advancing leads to near exhaustion,
retreating leads to regulated seeking—
nothing in the world compares to it.
All people follow what they permit
and abandon what they don't permit.
Knowing nothing compares to the Way
yet not following it—
such people don't exist.
Suppose someone desires to go south
without limit
and detests going north
without measure—
would they, because the southward journey cannot be completed,
abandon traveling south and run north instead?
Now what people desire
has no limit,
what they detest
has no measure—
would they, because desires cannot be exhausted,
abandon the path to desired things and choose what they detest?
Thus if permissible by the Way and followed,
how could reducing lead to chaos!
If impermissible by the Way and abandoned,
how could increasing lead to order!
Therefore, the wise discuss the Way alone,
and the cherished theories of petty schools
all wither away.
When people seek something,
what they desire never arrives in its pure form;
when they reject something,
what they detest never departs completely.
Therefore, no human action can be undertaken without applying proper measurement.
If the scale is inaccurate,
then heavy objects will hang high
yet people will consider them light,
while light objects will hang low
yet people will consider them heavy -
this is how people become confused about weight.
If the standard is wrong,
then misfortune may dwell in desires
yet people consider it blessing,
while blessing may reside in aversions
yet people consider it misfortune -
this is also how people become confused about fortune and misfortune.
The Dào is
the correct standard for all times;
to depart from the Dào and make personal choices
is to not understand where fortune and misfortune truly reside.
In exchanges:
trading one for one,
people say
there's neither gain nor loss;
trading one for two,
people say
there's no loss but gain;
trading two for one,
people say
there's no gain but loss.
Those who calculate choose what gives more,
those who deliberate follow what's acceptable.
Trading two for one -
no one would do this,
understanding the numbers clearly.
Following the Dào in action
is like trading one for two -
what loss is there?
Departing from the Dào to make personal choices
is like trading two for one -
what gain is there?
To exchange accumulated desires of a hundred years
for momentary dislike,
and still do it -
this shows not understanding the numbers.
If one deeply observes what's hidden and difficult to perceive:
those who slight principle inwardly without valuing external things -
such people don't exist;
those who value external things without inner anxiety -
such people don't exist.
Those who act contrary to principle without external danger -
such people don't exist;
those who face external danger without inner fear -
such people don't exist.
When the heart is anxious and fearful,
then the mouth may hold fine food yet not know its taste,
the ears may hear bells and drums yet not know their sound,
the eyes may see embroidered robes yet not know their pattern,
and though resting on light warm mats, the body feels no comfort.
Thus, even enjoying all things' beauty brings no satisfaction,
and if momentarily satisfied,
the anxiety cannot be shaken off.
So enjoying all things' beauty brings great worry,
possessing all things' benefits brings great harm.
In such cases,
is this seeking things?
Nourishing life? Or selling one's longevity?
Thus, wanting to nourish desires yet indulging emotions,
wanting to nourish nature yet endangering the body,
wanting to nourish joy yet assaulting the heart,
wanting to nourish reputation yet confusing conduct -
people like this,
even if enfeoffed as lords or called rulers,
are no different from robbers;
riding carriages and wearing crowns,
are no different from the footless.
This is called being enslaved by things.
When the heart is peaceful and content,
then colors less than average can nourish the eyes,
sounds less than average can nourish the ears,
vegetarian food and soup can nourish the mouth,
coarse cloth clothes and hempen shoes can nourish the body,
small rooms, reed curtains, straw mats, and simple furniture can nourish the form.
Thus without all things' beauty, one can cultivate joy,
without powerful positions, one can cultivate reputation.
If such a person were given the world,
they would do much for the world,
with little personal pleasure -
this is called mastering things.
Unverified words,
unseen actions,
unheard plans -
the gentleman is cautious toward them.
Human nature is evil;
what is good in it is artificial.
Now by human nature,
we are born with fondness for profit -
following this leads to
struggle and contention arising
while courtesy and deference perish;
we are born with envy and hatred -
following this leads to
violence and crime arising
while loyalty and faithfulness perish;
we are born with sensory desires,
with fondness for sounds and beauty -
following this leads to
licentiousness and disorder arising
while ritual principles and culture perish.
Thus following human nature
and indulging human emotions
must lead to struggle and contention,
conform with violation of culture and disorder of principle,
and end in violence.
Therefore there must be the transformation of teachers and models,
the guidance of ritual principles,
then courtesy and deference emerge,
conformity with culture and principle follows,
and order is achieved.
Viewing it this way,
then human nature's evil is clear,
and what is good in it is artificial.
Thus warped wood must await pressing frames and steam straightening
before it becomes straight;
dull metal must await grinding and whetting
before it becomes sharp.
Now human nature being evil,
must await teachers and models before becoming correct,
obtain ritual principles before becoming ordered.
Without teachers and models,
people become biased dangerous and incorrect;
without ritual principles,
they become rebellious disorderly and ungoverned.
The ancient sage kings, regarding human nature as evil,
seeing it as biased dangerous and incorrect,
rebellious disorderly and ungoverned,
therefore established ritual principles
and instituted laws and measures
to reform and adorn human nature and emotions
and correct them,
to tame and transform human nature and emotions
and guide them,
making all emerge from governance
and conform with the Dào.
Now among people, those transformed by teachers and models, who accumulate culture and learning, and follow ritual principles
become gentlemen;
those who indulge their nature and emotions,
content with willfulness and violating ritual principles
become petty persons.
Viewing it this way,
then human nature's evil is clear,
and what is good in it is artificial.
Mèngzǐ said:
"People's capacity to learn
shows their nature is good."
I say:
This is not so.
This fails to understand human nature,
and doesn't examine the distinction between what's natural and artificial in humans.
What belongs to nature
is endowed by Heaven,
cannot be learned,
cannot be acquired through effort.
Ritual principles
are created by sages,
what people can learn to master,
and accomplish through effort.
What cannot be learned or acquired through effort in humans
is called nature;
what can be learned and mastered, acquired and accomplished in humans
is called artificial.
This is the distinction between nature and artificial.
Now by human nature,
eyes can see,
ears can hear.
The clarity that enables seeing cannot leave the eyes,
the acuity that enables hearing cannot leave the ears;
clear eyes and acute ears -
clearly cannot be learned.
Mèngzǐ said:
"People's nature today being good
is because all have lost their original nature."
I say:
If so, then he's mistaken.
Now by human nature,
if born separated from its simplicity, separated from its endowment,
it must be lost and forfeited.
Viewing it this way,
then human nature's evil is clear,
and what is good in it is artificial.
What is meant by innate goodness is that
one does not depart from one's simplicity to make it beautiful,
nor from one's innate disposition to make it beneficial.
If the relationship between innate disposition and beauty,
and between mind and goodness,
is like the capacity for clear vision not departing from the eyes,
or the capacity for acute hearing not departing from the ears,
then it is said:
"The eyes are clear and the ears are sharp."
Now, human nature is such that
when hungry, one desires to be full,
when cold, one desires warmth,
when tired, one desires rest—
these are the genuine feelings and nature of humans.
If someone is hungry
but dares not eat before their elders,
it is because they intend to defer;
if tired but dares not seek rest,
it is because they intend to take over for others.
A son deferring to his father,
a younger brother deferring to his elder brother;
a son taking over for his father,
a younger brother taking over for his elder brother—
these two behaviors both go against nature and contradict genuine feelings.
Yet, the way of a filial son
lies in the patterns of ritual and righteousness.
Thus, following one's nature and feelings
would mean no deferring or yielding;
deferring and yielding contradict nature and feelings.
From this perspective,
it is clear that human nature is evil,
and goodness is a human construct.
Someone asks:
"If human nature is evil,
then how do ritual and righteousness arise?"
The response is:
All ritual and righteousness
are born from the constructive efforts of the sages,
not originally from human nature.
Thus, when a potter molds clay to make vessels,
then vessels arise from the potter's constructive efforts,
not originally from human nature.
When a craftsman carves wood to make utensils,
then utensils arise from the craftsman's constructive efforts,
not originally from human nature.
The sages accumulated thought and deliberation, and practiced constructive methods,
to generate ritual and righteousness and establish laws and measures.
Thus, ritual, righteousness, laws, and measures
are born from the constructive efforts of the sages,
not originally from human nature.
As for the eyes loving beauty,
ears loving sounds,
mouth loving flavors,
mind loving profit,
and the bones, body, skin, and texture loving ease and comfort—
these all arise from human nature and feelings;
they are felt naturally
and do not require effort to emerge.
What is felt but not natural,
and must await effort to become so,
is called a human construct.
This is the distinction between what arises from nature
and what arises from constructive effort.
Thus, the sages transform nature and initiate constructive efforts;
constructive efforts give rise to ritual and righteousness,
and ritual and righteousness lead to the establishment of laws and measures.
Therefore, ritual, righteousness, laws, and measures
are produced by the sages.
What makes the sages the same as the masses,
and not different from them,
is their nature;
what makes them different and surpass the masses
is their constructive effort.
The desire for profit and gain
is part of human nature and feelings.
Suppose brothers are dividing inherited wealth;
if they follow their nature,
loving profit and desiring gain,
then they will conflict and seize from each other;
but if transformed by the patterns of ritual and righteousness,
they will defer even to fellow countrymen.
Thus, following nature leads to conflict between brothers,
while transformation through ritual and righteousness leads to deference to others.
Whenever people desire to be good,
it is because their nature is evil.
The thin desire thickness,
the ugly desire beauty,
the narrow desire breadth,
the poor desire wealth,
the lowly desire nobility—
if one lacks something within,
one necessarily seeks it externally;
thus, the wealthy do not desire more wealth,
the noble do not desire more power;
if one possesses something within,
one does not seek it externally.
From this perspective,
people's desire to be good
is because their nature is evil.
Human nature
inherently lacks ritual and righteousness,
so one must strenuously learn to acquire them;
nature does not know ritual and righteousness,
so one must think and deliberate to understand them.
If left to nature alone,
humans would have no ritual or righteousness,
and would not know them.
Without ritual and righteousness, there is disorder;
not knowing them leads to rebellion.
Thus, if left to nature,
rebellion and disorder lie within oneself.
From this perspective,
it is clear that human nature is evil,
and goodness is a human construct.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Human nature is good."
I say:
This is not so.
Throughout history, what is called good
is correctness, order, peace, and governance;
what is called evil
is bias, danger, rebellion, and disorder—
this is the distinction between good and evil.
If human nature were inherently correct, orderly, peaceful, and governed,
then what use would there be for sage kings?
What use for ritual and righteousness?
Even with sage kings and ritual righteousness,
what could be added to inherent correctness, order, peace, and governance?
But it is not so;
human nature is evil.
Thus, the ancient sages, seeing human nature as evil,
considered it biased, dangerous, and incorrect,
rebellious, disorderly, and ungoverned,
so they established the authority of rulers
to oversee it,
clarified ritual and righteousness to transform it,
instituted laws and regulations to govern it,
and emphasized punishments to restrain it,
ensuring that all under heaven emerged into order
and aligned with goodness.
This is the governance of the sage kings
and the transformation through ritual and righteousness.
If we were to remove the authority of rulers,
eliminate the transformation through ritual and righteousness,
abolish the governance of laws and regulations,
and do away with the restraints of punishments,
then observe how the people of the world interact—
in such a case, the strong would harm the weak and seize from them,
the many would oppress the few and clamor against them,
and the world would fall into rebellion and disorder, leading to mutual destruction
in no time.
From this perspective,
it is clear that human nature is evil,
and goodness is a human construct.
Thus, those who skillfully discuss antiquity
must have evidence in the present;
those who skillfully discuss heaven
must have proof in humanity.
All arguments value having matching joints
and verifiable signs.
Thus, one can sit and speak of it,
rise and establish it,
spread it and put it into practice.
Now Mèngzǐ says
"human nature is good,"
but it lacks matching joints and verifiable signs;
one can sit and speak of it,
but cannot rise and establish it,
nor spread it and put it into practice—
is this not a grave error!
Thus, if nature were good,
one could discard sage kings
and abandon ritual and righteousness;
if nature is evil,
one should support sage kings
and value ritual and righteousness.
Thus, the straightening tool is made
for warped wood;
the ink line is created
for the crooked;
establishing rulers and clarifying ritual and righteousness
is because nature is evil.
From this perspective,
it is clear that human nature is evil,
and goodness is a human construct.
Straight wood does not need a straightening tool to be straight
because its nature is straight;
warped wood must await the straightening tool, steam, and correction
to become straight,
because its nature is not straight.
Human nature is evil;
it must await the rule of sage kings
and the transformation through rituals and righteousness,
and only then will it emerge into order and conform to goodness.
Judging from this,
it is clear that human nature is evil,
and goodness is a human artifice.
Someone asks:
"Since the accumulation of artifice in rituals and righteousness
is part of human nature,
that is why sages are able to produce them."
The reply is:
This is not so.
The potter molds clay to produce tiles;
but is the nature of tiles and clay the potter's nature?
The artisan carves wood to produce vessels;
but is the nature of vessels and wood the artisan's nature?
As for the sages' relation to rituals and righteousness,
they are similarly like the potter molding to produce them;
then are the accumulation of artifice in rituals and righteousness
truly human nature?
Concerning human nature,
Yáo, Shùn, compared to Jié and Zhí,
their nature is the same;
the gentleman compared to the petty person,
their nature is the same.
Now, would you consider the accumulation of artifice in rituals and righteousness as human nature?
Then why value Yáo and Yǔ?
Why value the gentleman?
The reason for valuing Yáo, Yǔ, and the gentleman
is that they can transform nature,
can initiate artifice,
and through initiating artifice, produce rituals and righteousness.
Thus, the sages' relation to the accumulation of artifice in rituals and righteousness
is also like the potter molding to produce them.
Judging from this,
then the accumulation of artifice in rituals and righteousness,
is it truly human nature?
The reason for despising Jié, Zhí, and the petty person
is that they follow their nature,
indulge their emotions,
content with wantonness,
thereby emerging with greed, profit-seeking, and contention.
Therefore, it is clear that human nature is evil,
and goodness is a human artifice.
Heaven does not favor Zēng, Qiān, and Xiàojǐ
and exclude the multitude.
Yet Zēng, Qiān, and Xiàojǐ alone were abundant in the substance of filial piety
and perfect in the name of filial piety;
why is this?
Because they were devoted to rituals and righteousness.
Heaven does not favor the people of Qí and Lǔ
and exclude the people of Qín,
yet the people of Qín, in the righteousness between father and son, the distinction between husband and wife,
do not match the filial respect, reverence, and refinement of Qí and Lǔ;
why is this?
Because the people of Qín follow their emotions and nature, content with wantonness, and neglect rituals and righteousness.
Is it that their nature is different?
"The person on the street can become a Yǔ";
what does this mean?
The answer:
All that makes Yǔ who he is
is his practice of humaneness, righteousness, laws, and correctness.
Now, humaneness, righteousness, laws, and correctness
have principles that can be known and practiced,
and the person on the street
all possesses the substance capable of knowing humaneness, righteousness, laws, and correctness,
all possesses the means capable of practicing humaneness, righteousness, laws, and correctness;
then it is clear that they can become a Yǔ.
Now, if you think humaneness, righteousness, laws, and correctness inherently lack principles that can be known and practiced,
then even Yǔ would not know humaneness, righteousness, laws, and correctness,
nor practice humaneness, righteousness, laws, and correctness.
If you say the person on the street inherently lacks the substance to know humaneness, righteousness, laws, and correctness,
and inherently lacks the means to practice humaneness, righteousness, laws and correctness,
then the person on the street
would internally not know the righteousness between father and son,
externally not know the correctness between ruler and minister. (
But this is not so). Now, it is not so;
the person on the street
all internally can know the righteousness between father and son,
externally can know the correctness between ruler and minister,
then the substance capable of knowing,
the means capable of practicing,
are clearly present in the person on the street.
Now, if the person on the street
uses their substance capable of knowing,
their means capable of practicing,
based on the knowable principles and practicable means of humaneness and righteousness,
then it is clear that they can become a Yǔ.
Now, if the person on the street applies themselves to learning methods,
concentrates wholeheartedly,
ponders and examines thoroughly,
adds days and extends time,
accumulates goodness without ceasing,
then they will penetrate spiritual intelligence,
and align with heaven and earth.
Therefore, the sage
is achieved through human accumulation.
It is said:
"Sagehood can be accumulated and achieved,
yet not all can accumulate it;
why is that?"
The answer:
It is possible but cannot be forced.
Thus, the petty person can become a gentleman
but is unwilling to do so,
the gentleman can become a petty person
but is unwilling to do so.
The petty person and the gentleman
have never been unable to exchange roles;
yet they do not exchange roles,
because it is possible but cannot be forced.
Thus, the person on the street can become a Yǔ,
this is true;
but the person on the street becoming a Yǔ,
is not necessarily so.
Even if they cannot become a Yǔ,
it does not harm the possibility of becoming one.
Feet can walk all under heaven,
yet there has never been one who could walk all under heaven.
Artisans, farmers, and merchants
have never been unable to exchange occupations,
yet they have never exchanged occupations.
Judging from this,
then what is possible
is not necessarily achievable;
even if not achievable,
it does not harm the possibility.
Thus, the difference between ability and possibility
is vast,
and their interchangeability is clearly impossible.
Yáo asked Shùn:
"What are human emotions like?"
Shùn replied:
"Human emotions are very unappealing;
why ask about them?
When wife and children are present, filial piety declines toward parents;
when desires are obtained, trust declines toward friends;
when ranks and emoluments are full, loyalty declines toward the ruler.
Human emotions!
Human emotions!
Very unappealing;
why ask about them?"
Only the worthy are not so.
There is the knowledge of the sage,
the knowledge of the scholar-gentleman,
the knowledge of the petty person,
the knowledge of the laborer:
Speaking much, it is patterned and categorized,
all day discussing its reasons,
the speech in a thousand moves and ten thousand changes,
its guiding categories unified,
this is the knowledge of the sage.
Speaking little, it is direct and concise,
reasoned and lawful,
as if guided by a plumb line,
this is the knowledge of the scholar-gentleman.
His speech is flattering,
his actions perverse,
his undertakings often regrettable,
this is the knowledge of the petty person.
Quick, glib, and sharp but without category,
miscellaneous abilities, broad but useless,
analytically fast, refined and skilled but not urgent,
indifferent to right and wrong,
regardless of crooked or straight,
aiming to surpass others as the intent,
this is the knowledge of the laborer.
There is superior courage,
middle courage,
and inferior courage;
when the world has the Mean,
dare to straighten one's person;
when former kings had the Way,
dare to practice their intent;
above, not following the rulers of chaotic times,
below, not conforming to the people of chaotic times;
where humaneness is, no poverty or hardship;
where humaneness is lost, no wealth or honor;
when the world knows him,
he wishes to share joy with the world;
when the world does not know him,
he stands loftily independent between heaven and earth without fear:
this is superior courage.
Ritually respectful and intent frugal,
great in trust and faith while轻视ing wealth and goods,
daring to promote and elevate the worthy,
daring to pull down and depose the unworthy,
this is middle courage.
轻视ing one's person and重ing goods,
calamity-prone yet widely excusing,
seeking only to avoid trouble,
indifferent to right and wrong,
the reality of so and not so,
aiming to surpass others as the intent,
this is inferior courage.
Fánruò and Jùshǔ
were fine bows of antiquity,
yet without the straightening frame
they could not correct themselves.
Lord Huán's Cōng,
the Grand Duke's Quē,
King Wén's Lù,
Lord Zhuāng's Hū,
Hélǘ's Gānjiàng, Mòyé, Jùquē, and Pìlǘ—
these were all fine swords of antiquity,
yet without grinding and whetting they could not be sharp,
and without human strength they could not cut.
Huáliú, Qíjì, Xiānlí, and Lǜ'ěr
were all fine horses of antiquity,
yet they required the restraint of bit and reins in front,
the threat of whip and crop behind,
and the driving of Zàofǔ added to it,
only then could they cover a thousand lǐ in a day.
Though a person may have a fine nature and a discerning mind,
they must seek out worthy teachers to serve,
and choose worthy friends to befriend.
By obtaining worthy teachers to serve,
what they hear will be the ways of Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, and Tāng;
by obtaining good friends to befriend,
what they see will be acts of loyalty, trust, respect, and deference.
That they daily advance in benevolence and righteousness without realizing it
is due to the influence that makes it so.
If they associate with unworthy people now,
what they hear will be deceit, falsehood, fraud, and hypocrisy,
what they see will be filthy, indulgent, depraved, and greedy behaviors,
and that they approach punishment and execution without realizing it
is due to the influence that makes it so.
The Tradition says:
"If you do not know the son,
look at his friends;
if you do not know the ruler,
look at his attendants."
It is all a matter of influence,
it is all a matter of influence.
The Son of Heaven has no wife,
meaning he has no equal.
Within the four seas, there is no protocol for him as a guest,
meaning he has no destination.
Though his feet can walk,
he waits for attendants to advance;
though his mouth can speak,
he waits for officials to announce.
Without looking, he sees;
without listening, he hears;
without speaking, he is trusted;
without deliberating, he knows;
without acting, he achieves—
this signifies the ultimate completeness.
The Son of Heaven
holds the utmost power,
his form is most at ease,
his mind most content,
his will never thwarted,
his form never labored,
his honor unsurpassed.
The Odes say:
"Under the vast sky,
none is not the king's land;
to the shores of the land,
none is not the king's subject."
This expresses it.
When a sage king reigns above,
and duty is practiced below,
then scholars and officials have no dissolute conduct,
the hundred officials have no negligent affairs,
the masses and common people have no corrupt or strange customs,
no crimes of theft or banditry,
and none dare violate the prohibitions of the superiors.
All under heaven clearly know that theft cannot lead to wealth,
that harming others cannot lead to longevity,
that violating the prohibitions of superiors cannot lead to safety.
By following the proper way,
people attain what they desire;
by not following it,
they inevitably encounter what they detest:
thus punishments are extremely sparing yet authority flows like water.
The world clearly knows that for those who commit crimes, even hiding, fleeing, or escaping is insufficient to avoid punishment,
so none fail to admit their guilt and plead.
The Documents say:
"Every man brings punishment on himself."
This expresses it.
Thus, when punishment fits the crime, it is authoritative;
when it does not fit the crime, it is insulting;
when rank matches worthiness, it is honorable;
when it does not match worthiness, it is base.
In antiquity, punishment did not exceed the crime,
rank did not surpass virtue,
so they could execute the father and employ the son,
execute the elder brother and employ the younger.
Punishments did not rage beyond the crime,
ranks and rewards did not surpass virtue,
clearly each was communicated according to their sincerity.
Thus, those who did good were encouraged,
those who did evil were deterred,
punishments were extremely sparing yet authority flowed like water,
governmental decrees were supremely clear and transformation occurred as if by spirit.
The Tradition says:
"When one man has goodness,
millions rely on it."
This expresses it.
In chaotic times, it is not so;
punishments rage beyond crimes,
ranks and rewards surpass virtue,
crimes are judged by clan,
worthiness is elevated by lineage.
Thus, when one person is guilty, three clans are exterminated;
even with virtue like Shùn's,
they do not escape equal punishment—
this is judging crime by clan.
If ancestors were worthy,
their descendants must be eminent;
even with conduct like Jié
and Zhòu, their rank must be honored—
this is elevating worthiness by lineage.
Judging crime by clan,
elevating worthiness by lineage—
even if one wishes for no chaos,
is it possible!
The Odes say:
"All streams boil and surge,
mountain peaks crumble and fall;
high banks become valleys,
deep valleys become hills.
Alas for the people of today,
why are they not warned!"
This expresses it.
By discussing and emulating the sage kings,
one knows what to value;
by using righteousness to manage affairs,
one knows what is beneficial.
By discussing and knowing what to value,
one knows what to cultivate;
by managing affairs and knowing what is beneficial,
one knows whence to act.
These two aspects
are the root of right and wrong,
the source of success and failure.
Thus, King Chéng regarding the Duke of Zhōu
listened in all matters,
knowing what to value.
Lord Huán regarding Guǎn Zhòng
employed him in all state affairs,
knowing what was beneficial.
Wú had Wǔ Zǐxū but could not use him,
leading to the state's destruction,
due to abandoning the way and losing the worthy.
Thus, honoring the sage leads to kingship,
valuing the worthy leads to hegemony,
respecting the worthy leads to preservation,
disdaining the worthy leads to ruin—
this is uniform throughout antiquity and today.
Therefore, exalting the worthy and employing the capable,
distinguishing noble and base,
differentiating close and distant,
ordering elder and younger—
this is the way of the former kings.
Thus, exalting the worthy and employing the capable
leads to the ruler's honor and the subjects' peace;
having distinction between noble and base ensures orders are followed without deviation;
having differentiation between close and distant
ensures enforcement without contradiction;
having order between elder and younger
ensures tasks are accomplished swiftly and there is rest.
Thus, the benevolent
are those who are benevolent in this,
the righteous
are those who differentiate this,
the principled
are those for whom life and death reside in this,
the loyal
are those who are sincere and careful in this.
To master all these and be capable
is to be complete.
Complete yet not boastful,
naturally good in oneself,
is called sagely.
Not boastful,
thus the world does not contend with one in ability, and one excels in employing one's efforts.
Having yet not possessing,
thus one is honored by the world.
The Odes say:
"The good man, the gentleman,
his demeanor is without fault;
his demeanor is without fault,
he rectifies the four states."
This expresses it.
Let me present the "Completion of the Phases,"
The world's calamity,
Folly and darkness, folly and darkness overthrow the worthy and good,
When a ruler lacks worthies,
Like a blind man without a guide
How bewildered he is!
Let me set out the foundation,
Heed the sages,
Fools who act on their own—affairs go unmanaged,
If the ruler detests those who merely surpass him,
And his ministers do not remonstrate,
Disaster is sure to strike.
Discuss the ministers' faults,
Reverse their actions,
Honor the ruler, secure the state, exalt worthiness and righteousness,
Rejecting remonstrance and covering up errors,
Fools who agree with superiors
Will surely bring calamity to the state.
What is meant by "incompetent"?
The state is full of selfishness,
Cliques circle the ruler and factions spread,
Keeping the worthy distant and the slanderers close,
Loyal ministers are blocked, and the ruler's power shifts.
What is meant by "worthy"?
They clarify the roles of ruler and minister,
Above they honor the ruler, below they love the people,
If the ruler truly listens to them,
The world becomes one, and all within the seas submit.
The ruler's curse,
Slanderers prosper,
The worthy and able flee, and the state then collapses,
Folly piled upon folly,
Darkness upon darkness,
They become like Jié.
The world's disaster,
Envy of the worthy and able,
Fēi Lián knew governance and appointed È Lái,
Debasing their aspirations,
Expanding their parks and gardens,
Raising high their terraces (and pavilions).
King Wǔ was angered, led his troops at Mùyě,
Zhòu's soldiers turned their spears, Qǐ then submitted,
King Wǔ treated him well,
Enfeoffed him in Sòng, establishing his ancestral line.
The world's decline,
Slanderers gather,
Bǐ Gān was disemboweled, Jīzī was imprisoned,
King Wǔ executed them,
Lǚ Shàng waved his banner, and the people of Yīn cherished him.
The world's misfortune,
Hatred of worthy scholars,
Zǐxū was killed, Bǎilǐ was displaced,
Duke Mù obtained him,
Strengthened to match the Five Hegemons, the six ministers implemented.
The world's folly,
Hatred of great Confucians,
Rejected and spurned, not accepted, Confucius was constrained,
Zhǎn Qín was thrice dismissed,
Chūnshēn's way was cut off,
The foundation completely lost.
Let me tend the foundation,
The worthy are thoughtful,
Yáo exists through ten thousand generations as if seen today,
Slanderers know no limits,
Dangerous, steep, and biased—they doubt this.
The foundation must be extended,
Distinguish the worthy and incompetent,
The ways of King Wén and King Wǔ are the same as Fú Xī's,
Those who follow them achieve order,
Those who do not follow fall into chaos
Why doubt this?
In all completion of phases,
Distinguish the methods and models,
The pinnacle of perfect governance reverts to later kings,
Shèn, Mò, Jì, Huì,
The theories of the hundred schools are truly inauspicious.
Governance returns to unity,
Cultivate it for good fortune,
The gentleman holds it with a heart like a knot,
The common people are of two minds,
Slanderers discard it,
And punish its form.
Water is perfectly level,
Upright and un倾斜,
A heart and method like this resemble the sage.
If a man has power,
Upright and employed, he must align with Heaven.
The world lacks a true king,
Worthy and good are in distress,
Violent men enjoy grain-fed meat,
While the benevolent have only husks,
Ritual and music are extinguished
And cease, sages lie hidden
While Mò's techniques prevail.
The classic of governance,
Is ritual and punishment,
The gentleman cultivates them, the common people are tranquil,
Illustrious virtue and cautious punishment,
The state being well-governed, all within the four seas are pacified.
The aim of governance,
Puts power and wealth last,
The gentleman is sincere in it and well prepared,
Abides in it steadfastly,
And deeply stores it
Able to think far ahead.
Thought becomes refined,
The glory of the will,
Devotion and unity bring spiritual completion,
When essence and spirit interact,
Unified and undivided,
One becomes a sage.
The way of governance,
Beautiful and ageless,
The gentleman follows it, excellent and good,
Below, to teach and instruct the young,
Above, to serve the ancestors.
The "Completion of the Phases" is exhausted,
But the words do not falter,
The gentleman follows the way, smooth and penetrating,
Honoring the worthy and good,
Distinguishing the calamities and evils.
Let me present the "Completion of the Phases,"
Speaking of the sage kings,
Yáo and Shùn exalted the worthy and personally declined power,
Xǔ Yóu and Shàn Juǎn,
Valued righteousness over profit, their conduct illustrious.
Yáo yielded to the worthy,
For the sake of the people,
Broad benefit and universal love, virtue was impartially bestowed,
Distinguishing order above and below,
Noble and humble had their ranks, clarifying ruler and minister.
Yáo entrusted the able,
Shùn met his time,
Exalting the worthy and promoting virtue, the world was well-governed,
Even with worthies
And sages, if they do not meet their age,
Who knows them?
Yáo did not boast of virtue,
Shùn did not decline,
He gave him his two daughters in marriage and entrusted him with affairs,
Great indeed was Shùn,
Facing south he stood, and all things were complete.
Shùn passed it to Yǔ,
The whole world,
Exalting virtue and promoting the worthy without losing order,
Abroad not avoiding enemies,
At home not favoring kin,
He gave it to the worthy.
Yǔ toiled (with heart) and strength,
Yáo had virtue,
Without using arms, the Sān Miáo submitted,
Raising Shùn from the fields,
Entrusting him the world,
He himself rested.
He obtained Hòu Jì,
The five grains were planted,
Kuí as music director made birds and beasts submit,
Xiè as Minister of Education,
The people knew filial piety and fraternal duty, honoring the virtuous.
Yǔ had achievements,
Controlled the flooding waters,
Expelled the people's scourge, drove away Gōng Gōng,
In the north, opened the nine rivers,
Connected the twelve islets,
Dredged the three rivers.
Yǔ spread the land,
Pacified the world,
Personally labored for the people's sake,
Gaining Yì, Gāo Yáo, Héng Gé, and Zhí Chéng as assistants.
Xiè, the Dark King,
Fathered Zhāo Míng,
Dwelt at Dǐshí, then moved to Shāng,
After fourteen generations,
There was Tiān Yǐ, who became Chéng Tāng.
Tiān Yǐ Tāng,
Discussed and promoted appropriately,
Personally yielded to Biàn Suí and promoted Móu Guāng,
The way of ancient sages and worthies—the foundation must be extended.
I wish to set forth my words,
The world in chaos hates the good and does not govern this,
Concealing faults and嫉妒 the worthy,
Long led by deceit and fraud, seldom without disaster.
How perilous!
The slope is made thus,
Sage wisdom unused, fools devise plans,
The front carriage has already overturned,
The later one does not yet know to change
When will it awaken!
Not awakened,
Not knowing the hardship,
Confused, losing direction, easily reversing high and low,
Loyalty does not reach above,
Eyes and ears are covered, the gate is blocked.
The gate blocked,
Greatly confused,
Reckless chaos and darkness know no end,
Right and wrong are reversed,
Cliques deceive the ruler and hate the upright.
Uprightness is detested,
the heart lacks measure,
crooked and perverse, one strays from the path,
blaming not oneself but others—
am I alone in thinking myself fine? Surely not without cause!
Unaware of caution,
consequences will surely follow,
regretfully persisting in error, unwilling to repent,
slanderers advance—
deceptive words breed cunning postures.
Human postures,
better to be prepared,
vying for favor, envying the worthy, mutual hatred and jealousy,
jealous of merit, slandering the virtuous—
below, gathering cliques; above, concealing and hiding.
When the ruler is obstructed,
he loses support and power,
employing slanderers, unable to control them,
as in the troubles of Gōng Chángfù—
King Lì was exiled to Zhì.
King Yōu and King Lì of Zhōu,
the reasons for their downfall,
were not heeding loyal admonitions, harming the faithful.
Alas, what kind of person am I,
to meet such times alone, born in an age of chaos!
Wishing to speak from the heart,
my words go unheeded,
fearing to share Wǔ Zǐxū’s fate, meeting disaster,
advising without being heard—
beheaded and cast into the river with Dúlù.
Reflecting on the past,
to caution myself,
order and chaos, right and wrong, can be discerned,
entrusting to "Chéng Xiàng" to convey my meaning.
Let me present the "Chéng Xiàng,"
speaking of ways to govern,
the ruler's principles are five, concise and clear,
if the ruler strictly adheres to them—
all below will be just and upright,
and the state will prosper.
Ministers and subordinates have their duties,
none should idle without work,
focus on fundamentals, economize, wealth will be boundless,
affairs follow the ruler’s commands—
none may arbitrarily assign tasks,
unifying the people’s strength.
Each keeping to their duty,
clothed and fed sufficiently,
ranks and robes clearly distinguished by degree,
benefits flow upward—
none may bestow favors arbitrarily,
who then gains privately?
The ruler’s laws are clear,
principles constant,
standards set, the people know the way,
advancement and retreat follow rules—
none may determine nobility or baseness,
who then curries private favor with the king?
The ruler’s laws are models,
prohibiting wrongdoing,
all delight in instruction, names remain unchanged,
those who cultivate them are honored—
those who deviate are shamed,
who would follow another guide?
Punishments fit the crime,
maintain their strictness,
subordinates cannot lightly use private influence,
crimes and misfortunes have their laws—
none may lighten or加重 penalties, authority remains undivided.
Let me tend the foundations,
clarity brings blessing,
the ruler fond of discussion must be good at planning,
refining the five hearings—
all affairs are managed, who but the ruler directs?
The essence of hearing,
lies in understanding the circumstances,
carefully applying rewards and punishments with clarity,
the evident will be captured—
the hidden will be revealed,
and the people return to sincerity.
Words have measure,
examined for their truth,
distinguishing truth from falsehood, rewards and punishments assured,
subordinates do not deceive superiors—
all speak from true feeling,
clear as the sun.
When superiors are open and perceptive,
the distant and hidden come near,
observing what is lawful and unlawful, seeing the unseen,
once ears and eyes are sharp—
officials respect laws and decrees, none dare act arbitrarily.
The ruler’s teachings issued,
actions follow rules,
officials carefully execute them without corruption,
subordinates make no private requests—
each acts appropriately,
setting aside cleverness or clumsiness.
Ministers diligently follow,
the ruler controls change,
impartial scrutiny and thoughtful deliberation bring order,
governing all under heaven—
later ages emulate this, forming a consistent code.
There is a great thing,
neither silk nor cloth,
yet patterns form its texture.
Neither sun nor moon,
it illuminates all under heaven.
The living use it to attain longevity,
the dead use it for burial,
city walls rely on it for strength,
armies rely on it for might.
Pure, it brings kingly rule;
mixed, it brings hegemony;
without it, perish.
I, ignorant, do not recognize it,
dare to ask the king.
The king said:
Is this not patterned yet without embellishment?
Simple to know yet profoundly orderly?
Revered by gentlemen, ignored by petty men?
Without its nature, one becomes like a beast;
with its nature, one becomes refined and proper?
Commoners exalted by it become sages;
lords exalted by it unify the four seas?
Extremely clear yet concise,
very smooth yet substantive,
I归结 it to Lǐ. Ritual.
Heaven bestows this thing,
to bestow upon the people below,
some receive much, some little,
often unevenly.
Jié and Zhòu used it for chaos;
Tāng and Wǔ used it for virtue.
Dim and bright,
vast and solemn,
it circulates throughout the four seas,
in less than a full day.
Gentlemen cultivate it;
Zhí uses it to break into houses.
Vast, it reaches heaven;
subtle, it has no form.
Through it, righteousness is upheld;
through it, endeavors succeed.
It can curb violence and enrich the poor;
the people await it for peace and prosperity.
I, ignorant, do not recognize it,
and wish to ask its name.
It is said:
Is this what brings safety in breadth and peril in narrowness?
Is it drawn to purity and repelled by impurity?
Deeply hidden yet outwardly overcoming foes?
Emulating Yǔ and Shùn, able to follow their traces?
In action and repose, relying on it for suitability?
The essence of vital energy,
the flourish of will and intent.
The people await it for tranquility;
the world awaits it for peace.
Clear, thorough, pure, and flawless—
this is called the wisdom of a gentleman. Wisdom.
There is a thing here:
at rest, it spreads calmly low;
in motion, it rises immensely high.
Round, it fits the compass;
square, it fits the square.
Vast, it matches heaven and earth;
in virtue, it rivals Yáo and Yǔ?
Fine as the tip of a hair,
yet filling the great cosmos.
Swift, it reaches the farthest extremes;
twisting, it chases and returns.
Majestic, all under heaven look up to it.
Virtuous and generous, it rejects none;
adorned with five colors, it forms patterns.
Coming and going, dim and weary,
it connects with the great spirit;
passing in and out very swiftly,
none know its gate.
Without it, the world perishes;
with it, the world survives.
Your disciple is not clever,
but wishes to describe this;
gentleman, set forth words,
please guess its meaning.
It is said:
Is this not something vast yet unblockable?
Filling the great cosmos without leaving gaps,
Entering crevices without feeling cramped?
Traveling far swiftly yet bearing no messages?
Coming and going obscurely yet impossible to barricade?
Violently arriving with杀伤 yet without hesitation?
Benefiting all under heaven yet showing no partiality?
It rests upon the earth and wanders the cosmos,
Befriending the wind and giving birth to rain.
In winter it brings cold,
In summer it brings heat.
Vast and spirited,
I ask to attribute it to cloud. Cloud.
There is a thing here,
Soft and delicate in form,
Transforming repeatedly like a spirit.
Its merit covers all under heaven,
Creating patterns for ten thousand generations.
Rituals and music are completed through it,
Nobility and baseness are distinguished by it.
Nurturing the aged and raising the young,
Depend on it for survival.
Its name is not beautiful,
Neighboring with violence.
Its achievement made, its body discarded,
Its task accomplished, its home destroyed.
Its elders abandoned,
Its offspring gathered.
Harmful to flying birds.
I am ignorant and do not recognize it,
I ask to consult Wǔtài for a divination.
Wǔtài divined and said:
Is this not what has a maiden's body
And a horse's head?
Transforming repeatedly yet not long-lived?
Excellent in youth but clumsy in old age?
Having parents yet without male or female?
Hibernating in winter and active in summer,
Feeding on mulberry leaves and spinning silk,
Chaotic in front yet orderly behind,
Born in summer yet disliking heat,
Fond of moisture yet disliking rain.
The chrysalis as its mother,
The moth as its father.
Three bowings and three risings,
Then its task is greatly completed.
This is called the principle of the silkworm. Silkworm.
There is a thing here,
Born in the mountains,
Residing in halls and rooms.
Without knowledge or skill,
Yet adept at tailoring clothes.
Neither stealing nor thieving,
It passes through walls.
Day and night joining and separating,
Forming patterns and designs,
Able to create vertical unions,
And also skilled at horizontal connections.
Below it clothes the common people,
Above it adorns the emperor.
Its achievements are vast,
Yet it receives no recognition.
Used in time, it remains,
Unused, it perishes.
I am ignorant and do not recognize it,
I dare to ask the king.
The king said:
Is this not what begins life large
And ends up small?
With a long tail and sharp point?
With a sharp head and a lingering tail?
Going back and forth,
Tying knots to accomplish its task.
Without feathers or wings,
It reverses and turns extremely.
The tail appears and work begins,
The tail lingers and work ends.
The hairpin as its father,
The tube as its mother.
It sews the outer layer,
And also connects the inner lining.
This is called the principle of the needle. Needle.
When the world is in disorder,
I present these anomalous verses:
Heaven and earth change places,
The four seasons reverse directions.
Constellations fall,
Day and night become dark.
The obscure rise to prominence,
Sun and moon hide below.
Just and selfless,
Are accused of manipulation,
Those who cherish public benefit,
Build towering towers and spacious halls.
Not privately blaming others,
Yet arm themselves with weapons.
Pure and complete in virtue,
Face slanderous mouths clamoring.
Benevolent men are deposed and constrained,
The arrogant and violent dominate with strength.
The world is dark and perilous,
Fearful of losing its finest.
The horned dragon becomes a gecko,
The owl becomes a phoenix.
Bǐgān was disemboweled,
Confucius was confined in Kuang.
How bright was his understanding!
How dense his encounter with inauspicious times!
How contrary his desire for ritual and righteousness to flourish!
How dark the world's obscurity!
The bright heaven does not return,
Worries know no bounds.
A thousand years must reverse,
Such is the ancient constant.
Disciples, strive in learning,
Heaven will not forget.
The sage clasps his hands,
The time is nearly at hand.
Stupid and doubtful,
I wish to hear the counter-verse.
Its "Little Song" says:
"Thinking of those distant places,
How blocked they are!
Benevolent men are suppressed and constrained,
Violent men prosper.
Loyal ministers are in peril,
Slanderers are employed."
Xuányù and yáozhū
They do not know to wear,
Mixed cloth and brocade
They do not know to distinguish.
Lǘjū and Zǐshē
No one introduces them,
Mómǔ and Diāofù
They delight in.
Taking blindness for sight,
Deafness for hearing.
Danger for safety,
Auspiciousness for ominousness.
Alas!
O Heaven above!
How can I be the same as they?
The Great Summary. The ruler who governs people,
Exalts ritual and honors the worthy to become king,
Emphasizes laws and loves the people to become hegemon,
Is fond of profit and full of deceit to face peril.
To be close to all four directions,
Nothing compares to the center,
Thus the king must dwell in the center of the world,
This is ritual.
The Son of Heaven has an outer screen,
The feudal lords have an inner screen,
This is ritual.
The outer screen—
Is to not wish to see outside,
The inner screen—
Is to not wish to see inside.
When a feudal lord summons his minister,
The minister does not wait for his carriage,
But dons his clothes in disarray and runs,
This is ritual.
The Book of Songs says:
"Upside down and inside out,
From the duke's summons I go."
When the Son of Heaven summons feudal lords,
The carriage goes to the horses,
This is ritual.
The Book of Songs says:
"I bring out my carriage,
To the pastures there.
From the Son of Heaven's place,
He bids me come."
The Son of Heaven wears the mountain crown,
Feudal lords wear black caps,
Great officers wear subordinate crowns,
Scholars wear leather caps,
This is ritual.
The Son of Heaven holds a jade scepter,
Feudal lords hold a tú scepter,
Great officers carry a tablet,
This is ritual.
The Son of Heaven has a carved bow,
Feudal lords have a red bow,
Great officers have a black bow,
This is ritual.
When feudal lords meet,
A minister acts as intermediary,
With their instructed knights fully deployed,
Leaving the benevolent to guard the home.
To recruit someone with a jade guī,
to inquire of a scholar with a bì,
to summon someone with a yuàn,
to sever relations with someone using a jué,
and to restore severed ties with a huán.
The benevolent heart of a ruler is established,
wisdom serves as its instrument,
and rites represent its fulfillment.
Thus, the king prioritizes benevolence before rites,
as Heaven's bestowal naturally follows this order.
The Records of Rites states:
"Excessive gifts harm virtue,
extravagant wealth destroys rites."
"When we speak of rites, oh rites,
are we merely speaking of jades and silks?"
The Book of Songs says:
"Things may be fine,
but only when they are appropriate."
If not timely and fitting,
not reverent in interaction,
not joyful in spirit,
even if fine,
they do not constitute rites.
Those crossing waters mark the depths,
to keep people from drowning;
those governing the people mark disorder,
to keep them from error.
Rites
serve as such markers,
the ancient kings used rites to mark the world's disorders.
Now those who abandon rites
are removing these markers.
Thus the people become confused
and fall into calamity,
this is why punishments proliferate.
Shùn said:
"I follow desires yet achieve order."
Therefore rites were created
for those below the wise down to common people,
not for making sages,
yet they also help in becoming sage.
Without learning, one cannot achieve:
Yáo learned from Jūn Chóu,
Shùn learned from Wùchéng Zhāo,
Yǔ learned from Xīwáng Guó.
At fifty, one cannot fully observe mourning,
at seventy, only the mourning garments remain.
In the wedding ceremony,
the father stands facing south,
the son kneels facing north,
the father toasts and commands him:
"Go welcome your partner,
complete our ancestral affairs,
reverently continue the line of your departed mother,
then you will have constancy."
The son says:
"I obey.
I only fear I cannot measure up,
dare I forget your command!"
What is called conduct
means practicing rites,
and rites mean
respecting the noble,
being filial to the aged,
deferential to elders,
kind to the young,
and benevolent to the lowly.
Bestowing on one's household
is like giving rewards to the state;
being angry with servants
is like punishing the common people.
The gentleman towards his son
loves him but doesn't show it outwardly,
employs him but not with special appearance,
guides him with principle but doesn't force him.
Rites take顺应人心 as fundamental,
thus what's not in the Classic of Rites
yet顺应人心
all constitutes rites.
The main aspects of rites:
serving the living -
adorning joy,
sending off the dead -
adorning grief,
military matters -
adorning authority.
Loving kin, maintaining old ties, rewarding merit, acknowledging labor - these are the gradations of benevolence.
Honoring the noble, respecting the respected, esteeming the worthy, revering the aged, deferring to elders - these are the principles of righteousness.
Practicing these with proper measure
constitutes the order of rites.
Benevolence means love,
thus creating closeness.
Righteousness
means principle,
thus guiding action.
Rites
mean measure,
thus achieving completion.
Benevolence has its proper neighborhood,
righteousness its proper gate.
Benevolence - if not in its proper neighborhood yet dwelling there,
is not true benevolence.
Righteousness - if not through its proper gate yet following it,
is not true righteousness.
Extending kindness without principle,
doesn't complete benevolence;
following principle without courage,
doesn't complete righteousness;
examining measure without harmony,
doesn't complete rites;
having harmony without expression,
doesn't complete music.
Thus it is said:
Benevolence, righteousness, rites, and music
ultimately converge as one.
The gentleman dwells in benevolence through righteousness,
then achieves benevolence.
Practices righteousness through rites,
then achieves righteousness.
Establishes rites by returning to roots and completing branches,
then achieves rites.
When all three are mastered,
then the Way is achieved.
Money and goods are called fù,
carriages and horses called fèng,
clothing called suì,
treasures and curios called zèng,
jade and shells called hán.
Fù and fèng assist the living,
zèng and suì send off the dead.
Sending off the dead not reaching the coffin,
condoling the living not reaching grief,
violates rites.
Thus traveling for festivities fifty lǐ,
rushing to funerals a hundred lǐ,
ensuring fèng and zèng reach timely -
these are major aspects of rites.
Rites are
the steering mechanism of governance.
Governing without rites,
governance cannot be implemented.
When the Son of Heaven ascends the throne,
the high minister approaches saying:
"How profound should be your concerns!
He who can eliminate troubles creates blessings,
he who cannot becomes a scourge."
Presenting the first strategy to the Son of Heaven.
The middle minister approaches saying:
"He who matches Heaven and possesses the lands below,
considers affairs before they arise,
anticipates troubles before they occur.
Considering affairs beforehand is called preparedness,
preparedness ensures excellent completion;
anticipating troubles beforehand is called prevention,
prevention keeps calamity from arising.
Considering matters only after they occur is called lagging,
lagging ensures affairs won't succeed;
considering troubles only after they occur is called distress,
distress makes calamity unavoidable."
Presenting the second strategy.
The lower minister approaches saying:
"Be reverent and vigilant without slackening.
While celebrants are in the hall,
mourners may be at the gate.
Calamity and fortune are neighbors,
none know their gateway.
Be prepared!
Be prepared!
The myriad people look to you!"
Presenting the third strategy.
Yǔ seeing plowmen working in pairs would bow in his carriage,
passing a village of ten households would always dismount.
Hunting too early,
holding court too late,
violates rites.
Governing people without rites,
any action will lead to failure.
Bowing with the head balanced is called bài,
bowing with the head lowered is called qǐshǒu,
and touching the ground with the forehead is called qǐsǎng.
A minister's retainer does not perform qǐshǒu,
not to honor the family retainer,
but to avoid usurping the ruler's prerogative.
With one appointment, one is ranked among the villagers;
with two appointments, among the clan;
with three appointments,
even clan members over seventy dare not take precedence.
There are high-ranking dàfū,
middle-ranking dàfū,
and low-ranking dàfū.
In auspicious affairs, respect for rank is emphasized;
in mourning affairs, closeness of kinship is emphasized.
Between ruler and minister, there must be respect;
between father and son, there must be affection;
among brothers, there must to be harmony;
between husband and wife, there must be joy.
The young are nurtured to grow,
the elderly are provided for.
Thus, Heaven and Earth give them life,
and the sage completes them.
Pìn means inquiry,
a visit of courtesy,
xiǎng means offering,
a presentation of gifts.
Sīdí means private audience,
a personal meeting.
The beauty of speech lies in
its solemnity and magnificence.
The beauty of the court lies in
its orderliness and dignity.
Those who serve as ministers
may remonstrate but not slander,
may leave but not resent,
may feel discontent but not rage.
For a dàfū, the ruler
inquires three times about his illness
and attends his funeral three times;
for a shì,
he inquires once
and attends once.
Unless to inquire about illness or offer condolences,
a feudal lord does not go to his minister's home.
After the burial,
if a friend of one's father or the ruler
offers food, one may eat it,
not avoiding fine grains and meat,
but should decline if there is wine or sweet liquor.
Residential halls should not surpass ancestral temples in grandeur,
informal clothing should not surpass sacrificial robes in finery—
this is ritual propriety.
The Xián hexagram in the Yìjīng
reveals the relationship of husband and wife.
The way of husband and wife
must be correct,
for it is the foundation of ruler-minister and father-son relationships.
Xián means influence,
to connect,
with the high lowering to the low,
the man humbling himself before the woman,
the soft above and the firm below.
The principle of betrothing a scholar
and the way of personally welcoming the bride
emphasize the importance of beginnings.
Lǐ is what people practice;
to lose this practice
is to stumble and fall into peril.
When a minor deviation leads to great disorder,
it pertains to lǐ.
Lǐ in rectifying the state
is like scales for weighing lightness and heaviness,
like the ink line for determining straight and crooked.
Thus, without lǐ, people cannot live,
affairs cannot be accomplished,
and the state cannot be tranquil.
The sound of carriage bells
should match the Wǔ and Xiàng when walking,
and the Sháo and Hù when hurrying.
The nobleman listens to the pitches and practices demeanor before going out.
Marriages are arranged after the frost descends
and cease when the ice melts. Within,
one should visit once every ten days.
When seated, look at the knees;
when standing, look at the feet;
when conversing, look at the face.
Standing, one looks ahead six feet, and six times that is six-six thirty-six,
making three zhàng six chǐ.
Elegance in form and sincerity in substance
complement each other as inner and outer,
embodying the mean in lǐ.
The ability to reflect is called foresight.
Lǐ entails
consistency between root and branch,
correspondence between beginning and end.
Lǐ employs
material goods for its practice,
distinctions of nobility for its ornamentation,
and variations in quantity for its differentiation.
Inferior ministers serve their ruler with goods,
middle ministers with their persons,
superior ministers with talented individuals.
The Yìjīng says:
"Returning to the right path,
what blame can there be?"
The Chūnqiū praises Duke Mù,
considering him capable of reform.
If a scholar has jealous friends,
worthy companions will not draw near;
if a ruler has jealous ministers,
worthy men will not come.
Those who obscure the public good are called benighted;
those who hide the worthy are called jealous;
those who serve the jealous and benighted are called treacherous.
Treacherous individuals
and jealous, benighted ministers
are the blight of the state.
Those who can speak it
and practice it
are the state's treasures.
Those who cannot speak it
but can practice it
are the state's vessels.
Those who can speak it
but cannot practice it
are the state's tools.
Those who speak of goodness
but practice evil
are the state's calamities.
Those who govern the state revere its treasures,
cherish its vessels,
employ its tools,
and eliminate its calamities.
Without wealth, the people's sentiments cannot be nurtured;
without education, the people's nature cannot be refined.
Thus, each family with five mǔ of residence land
and a hundred mǔ of fields,
devoted to their work without disruption of their seasons,
is thereby enriched.
Establishing the Grand Academy,
setting up local schools,
cultivating the six rites,
and clarifying the seven teachings
are the means to guide them.
The Shījīng says:
"Give them drink and food,
instruct and teach them."
Thus, the king's affairs are complete.
When King Wǔ first entered Yīn,
he honored Shāng Róng's neighborhood,
paid respect to Jīzǐ in his confinement,
and wept at Bǐgàn's tomb,
whereupon all under heaven turned toward goodness.
In all under heaven, states have outstanding scholars,
and each age has worthy individuals.
The lost do not ask the way,
the drowning do not ask ford,
and the doomed prefer solitude.
The Shījīng says:
"What I say is for duty,
do not take it as a joke.
The ancients had a saying:
'Consult the grass and firewood gatherers.'"
This speaks of seeking broad counsel.
Where there are laws, act according to them;
where there are none, proceed by analogy.
From the root,
one knows the branches;
from the left,
one knows the right—
all things differ in principle
yet uphold one another.
Rewards and punishments
must correspond to their categories to be effective.
Education and customs
must align with circumstances to be practiced.
For households with an octogenarian, one son is exempt from service;
with a nonagenarian, the entire family is exempt;
those with severe disabilities requiring care are exempt one person.
During parental mourning,
three years of exemption from service.
For lighter mourning garments like cuīshuāi and dàgōng,
three months of exemption.
Those following feudal lords,
newlyweds within a year,
are exempt for the period.
Confucius said of Zǐjiā Jū that he was a persistent minister,
but not as good as Yànzǐ;
Yànzǐ,
a meritorious official,
was not as good as Zǐchǎn;
Zǐchǎn,
a benevolent man,
was not as good as Guǎn Zhòng.
Guǎn Zhòng’s character
valued achievement over righteousness,
wisdom over benevolence—
a rustic man,
unfit to be a high minister of the Son of Heaven.
Mèngzǐ met King Xuān three times
without discussing affairs of state.
His disciples asked:
"Why meet the King of Qí thrice without discussing affairs?"
Mèngzǐ replied:
"I first attack his corrupt heart."
When Gōngxíng Zǐzhī went to Yān,
he met Zēng Yuán on the road
and asked:
"What is the ruler of Yān like?"
Zēng Yuán said:
"His aspirations are low.
Low aspirations make one disregard matters;
disregarding matters, one seeks no help.
Without seeking help,
how can he achieve anything?
He is like a captive of the Dī and Qiāng tribes.
He worries not about being bound,
but about not being cremated.
He covets autumn’s fine hairs,
harms the state without end,
yet persists—
how can this be called wise strategy!"
Like one who loses a needle,
