searching all day without finding it,
but when found,
it’s not that his eyes grew sharper—
he saw it by looking closely.
So it is with the mind in deliberation.
Righteousness and profit
are both inherent in humans.
Even Yáo and Shùn could not rid people of desire for profit,
but they made that desire not overcome their love of righteousness.
Even Jié and Zhòu could not rid people of love for righteousness,
but they made that love not prevail over their desire for profit.
Thus when righteousness triumphs, it’s an age of order;
when profit overcomes righteousness, it’s an age of chaos.
If superiors value righteousness, it overcomes profit;
if they value profit, it overcomes righteousness.
Hence the Son of Heaven does not speak of wealth,
feudal lords not of gain and loss,
ministers not of personal fortunes,
scholars not of trading goods;
rulers of states do not breed cattle and sheep,
ministers in office do not raise chickens and pigs,
high ministers do not deal in currency,
officials do not tend gardens—
from scholars upward, all disdain profit and do not compete with the people for livelihoods,
delighting in sharing and ashamed of hoarding.
Thus the people are not burdened by wealth,
and the poor have means to sustain themselves.
King Wén punished four,
King Wǔ punished two,
the Duke of Zhōu completed the task,
and by Kings Chéng and Kāng’s time, there was no more punishment.
Amassing wealth while scorning the needy,
burdening the people and punishing incapability—
this is how wickedness arises,
and punishments multiply.
If superiors love righteousness,
the people secretly cultivate it;
if superiors love wealth,
the people die for profit.
These two paths
are the crossroads of order and chaos.
A saying goes:
"Want wealth?
Endure shame,
cast aside all,
abandon old ties,
and turn your back on righteousness."
When superiors love wealth,
the people’s conduct becomes thus—
how can chaos not follow?
Tāng prayed during drought:
"Was governance excessive?
Did I oppress the people?
Why has the drought reached this extreme!
Were palaces too lavish?
Were harem influences too strong?
Why has the drought reached this extreme!
Were bribes rampant?
Slanderers promoted?
Why has the drought reached this extreme!"
Heaven gave birth to the people
not for the ruler’s sake.
Heaven established rulers
for the people’s sake.
Thus in ancient times, lands were divided and states founded
not merely to honor feudal lords;
offices were established,
ranks and emoluments graded,
not merely to exalt ministers.
The ruler’s way is to know people;
the minister’s way is to know affairs.
Thus Shùn governed the world
without micromanaging, yet all things flourished.
A farmer skilled in tilling cannot necessarily be a farming instructor,
nor can artisans or merchants.
Replacing the unworthy with the worthy—
no divination is needed to know it’s auspicious.
Using order to attack chaos—
no battle is needed to know victory.
When the Qí wanted to attack Lǔ,
they feared Biàn Zhuāngzǐ
and dared not pass through Biàn.
When the Jìn wanted to attack Wèi,
they feared Zǐlù
and dared not pass through Pú.
Not knowing? Ask Yáo and Shùn;
not having? Seek the heavenly storehouse.
It is said:
The way of ancient kings
is embodied by Yáo and Shùn;
the breadth of the six arts
lies in the heavenly storehouse.
The noble person’s learning is like molting—
shedding and transforming utterly.
Thus their walking emulates,
their standing emulates,
their sitting emulates,
their expressions and speech emulate.
No good deed is delayed,
no question is held overnight.
Good learners exhaust the principles;
good practitioners delve into the difficulties.
The noble person sets their will as if in adversity—
even if the Son of Heaven or high ministers inquire,
they respond with right and wrong.
The noble person, though destitute, does not fail;
though weary, does not act carelessly;
facing hardship, does not forget words spoken on the mat.
Without cold weather,
one cannot know the pine and cypress;
without difficulties, one cannot know the noble person’s unwavering integrity.
With light rain,
the Hàn River still flows deep.
For what encompasses the small becomes great,
what accumulates the subtle becomes evident;
when virtue is perfect, one’s demeanor is harmonious,
and when conduct is complete, one’s reputation spreads far.
The petty person, not sincere within, seeks outward display.
To speak without acknowledging one’s teacher is rebellion;
to teach without acknowledging one’s teacher is betrayal.
Betrayers and rebels—
enlightened rulers do not admit them,
Those who fall short in action
are excessive in words;
those who lack in trustworthiness
speak of sincerity.
Thus, the *Spring and Autumn Annals* praises sworn agreements,
while the *Book of Songs* criticizes frequent oaths,
for their underlying intent is the same.
Those skilled in the *Book of Songs* do not merely recite it,
those skilled in the *Book of Changes* do not rely on divination,
those skilled in the *Rites* do not just perform ceremonies,
as their inner purpose is identical.
Master Zēng said:
"A filial son's words are meant to be heard,
his actions are meant to be seen.
Words being heard
serve to please those afar;
actions being seen
serve to please those nearby.
When the near are pleased, they draw close;
when the far are pleased, they adhere.
Drawing the near close and making the far adhere—
this is the way of a filial son."
When Master Zēng was traveling,
Yànzǐ followed him to the outskirts
and said:
"Yíng has heard that
a gentleman gives words as gifts,
while commoners give wealth.
Yíng is poor and without wealth,
so I beg to borrow from the gentleman's way,
offering you these words: The wheel of a carriage
is made from wood of Tài Shān,
placed in a straightening frame,
and after three to five months,
it becomes a curved rim
that, even when worn, does not revert to its original state.
The 'straightening frame' for a gentleman
must be carefully chosen;
be cautious of it.
Orchids and gǎoběn herbs,
steeped in honeyed wine,
can be traded for a single wearing.
If a ruler is steeped in fragrant wine,
he can be swayed by flattery;
what a gentleman is steeped in
must be chosen with care."
A person's engagement with culture and learning
is like jade being carved and polished.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Like cutting, like filing,
like carving, like polishing."
This refers to the pursuit of learning.
The Hé Shì's jade disc,
in its rough state from the well village,
was carved by jade artisans
to become a treasure for the world.
Zǐgòng and Jìlù,
originally men of lowly status,
embraced culture and learning,
practiced ritual and righteousness,
and became renowned scholars under heaven.
Never tiring of learning and inquiry,
never wearying in cherishing scholars,
this is the storehouse of heaven.
A gentleman does not speak when in doubt,
nor before asking questions;
the path is long, and each day brings increase.
Having much knowledge but no closeness,
broad learning but no method,
loving many things but no steadfastness—
a gentleman does not associate with such.
If one does not recite in youth,
nor discuss in prime age,
even if capable,
one will not achieve completion.
When the gentleman teaches with single-mindedness,
and the disciple learns with single-mindedness,
rapid success follows.
A gentleman in office can enhance the ruler's reputation and alleviate the people's worries.
To hold a position without the ability is deceit;
to receive generous rewards without benefit is theft.
Learners do not necessarily aim for official posts,
but those who hold office must engage in learning.
Zǐgòng asked Confucius:
"Cì is weary of learning and wishes to cease and serve a ruler."
Confucius said:
"The *Book of Songs* says:
'Gentle and reverent, morning and evening,
in duties be respectful.'
Serving a ruler is hard;
how can one cease in serving a ruler?"
"Then Cì wishes to cease in serving parents."
Confucius said:
"The *Book of Songs* says:
'Filial sons never fail;
forever you bless your kind.'
Serving parents is hard;
how can one cease in serving parents?"
"Then Cì wishes to cease with wife and children."
Confucius said:
"The *Book of Songs* says:
'Set an example for your wife,
extend to your brothers,
and thus rule the family and state.'
Wife and children are hard;
how can one cease with wife and children?"
"Then Cì wishes to cease with friends."
Confucius said:
"The *Book of Songs* says:
'Friends assist each other,
assisting with dignity and grace.'
Friends are hard;
how can one cease with friends?"
"Then Cì wishes to cease and farm."
Confucius said:
"The *Book of Songs* says:
'By day you gather thatch,
by night you twist ropes;
hastily you repair the roof,
for soon you'll sow the grains.'
Farming is hard;
how can one cease in farming?"
"Then is there no cessation for Cì?"
Confucius said:
"Gaze upon the grave mound,
lofty it appears,
peaked it stands,
like a cauldron—
then you know where rest is found."
Zǐgòng said:
"How great is death!
The gentleman rests there,
the commoner ends there."
The *Airs of the States*' portrayal of love for beauty,
as the *Tradition* says:
"Fulfills desires without overstepping bounds.
Its sincerity can compare to metal and stone;
its tones can be offered in the ancestral temple."
The *Minor Odes* do not serve a corrupt ruler,
but withdraw to lower station,
lamenting current governance
while longing for the past;
their words are elegant,
their tones sorrowful.
When a state is to thrive,
it must honor teachers and respect mentors;
honoring teachers and respecting mentors ensures the preservation of laws and measures.
When a state is to decline,
it will despise teachers and belittle mentors;
despising teachers and belittling mentors leads people to indulgence;
when people are indulgent, laws and measures crumble.
In ancient times, common men became scholars at fifty.
Sons of the Son of Heaven and feudal lords were capped at nineteen,
and after capping, they attended to governance,
such was the thoroughness of their education.
If a gentleman is fond of someone,
it is because they are the right person;
if they are the right person but not taught,
it is inauspicious.
If one is not a gentleman but is fond of someone,
it is not the right person;
teaching someone who is not the right person
is like supplying food to a robber
or lending weapons to a thief.
Those who do not reflect on their own conduct
speak recklessly and err.
The worthy of old,
though lowly as commoners,
poor as ordinary men,
had insufficient gruel to eat,
wore ragged hemp clothes,
yet would not advance without ritual,
nor accept without righteousness—
why act otherwise?
Zǐxià's family was poor,
his clothes like a dangling quail.
Someone said:
"Why don't you take office?"
He replied:
"When feudal lords are arrogant to me,
I won't serve as their minister;
when senior officials are arrogant to me,
I won't see them again."
Liǔxiàhuì shared clothes with the gatekeeper yet wasn't suspected,
this reputation didn't come from one day.
Striving for gain like flea claws
only to lose one's palm.
A ruler cannot be careless in selecting ministers,
a commoner cannot be careless in choosing friends.
Friends are
means to mutual support.
If paths differ,
how can they support each other?
Spread fire on even firewood,
flames seek the dry;
pour water on level ground,
water flows to the damp.
That like follows like
is so evident,
observing someone through their friends
what doubt remains?
Choosing friends and influencing others,
one cannot be careless,
this is virtue's foundation.
The Book of Songs says:
"Don't push the great cart,
only dust will darken the sky."
Meaning don't keep company with petty people.
Pretentious and ostentatious,
seemingly wise but not.
Weak-willed and easily swayed,
seemingly benevolent but not.
Fierce, stubborn and fond of fighting,
seemingly courageous but not.
Benevolence, righteousness, propriety and goodness to humans,
are like goods, wealth, grain and rice to a family:
having much makes one rich,
having little makes one poor,
having none makes one destitute.
Thus failing at great things,
neglecting small deeds,
this is the way to lose state and self.
All things come by some means,
what goes out
is what returns.
Quell rumors,
avoid wealth and beauty.
Where calamity arises from,
begins from the slightest thread,
thus the gentleman cuts it off early.
Trustworthy speech
lies within bounds and limits.
When doubtful, don't speak;
unasked, don't speak.
The wise understand affairs
and comprehend principles,
one must serve them with sincerity.
Hence it is said:
"The gentleman is hard to please,
if pleased not by the Way,
he is not pleased."
A saying goes:
"Rolling pellets stop in hollows,
rumors stop at the wise."
This is why sectarian doctrines and heterodox schools detest Confucian scholars.
When right and wrong are uncertain
measure by past events,
verify with present things,
weigh with impartial mind -
rumors then cease,
malicious words die.
Zēngzǐ was served fish,
with leftovers,
said:
"Stew it."
His disciple said:
"Stewing may harm people,
better simmer it."
Zēngzǐ wept, saying:
"Did I have ill intent!"
Saddened he learned this too late.
Don't use my weaknesses against others' strengths.
Thus block and avoid weaknesses,
shift to develop strengths.
Clever but lawless,
discerning but perverse,
bold but riteless -
these the gentleman detests.
Speaking much but systematically -
a sage;
speaking little but methodically -
a gentleman.
Speaking much without principle, drifting endlessly,
though eloquent,
a petty person.
State laws forbid picking up lost items,
disliking people habitually gaining without distinction.
With distinction and duty,
one can embrace all under heaven and govern;
without distinction and duty,
even one wife one concubine bring chaos.
All people under heaven
have unique intentions,
yet share common approvals.
Discussing flavors, they approve Yìyá;
discussing music, they approve Shīkuàng;
discussing governance, they approve the Three Sovereigns.
The Three Sovereigns established laws
and instituted rituals and music, passing them down;
disusing these to create one's own -
how differs from changing Yìyá's recipes,
altering Shīkuàng's pitch-pipes?
Without the Three Sovereigns' laws,
the world need not await destruction,
states need not await death.
Drinking but not eating -
cicadas;
neither drinking nor eating -
mayflies.
Yú Shùn and Xiàojǐ were filial but unloved by parents;
Bǐgān and Wǔ Zǐxū were loyal but unused by lords;
Zhòngní and Yán Yuān were wise but impoverished in their time.
Forced into violent states with no escape,
then exalt their goodness,
promote their merits,
speak their strengths, not their weaknesses.
Obedient yet doomed -
slandered;
learned yet impoverished -
defamed;
cleansing but growing murkier -
the mouth.
The gentleman can make himself worthy of honor,
but cannot make others necessarily honor him;
can make himself fit for use,
but cannot make others necessarily use him.
Proclamations and pledges didn't reach the Five Emperors,
oaths and curses didn't reach the Three Sovereigns,
hostage exchanges didn't reach the Five Hegemons.
Confucius visited Duke Huān of Lǔ's temple,
where there was a tilting vessel.
Confucius asked the temple keeper:
"What vessel is this?"
The keeper said:
"This is probably the 'right-side vessel'."
Confucius said:
"I've heard of the right-side vessel:
empty, it tilts;
half-full, it stands upright;
full, it capsizes."
Confucius turned to his disciples:
"Pour water into it!"
Disciples ladled water and poured -
half-full, it stood upright;
full, it capsized;
empty, it tilted. Confucius sighed deeply:
"Alas!
How can anything full not capsize!"
Zǐlù asked:
"May I ask if there's a way to remain full?"
Confucius said:[186"With brilliant wisdom and sage knowledge,
maintain it with simplicity;
with achievements covering the world,
maintain it with humility;
with courage and strength comforting the age,
maintain it with caution;
with wealth encompassing the four seas,
maintain it with modesty.
This is the so-called way of reducing and decreasing."
Confucius served as acting prime minister of Lǔ,
and within seven days of taking office, he had Shǎozhèng Máo executed.
His disciples came forward and asked,
"Shǎozhèng Máo
was a well-known figure in Lǔ.
For you to begin your governance by having him executed—
is this not a mistake?"
Confucius replied,
"Sit!
I will tell you the reason.
There are five types of wickedness in a person,
and theft is not among them:
The first is a mind that is perceptive yet dangerous;
the second is conduct that is deviant yet steadfast;
the third is speech that is false yet persuasive;
the fourth is a memory full of sordid details and broad in scope;
the fifth is going along with wrongdoing and glossing it over.
If a person possesses even one of these five,
they cannot avoid being punished by the noble man,
and Shǎozhèng Máo had them all.
Therefore, his dwelling could gather followers and form crowds;
his speech could embellish evil and mislead the masses;
his strength was sufficient to oppose what is right and stand alone.
He was an outstanding villain among petty men,
and could not be left unpunished.
Thus, Tāng executed Yīn Xié;
King Wén executed Pān Zhǐ;
the Duke of Zhōu executed Guǎn Shū;
Tàigōng executed Huá Shì;
Guǎn Zhòng executed Fùlǐ Yǐ;
Zǐchǎn executed Dèng Xī and Shǐ Fù.
These seven individuals,
though from different times, were of the same mind,
and could not be left unpunished.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'My heart is filled with sorrow,
angered by the crowd of petty men.'
When petty men form groups,
that is indeed cause for worry."
When Confucius served as minister of crime in Lǔ,
there was a case of a father and son suing each other.
Confucius detained them,
and for three months did not pass judgment.
The father then requested to drop the case,
and Confucius released them.
Jìsūn heard of this
and was displeased,
saying,
"This old man has deceived me.
He told me:
'Governing a state must be based on filial piety.'
Now, he could have killed one to punish the unfilial,
yet he released them."
Rǎnzǐ reported this to Confucius.
Confucius sighed deeply and said,
"Alas!
If those above fail in their duties,
and those below are executed for it,
how can that be right?
Not educating the people
and then judging their disputes
is to kill the innocent.
When the three armies suffer a great defeat,
not all can be beheaded;
when prisons are in disorder,
punishments cannot be applied—
because the fault does not lie with the people.
To issue careless orders and enforce strict punishments
is tyranny;
life has its seasons,
yet exactions are untimely—
that is oppression;
to demand success without teaching—
that is cruelty.
Only after eliminating these three
can punishments be properly applied.
The *Book of Documents* says:
'Just punishments and executions
should not be hastily carried out;
I say we have not yet managed affairs properly.'
This means education must come first."
Thus, the ancient kings first set forth the Way,
and the rulers themselves practiced it;
if that did not suffice,
they honored the worthy to encourage it;
if that still did not suffice,
they removed the incompetent to caution others;
after three years of such efforts, the people would follow like the wind.
If personal example did not lead to compliance,
only then were punishments used,
and the people would understand their faults.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Grand Tutor Yǐnshì,
the pillar of Zhōu,
holding the balance of the state,
upholding the four quarters,
assisting the Son of Heaven,
so the people do not go astray." Thus, authority is stern but not tested,
punishments are set aside and not used—
this is what it means.
But in today's world, it is not so:
teachings are confused,
punishments are multiplied,
the people are bewildered and fall into error,
and then they are controlled—
hence, the more punishments increase, the more wickedness prevails.
A three-foot bank, an empty cart cannot climb it;
a hundred-ren mountain, a loaded cart can ascend—
why?
Because of the gradual slope.
A wall of several ren, people do not climb over it;
a hundred-ren mountain, children can climb and play on it—
because of the gradual slope.
Now, the decline of the world has been long and gradual,
so how can we prevent the people from transgressing?
The *Book of Songs* says:
"The way of Zhōu is like a whetstone,
straight as an arrow.
The noble man treads it,
the petty man sees it.
Looking back with longing,
tears flow in streams!"
Is it not lamentable?
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Gazing at the sun and moon,
my thoughts stretch far.
The way is so distant,
how can it ever come?"
The Master said:
"If we bow our heads in reflection,
will it not come?"
Confucius was observing the east-flowing water,
and Zǐgòng asked him,
"Why is it that when a noble man sees great water, he always observes it?"
Confucius said:
"Water, it abundantly nourishes all living things without acting,
resembling virtue;
its flow descends to the low places,
winding yet always following its course,
resembling righteousness;
its surging vastness, never exhausted,
resembles the Way;
if a channel is opened for it,
its response is swift as an echo,
it rushes into hundred-ren valleys without fear,
resembling courage;
in a container, it always levels itself,
resembling law;
full, it requires no leveling,
resembling fairness;
gentle and subtle, it reaches everywhere,
flowing in and out,
it cleanses and purifies,
resembling good transformation;
though it twists ten thousand times, it must flow east,
resembling determination.
Therefore, when a noble man sees great water, he always observes it."
Confucius said:
"I have shames,
I have contempts,
I have fears:
In youth, unable to study diligently;
in old age, having nothing to teach—
this shames me.
Leaving my homeland,
serving a ruler and achieving success,
then suddenly meeting an old friend,
without a word of the past—
this I despise.
Associating with petty men—
this I fear."
Confucius said:
"If one advances like an anthill,
I will join them;
if one stops like a hill,
I have done with them."
Now, if one's learning is not even like a wart or a growth,
yet they presumptuously wish to be a teacher to others.
Confucius traveled south to Chǔ,
was trapped between Chén and Cài,
for seven days had no cooked food,
wild vegetable soup without grain,
and his disciples all had hungry faces.
Zǐlù came forward and asked him, saying:
"I have heard:
Those who do good, heaven rewards with blessings;
those who do evil, heaven rewards with misfortune.
Now, you, Master, have accumulated virtue, piled up righteousness, and embraced goodness—
you have practiced this for a long time.
Why then do you dwell in such obscurity?"
Confucius said:
"Yóu, you do not understand,
let me tell you.
Do you think the wise are always employed?
Was not Prince Bǐgān cut open at the heart?
Do you think the loyal are always employed?
Was not Guān Lóngpáng executed?
Do you think remonstrators are always employed?
Was not Wú Zǐxū torn apart outside the eastern gate of Gūsū?
Meeting opportunity or not
is a matter of timing;
being worthy or unworthy
is a matter of ability.
There are many gentlemen of broad learning and deep strategy
who miss their time.
From this perspective,
those who miss their era are numerous,
why should I, Qiū, be the only one?
Moreover, the zhǐ and lán orchids grow in deep forests,
not failing to be fragrant just because no one is there.
The gentleman's learning
is not for attaining office;
it is for not being distressed in poverty,
not having his will decline in worry,
and his mind not being confused while knowing the beginnings and ends of fortune and misfortune.
Being worthy or unworthy
is a matter of ability;
to act or not to act
is a matter of human effort;
meeting opportunity or not
is a matter of timing;
life and death
are matters of destiny.
Now if there is a person
who misses his time,
though worthy,
can he act?
If he meets his time,
what difficulty is there?
Therefore, the gentleman broadly learns, deeply strategizes,
cultivates his person, and rectifies his conduct
to await his time."
Confucius said:
"Yóu!
Stay!
Let me tell you,
formerly the hegemon's mind of Prince Chóng'ěr of Jìn was born in Cáo,
the hegemon's mind of King Gōujiàn of Yuè was born in Kuàijī,
the hegemon's mind of Duke Huán of Qí, Xiǎobái, was born in Jǔ.
Therefore, those who do not live in obscurity do not think far,
those whose persons are not in hardship do not have broad aspirations.
How can you know I may not attain it under the mulberry's fall?"
Zǐgòng observed the northern hall of the Lǔ temple,
came out and asked Confucius:
"Earlier, Cì observed the northern hall of the Grand Temple,
I did not pause either,
turning back to gaze at the northern cover, all were joined,
is there an explanation for that?
Was the craftsman excessively cutting off?"
Confucius said:
"The hall of the Grand Temple
also has an explanation.
The officials employed skilled craftsmen,
according to beauty and joints patterned,
not that there was no good material,
but it is said to value pattern."
Being filial at home and respectful outside
are the small conduct of a person;
obeying superiors and being sincere to inferiors
are the medium conduct of a person;
following the Way rather than the ruler,
following righteousness rather than the father,
are the great conduct of a person.
If the will is settled by ritual,
speech is guided by categories,
then the Confucian Way is complete,
even Shùn could not add a hair's tip to this.
There are three reasons why a filial son does not obey commands:
obeying would endanger the parent,
not obeying would keep the parent safe,
not obeying is then loyalty;
obeying would disgrace the parent,
not obeying would honor the parent,
the filial son not obeying is then righteousness;
obeying would make one a beast,
not obeying would lead to cultivation,
the filial son not obeying is then respect.
Therefore, if one can obey but does not,
this is not being a son;
if one should not obey but does,
this is not being loyal.
Understanding the principle of when to obey or not,
and being able to practice it with reverence,
loyalty, trustworthiness, uprightness, and sincerity cautiously,
then one can be called greatly filial.
The tradition says:
"Follow the Way, not the ruler;
follow righteousness, not the father."
This refers to that.
Therefore, being able to labor and toil without losing reverence,
facing disaster and hardship without losing righteousness,
then if unfortunately not being compliant and being disliked
yet able not to lose love,
none but a humane person can practice this.
The Odes say:
"The filial son's supply never fails."
This refers to that.
Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Confucius:
"Does a son obeying his father's commands
constitute filial piety?
Does a minister obeying his ruler's commands
constitute loyalty?"
He asked three times,
Confucius did not reply.
Confucius hurried out,
and told Zǐgòng:
"Earlier, the ruler asked me,
saying:
'Does a son obeying his father's commands
constitute filial piety?
Does a minister obeying his ruler's commands
constitute loyalty?'
He asked three times and I did not reply,
what do you think, Cì?"
Zǐgòng said:
"A son obeying his father's commands
is filial;
a minister obeying his ruler's commands
is loyal,
what does the Master have to reply?"
Confucius said:[134"Petty man!
Cì, you do not understand.
Formerly, a state of ten thousand chariots
with four remonstrating ministers
would not have its borders reduced;
a state of a thousand chariots
with three remonstrating ministers
would not have its altars endangered;
a house of a hundred chariots
with two remonstrating ministers
would not have its ancestral temple destroyed.
A father with a remonstrating son
does not act without ritual;
a scholar with a remonstrating friend
does not do what is unrighteous.
Therefore, if a son simply obeys his father,
how is that filial?
If a minister simply obeys his ruler,
how is that loyal?
It is examining the reason for obedience that is called filial, called loyal."
Zǐlù asked Confucius:
"Suppose there is a person here,
rising early and retiring late,
plowing, weeding, planting, and cultivating,
hands and feet calloused
to support his parents,
yet he has no reputation for filial piety,
why is that?"
Confucius said:
"Could it be that his person is not reverent?
His speech not humble?
His expression not compliant?
The ancients had a saying:
'Clothe me,
feed me,
but I will not rely on you.'
Now rising early and retiring late,
plowing, weeding, planting, and cultivating,
hands and feet calloused
to support his parents,
if without these three faults,
then why would he have no reputation for filial piety?
Could it be that the friends he makes are not humane persons?"
Confucius said:
"Yóu, remember this,
I tell you:
Even with the strength of a champion of the state,
one cannot lift oneself,
not for lack of strength,
but the situation makes it impossible.
Therefore, if at home one's conduct is not cultivated,
it is the fault of the person;
if outside one's reputation is not illustrious,
it is the fault of friends.
Therefore, the gentleman at home practices conduct earnestly,
outside makes friends with the worthy,
how could he lack a reputation for filial piety?"
Zǐlù asked Confucius:
"The great officer of Lǔ using a bed while in mourning linen,
is that ritual?"
Confucius said:
"I do not know."
Zǐlù went out,
and said to Zǐgòng:
"I thought the Master was omniscient,
but the Master too has things he does not know."
Zǐgòng said:
"What did you ask?"
Zǐlù said:
"Yóu asked
whether it is ritually proper for a Lu minister to sleep on a bed while wearing mourning silk.
The Master said:
'I do not know.'"
Zǐgòng said:
"I will ask him for you."
Zǐgòng asked:
"Is it ritually proper to sleep on a bed while wearing mourning silk?"
Confucius said:
"It is not ritually proper."
Zǐgòng went out,
and said to Zǐlù:
"Do you think the Master does not know everything?
The Master is truly omniscient,
but your question was improper.
According to ritual,
when residing in a city
one should not criticize its ministers."
Zǐlù appeared before Confucius in splendid attire,
Confucius said:
"Yóu,
why this ostentatious display?
In ancient times, the river originated from Mínshān,
at its source,
its flow could barely fill a wine cup,
but when it reached the river's crossing,
without boats
and avoiding winds
one could not cross it,
is this not because the downstream flow is abundant?
Now your clothing is splendid,
your countenance self-satisfied,
who in the world would then dare to admonish you? Yóu!"
Zǐlù hurried out,
changed his clothes and returned,
appearing humble.
Confucius said:
Remember this,
I tell you:
those cautious in speech are not flowery,
those cautious in action do not boast.
Those who show off their knowledge and ability
are petty persons.
Thus, the gentleman knows what he knows,
and admits what he doesn't know -
this is the essence of speech;
he can do what he can do,
and admits what he cannot do -
this is the perfection of action.
With the essence of speech comes wisdom,
with the perfection of action comes benevolence.
Having both wisdom
and benevolence, what could possibly be lacking!"
Zǐlù entered,
the Master said:
"Yóu,
what is a wise person like?
What is a benevolent person like?"
Zǐlù replied:
"A wise person makes others know him,
a benevolent person makes others love him."
The Master said:
"You may be called a scholar."
Zǐgòng entered,
the Master said:
"Cì,
what is a wise person like?
What is a benevolent person like?"
Zǐgòng replied:
"A wise person knows others,
a benevolent person loves others."
The Master said:
"You may be called a scholar-gentleman."
Yán Yuān entered,
the Master said:
"Huí,
what is a wise person like?
What is a benevolent person like?"
Yán Yuān replied:
"A wise person knows himself,
a benevolent person loves himself."
The Master said:
"You may be called an enlightened gentleman."
Zǐlù asked Confucius:
"Does a gentleman also have worries?"
Confucius said:
"The gentleman,
before attaining his goal, enjoys the pursuit,
and after attaining it,
enjoys governing it properly.
Thus he has lifelong joy,
and not a single day of worry.
The petty person,
before attaining his goal,
worries about not getting it,
and after attaining it,
fears losing it.
Thus he has lifelong worry,
and not a single day of joy."
Gōngshū could not improve upon the marking line,
the sage cannot improve upon ritual.
Ritual -
the multitude follows it without understanding,
the sage follows it with understanding.
Zēngzǐ said:
"Do not treat family members distantly while treating outsiders intimately,
do not blame others for your own faults,
do not cry to heaven only after punishment has arrived.
Treating family members distantly while treating outsiders intimately -
is this not perverse!
Blaming others for your own faults -
is this not unreasonable!
Crying to heaven only after punishment has arrived -
is this not too late!
The Book of Songs says:
'Tiny stream at the source,
neither blocked nor dammed.
When the hub is already broken,
then enlarge the spokes.
When matters are already ruined,
then heave great sighs.'
What good does it do!"
Zēngzǐ was ill,
Zēng Yuán held his feet.
Zēngzǐ said:
"Yuán, remember this!
I tell you:
Fish, turtles, and crocodiles still find the deep pool too shallow
and burrow holes in it,
eagles and kites still find the mountain too low
and build nests higher up,
but when they are caught,
it is always because of bait.
Therefore, if the gentleman can avoid harming righteousness for profit,
then disgrace will have no way to reach him."
Zǐgòng asked Confucius:
"Why does the gentleman value jade and disdain mǐn stone?
Is it
because jade is rare and mǐn stone is plentiful?"
Confucius said:
"Alas!
Cì,
what kind of talk is this?
Would the gentleman value something because it's rare
and disdain it because it's plentiful!
Jade
is compared by the gentleman to virtue:
gentle, smooth, and glossy -
this is benevolence;
fine-textured and well-patterned -
this is wisdom;
hard and firm, unyielding -
this is righteousness;
sharp-edged but not cutting -
this is conduct;
breakable but not bendable -
this is courage;
flaws and beauty both visible -
this is sincerity;
strike it,
its sound clear and far-reaching,
stopping abruptly -
this is eloquence.
Thus although mǐn stone may be beautifully carved,
it cannot match jade's natural brilliance.
The Book of Songs says:
'I think of my gentleman,
gentle as jade.'
This expresses it."
Zēngzǐ said:
"If among companions I am not loved,
I must be lacking in benevolence;
if among friends I am not respected,
I must be lacking in respectfulness;
if in financial matters I am not trusted,
I must be lacking in trustworthiness.
These three faults lie with me,
why blame others?
Those who blame others are destitute,
those who blame heaven lack understanding.
Failing in oneself but blaming others -
is this not indeed misguided!"
Nánguō Huìzǐ asked Zǐgòng:
"The Master's school,
why is it so mixed?"
Zǐgòng said:
"The gentleman rectifies himself and waits,
those who wish to come are not refused,
those who wish to leave are not detained.
Moreover, at a good physician's door are many patients,
by the straightening tool lie many crooked woods -
this is why it is mixed."
Confucius said:
"The noble person has three principles of reciprocity.
Having a ruler whom one cannot serve properly,
yet demanding service from subordinates,
is not reciprocity;
having parents whose kindness one cannot repay,
yet expecting filial piety from one's children,
is not reciprocity;
having an elder brother whom one cannot respect,
yet demanding obedience from younger brothers,
is not reciprocity.
If a scholar understands these three principles of reciprocity,
then he can rectify his conduct."
Confucius said:
"The noble person has three reflections,
which cannot be neglected.
If one does not study when young,
one will have no abilities when grown;
if one does not teach when old,
one will leave no legacy after death;
if one does not give when possessing,
one will have no support when in need.
Therefore, the noble person, reflecting on adulthood when young,
studies;
reflecting on death when old,
teaches;
reflecting on poverty when wealthy,
gives."
Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Confucius:
"I wish to select scholars from my state
to govern the country with them.
May I ask how to choose them?"
Confucius replied:
"Those who live in the present age,
yet aspire to the ways of antiquity;
dwell among modern customs,
yet wear ancient attire—
how rare are those who do this and yet act wrongly!"
Duke Āi said:
"Then are all those who wear the zhāngfǔ cap, qú jù shoes,
sash belt, and carry the jìn hù tablet
worthy?"
Confucius replied:
"Not necessarily.
Those in formal robes and dark skirts,
wearing miǎn crowns and riding in royal carriages,
may have minds not set on rich food;
those in mourning dress and jiān shoes,
leaning on staffs and consuming gruel,
may have minds not set on wine and meat.
Those who live in the present age,
yet aspire to the ways of antiquity;
dwell among modern customs,
yet wear ancient attire—
how rare are those who do this and yet act wrongly,
even if there are some!"
Duke Āi said:
"Well said."
Confucius said:
"People have five grades:
the mediocre person,
the scholar,
the noble person,
the worthy person,
and the great sage."
Duke Āi said:
"May I ask what defines a mediocre person?"
Confucius replied:
"The so-called mediocre person
cannot speak good words,
and their heart knows no distress;
they do not know to entrust themselves to worthy and good scholars as a concern for themselves,
their actions lack clear aims,
their stillness lacks firm foundation;
daily choosing among things,
they know not what to value;
following things like a stream,
they know not where to return;
with the five senses as their guide,
their heart follows and decays;
such a one
may be called a mediocre person."
Duke Āi said:
"Well said!
May I ask what defines a scholar?"
Confucius replied:
"The so-called scholar,
though unable to fully master the Way,
must have principles to follow;
though unable to achieve perfect goodness,
must have a steadfast place.
Thus, knowledge need not be abundant,
but must be thorough in what is known;
words need not be many,
but must be precise in what is said;
actions need not be numerous,
but must be examined in their origins.
Therefore, when knowledge is already acquired,
words already spoken,
actions already taken,
they become as unchangeable as one's life and skin.
Thus, wealth and honor cannot add to them,
poverty and lowliness cannot diminish them;
such a one
may be called a scholar."
Duke Āi said:
"Well said!
May I ask what defines a noble person?"
Confucius replied:
"The so-called noble person
speaks with loyalty and trustworthiness,
yet claims no virtue in heart;
embodies benevolence and righteousness, yet shows no boastful expression;
has clear and penetrating thoughts, yet argues not in speech;
thus, appearing as if attainable,
this is the noble person."
Duke Āi said:
"Well said!
May I ask what defines a worthy person?"
Confucius replied:
"The so-called worthy person
acts in accordance with rules
without harming their essence;
speaks in ways that the world can emulate
without endangering themselves;
possessing the wealth of the world
without hoarding resentfully;
distributing throughout the world
without suffering poverty;
such a one
may be called a worthy person."
Duke Āi said:
"Well said!
May I ask what defines a great sage?"
Confucius replied:
"The so-called great sage
understands the great Way thoroughly,
responds to changes without exhaustion,
and discerns the nature of all things.
The great Way
is that by which changes occur
and all things are accomplished;
the nature
is that which determines principles, affirmations, denials, choices, and rejections.
Thus, their affairs are as vast as heaven and earth,
as illuminating as the sun and moon,
encompassing all things like wind and rain;
profound and sincere,
their actions cannot be followed,
as if succeeding heaven;
their deeds cannot be comprehended,
the common people placidly unaware of their proximity;
such a one
may be called a great sage."
Duke Āi said:
"Well said!"
Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Confucius about Shùn's crown,
but Confucius did not answer.
Asked three times,
he still did not answer.
Duke Āi said:
"I asked you about Shùn's crown,
why do you not speak?"
Confucius replied:
"The ancient kings
wore simple caps and collars,
yet their governance favored life and abhorred killing;
thus, phoenixes perched in rows of trees,
unicorns roamed the outskirts,
and the nests of crows and magpies could be peered into from below.
You do not ask about this, but ask of Shùn's crown—
this is why I did not answer."
Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Confucius:
"I was born in the depths of the palace,
raised by the hands of women;
I have never known sorrow,
never known worry,
never known toil,
never known fear,
never known danger."
Confucius said:
"Your question,
is that of a sage ruler.
I, Qiū,
am but a petty person—
how could I know of such things?"
The Duke said:
"If not from you, I have no one to hear it from."
Confucius said:
"When you enter the temple gate and turn right,
ascend from the zuò steps,
look up at the rafters and beams,
look down upon the mats and altars,
the vessels remain,
but the people are gone."
If you, my lord, reflect on this with sorrow,
then how could sorrow fail to come?
You rise at dawn to wash and don your cap,
and at first light you hold court.
If one matter is not properly addressed,
it becomes the start of disorder.
If you reflect on this with worry,
then how could worry fail to come?
You hold court at first light
and retire only after the sun has set.
The descendants of the feudal lords are surely waiting in the outer chambers of your court.
If you reflect on this with toil,
then how could toil fail to come?
If you go out through the four gates of Lǔ
and gaze upon the four suburbs of Lǔ,
you will surely see numerous ruins of fallen states.
If you reflect on this with fear,
then how could fear fail to come?
Moreover, I have heard:
The ruler is like a boat,
and the common people are like water.
The water can bear up the boat,
and the water can capsize the boat.
If you reflect on this with a sense of peril,
then how could peril fail to come?"
Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Confucius:
"Do the sash, the robe, and the ceremonial cap
contribute to benevolence?"
Confucius looked startled and said:
"How could you say such a thing, my lord!
Those in mourning dress with hempen staffs do not listen to music,
not because their ears cannot hear,
but because their attire requires it.
Those wearing embroidered ritual garments do not eat meat,
not because their mouths cannot taste,
but because their attire requires it.
Moreover, I have heard:
A good merchant does not guard against losses,
and an elder does not engage in trade.
As for whether it is beneficial or not,
you, my lord, surely know."
Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Confucius:
"May I ask about selecting people?"
Confucius replied:
"Do not select the aggressive,
do not select the glib,
do not select the garrulous.
The aggressive are greedy;
greedy,
the glib are disruptive;
disruptive,
the garrulous are deceitful;
deceitful.
Thus, a bow must be well-adjusted before one seeks its strength;
a horse must be tamed before one seeks its excellence;
a scholar must be trustworthy and sincere before one seeks his knowledge and ability.
If a scholar is not trustworthy and sincere yet has much knowledge and ability,
he is like a wolf or a jackal,
and one cannot approach him personally.
There is a saying:
'Duke Huán employed his enemy,
and Duke Wén employed a thief.'
Thus, an enlightened ruler relies on strategy, not on anger;
a benighted ruler relies on anger, not on strategy.
When strategy prevails over anger, the state is strong;
when anger prevails over strategy, the state perishes."
Duke Dìng asked Yán Yuān:
"Have you heard of Dōngyě Bì's skill in driving?"
Yán Yuān replied:
"Skilled he is indeed.
However,
his horses will bolt."
Duke Dìng was displeased
and said to his attendants upon entering:
"Is a gentleman necessarily a slanderer?"
Three days later, the stablemaster came to report,
saying:
"Dōngyě Bì's horses have bolted.
The two outer horses broke away,
and the two inner horses returned to the stable."
Duke Dìng rose from his mat and said:
"Quickly, summon Yán Yuān!"
When Yán Yuān arrived,
Duke Dìng said:
"The other day, I asked you,
and you said:
'As for Dōngyě Bì's driving,
skilled he is indeed.
However,
his horses will bolt.'
How did you know this?"
Yán Yuān replied:
"I knew it from the principles of governance.
In the past, Shùn was skilled in employing the people,
and Zàofǔ was skilled in employing horses.
Shùn did not push his people to the limit,
and Zàofǔ did not push his horses to the limit.
Thus, Shùn never lost his people,
and Zàofǔ never lost his horses.
Now, as for Dōngyě Bì's driving,
when he mounts the chariot and takes the reins,
the bits are properly set;
in walking, trotting, and galloping,
the rituals are fully observed;
in traversing dangers and going long distances,
the horses' strength is exhausted.
Yet he still incessantly demands more from them;
this is how I knew."
Duke Dìng said:
"Excellent!
Could you elaborate a little?"
Yán Yuān replied:
"I have heard:
When birds are cornered, they peck;
when beasts are cornered, they snatch;
when people are cornered, they deceive.
From ancient times to the present,
there has never been one who pushed his subordinates to the limit and yet avoided peril."
Yáo asked Shùn:
"I wish to attract the world to me.
How should I do it?"
Shùn replied:
"Hold fast to the One without error,
carry out the subtle without negligence,
be loyal and trustworthy without weariness,
and the world will come of itself.
Holding fast to the One like heaven and earth,
carrying out the subtle like the sun and moon,
with loyalty and sincerity abundant within
and radiating outward,
manifesting throughout the four seas.
How could the world be merely in one corner?
What need is there to attract it?"
Marquis Wǔ of Wèi planned affairs appropriately,
and none of his ministers could match him.
He withdrew from court with a pleased expression.
Wú Qǐ came forward and said:
"Has Your Majesty ever heard the words of King Zhuāng of Chǔ?"
Marquis Wǔ said:
"What were King Zhuāng of Chǔ's words?"
Wú Qǐ replied:
"King Zhuāng of Chǔ planned affairs appropriately,
and none of his ministers could match him.
He withdrew from court with a worried expression.
Shēngōng Wūchén came forward and asked:
'Your Majesty has a worried expression after court. Why?'
King Zhuāng said:
'I, the unworthy one, plan affairs appropriately,
and none of my ministers can match me.
This is why I worry.
In the words of the "Zhōngguī",
it is said:
"Those who secure a teacher for themselves become kings;
those who secure friends become hegemons;
those who secure advisers survive;
those who plan for themselves with no one matching them perish."
Now, with my lack of virtue and none of my ministers matching me,
my state is close to perishing!
This is why I worry.'
King Zhuāng of Chǔ worried,
yet you, my lord, are pleased."
Marquis Wǔ stepped back, bowed twice, and said:
"Heaven has sent you, Master, to awaken me to my fault."
When Bóqín was about to return to Lǔ,
the Duke of Zhōu said to Bóqín's tutor:
"You are about to depart.
Why not tell me of your charge's fine virtues?"
The tutor replied:
"He is tolerant by nature,
fond of relying on himself,
and cautious.
These three are his fine virtues."
The Duke of Zhōu said:
"Alas!
How can you consider others' faults as fine virtues?
A gentleman delights in the Way and its virtue,
so his people turn to the Way.
His tolerance
shows a lack of discrimination, yet you praise it.
you praise it.
His fondness for relying on himself
is what makes him narrow and small.
A gentleman may have the strength of an ox,
but he does not contend with an ox in strength;
he may run like a horse,
but he does not contend with a horse in running;
he may have the wisdom of a scholar,
but he does not contend with a scholar in wisdom.
Those who contend
are driven by a spirit of rivalry."
Yet you admire them. Their caution
stems from their superficiality.
I have heard it said:
Do not neglect to meet scholars.
When meeting scholars, ask:
"Have I been unobservant?"
If you do not listen,
then understanding will seldom come,
and seldom coming leads to superficiality.
Such superficiality
is the way of base men.
How can you admire it?
Let me tell you:
I,
as a son to King Wén,
a brother to King Wǔ,
and an uncle to King Chéng,
am not lowly in the world.
Yet those I formally visited with gifts number ten,
those who returned gifts and met me number thirty,
scholars received with due demeanor number over a hundred,
those who sought to speak and requested to state their affairs number over a thousand.
From these, I obtained only three true scholars
to rectify my person
and stabilize the world.
The way I obtained these three scholars
was not from the ten or the thirty,
but from the hundred and the thousand.
Thus, to superior scholars I show lesser demeanor,
to inferior scholars I show greater demeanor.
Everyone thought I excessively favored scholars,
yet thus scholars came,
and only when scholars came could I perceive things,
perceiving things then I knew where right and wrong lie.
Be warned!
You pride yourself on the state of Lǔ,
how perilous!
Those scholars who seek salary may still be treated arrogantly,
but scholars who rectify themselves cannot be treated arrogantly.
Those scholars who rectify themselves
abandon honor for humility,
abandon wealth for poverty,
abandon ease for toil,
their faces dark yet not losing their place.
Thus, the principles of the world do not cease,
and cultural achievements are not abandoned."
A saying goes:
"The border official of Zēngqiū
met the Chǔ chancellor Sūnshū Áo, saying:
'I have heard:
Those long in office are envied by scholars,
those with ample salary are resented by the people,
those in high position are hated by the ruler.
Now you, Chancellor, have all three
yet incur no offense from the scholars and people of Chǔ.
Why?'
Sūnshū Áo said:
'I have been chancellor of Chǔ thrice, yet my heart grows humbler;
each time my salary increased, my generosity broadened;
the more honored my position, the more respectful my courtesy.
Thus, I incur no offense from the scholars and people of Chǔ.'"
Zǐgòng asked Confucius:
"I wish to be humble but do not know how."
Confucius said:
"To be humble?
Is it not like the earth?
Dig deep and sweet springs are found;
plant it and the five grains are sown;
grasses and trees flourish;
birds and beasts thrive;
the living stand upon it;
the dead enter into it;
its merits are many yet it claims no virtue.
To be humble,
is to be like the earth."
Of old, Yú did not employ Gōngzhī Qí and Jìn annexed it;
Lái did not employ Zǐmǎ and Qí annexed it;
Zhòu disemboweled Prince Bǐgān and King Wǔ succeeded him.
Not drawing near to worthies nor employing the wise,
led to their deaths and states' ruin.
Some commentators say:
"Xúnzǐ does not equal Confucius."
This is not so.
Xúnzǐ was constrained by a chaotic age,
harried by harsh punishments,
above had no worthy rulers,
below encountered the tyranny of Qín,
ritual and righteousness were not practiced,
education and transformation did not succeed,
the benevolent were oppressed and bound,
the world was in darkness,
those of complete conduct were criticized,
the feudal lords greatly declined.
At that time,
the wise could not plan,
the capable could not govern,
the worthy could not be employed,
so rulers were blinded and unseeing,
worthies were rejected and not received.
Yet Xúnzǐ, embracing a sage's heart,
assumed a feigned madness,
showed the world foolishness.
The Odes say:
"Both intelligent and wise,
to protect his person."
This describes him.
This is why his fame was not prominent,
his followers not numerous,
his brilliance not widespread.
Today's learners,
obtaining Xúnzǐ's remaining words and teachings,
find them sufficient as models and standards for the world.
Where they reside, there is spirit-like influence;
where they pass, there is transformation.
Observing his good conduct,
even Confucius would not surpass him.
The world does not examine in detail,
saying he was no sage—
What can be done!
The world lacks order
because Xúnzǐ met an untimely age.
His virtue like Yáo and Yǔ,
few in the world know it.
His methods unused,
he was doubted by others.
His wisdom supremely bright,
following the Way and correcting conduct,
sufficient to be a guiding principle.
Alas!
How worthy!
Fit to be a sovereign.
Heaven and Earth unknowing,
favored Jié and Zhòu,
killed the worthy and good.
Bǐgān had his heart cut out;
Confucius was confined in Kuāng;
Jiēyú withdrew from the world;
Jīzǐ feigned madness;
Tiáncháng created chaos;
Hélǚ wielded power.
The wicked obtained fortune,
the good met calamity.
Now commentators
again do not examine the reality,
but believe the reputation.
Times and ages differ;
how could praise arise?
Not attaining to governance,
how could achievements be made?
With aims cultivated and virtue profound,
who can say he was not worthy!
